## 一、隐藏的镜像：热刺、曼联、切尔西、女子网球、英式橄榄球——都在犯"同一种错"
表面看这期节目是五个孤立的话题拼盘，但如果把它们叠在一张X光片上，你会看到**同一副骨架**：**跳过"机器搭建"，直接往里灌汽油**。
- **热刺**：以为问题是"没花够钱"，于是花 3 亿+ 请来 De Zerbi，赋予他 1980 年代式的"魔术师全权"。 - **曼联**：Ratcliffe 以为可以像收购化工厂一样重构一家足球俱乐部——低估了"文化—技术—青训"这台机器修复的时间常数。 - **切尔西 Clearlake**：把本该投向球场基建（一个能提升"发动机排量"的东西）的 20 亿英镑，烧进了球员市场，现在只能通过溢价 20% 的关联交易，来"保住估值面子"。 - **WTA**：把 CVC 给的 1.5 亿美元一次性抵押未来的钱——本应用于国际化、品牌、产品开发——**几乎全部倒进了奖金池**。 - **Eddie Hearn 想干的橄榄球**：主张"去掉薪水帽，让球员多赚钱"，而现实是 Prem 十支球队里六支资产负债表已经技术性破产。
**出人意料的观察**：这五个案例

item.title: [投资TALK君] ✨【投资TALK君1498期】甲骨文木星计划失手？损失惨重？资金链断裂？✨20260924#CPI #nvda #美股 #投资 #英伟达 #ai #特斯拉
item.dc:creator: 投资TALK君
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、瓶颈迁移史：AI 最终被 19 世纪基建卡住了

过去三年 AI 的瓶颈迁移路径本身就是一个反讽的隐喻——H100（芯片）→ NVLink（互联）→ HBM（内存）→ 现在停在了新墨西哥州的一份天然气管道审批上。整个视频最容易被忽略但最惊人的一个事实是：人类最尖端的技术堆栈，最终被一份州级空气质量许可证和几段管道钢管卡住了。

跨领域连接：这几乎完美复刻了 2010 年代德国的太阳能革命——最终不是电池技术限制了转型，而是输电线路审批限制了扩容。每一次能量密度革命，最后败给的都是地方规划委员会。AI 表面上是硅+算法的战争，本质上正在变成能源+规划许可的战争。这也解释了为什么 GEV、Caterpillar、Bloom 这些"老经济"公司突然被拉进了 AI 定价链条——它们是新瓶颈的守门人。

二、"泡沫延缓论"——最反常识的市场自愈机制

本次分析最反直觉的洞见值得单独拎出来放大：Oracle 的执行失败，反而在系统层面降低了 AI 泡沫风险。

  • 直觉链：项目延期 → 营收往后推 → 坏消息 → 拉低估值
  • 但真实链条：需求端持续增长 + 供给端因物理/审批瓶颈跟不上 = 供需缺口继续存在 = "供给过剩"的泡沫论证据被削弱

这构成一个奇特的悖论：Oracle 越"不行"，行业整体越"健康"。市场在周四已经用 CoreWeave 和 Nebius 的上涨定价了这个逻辑——单个玩家的执行失败，反而是行业稀缺性的价格确认。这几乎是"负面消息=正面信号"的教科书案例，能看懂这一层的人才真正理解 AI 周期还没到顶。

三、Oracle 正在扮演"AI 基建的准主权信用"

更深一层、几乎没人明确指出来的观察：Oracle 在这套 SPV 结构里扮演的角色，与 19 世纪美国州政府为跨州铁路建设提供收益担保是同构的。

SPV 借了 180 亿美金，抵押品不是数据中心的物理资产，而是 Oracle 未来的现金流承诺。这本质上是把 Oracle 的公司信用证券化并注入基建融资链条——就像州政府用未来税收担保铁路债券一样。

由此推出一个尚未被主流讨论的问题：当 AI 基建融资规模持续膨胀到 Oracle 市值的相当比例时，Oracle 的信用曲线就变成了整个 AI 基建圈的"影子国债曲线"。这也是为什么那笔 180 亿贷款跌到 89 美分并不是简单的流动性折价——市场正在重新为"Oracle 作为 AI 基建准主权担保人"的信用打价。加息只能解释 2–3%，其余 8–9% 的折价是这个身份的估值重估。

四、被忽略的结构性真相：Oracle 的"影子资产负债表"

一个几乎所有报道都漏掉的会计洞察：Oracle 在整个木星计划里几乎没有直接资本风险——它不是 SPV 股东、不是贷款方、不是开发商。它只是用"未来营收承诺"换取当下的算力优先权。

这在会计报表上是天才设计（不并表、不负债），但在系统层面创造了一个"影子资产负债表"：Oracle 真实的敞口远超财报数字，因为它的品牌、信用、股价都被绑定在一个它并不直接控制的物理施工时间表上。

跨领域连接：这与航空业过去 30 年用飞机租赁 SPV 持有飞机的结构完全同构——表面轻资产，实际重敞口。当年美联航、达美的租赁 SPV 结构在 2001 年、2020 年两次危机中都反噬了母公司。今天 Oracle 走的是同一条路：一旦木星计划从"延期"滑向"永久搁置"，那 180 亿贷款的债权人一定会通过合同追索链把风险反向压回 Oracle——force majeure 警告本身就是 Oracle 提前在打这个防御桩。

五、一个属于 2026 年的时间悖论

最后一个让人后背发凉的观察：审批周期正在变得比技术周期更长。

天然气管道审批推到 2027 年 2 月——这意味着从"决定建"到"能通电"的时间，已经超过了从"H100 发布"到"B200 出货"的整个 GPU 换代周期。监管时钟正在变得比摩尔时钟慢。这在人类工业史上是极其罕见的错配——通常是技术慢，规则跟得上。而现在，最快的技术被最慢的官僚流程套住了。

这才是 AI 时代真正的深层瓶颈：不是算力，不是数据，不是能源，是"批准速度"。

📝 转录文本

开场：一次由 Oracle 引发的 AI 基建全景讨论

周四的市场，Oracle 因为一条消息出现了比较大幅度的下跌，同时把 Bloom Energy（BE）这家公司的股价也带了下来。那整个 AI 的基建是不是出现了放缓？AI 本身是不是基本面出现了问题？今天我们借由这期视频，非常好的一个机会，来聊一下 Stargate 木星计划，把整个 AI 现在所碰到的问题全部展开去聊一下，最后回到 Oracle 这家公司基本面本身，接下去是不是遇到了非常重大的问题。

欢迎大家来到一个不单只聊新闻的专业美股频道，我是市场分析员小陶。今天这期内容我们就来做一个 Oracle 专辑，一起走入 Oracle 的世界。好吧，在开始之前，大家记得留言、点赞、加转发。

一、事情的原委：Stargate 与木星计划的合作结构

我先不聊今天的新闻，我们先从头去过一下，到底这件事情的原委是什么。

首先在 2025 年的时候，Oracle 和 OpenAI 之间扩大了 Stargate（我们称为"星门"）的这个合作。OpenAI 给了 Oracle 五年的订单，订单幅度达到了 3000 亿美金（300 billion），而 Project Jupiter（木星计划）是其中的项目之一。

这个木星计划是在新墨西哥州建立四座大的数据中心，总共加一起达到了 2.4 吉瓦。

二、真正的瓶颈：不是 GPU，是通电

整个数据中心的建造，我们知道要包括几点：

  • 第一点，选址——你要选定一个地址；
  • 第二点，这个地址本身，你建厂完之后，你要进行通电。

现在其实比起 GPU 来说——就是整个 AI 工厂，AI 工厂的话包括 GPU、包括互联等等——现在 AI 工厂不是一个瓶颈，现在那个瓶颈就是通电。

通电的方式有很多种，最便宜的其实是电网。但是现在因为对于数据中心建造这个需求非常的大，你要拿到电网的电，起码要排 5～6 年以后。那当电网的电非常紧缺的时候，这时候建造数据中心电哪里来？就需要靠其他的方式，比如说用 turbine。

那 turbine 利好哪一类公司？或者哪一类公司是提供 turbine——比如说像 Caterpillar，我们非常熟悉的；比如像 GEV；包括西门子。这几家公司都是提供 turbine。然后现在，因为 turbine 的产能现在也非常紧缺，并且如果你用 turbine 加上 diesel 的话，对于环境会有一些污染在那边。

所以现在改用什么？现在改用的是 Bloom Energy，它的天然气电池。但是天然气电池你要运行的话，你必须要有天然气的管道。

三、木星计划卡在哪里：管道与许可证

所以现在在新墨西哥州的这个木星计划遇到了什么问题？

  • 第一，天然气管道的审批遇到了阻碍，审批现在已经推延至 2027 年的 2 月份；
  • 并且还有空气质量的许可证也没有下来。

四、四方合作结构：Oracle、OpenAI、BlueOwl、SPV

那 Oracle 和 OpenAI 之间的合作，方式其实是这样的：

首先，OpenAI 说我需要这个算力，然后 Oracle 负责去建——Oracle 应该是这么说，Oracle 负责去提供这个算力，但是 Oracle 自己本身并不是这个数据中心的开发商。它去和 BlueOwl 之间合作，BlueOwl 下面又有一家 Infer，这做基建的一家公司。然后这家做基建的公司，它去建了一个 SPV，这个 SPV 本身是一家新公司，它其实是去负责贷款。

然后 BlueOwl 下面的这家基建公司负责去进行建造，或者是成为开发商。等这个数据中心建完之后，Oracle 承诺会直接去租赁这个数据中心能够提供的算力，然后再把这个算力提供给 OpenAI。

所以这个木星计划本身其实牵涉到了很多公司。而 Oracle 自己本身其实背后没有这个风险在那边——它的风险是什么？它的风险是：如果这一个木星计划往后延的话，对它来说营收就往后延了，它为 OpenAI 所提供的算力就要往后延了。因为算力没办法提供嘛，所以营收就往后延。

但是这个木星计划如果最终失败或者停产的话，从 Oracle 的角度来看，他们其实没有损失任何的钱——他们损失的是未来的营收。你就能够理解，因为他们也并不是这个新公司 SPV 的贷款方。

而且 Oracle 给这个 SPV 提供的是什么？它提供的是一个担保——就是等于是"未来你这个数据中心建完之后，我给你提供现金流"。然后这个 SPV 拿着这个现金流去向中小型银行进行贷款，贷款的体量是 18 个 billion，180 亿美金。稍后我会展开聊一下。

所以聊到这边，这背后其实是比较复杂的。所涉及的 parties 不单只是 OpenAI 和 Oracle，背后还有很多其他的一些公司，包括借钱的公司、给钱的公司和借钱的公司。

起码聊到现在，我们能够确定一点：这不是一个需求的问题，这是整个数据中心在建造或者这个木星计划在执行过程中的执行力问题。

五、周四那条新闻：force majeure 是自我保护

回到今天，回到周四的那条新闻——周四这条新闻说的是什么？说的是 Oracle 发出了一个不可抗力（force majeure）的警告。

那这么做的目的是什么？是保护自己。如果未来这个项目交付会延期的话，那 Oracle 会延期去支付租金。你数据中心都没有造好，我为什么要向你支付租金？这个租金是针对这个数据中心本身的——你数据中心都没有造完，我凭什么向你支付租金？

所以周四 Oracle 所发出的这个不可抗力警告，是用来保护自己的，当未来如果有延误的话。

当然，对于 Oracle 来说，它是有这个风险——就像我前面说的，如果交付真的延后，那 Oracle 28 年以后的营收也会延后。

所以像我前面说到的，这对于 Oracle 二期财年营收是没有任何影响的，因为木星计划的交付时间本身是在 2028 年。但是同时，如果 Oracle 的营收往后延的话——因为 Oracle 这个电是谁提供的？是 Bloom Energy 提供的——整个项目本身往后延，Oracle 的营收往后延，2028 年的营收往后延，那 Bloom Energy 同样的，它 2028 年的营收也会往后延。

六、Bloom Energy 的确认：订单没取消，只是可能延期

下面那个截图我们看一下，是 Bloom Energy 在周四美东时间下午 2:40 左右，他们和 Oracle 进行了沟通。先确定一下：Oracle 并不是取消这个 2.4 吉瓦的订单——2.4 吉瓦是非常大的订单——并不是取消订单，而是整个计划本身还是按原计划去执行，只是它最终会不会延期现在不知道。

但是既然 Oracle 发出了这个不可抗力警告，其实背后是存在延期的可能性。所以对于这两家公司来说，你只能这么去想：最后这个 2.4 吉瓦的 commitment、项目本身会不会完成？应该是会完成的，只是完成的时间点比原来的预期要往后延了。

也就是说，原来这个预期市场已经把未来的营收算进来，但是现在这个预期要往后推——推半年或者推一年左右。对于现在的股价来说，那一定是一个负面的影响。所以今天这两家公司的股价下跌是合理的。

七、180 亿贷款为什么跌到 89 美分：四个原因

同时在周四，还有另外一条新闻和这条新闻完全类似的：说到 18 个 billion、180 亿的贷款，现在的价格只有 89 至 90 美分（对 1 刀的面值）。

因为很多在写——很多媒体、自媒体也好，主流媒体也好——他们在写新闻的时候写得不清楚，只是说 Oracle 发出了不可抗力的警告，然后贷款本身 18 个 billion、现在一刀面值只值 89 至 90 美分，但没有说明白到底是谁借的这个贷款。你如果只是看标题的话，会以为这是 Oracle 的贷款——其实不是 Oracle 的贷款。

这个贷款本身是木星计划下面一个开发商 BlueOwl、它下面的公司所成立的 SPV。这个 SPV 去向 20 多家中小型银行一起进行贷款。

那中小型银行凭什么一起借出 200 亿美金？凭什么要借给 BlueOwl 下面这家公司呢？就是我前面说的：因为 Oracle 对这个项目本身进行了担保。如果项目完成的话，Oracle 未来会有不断的现金流进来。

类比：政府建医院的项目融资（project finance）

其实这种 project finance 在北美是非常常见的。我给大家举个例子：

比如说政府今天要造一家医院。通常来说，因为政府不会有这个钱，通常要去招商，找人愿意贷款去建这个医院。但是政府可以保证什么？政府可以保证：当你这个医院建完之后，我每年会给你拨款，或者未来每一个月会给你拨款。

那这个开发商本身，会拿政府的 commitment（当然前提一定是建立在医院能够建好、或者在几年之内能够建好的基础上），然后去外面进行融资。这些项目有时候可以有债务人，然后也可以有债权人——你可以以 equity 的形式去投资，都是可以的。

而通常这些基建项目其实比较受到一些长期投资者的欢迎，比如说一些养老基金。为什么？是因为如果你今天要建一个医院，或者建一条高速公路，那未来政府给这些项目现金流上的担保时间年限是比较长的——医院基本上 10 年、15 年，高速公路有些时候更长，20 年、30 年。这 20 年和 30 年的现金流对于养老基金投资者来说是非常有吸引力的。

但是这个项目本身凭什么外面能借得到钱？是因为有政府的担保。在这个例子里面其实是一样的——SPV（BlueOwl 下面的那家公司）凭什么能够借到钱？是因为有 Oracle 的担保。而 Oracle 的担保来自于哪里？来自于和 OpenAI 之间的订单。

贷款价格下跌的四个角度

有了这样的背景之后，我们来看第二点：这个贷款为什么会出现下降？价格为什么会出现下降？主要来自于四个角度。

第一，融资成本上升（加息）。 在这个加息周期里边——比如说现在美联储在加息，你在 2025 年美国财政部所举的债务，到 2026 年因为美联储的加息之后，价格一定会下跌。所以当在一个加息过程里边，你原本所举的债务本身的价格就会下跌。但是当这个债券本身接近于到期日的时候，它的票面价值就会慢慢回到 1 到美金——前提是项目本身或者公司本身不破产的情况下。所以说无限接近这个票面价值，因为当真的到期的时候，会把本金还回去，那这就是债券背后的本质。但是在这中间，你在加息过程里面，票面价值如果要卖掉或者要转手的话，价格就一定会下跌。

我去看了一下背后的条款：SPV 他们贷款的条款是 SOFR + 250 个基点。SOFR 就是隔夜利率，或者美联储联邦利率。联邦利率上次刚加了 25 个基点，所以加了 25 个基点这件事情本身就会使得价格下跌。但是它的价格从一刀跌到了 90 美分，加息本身不会使得它跌了将近 10%，对吗？

第二，Oracle 的信用风险上升。 也会使得这个贷款的价格下跌。为什么？因为 Oracle 是为这家 SPV 未来做担保的——严格来说，可能不能说它是做一个担保，它是给了一个承诺："如果你这个数据中心你造完之后，我会给你现金流"。但是 Oracle 如果自己的信用风险在上升的话，那你所承诺现金流去担保的项目本身，它的价格自然就会下降。这是我认为主要导致 SPV 贷款价格下跌的原因。

第三，流动性折扣。 因为你要在一级市场上卖掉的话，通常会有一个折扣价在那边。

第四，项目的完成风险。 就是我们今天所看到的事情——明显如果这个项目往后延，项目的完成风险往上升，那么以这个项目名义去贷的款的价格、贷款本身或者这个债券本身，自然价格一定要下降，因为风险上升了。

这四点全部加在一起，是我认为为什么导致这个价格下跌的原因。其中最主要的原因就是——因为 Oracle 的信用风险上升，所以使得贷款的价格下跌。

八、总结：这是执行力风险，不是需求风险

讲到这边，基本上我们把这件事情就讲清楚了。我来做一个总结：

首先，这件事情本身，它不是整个 AI 市场里边需求的风险。而在我们看整个 AI 市场里面有没有泡沫的时候，我认为最大最大的一个风险就是 AI 落地的风险——AI 落地是讲究需求。如果需求端这边出现问题，那整个市场就是有泡沫的。

所以第二点，我认为也不是供给过剩的风险。所谓有泡沫，就是你的供给超过了你的需求，或你需求不够高，或者你的供给太多了。所以泡沫的形成一定是供给超过需求。

从某种程度来说，这件事情本身，你说是不是对于 Oracle 有伤害在那边？一定是有的，因为未来营收可能要往后推了。包括 BE 来说，未来的营收也要往后推了。但是对于整个行业来说不见得是一件坏事，对吧？为什么？因为原本你在 28 年计划要上线的 2.4 吉瓦的算力，现在上线不了了。这个算力上线不了之后，变相就会使得其他能够去执行、或者能够把数据中心造起来的这些公司——大云也好、星云也好，对他们来说都是一个利好。

这就是为什么在周四这个市场里面，我们反而看到了 Nebius、反而看到了 CoreWeave 的价格出现了上涨。

所以我说它是延缓了交付。某种程度在需求——如果 AI 这一块需求持续强劲的情况下，其他有执行力的这些云公司是受益的。

九、风险的自上而下拆解

那整个的风险，它是由上而下的。我们来回顾一下：

  • 首先是 OpenAI。OpenAI 雇佣了、或者和 Oracle 之间合作。
  • 那 Oracle 有什么风险？Oracle 有融资风险、有执行力风险。对于他们来说，如果他们合作的开发商本身建数据中心往后延，那对于他们来说就是营收上的风险——数据中心建不了，营收就要往后推延。
  • 对于所有的大云公司也好、新云公司也好，都有执行力风险。如果你是大云，融资风险相对就会低一些；你是新云，就有融资风险在那边。不用看现在，因为 Oracle 现在体量相对来说是比较大的——对于这些新云来说，未来他们一定会融资的，因为他们要扩张的话，必须要融资。

顺着这个逻辑线，我们继续看下去，接下去就是数据中心的通电风险。

现在市场里边，AI factory 不是风险——GPU 本身它不是瓶颈（当然，HBM 现在仍然是一个瓶颈），GPU 不是瓶颈，然后互联也不是瓶颈；但是现在通电是一个瓶颈。整个 AI 数据中心里边明显看到了通电是一个风险。

那如果通电出现风险，我们再走到最后一步的话，就是交付要延后。交付要延后的话，营收就会出现风险。所以其实我在聊星云的时候有聊过：对于这些星云来说，包括对于 Oracle 来说，他们唯一的风险就是执行力风险。

十、彭博 Anna Wang 的转发：执行力风险 vs 信用风险

最后这边，因为今天这件事情在社交媒体上讨论非常的激烈，然后我看到彭博 Anna Wang 这个团队的 Anna Wang 自己也进行了转发，他说"将会有更多类似于 Oracle 的这种情况发生"。

我问他这是什么意思。我说你认为这是一个信用风险吗？因为我不认为是信用风险。我说这是一个执行力风险，Execution Risk。然后他说，他的意思是将会有更多的数据中心的建造会被延后或者取消。

但其实这件事情本身，我们仔细思考一下——这件事情本身它其实是 company specific risk，是仅限于公司自己本身的风险。而恰恰如果这些公司出现这些风险——就执行力风险——如果出现的话，对于整个行业来说不见得是一件坏事。

什么意思？这个前提当然还是建立在 AI 这一块仍然有需求的情况下，就是需求仍然增长的情况下。当需求仍然在增长，反而你在供给端、在提供算力这块跟不上，那只能……那这种情况就说明需求仍然会大于供给，起码在一段时间里面需求大于供给。当需求大于供给的话，整个行业里面就不会有泡沫。

所以怎么说呢？从泡沫论这个角度去看：如果今天 Oracle 真的交付、木星计划交付往后延，推到 29 年或者推到 30 年的话，对于整个市场来说其实是降低了、或者放缓了泡沫形成的过程。

十一、结尾

所以周四 Oracle 的这个事件本身并不是 Oracle 的信用出现了风险，而是 Oracle——你可以理解为——是 Oracle 的执行力风险。因为 Oracle 和他们合作的 BlueOwl、他们下面的这家公司所建立的 SPV 这家公司，在获取电力这方面出现了延后。那电力获取这块出现了延后，导致 Oracle 未来的营收有可能也会往后延。

所以这是 Oracle 自己这家公司本身的执行力风险。这个执行力风险也把它的合作商 Bloom Energy 的价格带下来。但是从长期的角度来说，这件事情本身已经被市场比较好地消化了。

那未来就看这一个项目本身会不会——是还是按照原来这个计划继续执行？如果还是按照原来这个计划继续执行的话，那今天这个下跌可以被涨回来；如果不能、或者说未来会有更多的计划往后延的话，那未来每次出现这种情况，股价都会出现下跌。

好吧，那希望通过今天这期视频，大家可以把整个事情的原委有一个非常全面的了解，并且对于这背后的风险有一个比较深刻的理解。今天这期内容就到这边，我们下期见。

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、瓶颈迁移史：AI 最终被 19 世纪基建卡住了
过去三年 AI 的瓶颈迁移路径本身就是一个反讽的隐喻——**H100（芯片）→ NVLink（互联）→ HBM（内存）→ 现在停在了新墨西哥州的一份天然气管道审批**上。整个视频最容易被忽略但最惊人的一个事实是：**人类最尖端的技术堆栈，最终被一份州级空气质量许可证和几段管道钢管卡住了。**
**跨领域连接**：这几乎完美复刻了 2010 年代德国的太阳能革命——最终不是电池技术限制了转型，而是输电线路审批限制了扩容。每一次能量密度革命，最后败给的都是**地方规划委员会**。AI 表面上是硅+算法的战争，本质上正在变成**能源+规划许可**的战争。这也解释了为什么 GEV、Caterpillar、Bloom 这些"老经济"公司突然被拉进了 AI 定价链条——它们是新瓶颈的守门人。
## 二、"泡沫延缓论"——最反常识的市场自愈机制
本次分析最反直觉的洞见值得单独拎出来放大：**Oracle 的执行失败，反而在系统层面降低了 AI 泡沫风险。**
- 直觉链：项目延期 → 营收往后推 → 坏消息 → 拉低估值 - 但真实

item.title: [Latent Space] Runway’s Bet Beyond Video: World Models, Robotics, and the Neural OS — Anastasis Germanidis
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的洞见：这是机器学习史上唯一一个"成功太多、失败太少"的领域

在几乎所有 ML 场景中，我们都在为正样本稀缺发愁——医疗数据里的罕见病、金融里的欺诈、语音里的边缘口音。但 Anastasis 在谈机器人 world model 时点破了一个奇特的反转：训练视频模型时，射门成功的视频远比射失的多，人成功系鞋带的画面远比失败的多。当 world model 要作为 RL 环境使用时，你需要它精确地"模拟失败"，因为动作模型只能在失败中改进。

这个观察让我联想到二战时对返航飞机弹孔分布的分析——真正决定生死的是"没回来的那些"。视频生成领域正在遭遇镜像版的幸存者偏差：互联网的视频语料库天然过滤掉了"世界如何出错"，而这恰恰是 embodied intelligence 最需要的信号。未来最有价值的视频数据集，可能是被 YouTube 算法压制的、笨拙的、失败的、令人尴尬的第一次尝试。

二、跨领域连接：Runway 的赌注其实是"重演麦克卢汉"，而不是重演 Sora

大家习惯把 Runway 归类为"视频生成公司"，但 Anastasis 反复回到的那句话——"界面本身也应是可学习的组件"、"你不再输出代码去渲染像素，你直接输出像素"——是一个远更激进的媒介论主张。这本质上是 1964 年麦克卢汉《理解媒介》里"the medium is the message"的技术实现版：应用程序作为"抽象层"其实是一个历史偶然，是硬件贫瘠时代的妥协。

再把这个观察与他谈到的另一个细节拼在一起——Refusion 用 Stable Diffusion 处理频谱图就能生成音乐、物理模拟数据作为 RGB 帧输入视频模型也能训练——一个更大胆的图景浮现出来："模态"这个词本身可能是一个人类学范畴，而非计算范畴。视觉、听觉、触觉是我们神经解剖学的产物，但对底层张量而言，它们是同一种模式的不同投影。Runway 的 world model 长远看不是在做视频，是在做一种媒介中立的现实压缩器——这与柏拉图洞穴寓言完全反向：Yann LeCun 认为学"像素输出"是在学阴影，但如果你能把阴影生成得毫无破绽，你就必然内化了那团火。

三、最出乎意料的观察：Gen 2 那个"周末项目黑客管道"其实预言了行业方向

Anastasis 轻描淡写地讲了一个几乎被行业遗忘的历史细节：Gen 2 是他"某个周末"想出来的——Gen 1 只能从深度图生成视频，于是他串了一个"文本→深度图→深度图到视频"的两段式黑客管道，把它称作 text-to-video。这在当时是技术能力不足下的凑合方案。

但注意他随后指出的：Reeve 和 Ideogram 在几乎同一天独立发布了一个"planner 模型先生成 bounding box，再喂给 diffusion transformer"的架构。今天所有生产级视频模型都在做 prompt completion pipeline。换句话说：一个因能力不足而拼凑的架构，几年后被重新发现为最优结构。

这里有个跨领域的深刻回声——生物进化里有个现象叫 exaptation：羽毛最初是保温结构，后来被"重新招募"用于飞行。Runway 的 Gen 2 是软件史上的 exaptation：一个应急拼装物，因为它意外地符合了某种深层的计算约束（模态分解 + 逐层规划），而变成了范式。这暗示了一个有趣的方法论：当你被迫做"两段式黑客"时，很可能你不是在妥协，而是在无意中触碰了问题的自然分解方式。值得研究的不仅是那些"scale up 就好"的胜利，还有那些"因为scale不够而被迫聪明"的中间解——它们往往是未来架构的化石标本。

四、隐藏的系统性真相：他真正在贩卖的不是 world model，是"反抗抽象"

把整场对话的所有主张串起来——神经操作系统、第三人称视频优于遥操作、omni model、清醒梦测试、界面即像素——你会看到一条隐秘的哲学骨架：Runway 系统性地反对每一层"人类为了让机器可管理而发明的抽象"。

  • HTML/CSS 是为渲染引擎发明的抽象——用界面 world model 直接消除。
  • 3D 扫描 + 物理引擎是为机器人仿真发明的抽象——用视频 world model 直接消除。
  • 模态划分是为神经科学发明的抽象——用 omni model 直接消除。
  • 应用程序边界是为工程分工发明的抽象——用统一模型端到端消除。

每一次抽象都是"因为我们算力不够、数据不够、方法不够"而产生的中介层。Runway 在赌scaling laws 会持续消灭中介层。这也解释了为什么他强调 New York outsider 视角——湾区的 ASI 叙事仍在讨论"如何让机器像人一样思考"，而 Runway 在讨论"如何让计算的层次结构本身崩塌成一张学习到的张量"。这是两种不同的乐观主义。

📝 转录文本

Runway's Bet Beyond Video: World Models, Robotics, and the Neural OS — Anastasis Germanidis

Cold Open: The Neural OS Vision

Effectively the end game of something like interface world models is you have a fully neural operating system. So I think Andrej Karpathy has written about that quite a while back, but it's — you know, I think to me it's a bit odd that, for example, with an interaction with an LLM of today, you have this LLM that can basically talk to you about anything. You can take the conversation any direction — it's very general, so it can solve all those different tasks — but you interact with it through a very rigid interface. And so to me it's just a matter of time before the interface itself becomes learnable and becomes part of the whole loop. Like, you're not just delivering — you're delivering an application end to end, and that means you're delivering the language model but you're also delivering the render and the pixels, and that's also a learnable component.

Sponsor Break

Before we get into today's episode, I just have a small message for listeners. Thank you. We would not be able to bring you the AI engineering, science, and entertainment content that you so clearly want if you didn't choose to also click in and tune into our content. We've been approached by sponsors on an almost daily basis. But fortunately, enough of you actually subscribe to us to keep all this sustainable without ads, and we want to keep it that way.

But I just have one favor to ask all of you. The single most powerful, completely free thing you can do is to click that subscribe button. It's the only thing I'll ever ask of you. And it means absolutely everything to me and my team that works so hard to bring the Inspace to you each and every week. If you do it, I promise you we'll never stop working to make the show even better. Now, let's get into it.

Welcome — Runway's Origin Thesis

Host: Okay, we're here with Anastasis from Runway with me and Vivu in the studio. Welcome.

Anastasis: Good to be here.

Host: Congrats on all your success and progress with Runway. You're opening offices all over the world. Did you envision this when you first started out?

Anastasis: Uh, not quite. I think even when we started, we had this idea that it was more a matter of when, not if. We were seeing the early generative models of 2016, 2017 and just extrapolating — assuming resolution quality increases predictably over time, there's going to be a point where most of content will be generated. And that was maybe the initial thesis of Runway: we will need, as a result of those generative models, to rethink how creative tools are made. And as we built out the research behind our generative models, it then became clear that they were useful far beyond that as well.

Host: And it is more obvious now with the real-world stuff and the world models that we'll talk about later. I'm just kind of curious how you go from a background in like ZDoc and computer vision into Runway. Take us back to those early conversations with Chris and whoever else was on your founding team.

From Interactive Art to ML Engineering

Anastasis: I was always split into those two worlds. One was — I had my own art practice. I was making a lot of interactive art for a long time. And then on the other side, I was working in startups. I was working as ML engineer, as a backend engineer at different companies. I've always been interested in coding and computation, and especially interested in simulation, and brought it back into my early artwork as well.

Host: Personal site has a few, right? Is there one we should pull up, just in case there's something that's like — I just like to go down memory lane. Okay, what is this?

Anastasis: So this was a project that I made, I think back in 2015, where I built this software that would give voice instructions to people in a gallery space. So it would basically coordinate interactions between people. It would first give you an identity — like, you're an architect, you're 30 years old, and you like sports — and then it would match you with another person. You have this completely generated interaction. Obviously language models were not quite there at the time, so it was a mix of some templates and some Markov chain generated text. And it would just completely simulate this small-talk conversation between everyone in the gallery space.

So I was always very fascinated on one end with generative models and the early machine learning work that was playing out at that time, but at the same time there was this separate thread of simulation and what it means — like, what can we learn about humans by creating those very simple models of their interactions and their behavior.

Host: Did you generate the prompts, or, you know, the "30-year-old whatever" — was it you generating them? How'd you like…

Anastasis: Exactly. So the program would just generate those from — yeah, a lot of it would be kind of Mad Libs style of, you know, you have lists of different professions, lists of different personality types, list of different ages, things like that, and then it would just combine those things together.

Anna Ridge Road — The First Runway Signal

And then maybe the next project we go is Anna Ridge Road, which was one of the first projects that we built with one of my two co-founders, Chris. This was taking Pix2PixHD, which was one of the early image-to-image models that Nvidia released back in 2016 or 2017. It was a model that would take a semantic map of a scene and then generate a photorealistic — let's call it — output. Obviously very early days, so it was not very high fidelity outputs, but it, I think, was the first image generation model that would generate at 1K resolution. And it was all trained on self-driving datasets, so the semantic categories it would support were only things you would encounter on the road — so it would be pedestrians, traffic signs, bikes, stop lights.

And so that was actually one of our first indications. We built this and people were making all this very surreal imagery of a million pedestrians or a million traffic signs or gigantic humans. And it was an indication that you could take a model that was trained on this very boring dataset — essentially of not that many interesting things happening when you're on the road — and then you can repurpose it and go very out of distribution and make something that was artistically compelling.

And that was — it's a summary of the thesis of Runway in some ways: you can take the same generative models, and if you look at them from another direction, if you build interesting tools around them and you give them to artists, they're going to do things that you don't expect.

Host: Very cool. I like the UX of it. Basically, you're just given an empty canvas — drag whatever, do whatever. And in the other one, you see everyone with wired headphones — that's a sign that it's very…

Host 2: Apple ads. Yeah.

From Post-Production Tool to Research Org

Host: Take us to today. You've been doing this for seven years at Runway. How have we got to this? Like, how do we go from driving simulator data to all this? You kind of cover the whole stack of generative media.

Anastasis: I mean, interestingly, we're almost back — you know, we're full circle. We're now applying our models beyond creative tools into real-world scenarios. But it was a long journey. Very early on we realized that the first version of Runway was a way to easily use the open source models of the day — things like Pix2Pix — and give them to artists. That was the initial idea: those models are too difficult to use if you're not a machine learning engineer — like, what happens when you give them to artists?

Very quickly we realized we needed to build a research org inside of Runway, and that happened maybe on year one. And a lot of the mandate there was: the image generation models of the time, the video generation models — most of the time there were barely any video generations at the time, but they were not quite there where they could be productionized and brought into tools that would be part of creative workflows. So we needed to push the frontier of the research.

And so maybe the first four years of Runway Research was almost happening in the background until there was a moment in 2022 with latent diffusion, with DALL·E 2 — you know, there was that step function change, and you guys maybe remember…

Host: I started Latent Space because of basically latent diffusion and stable diffusion, because I was like, wow, this is not only feasible, it is actually doable on consumer hardware.

Anastasis: Exactly. Yeah.

Between Pix2Pix and Diffusion: Green Screen

Host: I think the delta is also huge. Like, I learned Pix2Pix — this was intro to ML, the TensorFlow, the Jupyter Google Colab notebooks are like this — and then you have a sudden step function change with diffusion, whatnot. Any other sense that there were clear examples of what early diffusion were to get to here? Any other changes in key technology, research between 2018 when we started and 2022?

Anastasis: So one of the early works that we did in Runway was solving segmentation — image and video segmentation. It was a very important problem because most VFX involves essentially separating subjects. Rotoscoping — extremely manual process. Nobody enjoys doing that.

And so a lot of the early days of Runway was building this tool that was called Green Screen. And it was for a long time the main thing that people were using Runway for. It ended up being used in Everything Everywhere All at Once and a bunch of other high-visibility films and series. But that was essentially Runway for a long time — it was a post-production tool — until latent diffusion, generative Gen 1, Gen 2 happened.

Betting on a 1000-A100 Cluster

Host: Cool. I mean, let's go past that moment. You've come a long way — you started releasing your own models. Maybe describe that journey as well.

Anastasis: Yeah. So we got at a point in mid-2022 when it became clear that we're doing research at a fairly small scale of compute, and it became clear that scaling laws would apply to image and video gen in the same way that they're applying to language generation. So we made a big bet. At the time we signed this deal to build a cluster of a thousand A100s, which at the time — we were a Series B startup — was almost a slightly irrational decision maybe. But we really believed that if we trained a video model at large scale, we would get a great model at the end.

And at the time we set the goal, around fall of 2022, of: what does the latent diffusion / stable diffusion moment look like for video? And at the time the best model of the time was called CogVideo. It was one of the early kind of video models. It was 256×256 resolution, not very high quality. And so we decided we're going to build out this cluster and we're going to just invest in building out our own video model.

It became clear as we're training Gen 1 that it was difficult to get to fully — we wanted to build text-to-video, but it became clear to us that an easier starting point would be to start from video-to-video, because when you have a stronger conditioning, it's basically an easier problem to re-stylize an existing video versus generate a video from scratch. And so we released Gen 1 first back in — it was January of 2023.

Gen 1: Depth-Conditioned Video

Host: It's just a fun visual podcast — honestly, we can see February 2023. What was the state of stuff?

Anastasis: I mean, it's so interesting because at the time when you see those results, you think, this is so incredible. This is like — it's almost like image generation or video generation is solved. And then you look back a few years after and it's like — obviously, you get used to results very quickly with those models. But at the time, when we started seeing those results, it felt quite incredible — the level of quality you could get.

So Gen 1 was a depth-conditioned video model. It would take an input video, we would first convert it into the depth map, and then we would generate pixels with a latent diffusion model.

Host: Yeah, very effective. I didn't realize how distracting the blog post would be. Sorry.

Anastasis: Yeah, but one of my favorite examples of Gen 1 was — if you go up to mode three or mode two, there was this storyboard use case where people would basically make a city out of books or out of boxes, and then they would shoot a video with their phone and then translate it into a photorealistic output. There was all these ways in which those models were starting to be used for storyboarding.

And then if you go to mode 4 — of taking untextured 3D scenes and then turning them into photorealistic output. So we saw a lot of use cases early on where people that were familiar — Power VFX editors — would just take a Blender render and then they would get translated with Gen 1, or create a scene in Unity and then take a capture of a video of it and then re-stylize it.

So I still think video-to-video is powerful. We had a recent video-to-video model as well, and it's one of my favorite ways of using those models — essentially using them to use ground truth video as the initial inspiration and then translate into different styles or different outputs.

The Stable Diffusion Controversy

Host: But I think we're going to go into the rest of Runway and catch people up to speed today. I did want to cover the — let's call it — the Stable Diffusion controversy, or what happened with Stability AI. I think there was sort of two sides of the story. Part of that is a normal thing of people joining and leaving companies, but what is the retrospective now that there's been some years behind it?

Anastasis: Yeah, it's a very long story to go into. Which — I remember you actually wrote a really long post about — we probably cover the whole hour to go into it in more detail.

But essentially, there was the latent diffusion paper that came in — I think that was at the end of 2021. And then Patrick Esser, who was one of the researchers behind latent diffusion — he worked at Runway at the time — he built latent diffusion in collaboration with Robin Rombach and a few other folks back in the CompVis lab, the research group.

And after releasing the early latent diffusion model, the goal was: keep working on versions of the model, going to scale it up, incorporate new data, incorporate new tasks. And Stable Diffusion was basically the same model but trained on more compute and then with a few more tricks — like classifier-free guidance paper came at some point in the early 2022, which was a big prompting improvement — that improved results. It was trained on better data, so the aesthetic subset of LAION. But it was effectively the same underlying architecture.

And there was that big training run that happened on Stability's cluster. Stability financed that run. And looking back at that story, the work to build and train that model was done — it was a research project, it was done as part of the continuation of the latent diffusion work.

I think the model became very successful, and I think as a result of its success other companies tried to figure out the commercialization path for it. But for us it was very important that we make sure — it was meant to be an open source research project. And so we decided that we should continue releasing versions of it, since that was kind of the original goal of Stable Diffusion. And that led to releasing Stable Diffusion 1.5. There was maybe a day of a bit of miscommunication there, but ultimately that was resolved very quickly within hours.

Host: I just wanted to — you know, you are actually one of the main players in that journey, and so it's nice to hear from the source of what happened.

Anastasis: Yeah, I mean, I think it's all in the past now, I would say. Both companies — you know, Stability took its own path, Runway took its own path.

Building the Video Diffusion Stack

Host: It's pretty crazy — like, even since then, you've kind of got people at every level of the stack. You've got devs, creatives, artists, hobbyists — you got everyone using it. And for people that tried stuff early, they'll remember how hard it was to use regular diffusion, right? Like, nowadays you can use your favorite ChatGPT or whatever, give a sentence, get a beautiful output. But diffusion was — like, you know, the whole ultra HD 4K high resolution — like, prompting these things was very different.

Anything you learned on the tooling side, like from the offerings you guys have now — so, like, creatives, devs — you really took the research and brought it to everyone to use. Anything interesting there to share?

Anastasis: We had to build the entire model-serving infrastructure for video diffusion models. There was nothing else — because Gen 2 was the first text-to-video model, I think, out in the market. So many things that we learned over time.

I think the biggest one was — it was very clear early on that text-to-video was not going to be the answer. Like, people wanted a lot more control than that, and so we invested in building control on top of those models very quickly. How do you use the camera trajectory as control? How do you use an initial input frame as control?

So that was a very early learning for us with text-to-video. Gen 2 was an amazing step function improvement in the quality of video models, but it was used much more in an exploratory way, because there was nothing to ground it to. There was no reference that you could bring into it. There was no — you couldn't really control the camera motion, you couldn't control the object motion.

And so the first year in 2023 was really all about: what are all the interesting ways in which we can condition those models? And it was a lot of just post-training runs on top of the base model to figure out — how do people actually want to control them?

Controllability Wave — Motion Brush, Camera Control

And so there was this quick succession — we had this thing called Motion Brush, which was: you could basically draw arrows and dictate where things should move in the scene. There was Camera Control, where you could just describe how you want the camera to move in the scene. And because we work with filmmakers from most of the history of Runway, we immediately got this feedback and decided that this was worth investing in.

And so controllability became a big theme, I think, very early on as we were building those models.

Gen 2 — The Weekend Hackathon Pipeline

Something fun that I haven't really talked about too much was just how Gen 2 came to be out of Gen 1. It was a bit strange, because we announced Gen 2 months after Gen 1, and it was before Gen 1 was even generally available.

Gen 1 was a depth-to-video model — so it would take a depth map and it would convert it into RGB. And we couldn't get text or image-to-video to work directly, and that's why we started from depth-to-video.

But we had discussions of like, okay, we need to spend the next 6 months actually investing in text-to-video, maybe increasing the compute scale or the model scale, train a larger model. And I had this weekend project idea, which was: what if I take a model that starts from text input and converts to depth maps, and then use Gen 1 to convert the depth maps into RGB? And so Gen 2 was basically that.

Host: It's a hackathon pipeline.

Anastasis: But it looks good. And it worked pretty well. I mean, if with a knowledge that it has this two-stage pipeline, you can tell in some cases that the structure of the video looks a bit off, because you had to generate the depth first before you go into the output video. But it worked, and it allowed us to bring this to our users very quickly.

But it's actually — now it's interesting, because people are coming back to this almost two-stage approach. Like, if you look at the Reeve text-to-image model that came a few months ago, it had this planner model that would generate bounding boxes before it fed that into the diffusion transformer.

Host: Yeah, Ideogram also, the same day — I remember that was very strange that both of them came out the same day with the same exact innovation.

Anastasis: It's a small community, I think.

Host: I'm like, this is completely coincidental, right?

Anastasis: People talk. So yeah, there's definitely something to this approach. And obviously now, every single video generation model in production uses a complex prompt completion pipeline under the hood. I think that's no secret.

Host: Humans are terrible at prompting, I think, across the board. But yeah — like the original Sora 1 blog post even told you that what happens after your input is rewriting your prompt — it's much more descriptive about what you would want.

Anastasis: Exactly. And there was the DALL·E 3 paper beforehand that was the first public description of the fact that synthetic captions and really detailed captions work really well, and then Sora kind of built on that.

Camera Control as the Seed of World Models

Yeah. So it was 2023. We were kind of releasing all these updates to Gen 2 — like the Camera Control, Motion Brush. And there was actually something very interesting about Camera Control, because it was the first time that you felt that, instead of like — you were creating video, you were creating a short video — you were actually navigating inside the world. And I think Camera Control was maybe the seed of some of the ideas that we had around world models and really opening up that research direction.

We realized — it was this era, and this series of Gen 1 and Gen 2 models really proved to ourselves — yeah, this is the… So this is not the original Camera Control, this was the update to Camera Control on top of Gen 3. But yeah, I think it made those models usable to filmmakers.

Camera Control was very popular, and so we realized: there's one way of seeing those models, which is you're just treating them as content creation machines. And there is the other way, which is: you're predicting video, and in order to predict video well, you need to simulate the world in an increasing and increasing capacity. And if scaling laws apply on video just like they apply on language models, then as we scale the compute that we put in those models, then they're going to be able to simulate physics, they're going to be able to simulate human actions and dynamics increasingly well and predictably well.

That was the thesis about our efforts on world models. And we spun up this research group to just focus on world models and how do we turn the video generation models that we're building into something broader and something that would be useful beyond content creation as well.

Host: And that was roughly when?

Anastasis: Yeah, so that was in late 2023.

Anastasis: I mean, it's debatable whether it's a pivot. Like, arguably that's what you always had to do anyway, right? It's in a way an expansion of the applications of the models as they become more capable.

Anastasis: Yeah. So it just became — and if you looked at the outputs of Gen 2, it was not obvious to people that this would scale to become a general simulator of the world. And you start from 32×32 images of faces, and then by the time in 2018 you could generate street images at a 1K resolution. And it was kind of the same with world models — very early signs of something much bigger.

Anastasis: Yeah, especially watching the early old blog posts, you can really see the choppiness, the details.

Host: Like human civilization starting from random noise and then noising into…

Anastasis: Yeah, just run it.

"The Human Mind Is No Longer the Center of AI"

Host: I like the way that you guys phrased it when you announced it in June, which is — you had a sort of video essay: "the human mind is no longer the center of AI, our world is." Right? Which is — you know, let's call it the past 5 years of LLM-based AI is very much like trying to emulate human preferences and human speech, but now that's like mostly solved — I think that's some of the context of your essay, which you also wrote around the time. And now it's like the focus on modeling the world accurately.

Anastasis: Exactly. So the way we see it is — there is that initial mission statement of DeepMind, which is: solve intelligence and then use it to solve everything else. But I think starting from "everything else" could be valuable — of, you know, there is just so much complexity and detail in the world that in order to — that it's hard to learn directly from just human descriptions of the world.

Like, we're essentially saying that language models learn from everything that humans have written about the world — like our own understanding as of the 2020s. And there's just so much that we don't know and so much that's not captured by existing text — about both the low-level dynamics of the world. Like, we're not describing in detail — if I tell you to describe how you tie your shoes, that's a very difficult thing to describe in words, but it's very obvious thing to demonstrate.

And so I think there's — and, you know, more of a paradox — like, we're constantly underestimating all the complexity that goes into very — things that we do subconsciously as humans, and we don't even necessarily always have the words to describe them.

And so in my mind, simulating the world and simulating physics, simulating the dynamics of the world, has always been kind of underestimated compared to — we place too much emphasis on the things that are easy to talk about. But there's just all this complexity and richness of the world, that if we just try and train directly on that observational data instead of training on how people describe the world, we would learn something new that we wouldn't otherwise know.

Response to LeCun — JEPA vs. Pixel Prediction

Host: You think that the present architectural paradigm is fine. You don't need like another layer, like JEPA — you know, like another famous New York AI leader would say.

Anastasis: You know, we're a very pragmatic research lab. If we have evidence that an approach works better than the approach that we're taking, then we have no qualms to taking it. We just have seen no indication that video prediction itself doesn't scale.

And even if you look now — not just our work, but the work of others — you're seeing in robotics some of the most promising work starts from video prediction models and then you adapt them to also be action models, for example. So there is very little evidence that you need something else, and that your time is better spent on a novel architectural change compared to improving data and improving and scaling the current approach.

And so we don't have any indication that — there is that counter-argument — I think there was a tweet by Yann LeCun a few days ago that — you know, understanding the dynamics of the world is very different than generating cute videos. And your answer is: no, they're the same thing. My cat videos are the same as understanding physics.

Anastasis: Right, because if you want to generate — you know, obviously video models can cheat, and they could give successive shots of the scene in a way that doesn't require you to actually simulate difficult physics. There's always all these different ways in which you can hide the deficiencies of the model. And it's important not to be too tricked by the performance of the current video models. It's easy to cherry-pick examples and think that video models are further advanced than they actually are. So there is a lot more work that we need to do to improve those models.

But in my mind — very similar to language, like, you go from barely coherent sentences to something that could hold a conversation with a human to something that could operate autonomously for a day and create entire codebases. And the main difference — there's obviously some architecture improvements along the way, but the main thing is scale. And so it's the same bet for video, and we have no indications that this is saturating. Like, we have benchmarks that we use for measuring the physics of those models and we see those predictably improve as we scale those models.

Physics IQ — Scaling Laws for Physical Intuition

So if you want to pull up Physics IQ — it's one of those benchmarks that measures: how well does the model perform at all mechanics, or fluid dynamics, or optics?

Host: I'm curious if you've seen any emergence, any scaling law around this. Yeah — he's saying there is a scaling law, right?

Anastasis: Exactly. So the way those benchmarks work is — the researchers have gone and captured a few videos that are representative of different physical phenomena, and then you can take the first frame and then pass it through an image-to-video model and then generate a rollout that shows what should happen next. So you have a ball hanging from the ceiling, and then you use that as input, and then the model predicts how the ball should fall on the ground.

And this measures — you know, we have an intuitive understanding of physics — I know you can imagine what will happen next if I drop this bottle. So it's measuring that same intuitive physics understanding of those models. And we've measured that at different model scales — different compute scales — and we see that the score in Physics IQ predictably improves.

There's other tricks and techniques that you can make to improve the score even further, but even scale alone helps in the model learning better physics.

Plato's Cave — The Sympathy with LeCun

Host: My main sympathy with Yann LeCun is the Plato's cave allegory, right? Like, you're learning on the output of a thing, not the internal process of a thing. And it's very, very noisy. And you know, if only you could observe the internals of a thing. It's hard to observe the internals of a human mind. But you can very much observe — or at least we have a whole bunch of science and physics that we're ignoring on how to model physics and movement and gravity and other interactions — and we're just like throwing away all that and just saying "just scale data," which is very much the lesson of unsupervised learning, but it feels wrong. I think that's like the main idea.

Anastasis: I think the history of machine learning is "large feels wrong." It's a bitter lesson right now, is the simple answer to that.

Scaling Video, Long Context, and Gen 3

Host: I guess how much can you scale? So, like, even on the video generation side — like, there's one side of video understanding, video generation. Are we still going to have tools where it's like: I want to generate 2 hours, 20 hours? I mean, there's an inferral way to do it in batches and stitch it together, but do we just keep scaling? Do we just continue long generation, consistency, all that would scale? And like, tying it into where we're at now from Runway 2 to 4.5 — like, technically what advancements have we made to today, and then where do you see things still going?

Anastasis: So part of the answer is definitely scale, and that was — we learned that lesson in a big way with Gen 3. So Gen 3 was the model we released the year after, in 2024, that was a few months after Sora was released — so yeah, there's an interesting story of how that came to be as well.

Gen 3 for us was the first time that we really needed to build — basically, we had to learn all the lessons that the language model world learned in three years in the span of a few months. One of the biggest changes of Sora was using diffusion transformers instead of ConvNets. So a lot of the early latent diffusion models were all ConvNets for the diffusion model part. And the diffusion transformer paper came at some point in 2023. And it basically showed scaling laws for image diffusion transformers.

And we realized at that point that we needed to invest in infrastructure for model parallelism, for really scaling training to larger than a few billion parameter models. And we spent maybe most of the fall of 2023 building out our infrastructure for distributed training. And we had a lot of false starts and a lot of failure in trying to scale image and video diffusion transformers.

The Sora Existential Crisis

And at that point — you know, February 2024 — Sora comes out, and the results are very much superior to what Gen 2 could produce. There were a lot of chatter on Twitter about "Runway's done," "there is no way Runway will catch up." And if you remember also, OpenAI in the early 2024, it felt very — like, it's a formidable opponent now, but at that point they were on the top of their game. Nobody could even get close to them. There was maybe — Gemini, the first version of Gemini, had just released.

So when OpenAI came with Sora and it was such a big jump of quality, it gave — there was an existential crisis for a few hours. But the amazing thing about Runway — I think we've been around 8 years now, which is almost — we're a dinosaur in AI. And we had to — there was a lot of those moments — we had to learn, adapt very quickly, and build out skillset in the team that we didn't have. And so if you ask anyone what is their favorite time at Runway that was there during that time, it was that push in like 3 months to get to a model better than Sora.

And we scaled 10x the model size and the compute that we were training on. We figured out model parallelism — we had zero expertise in that — and then we came out with Gen 3 during that summer.

So that was a big turning point, I think, for the company where the research work grew very quickly. And we really started pursuing this vision of the general world model in earnest, I think, after Gen 3 was out.

Real-Time Video and Step Distillation

Host: Yeah. I mean, that's the amazing thing about building — when you're building there's no stack. You have to invent everything yourself. You have to be completely full stack. Now, I think there are inference specialists like Fal or whatever that can help with model serving, and I think you guys work with them as well. But yeah, at the time it was — it's very interesting to think about what you do when Sora comes out and people are questioning whether your company should still exist.

Anastasis: Yeah. And there was no VLLM of diffusion models — that we had to build the whole model-serving infrastructure and make things efficient. And a few months after we released Gen 3, we released the Turbo version, which I think was the first step-distilled model in production.

Host: That was a whole trend that we covered as well.

Anastasis: So that allowed us actually to serve those models at the larger scale, because I think the first version of Gen 3 was quite expensive to serve.

Host: You know, I think the whole trend in consistency models, lightning, and turbo and all these things somehow didn't really stick around. I don't know if you have any reflections on this, because at the time I was like, well, obviously everything should start with a distilled model first, and then you can upscale, right? Then basically your bigger models just turn into fancy upscalers. But like, you should always draft with a smaller model and faster model, right? Because you can get it so quickly, like near real-time.

Anastasis: Yeah, I would not be so sure to say that didn't stick around. I think that's — likely to — I mean, there's a lot of step-distilled models that are actively used in production. There's still obviously a gap in quality compared to the non-distilled model. But in my mind, we're still — you know, there is a two-to-three-year offset from language models. So it's just a matter of time before there is better distillation techniques.

We use — right now we have a real-time model, Chorus Characters, that I think is the largest deployment of real-time video models. That's a step-distilled model and it's actively being used. It's a very specific use case compared to a general video model. So this is by the way — this is Avatar Consistency Characters.

Yeah, so this is a talking avatar model. We were able to — we optimized the hell out of it — and it generates at 24 fps, and it's a step-distilled autoregressive video model.

From Bidirectional Diffusion to Autoregressive

So if we look at our world model direction, a big component of it is starting from the bidirectional diffusion that basically generates an entire video at once, and making it autoregressive. So you generate one frame or a few frames at a time. So there's a lot that goes into that pipeline of getting to a real-time model. It's first you need to make it into a causal autoregressive model, and then you need to do some additional step distillation to get it to actually be real-time. And I think that part is actually just starting.

I would be very surprised if we're — you know, two years from now — we don't primarily use real-time models. To me, real-time video generation is just inevitable that — you know, it has much better user experience, is much cheaper to serve, and the quality gap between the base model and real-time model is only going to close as we figure out better distillation techniques. And we made a lot of progress there internally on maintaining the quality of the base model when we distill them.

Host: How much of this is transferable? So, is it the same base model? Like, if you're doing diffusion across the whole sequence and you're converting it to step autoregressive distillation, is this like distillation where you still need to train both, you can use the same base and converter? What's that process like to go from regular model to something that's real-time on a technical level?

Anastasis: So the nice thing about diffusion models is you have two axes of distillation. So there is — you can distill to a smaller model, which resembles what you do in LLMs, or you can distill in terms of taking less steps — less diffusion steps. So you could take a model that generates in 50 steps and generate in 4 steps, and you have some performance degradation, but very often you get comparable outputs. So you can even take the large frontier model and distill it with step distillation and get to real-time performance. And that's what we've seen.

So depending on the use case, in some cases we might also serve with a smaller model, but in a lot of use cases we actually just use the frontier model and we're able to make it work in real-time.

Interface World Models — The Neural OS Demo

Host: I think this might be a good time to cut over to his laptop to show off some of the real-time stuff that you're doing.

Anastasis: This is one of the research updates that we did recently. So we've been working on getting our general world models to different applications. One of them that we think is very compelling is using general world models as essentially a universal interface to software.

This is a version of our world model that's called an interface world model. And the idea is that it essentially replaces the front end of a software application. It renders the pixels directly of an interface, and it's trained to predict what happens next as a result of a click or another interaction you have with the interface.

So this is all pixels — there is no HTML, CSS, React that's powering this interface. This is directly at the output of our real-time video generation model, and it takes clicks directly as input.

Host: And drags. Click and drag, right?

Anastasis: So it supports clicks, it supports drags, it also supports scrolling. And the amazing thing about this is that you can effectively describe in the prompt how you want different elements — like, what do you want the behavior of different elements to be.

So it's almost — you can turn an interface from a markup language description of an HTML interface — instead you can just describe the interface. You know, if I press this button I expect this to happen, if I press this button this should happen. And it's useful, we believe, both for prototyping, for just testing what different interactions would feel like.

You can also add audio to it. So it's a video-audio generation model, so you essentially describe both what the visual outcome should be of your click and also what the sound effect is that comes out of it. So we believe that's going to be a much more flexible way of building software. Just render it — just, you know, why generate the code that generates the pixels? Just generate the pixels directly. It's the end-to-end philosophy applied to front ends.

So we think there's a few interesting use cases. So you can build creative tools on top of it. We think that for any kind of use case that involves a lot of exploration — like an educational use case where you want to learn about a new concept and you want some kind of visualization and open-ended exploration — we think this is a very powerful approach.

You can imagine new forms of design, industrial design software that could emerge as a result of those models. And this is all generated in real time as well. So you can build a lot of interesting camera transitions and forms of interaction that are very difficult to build otherwise.

And one way in which we evaluate this is — what if you try to generate the same interface with Claude, by just prompting Claude: here's an image reference of my interface that I made in Figma or that I created somewhere else, create this particular interaction, which in this case is drag that object upwards. And beyond it being slower, it's also very difficult to capture some interactions by just fully with just LLMs.

So we think that this is likely to be the way that a lot of the future software in the future will be created. And one of the additional benefits is personalization — might be a lot easier done with those models. Like, you can essentially try out different prompts based on who's visiting the interface. You can more easily prompt engineer the interface to have larger-sized text for more accessibility reasons — or if you have a particular study preferences.

So we're very excited about this approach. It's obviously early days, and I think we'll need to make it more cost-effective as well to serve those models. Because running a real-time video model versus just purely rendering HTML — obviously the computational needs are much higher. But we do see a lot of potential in this approach to building front-end interfaces.

Interfaces as Ambient Simulation

Host: So we covered a similar thing with flipbook before, with our Ethan her episode with Grok Video. And I think it's very engaging visually. I think it's maybe good for education, but it does sound expensive. I think there's an upper bound to how expensive it will be, though, right? Like, you know, the inference cost will go down over time. You'll figure out ways to optimize it effectively. When it pauses, you're not receiving human input — you don't have to generate anything, right?

Anastasis: Yeah, I mean, you could also — in this case you have ambient motion. So there is parts of the screen that — you know, if you let's say you want to visit Paris and then you get this interface that you're allowed to explore. You have people walking, or things happening. It obviously makes it more expensive because you need to run the model all the time. Maybe you have some looping mechanism so you don't need to do that. But all those things I think is stuff we need to figure out.

Our first consideration is: let's make this clearly find some use cases where it's clearly a much more compelling interaction compared to traditional interfaces, and then it's a matter of time before it becomes more cost-effective to serve.

The Neural OS Endgame

Host: I'm curious if you extend this out 2, 3 years. So where do you see things going even further?

Anastasis: Effectively the end game of something like interface world models is you have a fully neural operating system. So I think Andrej Karpathy has written about that quite a while back. But it's — you know, I think to me it's a bit odd that, for example, with an interaction with an LLM of today, you have this LLM that can basically talk to you about anything. It can — you can take the conversation any direction, it's very general, so it can solve all those different tasks. But you interact with it through a very rigid interface.

And so to me, it's just a matter of time before the interface itself becomes learnable and becomes part of the whole loop. Like, you're not just delivering — you're delivering an application end to end. And that means you're delivering the language model, but you're also delivering the render and the pixels, and that's also a learnable component.

And the concept of applications might not necessarily — I think we need to figure out new abstractions for software. The concept of application comes from this idea that you need separate code bases to power each individual tool and each individual application. But you might think of something a lot more unified if you have a video model that's actually generating the interface as you go. So it can take context from an LLM and allow you to combine different functionalities that traditionally would live in different applications. So it's a way to solve software end to end effectively.

World Models for Humans, World Models for Agents

We also see this as a powerful way to train computer-use agents as well. In general with world models, there is those two directions: one is world models for humans, and world models for agents to train agents. And so for every new work of world models that we do, both uses become possible.

So this is a powerful synthetic data generator for training computer-use models. It could become a live RL environment that you could use to do online RL with a computer-use agent. And you can get wide diversity of different interactions, kinds of interfaces just generated on the fly, that improve how robust your agent becomes. So that's the same also with the world models that we're working on for a robotics use case as well.

Long Context and Error Accumulation

Host: Is there a research breakthrough that you're waiting for that would unlock the next set of use cases that you really want to pursue?

Anastasis: Long context is a very important one. So being able to maintain consistency for long periods of time. And that depends on the use case. So for our Characters model, for example, or for the interface world model, it's easier to maintain long sessions of interaction. If you go into more open-ended worlds that you navigate and you take arbitrary actions in — like, there is more, the context at which you can generate becomes limited much more quickly. So we see more degradation and error accumulation happening.

So the biggest challenge with autoregressive models is error accumulation — is basically you're feeding generative frames back into the model to generate the next frames, and if there is any small errors they accumulate over time. That's not a new problem — it's a problem that LLMs also have — and we've seen the ability to generate now really really long outputs. So it's a solved problem, but it's definitely still a challenge.

Host: Yeah. And what is the state of the art? So for Grok, it would be like 10 to 20 seconds of context going in there for video.

Anastasis: With our Characters model, we're able to generate up to 30 minutes of video autoregressively.

Anastasis: Yeah. So if we look at GWM Worlds, which is more our open-ended world exploration model, it's on the order of a few minutes.

Anastasis: Yeah, it's not the ideal game experience if you have to restart every few minutes. But I think, for certain kinds of experiences, you can work around it. Ideally you're able to just generate forever and it doesn't degrade. And I think that's a matter of time before we get there.

GWM Robotics — Accidental State of the Art

Host: This was your — you did a study on robotics. I think I also have just your Runway Robotics page though. Is this better?

Anastasis: So last year we released Gen 4.5. So that was our latest base model. And we've been, as I mentioned, doing all this work in world models. A lot of our approach to world models is: how do you take a bidirectional diffusion model and make it autoregressive and make it accept actions? So instead of being a video you watch, it becomes a simulation that you step in, and you can control it every step of the way. You can explore counterfactuals — like what happens if I take this action versus if I take this action.

And GWM 1 was the world model that we built on top of Gen 4.5. So we did all this autoregressive and then step distillation on top of Gen 4.5. And one of the biggest use case that we saw for GWM 1 was in robotics.

One thing we like to say is: we, as we scaled video models, we accidentally created a state-of-the-art model for robotics by just scaling video models. So we realized at some point, mid last year, that robotics labs started coming up to us and asking to use video models for synthetic data — kind of asking us to post-train our video models to work really well for robotics so that they can use that to basically generate variations. That was the first use case that we saw.

And then increasingly became clear that the models will be useful beyond just creating synthetic data to train robotic policies. They would also be very useful as simulators. So that means that you can use a video model online to test how your robotic action model performs. So you can take an action, roll out, and then get the outcome of the action inside the world model, and then continue that loop — like this closed-loop simulation — and you can use that to evaluate how well your robotics model works.

Real-to-Sim Correlation

And the biggest thing that I think you need to solve if you want to build a simulator is establishing real-world correlation — that if you take an action inside the world model, if you take the same action in the real world, you get a similar outcome. So that was a goal of some work that we did earlier this year.

So if you go to the first link — so that was essentially, we wanted to establish that real-to-sim correlation for our world model. So that if you do a series of actions inside the world model, and if you do the same actions in the real world, you get similar outcomes. And we took our GWM 1 model, and we used some benchmark data — there's this RoboArena benchmark that's very commonly used to evaluate how well do different action models perform. And we used the same scenarios and things and embodiment inside our world model. And we measured the correlation of how well did an action model perform inside the world model versus in the real world.

And we saw that we could get very good correlation between our world model and reality. And that means that if you want to evaluate how well your robotic policies perform, you can scale that much faster inside simulation instead of having to do that with actual physical hardware.

And so that was a first indication that our models could be quite useful in robotics. And we saw, as we're working with robotics labs, that became like the first use case where they could use video models in a way that fit into their training pipeline.

Solving Sim-to-Real Without 3D Scanning

Host: Can I ask what the difference was from 4.5 to solving that? So the sim-to-real gap has always been the issue, right? You train a robotics model on video data, it doesn't generalize to real-world, and the simulation had an issue. So it seems like you solved it. But how?

Anastasis: Yeah. So a big problem with simulators is: if you're trying to simulate rigid objects, like, it works quite well if you can describe the physics of objects very accurately. Then you're able to use IsaacSim or MuJoCo or one of the traditional simulators. But for more complex interactions — with cloth for example, or slippery surfaces — with all the complexity that you want to be able to solve with a manipulation, with an action model that solves manipulation tasks — it's very difficult and so time-consuming to build for each of those environments and each of those tasks.

Build the simulated version of that, the digital domain of that environment. Whereas with a world model, you just need to provide the first frame, and then you can roll out the policies inside the first frame. So whereas we compared it to methods that required, like, 3D scanning an environment, and then 3D scanning each individual object before you can bring that simulation — whereas with a world model, you just take a picture of the environment and then you're able to test how your policy performs.

The Third-Person Video Thesis

Our general thesis on robotics is: there are companies that are leveraging a lot of teleoperation data to train robotics action models. There is now companies that are using UMI data — which is essentially human egocentric video where humans use kind of robotic grippers to perform different manipulation tasks. And then there's companies that are focusing on egocentric data, which is you strap a GoPro on someone's head and then you capture them performing a task.

We think that all those are great sources of data for training robotics models, but the most plentiful source of video data is third-person video data. And how do we as humans learn how to perform different tasks? A lot of it is by observing others perform those tasks. We don't learn from first person. We obviously do some trial and error to learn different things, but ultimately, a lot of what we learn how to do in the world, we learn by watching other people do it.

And that's how — when you're pre-training a video model, you're essentially doing that. It's a lot of third-person video footage of people performing different tasks in the world — people doing sports, people doing household tasks. And our main thesis is that video pre-training — once you do that, you can then adapt a model to be useful in robotics use cases with way fewer hours of actual robotic data.

So you require way less teleoperation data, which is very difficult to scale. And even if you look at egocentric data, which is a bit more easy to scale compared to teleoperation data — which requires actual hardware — is still three orders of magnitude less of that that exists in the world compared to third-person video data out there.

And so our thesis is — and generally like the most plentiful source of data will ultimately win — third-person video data pre-training is the right starting point for models that you want them to generalize and be able to deal with new environments, new tasks, things that you haven't seen during training. That's the motivation for why we think our models are especially useful in robotics settings. And we've seen that to be the case as well.

Curriculum: Third-Person Pretrain → First-Person SFT

Host: You said pre-training. So maybe it's like third-person pre-training, first-person SFT. Is that like a curriculum that you can sort of introduce?

Anastasis: Exactly. So if we look at GWM Worlds — so GWM Robotics — the GWM Robotics, it starts from Gen 4.5.

Host: It's the same video diffusion backbone, right?

Anastasis: Exactly. Yeah. So you start from the base video model — the one you're using to generate cats and dogs and other interesting stuff — and then you fine-tune on a very small number of hours of robotic data. So it's something on the order of hundreds of hours, compared to — if you were to pre-train a robotics model, the current pre-trainings go up to hundreds of thousands or millions of hours of data. And you're able to get quite good performance quickly, because the model leverages all the things that it has learned about the world and physics and human dynamics and the tasks that people care about from pre-training.

And ultimately, you want those models to generalize. You don't want to just be able to perform the task that has been during training. And the diversity of actions and environments that you have with a pre-training video dataset is much larger than what you can realistically capture manually.

Compute Allocation and Unification

Host: How's the scale looking like for the post-training? Like, you still want to do — is it like roughly 90% of the compute in regular video diffusion model and then scale up a lot? Or do it like — we want different robotic models for different tasks, or just the one base really good world model can also apply to robotics?

Anastasis: So currently, we are post-training our models for specific embodiment for particular partners. So if they have a particular kind of single-arm robot, or bi-manual robot, or humanoid robot, we would post-train our GWM Robotics model on their particular dataset.

Over time we see the different variants of GWM unifying. Like, I would expect a year from now or two years from now, you have a single world model that can simulate manipulation task, it can simulate navigation — which is a lot of the gaming world models are navigational world models, you're moving around the space — and it will also simulate human behavior, so that's the Characters models.

So instead of having three different models, you have a single model that's able to — ideally — simulate what it's like to be in the world. You're moving around an environment, you're maybe performing different tasks, you're talking to other people, and that happens with the same single real-time video model that's generating that.

Self-Driving and World Action Models

Host: Do you think you can solve self-driving? So if you are learning to drive a car in a simulator, you have a world model — your robot is basically a car — can manipulate so many axes. How far off are you from something like that? So a really good ADAS system.

Anastasis: World models are definitely being applied to self-driving research right now, mainly for evaluation use cases. But our focus has been more on robotic manipulation. We've done some work on AV world models as well.

But yeah, we do think that world models and video models are the best starting point for both simulators and also policy and the action models. So that's the other side to this — is that once you have a great world model, then you can just add an action head and it can predict actions as well.

One way to think about it is: if you take the starting frame of a scene with a robotic arm, and you prompt the model — generate the arm picking up an object — and if it generates an accurate enough video, then it should also be able to generate the exact poses in 3D that the arm should take to perform the same action.

So this is the direction that's — now the popular term for it is world-action models, which is: you're starting from a video model and then you're adding an action head to predict the actions, and it becomes a policy essentially.

The Lucid Dream Test

So one thought experiment that I like to use — it's almost like the Turing test of video models, or like the Turing test of world models. I call it the "lucid dream test."

Host: You mean like the actual person lucid — lucid dream?

Anastasis: It comes from lucid rains, right?

Host: Lucid dreams — is telling you're dreaming while you're in a…

Anastasis: Yeah, exactly. So lucid dreaming is when you realize you're inside a dream and then you basically are able to control what happens in —

Host: No, there was also an inference guy called Lucid Dreams. Yeah. Quantization — very prolific person.

Anastasis: Yeah. So, let's say you have a VR headset, and you're in a room. And you're wearing a VR headset, and that VR headset — most of today's VR headsets have a pass-through mode, so you can see directly what's in front of you in the world, or you can obviously render something inside the VR headset.

And there's going to be a point where those interactive real-time video models become good enough where you wear the headset, and you're in the same room, and you're walking around, and you're interacting with objects, you're able to move freely in that room and interact with any object. And then at the end, someone asks you: were you using pass-through mode, or was this rendered or generated footage? And if you cannot tell for sure — if that was what you were seeing as you were interacting with and moving around the world — was generated or it was pass-through mode and was just what was happening in front of you.

That's an indication that the models have become good enough. And we're not close to that yet.

Counterfactuals — Why Failure Data Matters

And a lot of it is just this idea of really simulating dynamics and counterfactuals. Like, you know, if you ask a video model to generate a person scoring a goal versus a person failing to score a goal, it would do a better job at scoring the goal, because there is a bias from the training distribution — there's a lot more videos of the person succeeding at scoring the goal.

But if you have an interactive model, you want it to be able to generate counterfactuals — like, if I take this action versus this action, you want it to generate equally realistic outcomes. So that's, I think, the big gap between video models and world models — is that idea of the counterfactual generation.

And if you want a great model for robotics, you want to simulate failure very well. Because whether you're using it for evaluation or you're using it as — in an online RL loop in the future — you want to be able to have the model kind of try and fail to do things and improve. And so in order to do that, you need to be able to simulate things failing. This is the only domain where you have too many successful examples and not enough bad examples.

Host: It should be easy to generate failure.

Host 2: Oddly enough, I think, like, early image video models weren't good at being human-realistic, right? Like, you see a lot of the high-res 4K, like professional photography, but not just everyday life — like, normal picture, right? Everything looks like it's professionally generated, like professional pictures, but not just like normal — messy cables on a desk.

Video Agents and the Harness

Host: Okay, so there's this stuff — you know, one thing we also covered that you guys have video agents that you launched. I guess, how does the traditional, let's call it frontier, like autoregressive LLMs — feed in to all this? They're driving your robotics models, or they're driving your video agent production? Anywhere you see the overlap of autoregressive and diffusion, let's call it?

Anastasis: Yeah, so harnesses are really important across all those different use cases. So we have this Video Agent, which is essentially an LLM that is very effective at tool use of different image models, video models, and helps you through creating a project end to end.

So very often in a traditional advertising flow, you have a brief you start from, and then you generate a storyboard, and then you generate the video. A Video Agent — and Runway Agent — kind of helps you through that whole process, and it helps you also analyze performance data. For example: how well did this ad perform versus this ad? And then, generate me more based on those learnings — figure out what to generate.

We think that the harness is a very important piece of the pipeline. As I mentioned, all the production video models use some prompt completion that happens, and we expect that to become more and more complex and — you generate longer and more detailed descriptions before you use the diffusion transformer.

Omni Models — End-to-End Integration

I do think eventually, there's increasingly this unification into omni models, where you're training the models end to end to both do autoregressive text prediction and also diffusion as well. So you're predicting the next token, you may be doing some reasoning and planning of the scene, and then you're passing it into the diffusion head that's actually generating the pixels.

Host: Yeah, I think currently maybe only Gemini and Qwen do it. I'm not sure who — which of the Chinese models are omni — but yeah, it's not a very well popularized modality. I guess it's an interesting use case when you think about it, right? Because not only do you have to end-to-end language model reason, diffusion head generate — you don't have to output there, you can go back into, feed that output to the same model, reason again on improvements, and it can do a lot of loops just on its own. I guess the question is, like: do we need that, or can we just do agent scaffold, like, do it outside the model? Is there a big benefit to doing it in?

Anastasis: I think there's generally the trend of something is first done by a harness and then it becomes part of the model, right? So you had chain-of-thought prompting where you have to do this super detailed system prompts to get back, and now the model basically generates the reasoning trace by itself before it gives you an answer.

And in video models similarly, a lot of the video models of the early days were single-shot video models, and you had to use some kind of orchestrators — generate multiple shots in parallel and then turn it into an actual video.

Host: ComfyUI, just all over the spaghetti workflow.

Anastasis: And now you have multi-shot video generation, where you directly generate multiple shots, and there is a benefit to that. Because then the video model learns — to generate a single shot well, you need obviously to figure out a lot of stuff about the world. To generate multi-shot video well, you also need to basically get some video editing instincts. Like, you need to figure out what is the right pacing of shots.

And also LLMs are not that good at it. Like, they're not that great video editors. If you ask an LLM to take some videos and then auto-create an edited video out of that, it would feel uncanny. So I don't think LLMs are actually that good yet at being video editors. And I think there's benefit to learning that end to end.

So I would expect — you know, the trend in general is: the things that you need a harness for eventually get injected into the model itself, and you learn that end to end.
