item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：Bending Spoons 不是"科技公司"，而是"科技界的银行"
大多数人把 Bending Spoons 归类为"连续收购者"或"科技版伯克希尔"，但真正的隐喻其实是**银行**——他们的核心业务不是造产品，而是**把"僵尸资产"的现金流重新定价**。
传统 PE 做的是财务套利：低价买、砍成本、高价卖。Bending Spoons 做的是**技术套利**：他们建了一套 50+ 的专有"操作系统"，把这套 OS "刷"进任何被收购的公司里，就像银行用同一套核心账务系统处理不同储户的钱。**这套 OS 才是真正的产品，被收购的品牌只是"应用层"**。
这解释了一个非常有趣的悖论：Luca 直言几乎不做"客户侧协同"（AOL 卖 Vimeo 广告之类），但疯狂追求"后台协同"。因为**前者是营销幻觉，后者才是复利机器**。这与传统 conglomerate 的思路完全相反——GE、Berkshire 都强调品牌间的看得见的协同，Bending Spoons 恰恰放弃了这一层，反而胜出。
## 二、跨领域连接：他们复制的其实是"米其林三星厨房"的模式，

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Why AI Progress Keeps Surprising Even Its Researchers - Noam Brown
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"人口方程式"：算力 × 3 的静默复利

Noam Brown 抛出的那个数字——同样的算力每年能跑出 3 倍规模的"有效人口"——远比它听上去更具颠覆性。人们习惯把 AI 进展想象成"模型变聪明"，但他实际上是在讲智能人口的马尔萨斯式爆炸，只不过没有资源上限：因为在这个宇宙里，土地（算力）本身也在指数扩张。

真正意外的地方在于：连他也在保守估计。把 3x/年 的效率提升，与背景中同步指数增长的算力叠加，你得到的不是线性叠加而是指数的指数。这意味着到 2030 年代中期，"每个实验室内部住着好几个地球的人类级智能"不是科幻叙事，而是当前曲线的保守外推。人类历史上从没出现过一个系统，其"公民数量"在同一栋楼里每年翻三倍——这已经不是经济学问题，而是接近相变的物理学问题。

二、预测视界的坍缩：一个来自混沌理论的隐秘信号

最容易被听众滑过、但最应该让人后背发凉的，是那位研究员的一句话："我以前能预测未来 12 个月，现在只敢预测 3 个月。"

这句话的重要性不在字面，而在于它揭示了一个Lyapunov 指数正在上升的动力学系统。在混沌理论中，当一个系统的不稳定性增加，可预测的时间窗口会指数级缩短。研究者的"信心半衰期"从 12 个月压缩到 3 个月——按同样的比率外推，明年可能是 3 周，后年可能是 3 天。

跨领域联想：这与地震前动物的行为异常、心脏病发作前 HRV（心率变异性）的坍塌、金融崩盘前波动率的自相关消失是同一类信号——不是"进展加快"，而是系统正在进入相变前的临界区。Brown 在描述的其实不是速度，而是可预测性本身的解体。

三、下注文化背后的"系统性反向乐观偏差"

那个 Navier-Stokes 的 $1,000 赌局——Frontier Lab 的研究员押 2030 年，Brown 押 2027 年，结果两周后就实现——揭示了一个心理学上少有人命名的现象：

在指数系统内部工作的人，会系统性地低估指数。

这与"人们总是过度乐观"的常识完全相反。原因是：每一次被现实反超，研究者会更新自己的锚点，但更新的幅度总是不足——他们把最近的惊喜当作"异常值"而不是"新趋势线"，然后基于修正过的旧模型再做线性外推。这是贝叶斯更新中的先验刚性（prior stickiness），在指数环境下会累积成灾难性偏差。

最出人意料的推论：这意味着最悲观的 AI 时间线预测者，往往是离得最近的人——不是因为他们看得更清楚，而是因为每天的具体工作让他们看不到复利曲线。就像在飞机内部走动的人感受不到 900 km/h 的速度。真正准确的时间线预测者，可能反而是那些远离前沿、只看积分曲线的外部观察者。

四、隐藏的测量悖论：AI 加速无法被诚实度量

Brown 在讨论"AI 加速研究"时暴露了一个深刻的认识论陷阱： - 问"三年前的任务，今天用 AI 快多少倍"——答案是 100x - 问"今天的任务，没有 AI 会慢多少倍"——答案可能只是 3x

同一个现实，两个数字相差 30 倍。这不是测量误差，而是任务空间本身在被 AI 重塑：你会去做那些 AI 让你能做的事，不做那些它没帮助的事——因此"效率"这个词在指数环境下失去了稳定的分母。

跨领域连接：这正是经济学里困扰了三十年的Solow 悖论（"我们到处都能看到计算机，除了在生产率统计里"）的镜像版。经济学家最终发现，不是计算机没用，而是 GDP 这个度量本身跟不上计算机改造经济结构的速度。今天的 AI 加速也一样——我们没有合适的坐标系去度量一个正在重写自身坐标系的过程。

这或许才是"奇点"最诚实的定义：不是某个具体的时刻，而是我们的测量工具集体失效的那个区域。

📝 转录文本

一、基准情境：即便进展速度不加快，仅仅"维持"就足够眩晕

One thing that's been giving me a bit of singularity vertigo is realizing that even if the current rate of progress simply continues — so it doesn't have to speed up, literally just continues apace — as some of the other headwinds you talked about come up (right? that it's harder to find problems, it's more long-horizon, maybe by the 2030s compute can't keep scaling at this exponential level)… if we simply continue the current rate of progress, I think people are not taking seriously what that implies as we cross over beyond the human horizon.

Here are some of the things that it implies. I think it's really hard to reason about what smarter-than-human intelligences will be like, so let's just think in terms of human population sizes.

The current rate of progress makes it so that a given level of compute allows you to basically run a 3x bigger effective population every single year. And also compute is growing in the background anyway. So you could have a situation where each of the labs — by the end of 2030, probably much sooner, but let's say by the end of 2030 — has enough compute to run, let's say, hundreds of millions of human-level intelligences, based on where the capabilities will be at that point.

And then I think people are not taking seriously: the current level of progress means that a few years down the line, by the mid-2030s or earlier, you would have many Earths' worth of human-level intelligences within each lab — and they'll probably be qualitatively superhuman. But anyway, this is like a base case, I don't know.

Yeah, progress is really fast.

二、研究者自己也在被反复"打脸"：IMO 金牌与 Navier–Stokes 的赌局

And I think that's 100% true. It's worth pointing out: researchers are continually being surprised at the rate of progress.

If you look at what — even among researchers in AI — what were the projections for getting an IMO Gold in 2025? The idea that it could be done with a general-purpose language model, with no tools and no access to the internet — I think even people at OpenAI thought this was outrageous. They thought it was almost impossible.

And then you get to 2026, and literally two weeks before we got Navier–Stokes, I was talking with a researcher at a Frontier Lab about how long it would take to get a Millennium Prize. He was willing to bet me $1,000 that it would take past 2027 — he thought it would take until 2030. And I took that bet. But even I thought it would take longer than how long it's likely to take.

So people have been continuously surprised, even inside the labs.

三、预测窗口的塌缩：从 12 个月到 3 个月

I was literally just talking to somebody yesterday who was working on the Navier–Stokes effort, and he was telling me that he used to say it's really hard to predict where AI would be in 12 months — if somebody asked him, "oh, where are things going?", he would feel comfortable making predictions for the next 12 months, but beyond that, you know, he's just like "I don't know."

And now he's saying he just doesn't feel comfortable making predictions beyond 3 months.

So it is really true that things are going very fast right now.

Yeah.

And you talk about 2030 — like, I don't know what the world looks like in 2030.

That's the truth.

四、AI 劳动的全面自动化？内部加速与 Codex 支出

Yeah. Do you expect the sort of full automation of AI labor — or let's say 95% automation of AI labor — '28, '29, '30, '27?

I don't know. I just said I don't know what the world looks like in 2030.

I mean, we actually released a blog post recently on internal acceleration at OpenAI. We show, for example, that the amount that researchers are spending on Codex is — the top 1%, I think as of early August, were spending like $7,000 or $8,000 a day on Codex for internal use. That's on an exponential. It's going to keep increasing.

五、归因难题：人做的，还是 AI 做的？

And there's a question of: okay, if that keeps going, then how much do you assign to just the AI doing work versus the humans doing work? Is it 95%? Is it 5%?

It's actually really hard to reason about this for a few reasons.

First of all, if it's the human directing the AIs to do the work, then how much do you attribute to the human? How much do you attribute to the AI?

The other thing is that these AIs are jagged — they're exceptionally good at some things. For example, they're exceptionally good at looking over datasets and checking every single data point to see: is this of sufficient quality? You can disproportionately use the AIs for those things compared to previously. So yes, you're using AI way more than before, and it's making some things go 100x faster and 100x better. But there are some things where it doesn't make a huge difference yet.

And of course, if something is suddenly 100x faster and 100x better, you're going to do more of that thing.

六、测量的悖论：两种"加速"是两个完全不同的问题

So, are you comparing to a speed-up of like three years ago — versus, is the question more like: given what we were doing three years ago, how much faster are we able to do it now, versus given what we're doing now, how much slower would it have been three years ago?

These are actually two very different questions. So, anyway, it's really hard to measure.

I do feel confident in saying that things are going faster now than they were even a year ago because of AI progress, and I think that acceleration will continue. A lot of people in the field have very high error bars on this sort of thing.

七、如果非要给一个数字：3x 加速的震撼含义

If you had to put a gun to my head and ask me for a number — I could see things going 3x faster.

Yeah.

And that is huge, right? Already the pace of progress is incredible. Even if we don't get any uplift — like you said, things are going to go much faster by the time we get to 2030. We don't even know what that world looks like.

I think if we get a 3x uplift from internal acceleration, that is massive. Like, right now we're releasing — think about where we were three years ago. If we make that progress in one year, that's huge.

Right.

It'd be like going from not even having o1 — just having non-reasoning models — to Astra.

Yeah. In a single year.

Yeah, yeah.

八、不确定性本身的形状

So I do think things go faster. It could be that things only go 50% faster. It could be — I think it's unlikely, but it's possible — that things go 10x faster. There's a lot of uncertainty around this, and at least from my perspective, I have a lot of uncertainty about it.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

观看原视频 →

## 一、被忽视的"人口方程式"：算力 × 3 的静默复利
Noam Brown 抛出的那个数字——**同样的算力每年能跑出 3 倍规模的"有效人口"**——远比它听上去更具颠覆性。人们习惯把 AI 进展想象成"模型变聪明"，但他实际上是在讲**智能人口的马尔萨斯式爆炸，只不过没有资源上限**：因为在这个宇宙里，土地（算力）本身也在指数扩张。
真正意外的地方在于：*连他也在保守估计*。把 3x/年 的效率提升，与背景中同步指数增长的算力叠加，你得到的不是线性叠加而是**指数的指数**。这意味着到 2030 年代中期，"每个实验室内部住着好几个地球的人类级智能"不是科幻叙事，而是当前曲线的**保守外推**。人类历史上从没出现过一个系统，其"公民数量"在**同一栋楼里**每年翻三倍——这已经不是经济学问题，而是接近相变的**物理学**问题。

item.title: [GoldRepublic Global] Luke Gromen: 53 Countries Defaulted at This Debt Level — We're Next
item.dc:creator: GoldRepublic Global
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"两个方向都通向同一个悬崖"——货币政策的量子叠加态

Gromen 最反直觉的判断，其实是把美联储放到了一个逻辑陷阱里：加息和降息都是通胀性的。这不是政策失误，而是系统的相变（phase transition）。想想水在 100°C 时的状态——加一点热量它变成蒸汽，减一点热量它凝成液体，但在临界点上，"加"与"减"的方向已经不再决定结果，能量密度本身才是。

美联储现在正站在这个临界点上：降息 → 美元贬值 → 大宗商品飙升 → 通胀回来；加息 → 政府利息支出爆炸 → 财政赤字加剧 → 财政主导地位 → 通胀回来。这不是货币现象，是财政引力场把货币政策吸走了。这就是为什么 Gromen 说"美联储比人们意识到的更被逼入死角"——他描述的其实是一个决策变量已经从系统中消失的状态。

二、意想不到的观察：Bitcoin 是煤矿里的金丝雀，而黄金是煤矿本身

大多数分析师把 Bitcoin 和黄金当作同一交易的两个表达（debasement trade）。但 Gromen 埋了一个非常精妙的层次结构：Bitcoin 是先行指标，黄金是终局资产。

这在信息论上非常优雅。Bitcoin 的流动性更薄、波动性更高、投机成分更浓——正因为如此，它对边际资金流入反应速度最快。而黄金是被央行、主权基金、传统资本压舱的"深水层"，反应慢但代表结构性再定价。

跨领域连接：这跟神经科学中的"预激活神经元"一模一样——大脑决策前 200 毫秒，某些边缘神经元会先放电，虽然这些放电不构成决定本身，但它们的模式提前泄露了决定的方向。Bitcoin 就是宏观系统的预激活神经元。如果你想观察黄金的下一波结构性上涨，不要看黄金——看 Bitcoin 何时脱钩于纳斯达克，重新与实物资产同步。

三、"我宁愿仓库里有铜，也不要银行里有现金"——这句话本身就是历史信号

这句话不是投资建议，是恶性通胀的语言学化石。Gromen 特别提到："每一次世界上的恶性通胀，都是从人们开始说这种话开始的。"

这里藏着一个社会学的相变机制：当足够多的人从"资金 → 资产"的心智模式，切换到"资产 → 资金"的心智模式时，货币的社会契约层就崩塌了。魏玛德国、津巴布韦、委内瑞拉，甚至最近的土耳其，都遵循同样的语言学序列：先是精英开始持有实物（铜、铁、房、金），然后中产模仿，然后普通人恐慌性抢购日用品。

跨领域连接：这跟生态学里的"营养级联崩溃"（trophic cascade）完全同构。当顶级捕食者（在这里是"对法币的信任"）从生态系统消失，整个食物网不是缓慢退化，而是几周内重构。Gromen 说"不是几年，甚至不是几个季度，而是几个月"——他其实是在描述一个营养级联的倒计时。

四、最容易被忽略的隐藏结构：债券市场"挤进"黄金市场的物理不可能性

"You're going to see gold rise because basically the bond market is going to try to fit itself into the gold market."——这句话值得反复咀嚼。

全球债券市场规模约 130 万亿美元，黄金市场（可投资部分）约 15-20 万亿美元。当哪怕 5% 的债券资金试图"迁移"到黄金——那是 6.5 万亿美元冲击一个能吸收几千亿的市场。这在数学上不是"上涨"，是"重估"。

物理类比：这就像把大西洋的水通过一根花园水管排空。水管不会"流得更快"——水管会爆裂。所谓黄金"暴涨到 5000/10000 美元"，不是黄金变贵了，是债券作为财富储存工具的功能性失效被市场瞬间定价。

真正的启示不是买黄金，而是：任何依赖债券作为"无风险抵押品"的金融结构（回购市场、保险公司准备金、养老金匹配、银行资本充足率），都在一个正在消失的地基上运行。这才是 Gromen 说的"53 个国家在这个债务水平违约"的深层意义——违约不是事件，是抵押品消失的必然算术。

📝 转录文本

开场：核心观点速览

Both Fed cuts and Fed rate hikes are inflationary at this point. Doesn't matter what they do. The next recession, we're saying yields are going up in the long end. Maybe they'll go down for like one little second, but they're gonna scream higher.

I would rather have copper in my warehouse than cash in my bank. That's how every hyperinflation in the world has ever started. That's what people say at the beginning of hyperinflation.

You're gonna see gold rise because basically... you're going to see gold rise because basically the bond market is going to try to fit itself into the gold market. And by the way, I think probably one of your early indicators will be Bitcoin.

We're not talking about years. We're probably not talking about quarters. We're probably talking about months until that tipping point is reached. I think the debasement trade is back on, which makes me want to buy gold, Bitcoin, silver.

主持人介绍与欢迎

Welcome to the Macroscopic Podcast. My name is Alex... Welcome to the Macroscopic Podcast. My name is Alexei Joronoff and I'm the host, and this is presented by Gold Republic. And today I have the extreme pleasure and honor to welcome on this podcast Luke Gromen.

Welcome, Luke.

Thanks for having me here, Alexei. It's great to be here. It's great to finally catch up.

It is. As I told you already before, I've been following you since years, and I think you've definitely been one of my top macro analysts out there. Lyn Alden and you... Lyn Alden and you were actually one of the people I followed the most back then five, six years ago, when I started really digging deeper into this journey of trying to understand this very complex monetary system.

第一问：最"异端"的货币观点

And one of the first questions I ask the guests who appear for the first time on my podcast is the following: what is your most heretical view on the monetary system? And this might be a bit of an easy one for you.

I think my most heretical view... well, view on the monetary system is that both Fed cuts and Fed rate hikes are inflationary — on the monetary system, is that at this point, doesn't matter what they do. They are, they are much more cornered than people realize. And I think that is very much a variant perception.

追问：为什么方向已经不再重要

Why does it not matter if the Fed hikes rates or cuts rates — in this case, Warsh, who was supposed to actually cut rates for his president? It's, uh, for his, uh, for his president... um, why does it matter?

Because if you cut rates with inflation above target...

item.title: [a16z] Replit CEO Amjad Masad on What Young People Should Learn in the AI Era
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个让人意外的观察

1. "毛刺人"（The Glitch Person）作为文明的免疫系统

Amjad 引用《城市与星辰》的隐喻表面是在说"叛逆青年很珍贵"，但更深的洞察是：一个高度优化的系统必须依赖故障来更新自己。这与生物学中的"体细胞超突变"（somatic hypermutation）惊人相似——免疫系统故意在B细胞的抗体基因区制造错误，以生成能识别未知病原的抗体。也就是说，进化从不奖励精确复制，进化奖励可控的错误。今天的大学是一个"高保真复制系统"——它太擅长把 18 岁的人复印成"合格公民"，因此它正在制造一个没有免疫力的文明。Peter Thiel 奖学金、Replit Academy 这些实验的真正意义不是"造更多创业者"，而是给社会补充"故意的错误率"。

2. Replit CEO 谈教育，却泄露了他对"公司"的秘密判断

注意他中段突然插入的一句："the future of companies is going to change... the company will run itself... a self-driving company." 这句话表面上是跑题，但如果你把它和整段对话叠加看，会发现一个惊人的对称：他对未来"学校"的设想（无年级、无考勤、以兴趣为绳、AI 提供个性化路径）几乎就是他对未来"公司"的设想。也就是说 —— 他不是在设计一所学校，他是在为自己未来的自驾公司训练第一批操作系统兼容的员工。Academy 是 Replit 的用户获取漏斗的最上游，同时也是"新型组织形态"的 alpha 测试。学校即产品原型。跨界连接：这是硅谷版本的"耶稣会学院"——16 世纪耶稣会通过办学校，把自己的世界观装进未来精英的操作系统。

3. "过早优化"这一编程术语被他用来批判 VC，其实指向了一个更黑的真相

他把过早融资比作"premature optimization is the root of all evil"，又把它类比为音乐产业的剥削性合约——这已经很尖锐了。但更深一层的意外是：当资本能够以极低成本"预订"一个年轻人的十年，它本质上在做的是"人生期权的贱卖套利"。就像高频交易之于股票——市场深度不足的地方，越先出手的人赚得越狠。18 岁人生"深度不足"（他还没搞清楚自己是谁），所以任何一个提前锁仓的资本方都在做认知不对称套利。这解释了一个悖论：为什么"YC 给 50 万"和"斯坦福给一门课"其实都是同一种东西的两个变种——两者都在贴现你未成型的自我，只是一个用金钱贴现，一个用学分贴现。真正稀缺、真正未被制度化的，是他反复强调的那个"中间地带"：不承诺、不打分、不锁仓的两年。

一个隐藏的系统性真相

整场对话里 Amjad 从"要做异端"讲到"要respect the elders"，从"disagreeable"讲到"interpersonal skills"，看起来在自我矛盾。但如果把这些放在一个坐标里看——他其实描述的是创业者的"张力管理"：一个人身上必须同时住着两个不兼容的人格（Julian Jaynes 会说这是二分脑的现代版）。这和顶级围棋手、顶级即兴爵士乐手的特征是同构的——在结构里保持自由，在自由里维持结构。真正稀缺的不是叛逆，也不是服从，而是能在两者之间高频切换的"元灵活性"。这也解释了为什么他强调"discernment 只能通过 reps 获得"——因为你不能被教会切换，你只能通过反复失败学会切换的时机。这就是他真正想构建的教育：一个允许你以低代价练习切换的道场。

📝 转录文本

开场：年轻人的真正效用

Ultimately, the utility of young people is to question deeply held beliefs, is to be heretics. And in today's college, it actually the opposite. It kind of beats any outside thought out of them. I just really want to see a world in which it's okay if you want to go on a side quest and go do something that's kind of oddball, but also might end up being super amazing if it works out.

The future of companies is going to change. The whole industry has changed. It's a complete reset on a technology perspective. I'd want to go to a college that's not prescriptive about what I learn. I'm motivated by what skills can it give me in order to achieve what I want to build. One of the core tenants of the academy sidesteps this problem entirely. We don't care if you graduate or not. We don't have grades. We don't have tests. The amount of weight to push against should be a lot less.

When you see a 18-year-old that is really inspiring to you that you're like, I got to spend time with this person. What are they doing that is capturing your interest?

《城市与星辰》：一个关于"毛刺人"的寓言

I think the first thing is that they — as we were talking — uh I remember this sci-fi story that I read once. It's called The City and the Stars, and it's about this future city that's governed by AGI. We sort of invented AGI. It's now governs all of our lives. It solves all all problems, all human problems. There's no wars, there's no disease, everyone lives forever, and people spend their time working on like a thousand-year art projects and doing all sorts of random things to fill up their time.

But they found this problem where they accumulate so much knowledge and memory it becomes like harder to keep it all in their heads. So they invented this technology where they go into some kind of laboratory and they compress their memory — sort of like context compression that we do with AI today. They go through all the memories and they compress them, and then they go through a boot camp to retrain them for their life. So they invented a new way to be born. But it's not — you're not fundamentally a new person. You're still the same person. You're just editing your memory.

But there's a glitch that happens in this system, in this machine, and there's a new person that is fundamentally born new. And he immediately starts causing problems. In the boot camp he starts doing weird things, new things, and everyone's like, "Whoa, that's crazy. You shouldn't be doing that. That's not how we do things." It becomes very disruptive.

And then when they go out into this like city, he starts asking questions like, "What's out there? What's in the stars? What's outside our city borders?" They're like, "We don't talk about outside our city borders."

Sounds like Silo a little bit. "It's probably dangerous out there." Yeah. A little bit like Silo. A little bit like Fallout.

Um, and I don't want to get into the spoilers too much, but eventually — that's what he has — so much drive to change things and go discover the stars. That's why it's called The City and the Stars. The story unfolds in that way and he finds all sorts of interesting things out there.

大学的真问题：它把年轻人变成了什么

And I'm reminded of this because as we're talking about what is college and what is it for, I think a related question is: what is the utility of young people in society? And I think ultimately the utility of young people is to question deeply held beliefs, is to be heretics.

And in today's college it's actually the opposite. It kind of beats any outside thought out of them, right? It tells you you're stupid. We've figured everything out. You need to learn our way, and we need to prepare you for the outside world so you can get a job and be a perfect citizen and go get married, have kids, and get a house and a car and live happily ever after. That world doesn't exist anymore. You can do really well in college and you can still be unemployed with a huge debt.

But not only that, I think the real civilizational missing opportunity is that person in The City and the Stars. It took a glitch to get someone with a clear mind to be able to question deeply held beliefs. And every one of us — we probably have blind spots in society. We have a lot of blind spots in Silicon Valley. There's a lot of ideas that don't come out of Silicon Valley, because there's a monoculture here. There's a certain way of thinking. Every culture is somehow a monoculture. Even the most radical cultures like Silicon Valley.

And so what do you need from young people? You need them to experiment. You need to encourage them to try impossible things. And every now and then they're going to have a breakthrough that once we thought was impossible and now it's suddenly possible because the technology changed, something changed. So college ultimately should be about that. Let's get these people with clear minds, zen mindsets, first-principles mindsets, and encourage them to go question the deeply held beliefs.

如果你 18 岁：理想中的大学

No, I think that's well said. I mean, imagine if you were 18 today and you were able to design your ideal experience — in terms of how much you go to class, to what projects you work on, to what kind of deep study you would engage in, to what you'd want to study. What are some principles that you would add to that, in terms of how you wish, if you could redo 18 to 22, but in 2026, how you'd think about it.

Yeah. I'd want to go to a college that's not prescriptive about what I learn. I want to be in an environment where there's a lot of different paths — like, there's a class about something totally I haven't even thought about, it's outside my world.

乔布斯的书法课

Right. We're talking about the story with Steve Jobs. One of the most inspiring speeches he gave is the Stanford commencement speech, and he talked about connecting things backwards. And so the way Steve Jobs approached college, I think it's the ideal experience of college — where he went to Reed College but he couldn't afford it, so he dropped out but kept dropping into different classes. One of them was calligraphy.

And in the calligraphy class he didn't know why he was interested in it, and he just did it and learned it. Later on when they were inventing the Mac and inventing user interfaces, they're like, "Oh, we should have proportionally spaced fonts, we should have — people should be able to select fonts." And that was a direct callback to his college days learning about fonts and calligraphy.

And so this meandering that I think modern society thinks is sort of useless — I think it's actually the most useful in college. Totally. Yeah. I think it's both not being afraid to spike in something — like a lot of people just show up because they're too broad and not really amazing at anything. Follow that to its conclusion, see how good you can get at it. While also having a baseline of interpersonal skills, or just being — the right beable.

Yeah. Be likable — and in a way that's not contrived or fake. Just truly authentic. Because people want to support people who are good people. But the most endearing thing is: you can nerd out on something obscure and interesting.

Totally. Yeah. Awesome job. Thanks for — Thank you so much. Thanks for having me.

item.title: [Latent Space] 🔬Bio-security is an AI Arms Race - Eric Nguyen (CEO, Radical Numerics)
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的洞察：进攻方即最佳防守方——"双重使命"背后的深层结构对称性

Eric 提出的最关键的哲学转折不在于"我们要做生物安全"，而在于一句几乎被顺口带过的话："一个擅长生成的模型，也天然擅长判别一个序列是否致病。"

这不是一句公关话术，而是一个深刻的信息论对称性。语言模型的生成 = 概率密度估计，判别 = 同一个密度函数的另一种查询方式。它意味着：在 DNA 空间中，攻防不是两种不同的技术，而是同一个数学对象的两次读取。

这带来一个惊人的推论：Radical Numerics 事实上是把自己变成了 AI 时代的"核武器扩散管制局"的技术底座——因为其他任何试图追赶其防御能力的机构，都必须先追上其进攻能力。这是一种通过技术不对称建立的、隐蔽的准公共治理权。听起来像 OpenAI 的"我们必须走在前面才能保证安全"叙事——但在生物领域，这个叙事第一次拥有了严格数学根据，因为在 NLP 里"更强模型 = 更安全"从未被证明，而在序列空间里生成器与鉴别器共享权重是结构性事实。

二、跨领域连接：这不是"AI + 生物"，这是 压缩理论 × 演化论 × 密码学 的三体缠绕

一个被 Eric 一笔带过、但极具颠覆性的暗线是：DNA 是物理世界压缩进化学空间的"log 文件"。他说 "genome is the imprint of the physical world into DNA"。这句话如果沿着信息论展开：

  • 演化 ≈ 数十亿年的随机梯度下降，损失函数是"能否留下后代"，训练数据是整个物理宇宙。
  • 基因组 = 该 SGD 的模型权重快照。
  • 预训练 GLM 就是在解压这份权重——不是在学 DNA 的语法，而是在学物理世界通过生物筛选后残留的规则。

这解释了 RNA 适配体链式思维那个让 RJ 意外的结果：模型从未见过 RNA 二级结构，为什么能沿着适应度轨迹外推？因为它学的从来不是 RNA，而是"什么样的序列演化会走向更优"这种元规则——一种从 DNA 学到的、跨模态可迁移的演化动力学先验。

更疯狂的类比：这与密码学中的可延展性攻击 (malleability) 惊人相似。Microsoft 的 "paraphrases" 工作证明你可以在保持功能的同时改写序列——这本质上是同态加密的生物学版本：功能不变、密文形式任意。这意味着生物防御体系正在被迫从"字符串匹配"升级为"功能语义匹配"，就像密码学从 MD5 升级到语义等价性验证一样。Radical 正在做的是 DNA 空间的"函数指纹识别"。

三、最容易被忽略但也最重要的一点："专家的悲观主义"是这个领域最大的隐形债务

Eric 在最后回答"想移除什么瓶颈"时，第一个说 GPU（他自己都笑称是套话），第二个说的东西才是真正的信号："越是领域专家，越倾向于对这个领域悲观。"

这句话表面平淡，实则藏着一个跨越所有学科的元规律——我称之为 "熟练度陷阱 (Expertise Trap)"：

  • 每个领域的资深从业者被训练来识别"为什么某件事不可行"，因为这是防止犯错的最优策略。
  • 但颠覆性突破恰好来自"应该不可行"的方向——这也是为什么 CRISPR、AlphaFold、mRNA 疫苗几乎都由领域边缘的人推动。
  • Eric 自己是最好的例子：他花六个月在斯坦福被几乎每一位生物学家告知"生成 DNA 是愚蠢的想法"，然后他做出了 Evo。

这与 Thomas Kuhn 的"科学革命结构"、与硅谷 VC 的"contrarian and right"、与围棋 AlphaGo 走出人类三千年从未考虑过的第 37 手，是同一个现象在不同层面的表达。

一个出人意料的推论：AI 之所以在生物学上突破如此之快，恰恰因为 AI 研究者不具备生物学家的悲观性先验。他们没有被教过"什么不可能"，所以他们做了不可能的事。这也预示着：未来 5 年生物学最大的突破，可能不会来自生物学家，而来自那些"知道足够多以理解问题，但不知道足够多以放弃"的杂交者。

Radical Numerics 的招聘哲学——"领域专家 + 仍是梦想家 (still dreamers)"——本质上是在系统性地筛选具有"反熟练度陷阱"免疫力的人。这是一种极其罕见的组织设计。

四、一个额外的、我忍不住要指出的模式

注意 Eric 反复回避回答的一个技术问题：Omni 是自回归的、扩散的还是别的？他说"我们不把自己绑定在特定训练目标上，我们用工具箱里的每一个工具。"

这句话在 AI 语境下听起来像常规发言，但在生物学语境下是革命性的——因为整个现代生物学的方法论根基就是"控制变量、单一机制、可复现"。Radical 的姿态是："我们不在乎机制的纯洁性，只在乎能力涌现。"

这实际上是把工程学的兼容主义 (methodological pluralism) 移植到生物学——一个被"分子生物学中心法则"训练了 70 年的领域。如果这种方法论真的在生物领域取得压倒性成功，它可能会从根本上重塑生物学作为一门科学的自我认知：从"追求机制理解"转向"追求可预测的操控"。这是库恩式的范式转移前夜的味道。

📝 转录文本

🔬 Bio-security is an AI Arms Race — Eric Nguyen (CEO, Radical Numerics)

Channel: Latent Space

Cold Open — The Arms Race Framing

"The design side is going to get more capable. The defensive side needs to try to get ahead. So I think inherently there is this arms race style dynamic that the defensive side has been far, far lagging. And so what we want to do is bring the defensive side to par essentially.

We felt it was important as a lab that a team that was both building the design capabilities is actually also best suited for building the defense capabilities — because they're basically the same models. A model that is good at generating turns out is also very good at discriminating or predicting if a sequence is pathogenic or not.

For us, we as a company thought it was very important to have a dual mandate. It's this idea of essentially being cognizant and feeling responsible for the capabilities that we're enabling on the design side. So if we're going to create models that can design function into sequences, we believe and see a gap in companies being able to safeguard that technology."

Introductions

Welcome to Latent Space. I'm Brandon. I build RNA therapeutics at Atomic AI. I'm joined by my co-host RJ Honake, CTO and co-founder of Miraomics. Today, it's a pleasure to have with us Eric Nguyen, CEO and co-founder of Radical Numerics.

Eric got his PhD in Chris Ré's group. He spent a lot of time thinking about how to do long-context genomic models before long-context or genomic models were cool. He was the first author and I think basically visionary behind the Evo generative model — one of the first generative genomics platforms — developed Evo 2, which naturally led into Radical Numerics.

Thank you for being here. Did I miss anything?

That sounds great. Cool. (Laughter) Welcome. Thank you.

What Is a Genomic Language Model?

So Eric, let's talk about Omni and the blog posts that you guys did about the benchmarking. But I want to hear first — OK, what is a genetic language model? Why do I care? What does it do? And then let's talk about the top-line results from the blog post.

So a genome language model, or GLM, is a large language model trained on DNA sequences. So very much like natural language and chatbots you see, but not trained on words or natural language — but on the raw fabric of life, which is these sequences of letters that make up DNA.

We ourselves — our company, our team — is known for creating the first generative genomics models, which are models trained on DNA not just to read, but also write, meaning able to generate new sequences of DNA. And we felt this was an area that was overlooked, and that if AI could read and write DNA, it could change a lot — you know, science of discovery and understanding of human health and how to treat it. And so we felt that it was a big opportunity to train AI on the genome.

What can you do with a model like this?

Great to start. For us, when we first started working on DNA models, we worked on this model called Hyena DNA, which is a large language model, but it used a convolution instead of attention. A little more technical detail: DNA has this property that, well, it's very long. At the time, these large language models had limited constraints on context — being able to fit long sequences. And so we were looking for a more efficient algorithm to be able to handle something like DNA.

And so we came up with this what we call the Hyena operator — uses convolutions. Long story short, it let us process longer sequences, in this case up to a million, and at the time was the largest context for a language model. And what we did with it was essentially used it to read DNA, predict function. So given a sequence of DNA, string of characters, we predict its regulatory function, its effect on a genome.

And this is interesting to scientists because a lot of the DNA in our bodies — perhaps people are less aware — but actually we don't know that much about our genome. We know it obviously encodes the information for making us us and all the different complexities and potential diseases. At the same time, the grammar rules about how the combination of those letters are sort of formed — what they encode, function and traits — is not fully understood.

And so the hope was using these DNA models, language models, to be able to map some function from the raw DNA sequence. And so our first-generation models were able to show that yes, we can train AI to be able to read and understand, to some degree, DNA sequences — and especially what we call the longer-range interactions, meaning over sequences. If you use chatbots, for example, if you've heard the phrase "context rot" — the longer the input you put into a language model, it starts to deteriorate.

And so being able to pick up long-range information and sort of patterns, motifs, grammar over long sequences was what we were trying to accomplish. And so we showcased in that first generation of Hyena DNA that that was possible over a million context.

Evo — From Reading to Writing DNA

And then really what started the field now known as generative genomics was the model called Evo. And Evo, we should try to showcase, there was this idea of not just reading DNA, but being able to generate it. And so we wanted to accelerate essentially how biologists and scientists have learned from biology, and particularly genomics.

And we felt like this whole field of generative AI being applied to language — great, accelerated, obviously, our understanding and ability to manipulate the natural language. But here's this other language — DNA in the genome — that we don't understand. And it's barely being applied with AI. In our pit at the time, a few years ago, models that we saw were really small, short context — so they can only pick up small patterns and limited context. And none of them generated DNA. So they all just would read.

And we felt that the idea of generation was so powerful and transformative in natural language — what if we could bring that to biology, and DNA in particular?

What does generation unlock?

What can you accomplish that you can't do in a lab? What does that unlock for you if you could do that very well?

I think one of the first things that we showcased that got folks sort of intrigued by the potential of this was a CRISPR-Cas system — it's an enzyme that's able to cut DNA itself.

And I think what was particularly enabled by the Evo models was the ability to generate over not just one modality or one type of sequence, but spanning multiple modalities and spanning multiple scales. So CRISPR-Cas — it's a molecule made up of both RNA and proteins. And so at the time you hadn't really seen models that can generate multiple modalities. They had protein language models that can generate proteins; sometimes you had RNA models that can generate RNA — but you didn't have a single system to sort of co-design.

We showcased that a single DNA model — sort of the foundation of both of those (from DNA you can get RNA and proteins) — that you can design a single system to generate and also function in the real world. So we asked Evo — we showcased it a bunch of natural CRISPR-Cas systems and essentially asked it: can you make a new one? And we were able to sample from that model that we trained. And indeed we showcased that Evo was able to discover a new CRISPR-Cas system.

And folks were intrigued by it — cover of Science Magazine. And later I got to give a TED talk about the work, which is interesting because obviously the audience is very general, and so trying to make: what is CRISPR-Cas system? What is DNA and how do you generate it? Why would you generate it? All sorts of fun topics.

The First AI-Designed Genome

And I think the even more intriguing, exciting thing that scientists — eventually just last year — showcased what you can do with a generative DNA model was to generate the first genome from scratch using AI.

So this is something not possible by humans. Humans usually, you can think of it like copy and paste parts of other genomes or other DNA, put it into something else — but they would just take out small motifs that they know the function and they understand the rules. But to build something from scratch, from the ground up, had not been done before at the genome level.

And so Evo turns out was able to generate a functional genome. And in this case, it was known as a bacteriophage, also known as a virus.

And this was a key turning point for, I think, the scientific community and for us as a company, Radical Numerics — because we felt this was such an indicative manifestation to create a whole organism, not existing in nature, but also the potential harm that that means as well. If you can control, if you can manipulate the fabric of life itself, control its function — what kind of implications does that mean? What are you enabling into the world?

And so we actually got a lot of feedback, a lot of comments, a lot of outreach from folks — both excited and concerned about this kind of capability and just the trajectory. This is the early stages, the first thing one can sort of project and imagine what this could lead to.

The Dual Mandate: Design AND Defense

And so we felt as a company it was important to not only push on the biological design capabilities of these models, but also the ability to use them as defensive tools for the potential of misuse and biological risk that emerges.

And I think indeed a lot of companies, a lot of frontier labs are also being concerned about this emerging risk — AI models being capable of designing biological sequences. And at the same time, it's being mostly attacked from like a natural language standpoint, like safeguards. And things like Claude — if you talk about viruses, it'll just like shut you down, which is great. I think to some degree you need safeguards at the natural language level. But I think what you also need clearly is safeguards at the biological sequence level too.

So you need models that not just can understand language, the trajectory of your chat, but to understand the substrate itself. That's the next step and ultimate limit. If you can have models that can understand if the sequence is pathogenic or virus, that's the level of defensive capabilities that you want.

And then being able to push that out into surveillance systems, national security — of being able to monitor emerging sequences in environment — this is what that kind of capability makes possible. And then we think bringing this frontier technology to that community as well is also important, just as important as using this for human health, which is what we primarily focus on.

From Evo to Omni — Alignment and Post-Training for DNA

There was this evolution — Hyena DNA, then Evo, Evo2, and now Omni. Can you talk about how Evo/Evo2 struggled to beat specialized models across many tasks, whereas Omni is actually able to outperform them now?

So yeah, Evo was intriguing to folks in many ways — showcased the potential for applying to multiple types of modalities. But it still in many ways underperformed sort of the specialist DNA models, especially on human genomics. And so although Evo was competitive, it still wasn't state of the art or kind of pushing the needle. And so some parts of the community thought like, why use a giant LLM when I can use these smaller, more specialized models?

And so what we wanted to do with Omni was, amongst many things, but one of the first things was to showcase this idea of mid-training and post-training, or broadly alignment.

So the way we think about language models in bio and genomics in particular is that mostly we've only seen base models trained. So they're pre-trained, but they're basically unaligned. So in the analogous space for natural language: it's like you're doing all the pre-training, but to make it actually useful in the real world and answer questions that users actually want — and that it is in the form factor they find actually informative — there's a bunch of alignment and post-training and mid-training done to get the models to be production-ready and actually useful.

And so we felt Evo was just showcasing the potential of that pre-training, but Omni is a step of actually making it useful for folks like scientists. And so we spent a lot of time on alignment and mid- and post-training — which is essentially showcasing tasks in the form that people generally would want to understand about genomics.

Given a wild-type and a mutation sequence: help me find the causal variant. These types of questions and form factors for how you might want to analyze genomics doesn't just emerge necessarily easily on its own from pre-training. Pre-training is this next-token prediction task or infilling. And basically I think of it as like the raw pattern-making ability that you're teaching it is in the pre-training. But then taking those learned embeddings or features and pointing at specific tasks — or a bunch of tasks really — and aligning it, meaning having it show you the output in a way that's meaningful to you, takes a little bit of teasing and manipulating.

That so far — like the frontier natural-language labs are the ones that drive that research in the natural-language community. And so we wanted to bring a lot of that research and more to genomics.

An unexpected preview

And so I think Omni is really just a preview to showcase that potential. And I think once you do that, even just a little bit, we were surprised that it did start being state of the art and pushing the boundaries — not just being effective at multiple tasks just broadly like Evo was, but actually pushing the frontier of each of those areas: variant effects prediction, causal mutations for disease — it could start actually being useful for human genomics.

And so we're really excited to share that with folks. And it was just a preview in that sense because we were still actively training and incorporating additional techniques into the model, like additional modalities. But I think we were basically too excited and we wanted to get this in the hands of folks faster.

And some of the feedback we got, in early interest: lots of hospital systems, nonprofits that have tons of genetic data. For example, they know there's some kind of condition or symptom for the patient, but they can't figure out which parts of the DNA are causing it. So they've got these VUSs — variants of unknown significance — that we're extremely excited to apply these models to and actually help diagnose a lot of these patients. That is one example of a real-use application.

What Does "Alignment" Mean for a Genomic Model?

I'd like to talk more about applications in a bit, but I'm curious just from a technical standpoint — what does it look like to align a genomics model? With LLMs there's chain-of-thought, RL, a clear paradigm. What does that look like for a genomic model?

Yeah, I mean, I think in many ways one could describe it as fine-tuning, but then introducing — I'd say — sort of the key components are the right structure of the inputs. So feeding them in a certain sequence so that the model is aware that a certain task is being asked of it.

So there's a mix of special tokens: you can think of it as, if you're gonna do disease prediction for disease A, expect this special token. Just kind of like a way to prompt it. If you expect it to do design, have another special token. And then showcase the examples, kind of like in a chain-of-thought manner, meaning showcase a sequence of desired outputs and the trajectory of it.

This is a little vague, sort of intentionally, because it's part of our secret sauce that we're still developing. And I think over time we wanna showcase more and more of it.

But in many ways it does mimic a lot of the natural-language community. A lot of it is fine-tuning, but really it's also carving out specific datasets that we want it to focus on and then structuring the questions or tasks in specific ways — as opposed to pre-training. Pre-training is really just feeding it in everything, and really and just doing next-token prediction or mask infilling if you're doing masked-image modeling. And it has no sense of like this Q&A type structure where you have a question, a prompt, and then an output.

And you could think of mid- and post-training as starting to showcase: given this type of input, I expect this type of output — whether it's score, prediction score, or design. That is largely the mid- and post-training. And post-training also includes things like reinforcement learning too. But I think the bigger steps are introducing structure of like question and answering.

Multi-head vs. unified models

Do the models have multiple heads that are task-specific, or are you training one set of heads that can answer multiple questions?

Yeah, broadly — I think we're flexible on this. Sometimes you can use different heads, but the idea for us is to unify more so. And so I think in early experiments we did have different heads. In some cases the different heads do better; in some cases a unified single head, a single model does better. And so I think we're flexible on that. But I think broadly the direction that we are moving toward is a single.

And the reason for a special motivation for that is that we're trying to unlock a lot of generalization. And I think the more unifying we're able to make these models, I think that's when you see more emerging capabilities happen.

And in large part, that's what motivated the DNA work. We felt like a lot of models were specialized into other modalities, a little more downstream from DNA — so like RNA or proteins or molecules. We largely felt DNA is the foundation and that from DNA you can learn a good deal of other modalities, potentially all of them. And I think other modalities is a sort of like additional context that you're showing the model. That's how I kind of view it philosophically in my head. But yeah, the idea that single models unifying across modalities, scales is what the lab builds toward.

Understanding Variants — The ClinVar Benchmark

Can you walk through a few of the tasks you talk about in the blog?

Sure. One of the areas that we thought was really interesting for showcasing in this particular release for Omni was on understanding variants and their effects — which are essentially, in DNA, a change in a position, changing the letter of one of the other three letters in your genome in DNA. Sometimes can cause a disease, and sometimes it doesn't do anything. Actually many times it doesn't do anything. But there are specific areas in your genome that if you have a different variant or a different letter there, it can cause disease.

And in many cases, because the combinations of these changes in the genome — over 3 billion letters — it's so vast that for clinicians and scientists we actually know only a very small portion of which variants are causal to disease or not.

And so there's these benchmarks from folks who collect variants — different hospital systems and clinics — and some are known and some are still unknown. Folks have created some benchmarks from ClinVar or TraChim to basically: the idea is given a mutation in a DNA, can you tell if it's gonna cause a disease or not?

And so this is a very good setup for DNA models because they're probabilistic. And so when you do make a change, it basically can modify its confidence or their probability of predicting a next letter.

And in this case, we've sort of leveraged that predictability of these models. They've essentially seen and been trained on so much DNA, in particular human DNA. They kind of understand what's common — and usually common or conserved across different other folks usually typically means healthier. And so if it's less common — you can think of it this way — if it's less common, the model can pick it up and sort of predict that it's potentially pathogenic or disease-causing.

Coding vs. non-coding regions

And so we've taken some of these benchmarks. And when you introduce a variant or a mutation, there's different types of mutations and variants. So sometimes you can delete a letter altogether, you can just flip it, you can remove big portions of the DNA — but these are generally single variants.

And in this case, this is where previous DNA models really struggled, especially on humans. And so we showcased that not only is it competitive or capable for humans, but in many cases it's state of the art — and actually most of these cases it's state of the art.

And I think the exciting part is that areas where other models that were currently on the frontier — they still were lagging behind quite a bit in terms of where in the genome. So in the genome, there's coding and non-coding regions — like protein areas, protein regions.

Meaning areas that are actually coding the structure of a protein versus other areas that do other things like regulate what genes are expressed.

Yeah — and so these non-coding regions are largely regulatory. They kind of control how much or when to use a certain gene or turn them on. And in many cases, these non-coding regions — these regulatory regions — variants, their mutations there are much harder to predict if they cause disease or not.

And I think what's exciting about the new generation of models we're building with Omni is that that's where we shine especially. The models are able to pick up mutations and be able to distinguish if it's disease-causing in these non-coding and especially long-range areas.

So I think this is particularly exciting to a lot of geneticists that have struggled to use traditional bioinformatic tools or statistical methods, because they've largely focused on coding regions, which is only about 1.5, 2% of the genome. And turns out many, if not most, of the diseases are in these non-coding regions. And so there's been a real desire to build models that can actually pick up these disease-causing variants in these non-coding regions.

The Borzoi Column — Supervised vs. Unsupervised

For the listeners: there's this column on this benchmark chart called Borzoi, reference number four in the blog post. Could you talk about what this column represents?

Yeah, great point. So what we show in this benchmark here is really taking some of the representative models — or the strongest models — in the deep-learning side and also in the traditional methods.

So we have Evo2 — the latest previous genomic model that our team had worked on. And then Borzoi — it's also a DNA model, but a very different kind. Essentially it's a supervised model that predicts, from DNA, functional genomic tracks. So it too is inherently multimodal, but it's not a language model. So it doesn't predict like a next-token prediction — it goes from a DNA sequence directly to a functional genomic track like chromatin flexibility or gene expression.

And these tracks have been annotated extensively by people writing their dissertations and whatever.

Yeah, right. So the big difference there is that it's a supervised task. So it requires labeled outputs. And in our case, these language models — they do not require labeled outputs. So you're doing raw pre-training on unannotated sequences.

So why is that desirable? Well, it's a lot more data — a lot more genomic data that's not annotated. Actually most of it, pretty much in many ways, almost all of it is not annotated. And so being able to learn from an unsupervised manner is hugely desirable.

For us, we wanted to showcase the benefit of pre-training on raw genomic sequences and comparing it to state-of-the-art models in other spaces in DNA.

How does likelihood turn into a score?

When you say it's unsupervised, how does the unsupervised property work? How do you convert the output to an actionable ranker or score?

What I talked about before is: to train the Omni model, it's pre-trained so it's unsupervised. But when you're pointing at a specific task, there is a supervised step. So it's just taking a smaller dataset that is labeled.

But essentially what we're doing is using the likelihood scores. So the raw outputs of the language model — which basically you can think of it like a probability for predicting what the next letter is. We can essentially showcase the probability score, the likelihood score, for the mutation versus the wild type — so that's seen in the reference genome versus the mutation in this particular case. And then we'll have two scores. And then you can think of it as like using a ratio of the two to showcase basically how different is this mutation from a normal or baseline. And then that's — you could think of it as like a surprise factor that the model is able to use and leverage. And then we can use that to essentially score an actual prediction for disease or not.

Is Omni autoregressive, or diffusion or something else you can't tell me?

(Laughing) Yeah, this time we're not describing the exact makeup. But Evo was autoregressive — I think that was the first large-scale autoregressive [genomic model]. And so I think for us, we don't tie ourselves down to a specific training objective. We use every tool in the toolbox essentially.

But for the specific benchmark, you're going along and you're just using the likelihood distribution of the tokens.

And some tokens are unlikely because of some evolutionary constraint — this doesn't show up often, and because it doesn't show up often across genomes, it is probably going to cause problems and people will not survive, so on. So that's basically your ranking metric.

Yeah, it's one interpretation of how the model is thinking about it. And very similar to natural language — you can describe the same kind of paradigm.

And there's additional cases in mid- and post-training to leverage more than that. Because we can teach it specific structure and benchmarks so that it can build on top of what you just described — which is like what's common in nature — but also because it's a specific task for disease-variant prediction, then the model has additional training introduced during mid-training to showcase, to add additional learning power essentially.

Examples of mid-training signal

What are some examples of that?

Again, probably secret sauce to some extent — but can give just a gist. We would actually throw in the score itself. That ratio I mentioned — a ratio of wild-type versus mutation — I would say that's more of a zero-shot method where you don't even have to do any mid-training. And that's what Evo2 is doing in particular in this column. So Evo2 is not fine-tuned essentially.

There's an EVE column — where people are basically fine-tuning, using the scores from Evo2. That's from Goodfire. And that's also folks that we greatly respect, and they kind of showcase that these models are able to be state of the art when you can fine-tune them as well — not just zero-shot.

And then our model is introducing sort of a step above that — not just fine-tuning, but also introducing structure (by structure I mean the format of these benchmarks) into the model itself. That Q&A style formatting during mid-training is what gives us an extra boost even.

I see. And extra boost — but I think the other benefit too, that we didn't emphasize too much in the blog, but I think it's really convenient for practical use for scientists: is that you don't — you're doing this without taking the embeddings and then tapping on a head and then doing some regression, which is an extra step, extra hurdle. Can you imagine ChatGPT, if every time you asked a question you had to like fine-tune it for a certain domain?

We've done it so that the model is flexible during mid-training to be trained on many tasks at once. And so the fine-tuning — that last step of training the embeddings — doesn't have to be done. It's out of the box at that point. You just prompt in a certain format and it will — that sort of format tells it which task you're gonna do, and then we'll output the answers in that desired format, basically.

Yeah, the short answer is: we're extremely cognizant of the risk of data leakage. And extremely hard to not mislead or be careful. Yeah, cool. And state of the art for a reason: which is sort of by design, they'll take the best methods and kind of do an ensemble. Chain-of-Thought for DNA

I'd be interested to see — there's some discussion of chain of thought. That broke my brain a little bit when I was first hearing about that.

Yeah — I think this is really just a taste of where we think the design capabilities can move toward and way more usable for folks.

So chain of thought stems from the natural-language community. I believe Jason Wei at OpenAI showcased the first examples. And really what the breakthrough there was showcasing that these language models performed better when you just show your work, essentially. You showed the steps of how you came to a conclusion or an argument. And it turns out — even if they were like simple steps — but it just gave the model a chance. Maybe it's sort of like philosophically who knows exactly why it works, but essentially feeding more tokens in and giving it more scratch space to think.

And so people just think this is the beginning of reasoning for these language models — this ability to kind of get to an answer by thinking to itself, by itself. And so it seemed quite successful in language — very successful. And that's why you have a lot of agents that just spend tons of tokens, right? Just showing its work. In many ways it stems from this chain-of-thought paradigm.

And in biology, we saw very little of that. We started to see some of that in protein design a little. And so we wanted to push that and showcase that — well, at first explore it — is that possible in DNA? What does that even mean in genomics? Because you don't really have words that describe its thinking. So how do you take that same paradigm and introduce it to a DNA language model?

The RNA aptamer experiment

And so what we did was a simpler version, in so many ways. We had this dataset of RNA aptamers — so just think of it as these desired sequences with some kind of fitness score associated with them. So we took this large dataset that had RNA input and a fitness score. The fitness score go high, it's good. It's the simplest version. It's a big dataset.

And so what we wanted to showcase was that if we show the model progressively better RNAs in a series of steps with its score — so you have like low scores first and then you gradually move up the chain — can the model continue that trajectory on its own? And then in the final step, does it self-optimize to a point where it's like the best score it can get? That was the experiment.

Can we do that? And so we took a dataset — a large dataset of aptamers. We held out a portion of like the best-performing ones and we showed it only the lower ones, but then we ranked it. So we showcased lower scores with the RNA aptamers, and then progressively got higher, and then asked the model to just like continue with that pattern. And it turns out it was able to recapitulate some of those higher scores that we had not shown it yet.

We were actually in the process of validating this in the wet lab right now. So we didn't get to show it here. But we wanted to know — actually, can it not just do this in silico, which it can (it showcased that it was able to continue this trajectory and create plausible aptamers with higher fitness scores)?

And now we think this is — you know, obviously if this works in the lab — we think this is a hugely, hugely valuable paradigm that can be pretty much applied to every other type of biological sequence. That's usually what you have: you have sequence, you have some kind of fitness score, desired output. And if we can get models to eventually learn that structure and just show a series of progressively stronger sequences — the model can then predict the rest. That's a very powerful paradigm.

Why did RNA work? A surprise

Honestly a bit surprised about this — that specifically this task saw a strong improvement. Maybe my personal bias, but RNA is somewhat notorious for not having good co-evolution data. For viral genomes there is strong evolutionary pressure, but for mammalian, usually RNA does not have evolutionary pressure. The predominant pressure is like RNA will carry coding information. Genomes carry lots of different information. So I'm wondering — where do you think this capability might have emerged in this language model?

That's a good question — and honestly I'm not sure. Like, we're surprised too. One, because the model is pre-trained on DNA and it's really just mid-trained on RNA, very, very in a small way. Yeah, I think what your intuition about DNA having a lot of evolutionary effects or information is probably where. And so I think this is hinting at the idea of why we think it's so important to pre-train on DNA genomes and genomes first, and then sort of add additional modalities on top — because you get a lot of transfer. And you want the modality generalization is the thing that we're working toward.

General biological intelligence

You know, what I didn't talk about as a company as well, is this idea of building toward general biological intelligence, where we are unifying a lot of the different so-called languages or modalities of biology. At the end of the day, they stem from DNA. And I think people have not exploited that fact as much. It's usually really specialized — the domain-specific, modality-specific models — and not leveraging a lot of inherent shared structure from other modalities.

And so one example of that is: you know, when people talk about virtual cells — a little bit of a tangent — but they tend to focus on just RNA and transcripts, and they want to generalize to describing an entire cell. But obviously a cell is a lot more things than that.

In my mind, if you want to learn a system, you want to learn from all the signals or sensors of that world or that system. If it's a cell and you want to fuse — you want to understand the DNA, you want to understand the metabolomics, the epigenomics, proteomics — and that's when you get closer to like, quote-unquote, a virtual cell.

And in our minds we don't even want to stop at just the cell, but we want to fuse all of these sensors across all of biology.

Will it get us to a super intelligence that understands every component and nuance of biology? Who knows? But I am confident that this type of paradigm will get us a hell of a lot further than we are now. That's my bars. Can you make something far more useful than now?

Are you focusing on eukaryotic cells? Human genomes? Viral genomes?

Yeah, absolutely. We are interested in all domains of life. And sort of got a lot of feedback from folks asking: what are these models useful for? But I think there's opportunity to apply these models generally to every form of life. So we absolutely are interested in prokaryotes and viral. Viral in particular we care about, especially for biodefense and biosecurity especially. More applications: AMR, rare earths

So another example is for the antimicrobial resistance — I think that's something we're very interested in as well. And the ability to selectively target specific bacterial strains or kill bacterial strains. Yeah — that's measured basically a score zero to one of how effectively that is done. And so showing progressively more effective phage genomes and their associated scores for effectiveness fits that paradigm very well.

There's another design task that we're working with a national lab to do this with as well. And an area that is quite different for us — but it's on designing proteins to extract rare-earth minerals.

And so it turns out that you don't just care about proteins that could bind to something, but you want it to be selective. You want it to bind to one type of rare-earth mineral. And so you have scores associated with how much affinity or binding affinity for each type of mineral. We wanna essentially do the similar exercise with rare-earth minerals and show it a series of progressively desirable scores — not just for binding to this, but like lower binding scores for other ones. You can selectively do it.

So I think the creativity in which you can showcase sequence and desirable sequence with some kind of fitness or functional output is a relatively intuitive way for people to design — just prompt, by just prompt engineering essentially — which I think is very exciting to explore more.

Context matters — the rare-earths thesis

Rare-earth mineral extraction is interesting. Maybe you wouldn't have a comparative advantage compared to other techniques, because it seems like your strengths are probably in larger-scale design across entire organisms, but focusing on individual proteins — that may be much more of a structural task. And going to talk about ClinVar — the argument is that the model now is a really good statistical representation of what type of mutations are common or not. If you want to do design and understand structure — for disease, that's more natural in a population-genomic way. So where do you think your strongest competitive advantage is? And do you think your model understands structure in addition to function?

Yeah — I'd say what drew us to this particular application — rare earths — and our strengths in general, why we thought it might be suited for it, is two things.

One is I think in areas where context matters. So yeah, you're right — a protein-design task where you're just designing maybe not naturally where we see ourselves competitively advantaged. But in the rare-earths case, our hypothesis is that context matters. And what matters here possibly is certain microorganisms with proteins that have the function that we desire — we can potentially prompt and provide it context for: this is the neighborhood in which — tell Omni, this is the neighborhood of genomes or microorganisms that you should search for new proteins.

So it's really sort of like a mining exercise. And what we can showcase to our models that other folks can — for like protein-structure models — is that we can feed in non-coding regions before that gene of interest or that protein of interest, and then ask for the model to provide variants. So like, mutate this protein — but know that you're in this microorganism — but show me different variants that you've seen in nature, or combine different things that you've seen in nature, given this context.

And I think that is one reason why we can make very evolutionarily diverse sequences and potentially phages. Folks have used Evo models to do this with toxin-antitoxins and a similar technique — they've prompted on things upstream from the proteins of interest, and then asked the model to kind of generate a bunch of plausible other ones.

And I think this case for rare earths — that's super exciting because then we can come up with plausible variants and then test them relatively simply for what they bind to and selectively bind to. Which I think is really interesting for this partner who cares, for example, about securing the supply chain of rare earths for the US strategically. And so we thought that's absolutely something that is worth supporting.

So your point is — not just you're designing a protein, but you're designing an organism which generates a protein, and this protein has an action. But the way to design this — you need to understand how through the tree of life interactions of proteins with rare earths or certain minerals have occurred.

Yeah — I'd say in this particular case for rare earths, we're not really interested in the organism, like designing the whole organism. But I think the organism does tell us about what proteins are plausible and the way they evolve — not just around the protein itself, but also the regulatory elements around it. And it helps us narrow and provide additional context.

I guess I think of the genome or DNA broadly as sort of the imprint of the physical world into DNA. And so there's parts of the DNA that we want, but the things around those parts that we want also tells a little bit about the context of where it came from and how it came to be — in its function. And so I just think of it — can we come back to that word — but context. I think context matters in many of these applications, or at least in some of them.

(Laughs) Yeah — I think context matters a lot in biology. I think maybe one of our big bottlenecks is the lack of context, and how we as humans mostly approach biology in terms of a very engineering [way], like let's isolate individual systems. And systems biology approaches — very hard to get any sort of meaningful quantitative predictive power.

The Stanford / Hyena origin story

You and your team, your collaborators, have a long history of these state-space models, doing pushing context. Also — how you go in a first-principles way, diving into the architectures of how GPUs work and designing models which are exploiting the architecture of GPUs.

Yeah, absolutely. If you wanna distract our researchers at Radical Numerics — this is how you nerd-snipe them. You talk about long context and kernels, GPUs — then they're like: wait, did someone say kernels? And they start trying to figure out how to make things fast.

Yeah — long contexts hold a special place in my heart because that's what I focused on in my PhD at Stanford. And that's how we started thinking about DNA. And going back a little bit for fun: we were looking at working on language models in general, and then we noticed our models were good at long context. And so that's the progression of how we started working in the space — it was like: oh, these models seem to be really efficient on long context.

We were like, DNA's gotta be the longest — three billion base pairs.

And we started thinking like: OK, what's being done there? Like what kind of context lengths are people doing there? They're doing super short. They're doing like one or 2000 base pairs or tokens at a time. It's like way smaller than what one would want for DNA. And so it's clearly a need there, and overlooked. And we saw it as a way to initially — like, let's see if we can do something that we had no idea if it was gonna work, and no idea who would want it. And so we just started tinkering around.

And it turns out out of the box — relatively out of the box — it was doing pretty well at reading DNA. And then it led to: OK, people keep asking about DNA. Pitching Evo — six months of "that's a stupid idea"

And then for some reason we alighted on this idea of: well, no one's writing DNA. Can we get it to write DNA? And that was a really simple question. But in hindsight it almost seems obvious that yeah — you would wanna write DNA and design it. But when I was first pitching the idea of Evo to folks, I spent six months (which I guess in bio-words is not that long, but I spent six months) going around saying: hey, if I generate DNA, would you find that useful? Like, what would you do with it? Would you back us? Would you wanna be a part of this?

And crazy enough, most, almost every scientist at Stanford I talked to thought it was a stupid idea. Like: this would be so cool, generating DNA, how much would we accelerate the field? And then people would say like: what would you do with it? I'm like: I don't know. And then I would get that comment — or comments like "that's not possible." Like: we as humans don't understand the rules — how could you expect an AI to learn it? You can't even tell if it's right or wrong. Like you can't tell the AI yes, that's right or wrong — how can you expect it to learn it? Or there's too many repeat characters, or DNA is too noisy of a distribution — there's no real rules and there's just a bunch of junk in there.

I heard all the reasons. And I was just so stubborn about it. There's gotta be a use case for being able to generate DNA. I just — it just feels right. And I didn't know what it was. So it really was an experiment of: like, what happens.

The first Evo checkpoint

And so when we first trained Evo, I remember we had no idea if it was gonna work. We had no idea. We didn't know what thing was gonna emerge. We just thought: let's just train a big one. Which is kind of ridiculous. But somehow folks were like, sure, why not — let's see what happens. Let's pay some money for the GPUs and let these crazy kids train the model.

And I remember when the first result came back and it kind of like gave us chills — like, oh, maybe there's something going on. Which was: somebody took the model checkpoint, the first one, and threw it at a protein gym — one of the protein benchmarks. And [it] turned out to be competitive with protein-specific models. And we were like: OK, that is pretty surprising because we never told the model what's proteins versus not. And there's actually — you know, there's also protein and DNA. So there was one piece — I think it was just surprising that it was actually competitive with protein-specific models.

And this was like the first experience. And then they just kind of kept on coming, one after another. And it was like: oh, this competitive here, oh, it's state of the art on RNA and our DNA. And we started seeing like: oh, it can learn across different modalities, not just DNA. And then we felt like: OK, there's something there.

And so it kind of went from there. And then folks at NVIDIA were like: let's back Evo2, let's make this even bigger. And then Greg Brockman from OpenAI was like: I'll take a break from OpenAI and take us four months of a sabbatical and help these crazy kids out. And, you know, then we're Slack-messaging Greg Brockman at 3 a.m. trying to debug our code — which is wild.

Yeah — so the trajectory was very surprising in many ways. But at the same time, you still got a lot of feedback like: what are these models good for? What are they useful for in the real world? And so that's really motivated us to start a company.

We thought what we showed was just really just a taste — from like an academic flavor. In a similar way, the language models when they first [came out] — you know, if natural language came out, people asked some of the questions like: what are these things good for? Oh, cool, it can write some jokes for me. Is this gonna lead to an all-composing AGI that can automate everything? They did not think that. They thought it's like a toy — it's got emerging capabilities and they would extrapolate the potential. And in many ways I think what we're seeing here is even more exciting or reminiscent of that trajectory for DNA.

But Evo2 even was showing the bacteriophage — and that wasn't a persuasive — I mean, that's almost a scary example. So the people didn't see that, like — that isn't a light-bulb moment for people.

Yeah — so I mean, and some people — I think either fair or rough critiques, you can even play devil's advocate and say: what it's generating is pretty close to nature, and you're kind of recapitulating just a small variance. And so there's a lot of ways to critique and kind of minimize the potential, which can be fair argument.

Like, so I think at this point, we think what is more important is not just pushing on the science and like — cool, this can be done, and kind of leave it there as a sort of thought experiment. But like: how do we actually use this to improve human understanding of disease, improve treatments, make better rare-earth mineral extractors? How do we actually make this useful is what we care about now as a company, in addition to some of these more scientific questions.
