But so far what we've showcased and been excited about is looking, really analyzing the embeddings and some of the activations in the model.

And so this idea of Mech Interp for bio is borrowing a lot from the natural-language community. Currently, you could think of what the models are doing is compressing a bunch of information it's seen. And so in this compression, it's really basically distilling it down into the key components, key patterns, that helps it understand the data or learns the distribution of the data.

And so what we're trying to do is probe the models to see what did the model distill into its weights and its activations — or sort of like the outputs. And so for us, we started off with a lot of the outputs of the model — so the activations. And we wanted to see: what kind of structure, what kind of visualizations, can we see that help us understand some of the complexities of DNA (which is a ton)?

And so some of these complexities can range around GC content, certain motifs of transcription factors — there's a bunch of regulatory types of patterns and motifs that the model, we believe, has to pick up to be able to do its tasks. To understand whether a disease is caused by a variant. And generally it's going to compress all these different motifs and distill them into the model weights. And so our job is to then find these and see if we can distill a pattern or structure that can be generalized to other cases where we don't understand the patterns. So that's sort of largely the goal.

From GC content up to disease

So in this case, GC means the two nucleotides — the fraction of those in a sequence.

Exactly, yeah — so the fraction of the G and C letters in a genome, which is amongst the more simpler things. But also simple things as repeats, number of motifs. I think transcription-factor (TF) motifs is another one that is especially interesting for folks. Because eventually we're going to get to a case where we can design transcription factors — meaning we'll have certain transcription-factor patterns via like ChIP-seq modalities. Transcription factors are — well, you can go ahead.

Transcription factors are molecules that bind to DNA, and they would alter essentially the gene-expression pattern. And so it has this regulatory effect that doesn't modify the DNA itself, but can modify sort of the effects of DNA in the products that DNA makes. It can have a lot of implications on — well, pretty much everything in your body. So it can modify disease states — it can modify — I guess that's a lot of aging-related research is around transcription-factor design.

And so we think being able to understand some of the motifs via DNA — but also additional modalities — will eventually let us be able to design transcription-factor patterns as well. And so I think this is very exciting. In many ways, the combinatorial space of learning these transcription factors — like what binds and where they bind and what effects it causes — is just far too vast to be able to do this in a manual way. And so we want to take a data-driven approach to learn some of these motifs.

The complexity here is partly because the transcription factors themselves — coding genes — and so those can regulate each other. And so that you have this — that's where that combinatorial effect comes.

So like — narrating for the listeners-only — we're kind of marching through these increasingly complex and higher-level factors all the way from GC content. We started, now we're looking at disease — which is maybe the most complex thing or you are pointing towards in this analysis.

Yeah — so I think our first idea for previewing this was, and what we're working toward broadly, is this idea of mapping the manifold of disease. So a manifold — there's like the sort of representation space of what disease looks like to a model in terms of the output scores or embeddings. We believe that there's a lot more structure that can be gleaned from understanding some of these outputs.

And so mapping this manifold — or the landscape of the structure of disease (and obviously there's many diseases) — would be a big exciting area of research for us to actually drive motivation for Mech Interp in bio.

I think we're just really scratching the surface. Because if you can glean this much of insight potentially from just DNA (which is in my mind just one of the sensors that you want to ultimately fuse into modeling biology), then being able to do something similar across all modalities — by "all modalities" I mean protein, RNA, epigenomics, ATAC (chromatin accessibility) and methylation patterns — all these other different types of molecular phenotypes around DNA — just presents such a huge opportunity that this kind of lay in front of us, that is all green space, greenfield.

No — I haven't seen anybody do this level of sophisticated techniques from machine learning, deep learning, into what I think is gonna be the most important, impactful area of understanding and applications for AI. That's what we're excited about. And I think we're just showing a preview — very simple preview from the DNA-only models. But in our next generation of models, which will be increasingly multimodal — we're talking dozens — it's a very exciting moment for us.

Sidebar on that — is language, natural language, one of the modalities?

Not yet — oh yeah, yeah, but it will be. So I'd say there's a lot of questions about how to fuse that with bio, but I actually think it's pretty — will be relatively straightforward. I think the more tricky part for us is actually how to fuse the biological signals more so. Fusing language, there's a lot of examples with that — with like image and video space. So we feel pretty good about that. And we've done some early experiments with language.

And I think that will make it extra accessible for folks when you connect it to language. But I think the part — the recipe — that folks still are trying to figure out is how to do this across biological modalities.

It just seems like a natural way to be able to do chain-of-thought, right?

Exactly — yeah. Absolutely. And I think, especially when you start having chain-of-thoughts from orchestrating tools — things like Claude Science — I think the idea of incorporating language, I think, is already in a lot of people's minds.

Biosecurity — The Dual Mandate in Practice

If you don't have any questions, let's talk about the biosecurity stuff.

For us, we as a company thought it was very important to have a dual mandate, what we call a dual mandate. And it's this idea of essentially being cognizant and feeling responsible — or wanting to feel responsible — for the capabilities that we're enabling on the design side. So if we're going to create models that can design function into sequences, we believe and see a gap in companies being able to safeguard that technology and make sure that it's used responsibly, increasingly more.

I was just at a panel last night — a panel on AI scientists, agents that can do scientific discovery. And one of the last questions was: what are some of the biggest risks or doomsday scenarios with AI learning about science? And every one of them talked about biological weapons. And at the same time, I was curious — because I was like: OK, so then what are any of these folks doing about that? And basically I didn't hear anything about that. And these companies — I won't say the names — I look at the companies, they don't have big efforts in those spaces.

So anyways, we felt it was important as a lab — that a team that was both building the design capabilities is actually also best suited for building the defense capabilities. Because they're basically the same models. A model that is good at generating turns out is also very good at discriminating or predicting if a sequence is pathogenic or not.

So we felt it was not just from a principle standpoint necessary to work on both biosecurity and the design — but that it was strategically, it just made sense as well. And so we felt this resonated with our team, but also the broader community — folks in the US government and abroad even — that there was a clear gap in need for a type of entity to exist to do this. And so yeah, we felt it was necessary to build it into our mission.

The four pillars of biodefense

For us, biodefense/biosecurity sort of has three or four different pillars of strategy:

  1. Detection and surveillance — broadly, can you detect from the environment if a sequence has a pathogen in it, something that can cause disease? Let's say from swabs at an airport, a nasal swab, or a sewage system — collecting samples.

  2. Attribution — once you've detected a danger, can you figure out where it came from? Is it natural? Is it from a rival country abroad? Is it engineered by a human from a specific lab in a country? And that helps you figure out what to do about it.

  3. Countermeasures — so once you've detected, figured out where it's from, what do you do about it? Can you make a counter-agent? Can you make an antiviral or antimicrobial?

  4. Deterrence — but that's more of like a government kind of level thing.

So we focus primarily on the first three.

So we create tools that, given a sequence, [can] detect if it's pathogenic — but also what we felt was missing from the community was not just detect broadly if it's pathogenic, but characterize the heck out of it. Meaning: what parts of the sequence are dangerous, what genes, for example. Attributing where it came from — being able to not just look at its sequence and match it to a database, but be able to attribute its signatures.

And then also a big component to make this effective in the first place: the community, the biodefense community, broadly focuses on sequence matching. So they'll take a sequence and they'll basically align it to a known database and see: have I seen this before? Does it match this list of known pathogens?

But I think what's emerging, and a concern for a lot of labs, is: well, one — new stuff. Right? If it's not on your list. And two — things that were intentionally obfuscated to not be detected in sequence space, meaning the letters matching up exactly, but also function space. Because basically models that we're enabling now — they will be able to be function-aware or structure-aware. And so that means, for concretely, you can have a sequence that has the same function like a pathogen, but actually look different in terms of the letters.

And you can imagine basically what we have on the screen here still is this Mech Interp thing — and there's this sort of manifold that the model constructs internally that is kind of coding for these, among other things, functions. So you can imagine how it would be able to say: oh, well, that's maybe genetically quite different, or at least somewhat different, but it still has a similar function.

Exactly, exactly. So what we talk about in our defense blog is this idea of things that can function similarly — they can start having separation in terms of what the sequence looks like, while maintaining the same functionality. So this can happen in nature sort of naturally, but also what these AI models allow you to do is also intentionally do that as well. So have the same function or functional capability, but have diverse letters — diverse spelling, but describe the same thing basically.

Paraphrases and DNA synthesis screening

And so in this case, this work from Microsoft called paraphrases — it's like kind of rewiring things — where they showcase that you can, for example, use protein language models to essentially keep the same structure (which structure implies similar function), but then change the spelling.

And not just that — they wanted to test that if you have this capability and you send this through existing detection systems, would it break the system? Like, would it actually detect it or not?

And I think one of the interesting facts that maybe the general public — but most biologists know — is that there's these DNA synthesis companies, right? Where you can basically send a design of sequences and get back a DNA molecule like it's an Amazon package. Like you just send it off, and they'll send you the physical DNA of the design. They'll manufacture it for you. And this runs the scientific community — right? It's the pipeline that allows people to do research and understand biology and make drugs and everything. So it's prevalent and it's public.

And so I think one of the concerns for folks is — well, and one of the concerns for us when we first started working on this — was in a world, for example, where agents are prolific online — presumably billions and trillions of agents building and taking all sorts of actions on the internet — it's wild that they don't have any tools to basically tell them if it's making anything dangerous or not.

And so that was literally our first motivation — of like: we should probably make something that can detect if something is dangerous or not.

So you guys filter for these manufacturers so that they can say: what am I making here? Is this dangerous or whatever? And maybe you could have an exception if you were like some licensed lab and I'm doing something dangerous, I know I'm doing it, please let me do it anyway.

All sorts of cases. So that's one scenario. To be fair, many of the DNA synthesis companies have detection tools, but I would strongly hypothesize that they're not AI-based, and fairly they're probably not robust. Yeah, they're all pattern-matching mostly.

The ROC-curve problem

Sorry, maybe I should ask this question later. I'm just curious about — we've all, everyone who is working in bio has tried to use Fable and it's illegal, literally everything you type in.

(My website for example.)

You can't do anything in Fable without [it triggering]. But in terms of people, scientists exploring synthetic biology and creating new sequences and designing new sequences, it seems like it'd be very hard to have an ROC curve which you can live on that doesn't impede novel scientific research for legitimate purposes. How do you avoid — even with an F1 of 0.9, which you're not even close to right now — I think that still could easily, if there are billions of sequences generated a day or at least a year, I mean, it seems like a very hard balance.

Yeah — it's a tough question. So I think broadly, the way we look at it is: if we thought about it like "how do we 100% stop the dangerous design" — I think it's a harder question to ask. I think the question we asked is: on the capabilities design side, there's plenty of folks pushing the frontier of that. When we look at the defense side, do we see frontier technology being applied there? And the answer to that was no. So we saw this huge gap, and we wanted to sort of aid — come to its defense, come to its aid — to give it a boost.

So I think from that perspective, it's an easy choice for us to say: let's push, let's bring that to a better head-to-head match against the design side. Is it gonna solve everything? Well, I think that's what we're gonna aspire to be, but realistically, there's always gonna be cases where it can get around. And I think that's — that's a big motivation for why we think, safety for language models and chatbots is one layer, but also you're right — there may be things that kind of just get out there, get past that anyways.

And so what do you do about those cases? It's already past the chatbots. It's already aided someone into making dangerous sequences. So it's out there. I think the cool thing about our tools is that what we're building is tools for the folks that care about things that's already out there — out in the environment — that's made it somewhere. And now there's this whole ecosystem that we wanna build into that does the surveillance, that does the attribution, that does the countermeasures. We wanna boost that community, right? And build stronger tools for that space.

Does it have to be perfect to be useful there? I don't think so. I think we can be helpful and move the biodefense community forward in terms of bringing AI technology and AI frontier technology to their aid without being perfect in it.

Maybe another thing to say — the threat model, it's not even clear what threat model you're actually trying to defend against at this point. But the capabilities don't currently exist at all. So you provide something and now this can be worked on in terms of a larger regulatory framework or government or nonprofit, whatever, larger framework. It now provides you a tool that the community can build upon. Even if it's not perfect, it provides a starting point. And if you don't have a tool, then you can't do anything.

Yeah — the bar is the improvement. So the bar is: where are you at now? Can we move the needle? Can we move beyond sequence-based matching, alignment-based matching? Absolutely, I think there's tons. And I think the interest is only growing. I think we're hitting a lot of chatter at the regulatory side, from different politicians and different folks in think tanks. It does seem like folks are mobilizing. So we're optimistic that this gets out and is more top of mind for folks to actually take action, as opposed to just talking about it.

Because right now it does feel like there's a lot of talk. And one of the reasons why we felt like: let's build tools and put it out and give access to people. Because there's been a lot of talk about AI companies saying we should do biodefense. But then — OK, what does that mean? What are you gonna do about it? And so that was our approach.

The arms-race pushback

So I can just steelman this for a minute. If you are on the frontier, which it seems like you are and you certainly strive to be, you're moving the frontier of the attack and the defense at the same time. So right now, what you're doing clearly helps. But — if you're on the frontier, then that doesn't really matter in the long term. So how do you think about that? I mean, I guess you just have to nerf what people are doing or something.

Yeah — the mindset [I was] hoping to get folks to start thinking about it as less of a "oh, let's make a biodefense tool and call it a day." It's basically an arms race. Similar to the cybersecurity community — you're gonna make better technology, especially with something like Fable, that can potentially attack. And that means you're gonna have this back and forth. The design side's gonna get more capable. The defensive side needs to try to get ahead. And then that just motivates other folks to do past that too, on the design side.

So I think inherently there is this arms-race-style dynamic that — the way it appears to us is that the defensive side has been far, far lagging. And so what we wanna do is bring the defensive side closer to par essentially. So that's the mindset — I picture, or the framing I think about it.

The cybersecurity analogy is interesting, but I think it differs in some key points. First of all, with cybersecurity with a sufficiently strong model, you might actually be able to close all loopholes which are not sociological. You could in principle catch every single exploit. And then you can patch them. As long as people stay updated, you're secure. We have fixed genomes. So you can't patch a human. So the attack surface — the way that you're defending — is much harder. But then maybe the converse is that it seems much less likely that someone would have the incentive to go on offense to the same degree. And also the barrier to entry to success — even if you can print out arbitrary DNA and the process of going from that to making a successful virus, especially one which doesn't kill the person designing it — is actually quite large. So what is, in your opinion, the single biggest threat we actually have? What would keep you awake at night?

One — it's hard to get in the mindset of a person wanting to design a bioweapon. So we're not trying to necessarily think of all the potential people or scenarios that bad actors might work on.

What I think broadly what I worry about is: we're lowering the bar for how much expertise is needed and the speed at which folks can engineer these kinds of things. And that means the volume is gonna just exponentially increase at some point.

And so there's a mix of — yes, there's intentional worries. Because there's certainly state actors that have had biological programs, very, very, very large ones. And one of our advisors on a company has physically seen these facilities and decommissioned them. And so we've heard a lot of stories about states actually being motivated to create such weapons. That is one concern. And I think during peacetime it's less scary. During wartime it's particularly scary.

I think the unintentional ones are also things that in my mind potentially more likely in the near term. Where folks do try to generate things and control function, and inadvertently things that maybe they tried to make a certain thing to understand and to study, but it got out — because these things can be hard to contain, for example, and they just have a leakage. So I think those scenarios potentially seem the most likely.

Does it keep me up at night? Not necessarily. I'm much more overall an optimist. I think building this type of technology is ultimately a game that you weigh out the pros and cons and the costs and benefits. I think the benefits far outweigh the potential harm. And so that's why we work on it. Because ultimately we do think it's going to be an engine for discovery and human health improvement.

But at the same time, we just felt that the defensive side was sort of losing this arms race. And so we work on it as well and try to push the frontier. But I'd say overall, I think as a community, as researchers, but also folks in the policy side — I think the community is resilient enough and has the ability to mobilize to get ahead of it. And so I'm very optimistic about it.

Closing Questions

The bottleneck question

We have two questions that we like to ask every guest. The first one is: if you could, by fiat, remove a bottleneck that is important to you, what would that be?

Interesting. Could I get two answers on this one?

Sure.

The first one is kind of a cop-out because every AI lab says this — like, GPUs. (Laughter) We've gotten the answer a few times. We can use GPUs.

The other one, which I think is a little more philosophical — I think in this space, in what we're trying to aspire to do, is reinvent how scientists do their work in this space. And I think one hurdle we run into is folks who — and you see this in many domains — folks who: the more expertise you have in something, the more pessimistic you become about that space. And I think you especially see this in bio, where you know a disease area or modality so well, and then someone introduces something else new, and you're like: oh, but what about this and this and that? And they're very pessimistic — and probably rightfully so.

I think what I've noticed at the company — what we strive to do, and the folks that we try to bring in — are domain experts that do know that field, but also are still dreamers. Meaning they still do have that imagination and desire to change how things are done. I think that barrier we see that a lot in the field. I think if we embrace that more, we can see a lot more progress and step-change that I would love to see.

The takeaway

Brings us to the last question — is there something that you want the audience to take away, a single message?

Yeah. I think one message is: I think folks have had, especially in the AI research community, felt like there was a choice they had to make sometimes — to either work on the frontier of AI technology, and that was like consumer-related apps or enterprise-related apps, and they just had to work on chatbots. And that's the cutting-edge technology.

But also, I think when people think about the true potential of what AI can do — and I think a lot of it is about improving human health, understanding our biology — but people have felt like they have had to choose. And if I work in that space, I can't work in the frontier of AI.

And what I would like people to take away is that you don't have to choose. And I think we can work on things you truly care about that you think will push humanity, and work on cutting-edge technology. And that's what we're trying to build at Radical Numerics.

Yeah — and I mean, clearly, and I encourage people to read the blog posts, the architecture, the Mech Interp. There's a lot of innovation that is going into building these models. And I firmly believe that biology is really on the forefront of AI.

Awesome. Yeah. Glad you feel that way. Amazing. Thanks for joining.

Yeah, thank you for — that was fun. Making the long trip. That's a long way. Anytime. Thank you. Precious invite. I had a blast. Great. Thank you. Thank you.

🎵 (Music playing)

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的洞察：进攻方即最佳防守方——"双重使命"背后的深层结构对称性
Eric 提出的最关键的哲学转折不在于"我们要做生物安全"，而在于一句几乎被顺口带过的话：**"一个擅长生成的模型，也天然擅长判别一个序列是否致病。"**
这不是一句公关话术，而是一个深刻的**信息论对称性**。语言模型的生成 = 概率密度估计，判别 = 同一个密度函数的另一种查询方式。它意味着：**在 DNA 空间中，攻防不是两种不同的技术，而是同一个数学对象的两次读取。**
这带来一个惊人的推论：**Radical Numerics 事实上是把自己变成了 AI 时代的"核武器扩散管制局"的技术底座**——因为其他任何试图追赶其防御能力的机构，都必须先追上其进攻能力。这是一种通过技术不对称建立的、隐蔽的准公共治理权。听起来像 OpenAI 的"我们必须走在前面才能保证安全"叙事——但在生物领域，这个叙事第一次拥有了严格数学根据，因为在 NLP 里"更强模型 = 更安全"从未被证明，而在序列空间里生成器与鉴别器共享权重是**结构性事实**。

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、隐藏的心理钩子：他童年"路灯焦虑"与今日"稳定币福音"是同一件事

John 反复讲的两个故事看似无关——小时候等待路灯亮起时的心痛（因为爸爸要去做第二份工作），以及现在痛斥"银行把 4.5% 利息吞掉、只给客户 10 个基点"——其实是同一段创伤在两个时空的回响。他不是在做商业布道，他是在为童年那个无力的男孩追讨迟到几十年的利息。这解释了一个悖论：为什么一个华尔街老将会主动放弃 Coinbase 的短期利润去做"复利返还"？因为对他而言，10 basis points vs 3% 复利 20 年 = "一年学费" = 他父亲不必打第二份工的那个平行宇宙。华尔街最坚定的稳定币收益派，动机是心理学的，不是金融的。

二、最反直觉的观察：泡沫是"文明的孵化器"，理性投资才是创新的敌人

他引用与 Nouriel Roubini 合作的研究抛出了一个几乎没人敢说的结论——资产泡沫期，相关技术专利申请量增长 4 倍。这意味着：如果所有人都变成"冷静的价值投资者"，人类的技术进步会立即减速。这是一个跨领域的连接——它与古生物学的"寒武纪大爆发"、演化生物学的"间断平衡理论 (punctuated equilibrium)" 完全同构：物种进化不是匀速的，而是在环境剧烈波动（≈泡沫）时爆发式跃迁。John 甚至说"我为医疗科技祈祷泡沫"——这话在传统金融圈是异端，但如果你相信熊彼特的"创造性破坏"，泡沫就是资本主义的发烧机制：不舒服，但杀菌、逼迫免疫系统进化。AI 巨额估值不是问题，AI 从来没出现泡沫才是问题。

三、被大家忽略的暗线：他其实在用同一把"未来价值电子表格"贯穿三件事

请注意 John 表面上在讲三件互不相关的事：(a) 让 9 岁女儿在便利店冲动消费前用 App 算 "6% 年化 20 年后是多少钱"；(b) 预测市场比民调准，因为 "skin in the game"；(c) 债券投资者不敢冒险却将 100% 输掉退休。三者是同一个认知手术：把隐性成本强制变成显性数字。冲动消费的隐性成本 = 未来 120 美元；投票民调的隐性缺陷 = 没有下注就没有真实信念；保守储蓄的隐性风险 = 通胀吃掉退休。他在个人层面、社会决策层面、宏观资产层面用同一把工具切开了同一种病——人类系统性地低估"不作为"的成本。这甚至可以外推到跨领域：气候政策的失败、创业者的路径依赖、婚姻中的沉默成本——所有"看起来最安全的选择"都在偷偷贷款给你，利率复利到你老年账单一起到期。

四、一个刺耳的意外：AI 民主化叙事是骗散户的，"绵羊与狮子"才是真相

当被问到"15 岁孩子用 Claude 是否能挑战 Citadel"时，他不给外交辞令，直接说 "I'm a seller on that." 这是整个访谈最具颠覆性的一段——它戳破了当下最流行的"AI 平权"叙事。他的逻辑冷酷但成立：Citadel 拥有的每一样东西，散户拿到时已经是它们十年前的版本 + 加了类固醇。这就产生一个让人不安的推论：AI 越强，散户与机构的差距不是缩小，而是被拉到光速差。这也解释了他自己的建议 (buy and hold ETFs) 为什么与他给孩子的教育 (培养金融素养) 表面矛盾——前者是承认"游戏规则不公平"，后者是为下一代抢夺"设计游戏规则的席位"。他不是在教女儿投资，他在教她如何不做那只绵羊。

五、跨领域彩蛋：那位瑞典物理学家的一句话，是整个 AI 产业最深的护城河

"When you shrink power into a smaller and smaller place, we have a name for it: the bomb."——这是全片最优雅的一句物理学玩笑。它揭示了一个几乎所有 AI 投资人都忽略的物理天花板：AI 的瓶颈最终不是算力、不是数据、不是模型，而是"能量密度"。这与热力学、军事史（核武发展）、生物进化（线粒体效率）在深层相通——所有"智能"的上限最终都是能量管理的上限。这就是为什么 John 说 "picks and shovels = 电力和电池"，而不是芯片。所以真正的问题不是"谁做出更好的 LLM"，而是"谁能把电池做得像不会爆炸的炸弹"。谁破解这个物理悖论，谁就拥有下一个十年。

There's a very elegant legal argument about who has control over that — I won't pretend to be able to convey that argument. But in the meantime, prediction markets are showing incredible informational value that you should not throw out with the bathwater because you're concerned about the societal impact of gambling.

十四、为什么预测市场准确？—— 群体的宽度与深度

>> We know that prediction markets are very accurate when it comes to data 100%. But why is it accurate?

>> Because — curated crowds. Crowds aren't that wise. Curated crowds are very very wise. There's a natural curation that occurs when you have a specific market venue that people are drawn to, and you get the best of all worlds. You get breadth of market, depth of market, and you get a degree of curation around that market. And that's when crowds are really really smart.

>> Explain that breadth and depth.

>> So if you put a completely random 100 people in a room and asked them a really tough question about physics — solve this physics problem — more than likely you probably aren't going to be able to do it. Now, if you have a completely random million people in that room, there's a higher probability they get closer to the answer, but still probably they won't be able to do it. But if you get 100 people in a room of the top mathematicians and physicists, they have a better chance of doing it than if you have 5 million random people.

Curated large crowds do better and better at solving complex problems. Random assemblies of people — it's a coin flip.

But I will say this: there is even value in knowing what large random groups of people do. Because prediction markets are like futures markets. Futures markets on January 1st are really bad at predicting the closing price of crude oil on December 31st. They're not savants — they can't predict the future. But they get better and better as the year goes on, and they get better and better than random prediction.

Day one — a year from now — a coin flip is probably as good as a futures market at predicting what the closing price of crude oil will be on December 31st. But as you get closer and closer to that day, they get better and better than a coin flip.

Now, the time that's passed is not useless. Because as a trader, I want to know the consensus at any point in time. So all of that information is incredibly valuable. But they're not magic. So we want them to be active and liquid because we want that information. And then they do get really really good — and way better than random prediction — at solving that problem of price prediction as you get closer to the event.

Skin in the Game 与 Hammurabi's Code

>> Let me just add to that if I may, John. So there's an element of financial gain involved that makes it accurate — because this is why some economists have told me that the reason polls on elections have not been as accurate — >> No skin in the game. >> — as prediction markets is because those same people, the curated crowd, have no skin in the game when it comes to polls. And so they don't participate, but they participate in the prediction market.

>> Nassim Taleb — another brilliant guy who hates crypto, but he's a brilliant guy, and we should listen to him. We should listen to people who have different views from us. Nassim Taleb talks about — I think it's Hammurabi's law — that in one culture, the rule was: if you were a bridge designer and the bridge collapsed, they buried you under the stones.

So this notion of "skin in the game" is extremely evident. Couldn't agree more. Now, there are negative, perverse financial incentives that can develop, but it's a delicate ecosystem. But in general, it is known that curated crowds scale in intelligence.

信息市场，而非预测市场

>> In Asia, there are a few companies building prediction markets, and they frame it as "the information market." >> I agree with that. I think we should think of them as information markets, not prediction markets. I agree. >> Could you explain why?

>> Because — to your point — polling was a good science when we didn't have the ability to gauge actual sentiment. When we didn't have people's opinions in digitized form. When we didn't have the ability — meaning Twitter, meaning X, right? — when we didn't have the ability to get the X firehose engaged sentiment of very large groups of people. Calling up a thousand people and getting a statistically relevant sample set was the best we had.

So information — trading is always about having, using, the best information available. No one has perfect — if you have perfect information, you're insider trading, right? By definition. So unless you have inside information, you're trading on imperfect information. And so it's all about just having slightly better information than my competitor. That's all I need.

And knowing the views and beliefs — the behind-the-scenes views and beliefs from 10 million people — is better than interrupting a thousand people at dinner and getting their non-unbiased belief. Anonymity has value. Understanding how people act versus what they say — what they do versus what they say they do. All of that is valuable information, and it can be used by professional traders to make better-informed decisions.

十五、散户 vs Citadel：绵羊与狮子

>> How are the world's best algorithmic trading companies and funds — the Citadels of the world — going to compete in a world where the average 15-year-old with OpenAI or Claude is going to build a bot that does pretty much the same thing?

>> I'm a seller on that. I think good luck competing with Citadel for a long time. I don't care if you have Claude. I don't care how good you are — Claude. >> Until everything is run by agents? >> Yeah. And even then, not all agents will be created equal. And I guarantee you, Citadel will have the best agents. Jane Street will have the best agents.

So that's why I always tell you: be careful about day trading. You're a sheep amongst lions. It's very, very challenging. Buy and hold, invest in ETFs. I don't think you can compete. Whatever you have in your home, they have on steroids, and they've had it for longer than you.

>> Yeah. Okay, fair enough. >> There is this index that shows retail investor does not outperform the NASDAQ. >> Right? We know, by the way, 75% of hedge funds don't outperform the S&P's. That's not just — >> Well, what are people trying to do then?

>> I try not to judge. I think it's hope. I think they want to believe that they have the ability to outperform. It's ego. Why do people buy lottery tickets? Because somebody won, right?

So I think there's an element — I believe in an element of freedom that everyone should be allowed to take that chance. I think that with a reasonable amount of your wealth, it's probably smart to do so, because we should all have hope. We should all swing for the fences with something in our lives.

But in general, the average investor who doesn't have the ability to monitor markets at least 5 hours a day at minimum would do better off investing in pooled vehicles — Bitcoin, ETFs, things like that. But I don't want laws that tell people what to do with their money. That's why I shy away from restrictive laws about things like prediction markets.

十六、给孩子的金融教育与"未来价值电子表格"

>> My last question to you: you've got two kids, like you said. Would you encourage them to study finance?

>> So my 12-year-old daughter has a show on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange — >> You're kidding. Wow. >> — Children's Financial Network — where she interviews big investors and she asks them how they teach their kids about money.

So it is a constant source of conversation in our home. And I think the schools do a horrible job of teaching children financial literacy. And so I think it's incumbent upon all of us — not just in crypto, but in TradFi — to strongly encourage our children to find joy in this particular topic.

>> What is one rule you teach at home?

冲动消费的未来价值 App

>> It's kind of near you. I have a little — I moved it to Claude — I used to have a little spreadsheet on my phone that computed future value.

Money should be for joy. So I don't want to be that "look at everything on the net present value basis" person. But if we walk into a store and want to buy X, and they say "oh, X was great, I also saw Y" — impulse purchase — I make them put the present value of that impulse purchase into this little app (now spreadsheet), and it pops out at a 6% annualized return what that would be in 20 years.

>> Wow. >> And I ask them: "Are you sure you want this? Because this is what you're giving up."

So — opportunity cost and future value calculations. They're super simple to understand. And it forces you to make smart decisions. So: "Sweetheart, would you like this or would you like $120 in 20 years?" And we do it. We have it on my phone. We do it all the time. And their kids are smart. I'd say 80% of the time they go "yeah, I want the 120 bucks." Sometimes they go "I want the toy." But that's okay — they're making an informed decision at that point.

>> I'd be curious to see how their decisions progress as they age. Maybe you can do it every year and track that. >> My 12-year-old does it all the time. She has the math in her head now, and she rounds it up, and she says "you know what, this isn't worth it, Daddy." But now she tracks it, so I have to give her that when she's older.

But I think just basic lessons in opportunity costs. What does it mean to take on risk? When is risk a good risk versus a bad risk? Kids are really smart. They understand this stuff.

>> Excellent. Do you do that when you buy things too? >> All the time. All the time. I think about when I'm 80. We all value different things. I value safety and security. I'd rather have the security of knowing the money's there than the shiny thing. That's my personality. I don't judge other people for how they think about it.

But I think you just have to teach — that's a non-intuitive thing. That math is non-intuitive. And so I think you have to be taught that. I was lucky enough to be taught that at business school. And I think these are not hard concepts. We put jargon around things to make it seem more complicated than it is. Future value versus present value is not a difficult concept.

关于那个"未来自己敲窗"的表情包

You know, there's a meme going on that my daughter has showed me about — like — your future self screaming because you're not studying. All the kids are doing this meme, and it's like — it's funny to them, but it's sad to me. It's like a grown person seeing their teenage self not studying for the test, and like, banging on the window. It's horrifying as an adult. The kids think it's funny.

And I'm trying to help her understand why that's so popular — because it's speaking to a universe of people who wish they could go back in time and make those smart decisions, but they weren't given the ammunition to do so. It was unfair of them. It was unfair to expect them to do that.

So that's what I try to teach — not just my kids. I teach at schools, and I do as much as I can. And my daughter and I are working on a little YouTube video channel that we hope to push out just for that reason. Children's Financial Network. We try to teach kids in fun ways using games we make on Claude — things like opportunity cost and all that stuff.

十七、地位游戏与父亲的第二份工

>> My last question for you: you live in New York. >> New York City. Yes. >> Yes. And people — that was a very obnoxious thing, that was — when you ask somebody, say, "New York" and they go "I live in Staten Island." >> Which I grew up in. I grew up in Staten Island. New York City. I'm very snobbish there. Yes.

>> What — do you ever play the status game? You have to up your car, your houses.

>> I grew up — my mom worked three jobs. My mom cleaned toilets. My dad worked two jobs. I remember when he used to come home from his first job. I used to be waiting for him with my baseball mitt to play catch.

And I remember waiting for the street lights to go on and being very sad and anxious — because I knew they were about to come on, because when the street lights went on, my dad had to get into his car and go to his second job.

And so — no. But I don't want to virtue signal here. I don't begrudge people who want to work hard and have toys. I'm just not — I just didn't grow up like that. So it's just not important to me.

But you know, I have a status of like wanting my daughter to get straight A's. That's my status. So I pay for tutors and things like that. We all splurge on things.

Don't judge. Find out what's important to you. Try to give back a little bit. It's the best you can hope for.

>> That was a beautiful ending. >> Yeah. Well, thank you very much.

尾声

>> I encourage everyone to check out John's daughter's channel. >> Oh, thank you. >> What is it called again? >> The Children's Financial Network. >> Children's Financial Network. And also, you were featured in the book Rigged: The True Story of an Ivy League Kid Who Changed the World of Oil. We don't have time to go over that book, but — >> This one. >> Yeah. What was your — ? >> I was lucky enough to be in a place where I was tasked by the New York Mercantile Exchange to build the first ever oil exchange in the Middle East. >> Yeah. Okay. Check out that book. Check out his channel. Check out our channel. Subscribe.

Thank you very much for watching. Thank you, John.

item.description:
## 一、隐藏的心理钩子：他童年"路灯焦虑"与今日"稳定币福音"是同一件事
John 反复讲的两个故事看似无关——小时候等待路灯亮起时的心痛（因为爸爸要去做第二份工作），以及现在痛斥"银行把 4.5% 利息吞掉、只给客户 10 个基点"——**其实是同一段创伤在两个时空的回响**。他不是在做商业布道，他是在**为童年那个无力的男孩追讨迟到几十年的利息**。这解释了一个悖论：为什么一个华尔街老将会主动放弃 Coinbase 的短期利润去做"复利返还"？因为对他而言，10 basis points vs 3% 复利 20 年 = "一年学费" = **他父亲不必打第二份工的那个平行宇宙**。华尔街最坚定的稳定币收益派，动机是心理学的，不是金融的。
## 二、最反直觉的观察：泡沫是"文明的孵化器"，理性投资才是创新的敌人
他引用与 Nouriel Roubini 合作的研究抛出了一个几乎没人敢说的结论——**资产泡沫期，相关技术专利申请量增长 4 倍**。这意味着：如果所有人都变成"冷静的价值投资者"，人类的技术进步会立即减速。这是一个跨领域的连接——它与**古生物学的"寒武纪大爆发"

item.title: [Mercatus Center] Why Americans Still Argue About the Founding with Thomas Merrill
item.dc:creator: Mercatus Center
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、当"美德的梦"成为自我欺骗的引擎

Merrill 对杰斐逊最锋利的诊断藏在一个看似矛盾的观察里：让杰斐逊背叛《独立宣言》的，不是他的利益，而恰恰是他对"自己是有德之人"的信念。传统的道德叙事总把私利视作原罪——利益扭曲原则、金钱腐蚀灵魂。但杰斐逊的悲剧走得更深：他之所以能在 1790 年后逐渐沉默、在密苏里危机中站到日后卡尔霍恩阵营的一边，不是因为他放弃了自然权利，而是因为他太确信自己"手里握着正确的观念"。"我脑子里有对的东西"这一自信，反而成了他不必真的去做什么的许可证。

这里有一个几乎令人不寒而栗的结构性发现：杰斐逊在《独立宣言》被删除的那段关于奴隶制的文字里，把责任全推给英王——"是他把奴隶制强加给我们"。Merrill 称之为"无辜的暴君"（the innocent tyrant）叙事。这不是虚伪，虚伪太表层了；这是一种更精致的道德结构——把自己塑造为受制于外力的正义者，就无需真的承担改变现状的代价。这个模式在今天几乎无处不在：AI 公司一边警告"超级智能会毁灭人类"，一边加速训练前沿模型并游说限制开源竞争者；ESG 部门的存在本身就成了继续原有商业模式的免罪符。杰斐逊是第一个"表演型自由主义者"，而我们仍活在他开创的这种修辞政治里。

二、一个被忽视的结构陷阱：农业共和主义与奴隶制的物质捆绑

大多数关于建国的讨论把杰斐逊的"自相矛盾"看作观念层面的张力：洛克式的自然权利 vs 古典共和主义的公民美德。但 Merrill 让人看到一个更硬的东西——杰斐逊心中的"美德公民"（自耕农、有土地、能对抗僭主的独立人格），在美国南方的物质条件下，几乎必然要靠奴隶制来维持。他崇拜的那种"上帝的选民"式的农民，其经济基础就是奴隶劳动。于是他的政治联盟——那些能对抗汉密尔顿式金融权力的"农业利益"——恰好就是最深陷奴隶制、日后会孕育出卡尔霍恩派的那批人。

这是一个跨领域的深刻教训：一种理念的道德纯洁性，可能被它所依赖的物质基础悄悄取消。这正是当代技术批评里最难谈的部分——"清洁能源"依赖刚果的钴矿童工，"数字自由"跑在被剥削的东南亚内容审核员之上，"开放科学"由能源密集的算力堆出来。杰斐逊不是没看到矛盾，而是他的整个政治想象力被物质基础反向殖民了：为了保护他心中的"美德共和国"，他必须保护那个让美德得以存在的、不义的生产关系。这是任何一场以"高尚理想"为名的政治都要面对的镜子。

三、一个反直觉的历史因果重排：真正塑造 20 世纪美国的不是 1776，也不是 1619，而是重建时代

这是全场对话里我认为最反常识、也最有政治后果的观察：南方在战场上输掉了内战，但在思想战场上赢了重建。Merrill 提醒我们，1619 和 1776 之争其实都过度聚焦于"起源"——仿佛美国的原罪或荣光在最初一刻就已铸就，此后只是展开。但决定 20 世纪美国种族秩序的关键决策，发生在 1865 到 1900 之间：谁被允许投票、谁的暴力被合法化、哪种历史叙事进入教科书。起源叙事的过度加权，恰恰是逃避近代责任的一种方式——把问题推到"建国父亲"身上，就不用面对我们自己的祖父辈做过什么。

这个因果重排揭示了一个更普遍的模式：当一个共同体反复争论"我们从哪里来"，往往是为了不谈"我们最近做了什么"。这一点惊人地适用于当代科技史。硅谷不断讲述"两个年轻人在车库里"的创世神话，是为了掩盖 2010 年后的一系列关键决策——广告驱动的注意力商业模式、算法推荐的规模化部署、并购竞争者以垄断数据。起源崇拜与近期责任的规避，在结构上是同一件事的两面。

四、一个令人不安的对称性：进步派与保守派共享同一套元结构

Merrill 顺口说出的一个观察值得单独放大："进步"（progressive）和"保守"（conservative）这两个词本身就是相互定义的，它们都是关于"你对变化的态度"的立场，而不是关于"我们要走向什么样的政体"的立场。古代政治学问的是"什么是好的政体"（regime），现代政治问的是"变还是不变"。这意味着——当代美国左右两派，在深层结构上共享着同一个哲学框架，只是分居在时间轴的两端。

这个观察让人后背发凉，因为它解释了为什么政治辩论会陷入某种"结构性同构的对骂"：双方都缺乏对"好生活"本身的实质性描述，只能不断攻击对方对"变化速度"的判断。这也是为什么"后自由主义"（post-liberalism）的兴起并不是复古，而是一次真正的哲学位移——它试图把政治重新拉回到"共同善"的实质讨论。跨到技术领域看，"AI 加速派"（e/acc）与"AI 安全派"其实也是这套时间性立场的翻版：都不问"我们究竟想要什么样的人-机共存秩序"，只争"该跑多快"。真正稀缺的，永远是关于"好"本身的实质想象。

五、"对话的内在无政府主义"作为文明的免疫机制

最后一个让人意外的连接：Merrill 用来描述好的经典阅读研讨课的那个短语——"the inner anarchism of a genuine conversation"（真正对话的内在无政府主义）——其实是一个可以推广到整个自由社会的免疫学原理。经典之所以不会变成教条，恰恰是因为经典之间彼此矛盾：读阿里斯托芬的《云》时苏格拉底否定宙斯，读奥古斯丁《忏悔录》时又满纸上帝。学生被迫在矛盾中自己拼装意义。

这与算法推荐系统的问题形成刺眼的对照。推荐系统把"对话"优化成了"共识"，把"矛盾的经典"替换成了"相似的内容"，于是文明的免疫系统就被抽走了。杰斐逊说宪法应该每 19 年重写一次——他真正抓住的是同一个直觉：任何秩序的正当性都必须由每一代人重新自我立法，否则就会退化为祖先崇拜。而每一代人要能重新立法，就必须先能真正地不同意彼此。这或许是这场关于 250 年前的对话，留给 2026 年的我们最锋利的一份遗产。

📝 转录文本

Why Americans Still Argue About the Founding — with Thomas Merrill

主持人开场

Welcome to Virtual Sentiments. I'm your host, Kristen Collins.

On today's episode, I talk to Dr. Thomas Merrill. Tom is an associate professor in the School of Public Affairs at American University, where he directs the Lincoln Scholars Program, a core techs program for first and second year students. He is the author of Hume and the Politics of Enlightenment, published in 2015 by Cambridge University Press, and he has edited a number of volumes, including The Political Thought of the Civil War, and is a co-editor of the journal American Political Thought.

We discuss Tom's work on early American political thought, especially the writings of Thomas Jefferson, author of the Declaration of Independence. This episode concludes a set of episodes on the 250th anniversary of the American founding, with earlier conversations with Laura Field and Osita Nwanebu. This episode focuses more directly on the historical context of the founding.

We talk about how the tensions and self-contradictions within Thomas Jefferson's long career make him, in Tom's words, "a tragic figure." We talk about how, even as we celebrate the principles of liberty and equality set down in the Declaration, we must also acknowledge the dark side of the founding and the dark sides of our founding fathers, especially as they relate to the legacy of slavery.

Thomas Jefferson was a complicated figure, and by studying him, warts and all, we learn not only about the intellectual strengths of the Declaration's defense of equal rights — which subsequent Americans drew on to overturn slavery and other inherited hierarchies and forms of domination — but also the dangers of self-righteousness, which can blind us to the political implications of our ideas and of the coalitions that we build. Sometimes, even with the best intentions, our actions might lead us down paths contrary to our values and hopes.

And we also talk about the value of higher education, and great books programs in particular, for helping us have difficult conversations about the past while also providing a space to learn from each other, to disagree, and to see how disagreement helps us learn and grow. These are spaces governed by equal respect that provide opportunities for students and teachers alike to reflect on ourselves and our own beliefs.

This episode concludes our regular episodes of this fourth season, although we'll have another crossover episode with my colleague Pete Becky at the Hayek Program podcast next month. If you enjoyed this episode, feel free to check out the rest of this season and our past three seasons. And if you've been an avid listener of Virtual Sentiments, then please share a positive review on your favorite podcasting platform and subscribe or follow so that you don't miss a new episode, especially when our next season premieres. You can also subscribe to my free Substack where I post about each episode and more at Theory of Virtual Sentiments.

Before we get to my conversation with Tom, I also want to thank my fantastic producer, Jacob Ngo, who has made this season such a stellar set of conversations. Thank you for all your hard work.

Without further ado, I hope you all enjoy this conversation with Tom as much as I did.

对话开始：为什么建国仍在被争论

On today's episode of Virtual Sentiments, I talk to Dr. Thomas Merrill. Tom is an associate professor in the School of Public Affairs at American University, where he is also the director of the Lincoln Scholars Program, as well as the associate director at the Political Theory Institute. He is also the editor of the academic journal American Political Thought, and he is the author of Hume and the Politics of Enlightenment from Cambridge University Press, and has edited a number of volumes, including The Political Thought of the Civil War.

Tom, thank you so much for joining me today.

Thanks for having me. It's great to be here.

I'm so excited because this year is a really big anniversary for America. It's the 250th anniversary of the American founding. We are recording this in August, but just last month we had a lot of big celebrations here in D.C. across the country. And this conversation I really see as a part of a small series of episodes that we're doing here. We have an episode with Laura Field on her work and how some people draw on the founding today to critique liberalism or modern liberalism as they see it. And we have an episode with Osita Nwanevu on his work on reflecting on the founding for developing a future vision of America.

And so I kind of thought this episode would really help us get — give a lot of historical context, right? And so I think always when we look back on the founding, we look back at it from our present perspective, but your expertise will really help us kind of give ourselves a deep historical perspective from which we engage with the founding. I think theorists, we often talk about the idea of like the past being like a foreign country in a lot of ways and sort of acknowledging that difference from our time, while we inevitably are going to be kind of looking back through our own lenses and in our own state of things.

They're sort of the predicates to say, yes, the first part of that is true. And so it's providing the evidence for the claim.

And then it concludes with the conclusion, right, which is if you've got a right to rebel under these circumstances, these circumstances exist. Therefore, you know, we are going to rebel. That's the punchline of the declaration.

Sure. You know, it's a great question. And because the founders shape our lives, we have — we are very interested in like who they were as human beings. And I always say that when you love something, like everything has got dark sides, right? You have to pay attention to the whole thing, right?

And so this question about Sally Hemings is extremely interesting. And so now scholars believe that Jefferson was in a long-term relationship with a woman named Sally Hemings who was an enslaved woman. We believe that it started in France, that Sally Hemings was a teenage — basically like an au pair for Jefferson's daughters.

And now the context is important. Jefferson is married. Jefferson — we think of him as an Enlightenment figure, but he also has these like very romantic in the sense of early 19th century kind of like novel, like Heathcliff or something like that. So Jefferson is married. His wife dies — childbirth, I believe, but in the early 1780s — and he's devastated. And he never has another — he never gets married again. So far as we know, there's never like a serious relationship with a woman, except for Sally Hemings.

Now, the interesting thing about Sally Hemings is that the whole milieu is already so affected by relationship between slave owners and slave women, right? That miscegenation — like, you know, mixed race, which I'm not totally comfortable with the phrase itself — but Sally Hemings herself is the product of, we believe, a union of Jefferson's wife's father with an enslaved woman who is already the product of a previous union between a white man and a black woman. So, which is to say — and this is the thing that's really weird — is that Sally Hemings is Jefferson's wife's half-sister.

Oh, wow. Okay?

Yeah. And by reports, she's quite light-skinned and that she looks like the half-sister. Yeah. Okay? So, I think one would need some sort of deep psychological account. Yeah. Right? Like, you know, some Freudian thing that Jefferson is, in a way, having a relationship with the closest thing he can get to this deceased wife. So that's what we know from the background. Scholars think — and I have to give a shout out to the scholar who's done the most amount of work on this, which is Annette Gordon-Reed at Harvard. And her account, which I don't know enough to judge whether or not it's true, she believes that Sally Hemings and Jefferson got together in France and that Sally Hemings was able to force Jefferson to cut a deal with her. And from what we know, it looks like the Hemings family was treated in a different way than other enslaved families. So that's a great question. So I run a program that's a core text program and which is in some ways modeled on St. John's College in Annapolis. But our — sort of the ideas of the program are, number one, we're reading and discussing big questions in community, and that it's a practice, it's not a teaching.

So, you know, in two weeks, I'm going to be sitting down with a bunch of 18-year-olds, and we're going to be starting on Plato's Apology. But when we sit around a common table, when we come to the table, we come as equals. And we're trying to use the text to raise big human questions. We're not trying to learn about the text. So — we're both political theorists. We've been in classes where the professor will present a survey. There's a place for that. It's totally useful. That's not what we're trying to do. I think that kind of education — number one, it puts you in community with other people, which we badly, badly need. And there are going to be people who disagree with each other. And I do — I don't want to make big claims about what liberal education can do. I do think that it could moderate our politics by allowing people to engage from a place more of self-knowledge rather than a place of — and just recognizing that the world is actually complicated, that it's not — you can't boil it down to this one thing. So, yeah, so I think there is a kind of practical wisdom that comes out of liberal education that is good for people if they're going to go into a job after college, if they're going to go into politics after college.

Yeah, totally. No, I think that's really correct. And I think that the danger of the great books thing is that it gets reduced to "here's the books that a serious person has to read." And that leads to, you know, people feeling insulted. And, you know, there's a whole debate. It's a certain amount of contingency about who ends up on the list. But look, I mean, the books are there because of the seminar. The seminar is the crucial thing. And in the seminar, you know, the conversation is open-ended. The text is an incredible resource. But you're there trying to figure things out for yourself. And there's a kind of inner anarchism to a genuine conversation, to a genuine seminar conversation, that is the necessary counterweight to "we have these books that are important."

And I would also say you have to think about a class like that as defined by the set of texts and the texts contradict each other, right? They're not all on the same page. But we, you know, we are all — we're in the class, we're called to take each one of those texts seriously. So we'll read Aristophanes' Clouds, right, where the character Socrates says there's no Zeus, right? And then we'll read the Confessions, and, you know, it's all about God all the time. How does a person make sense of that? How does a person navigate like what those different worldviews look like. That's the promise of [it]. Yeah.

收尾：分歧、人的尊严、以及杰斐逊会想看什么

Yeah, yeah. No, I think that that makes — that's a great way to put it. I mean, I think we're nearing a kind of natural end of the conversation. Is there anything that we didn't get to do justice to in your mind that we'd like to talk about?

Um, well, I mean this — there have been lots of people in American history who have had the conversation that we just had, right? And I think, you know, one thing that lots of people do, but we could do more in America higher education. Frederick Douglass has that speech on "What to the Slaves of the Fourth of July." It's a profound meditation on these things that I think gives ammunition or gives support to a lot of different positions on the political spectrum. I think that's the — especially on conversations around the founding. I think it would be good if American universities could say, "look, we're going to have this conversation. All views are going to be at the table. We welcome, you know, whatever anyone wants to say. We're going to talk this through. We're going to attend to this text." I think that would be a healthy way of trying to grapple with this thing. Too often universities want to avoid serious disagreement.

Yeah. And I think that's a mistake.

Yeah. No, and I do think — I think just as a general thing, you know, disagreement is such a key part of, I don't know, a free society and learning. And I think I also think a lot of people want that, I think. And I think there's a lot of even people who disagree. I definitely know people who are younger who, and part of it is, you know, is COVID and the anxiety, you know, and to be clear with COVID, it's not just, yes, you know, people, you know, lockdowns and not being — or I don't want to say lockdown because it's complicated in the U.S., but yes, like COVID, you know, people were home, students weren't able to be in schools, right? And that itself was hard. But also, if people had been in schools more and had been COVID, that also would have been very hard and scary for students as well. So either way you cut it, that pandemic was going to be really rough on the young generation.

And I think for younger people who — I definitely know there are people who are — shy, who are, you know, worried about expressing themselves. And it's not that they don't want to, it's that they kind of want to learn those skills and to be engaging in that. And in fact, and I would say like in our seminars, I definitely think like our fellowships, we really do create space for critique and disagreement and engagement and also in a way that I think is welcoming and I hope and it seems to be something that where people feel comfortable to do that. And I think especially kind of the more spaces we have like that the better for [it]. And it won't be, you know, I think as we've just been talking about the founding, we've been talking about politics, we've been talking about like major conflicts and interests and all sorts of parts of politics that have nothing to do with what happens in a classroom, and a classroom is not going to change that. But it is a key part, I think, though, of also this idea of also retaining this vision of, you know, rights matter and also civic skills matter and habits matter and the culture we create matters.

Yeah. Can I connect this back to the earlier part of our conversation that, you know, the sort of the core idea of the Declaration of Independence — [if you'd] leave aside all the complications — you know, all men are created equal, human beings are created equal — it's a vision of human dignity that — and I think liberal education, you know, within organizations, there's something to be said for aristocracy, for people making decisions. But liberal education is a space in which we come to the table as equals and it's meant to be a space for people to practice working out their own takes on things. And it's founded on a basic belief of human dignity. And so I just don't think that we should let go of that or lose sight of the fact that we might do it badly certainly as a country. We've messed up in, you know, many, many different ways. But there's something praiseworthy and noble about that that we need to hold on to.

Yeah. And that kind of — and having that shared commitment to having that equal respect is crucial. And I think, you know, from the point of — I mean, I think partly Jefferson, if you were around today, I'm sure there'd be a lot of complicated things but he'd be like, "guys, you're in charge of your own fates. You don't have to sit around waiting for those stupid founders to solve your problems."

Yeah. Do you know The Onion? One of my favorite Onion articles is if the founders were around today, they'd be too busy shoving things into a garbage disposal and it's sink-shrink.

Yeah, just seeing how it works. I think that's — you know, as a political theorist, as somebody who loves reading all these dead figures, I mean, it's always humbling to remember if they were alive today, they would not want to talk to us about all these ideas. They'd want to just see all this crazy junk that we have now.

Right, right, right, right, right. Okay. Well, I really love talking to you so much, Tom. This is really fantastic. I could keep going, but I think this is a nice bit of conversation to share with people. So thank you so much for joining us.

Thank you. I appreciate it. It's a great thing that you're doing. Oh, thank you. And, you know, look forward to hearing the episode and seeing the others.

Yeah. Thank you. Awesome. Awesome. Yay.

主持人结语：从杰斐逊到 AI —— 自义的危险

As usual, I want to wrap up with a few reflections on Tom's great insights.

Tom gave us a great overview of the historical context of the founding and of America's early years. And in doing so, he helped us avoid the pitfalls of either excessively glorifying the founding fathers, nor completely vilifying them either. Instead, we see how they were working within a particular political economic moment that inspired and constrained their actions and writings.

I loved Tom's points about how the tensions and contradictions of the founding become easier to comprehend if we think of the founding as a nascent civil war. Both Tom and Osita Nwanevu get at this in their works. Especially as the early Americans work towards the U.S. Constitution, they make a lot of compromises in accommodating slavery, which was in the interests of many of the participants in these political discussions. And they do this in order to keep the country acting as one whole and establish the modern American state. We cannot ignore how this political history continues to shape our culture, as well as Americans' sense of national identity and the meanings of these founding texts, like the Declaration and the Constitution, to our own politics today.

I love Tom's arguments about Jefferson being more than a hypocrite or hero, but a tragic figure. And you can read the essay where he discusses this in the show notes. For me, the appeal of this thesis has as much to do with Jefferson and understanding him in context as it does with the timelessness of the lessons that his story may hold for us today. Often we think that people fail to realize good moral values in our actual political reality because of things like the corrupting effect of self-interest. And I do think interest is important. We need to understand how interest motivates behaviors, both in private and public spheres, and how the pursuit of interest can be at odds with one's principles and values, as well as the good of society. But this does also distract from the fact that the risks of self-righteousness, a faith in one's own virtue or moral goodness, might end up being its own source of self-delusion. Confidence in my moral infallibility might make me turn a blind eye to the dangerous beliefs and actions of my political allies, or neglect that we actually do not share the same values at the end of the day, or it might mean that I end up acting in a manner that is ironically even more likely to create the suffering or bring about the dystopian world that I am trying to avoid in the first place.

We didn't talk about tech and AI much in this episode, but since Virtual Sentiments is all about using historical perspective to think deeply about digital technologies today, I will just be explicit that when I think about these aspects of Jefferson's legacy, I actually think a lot about the most pressing topics of discussion today, which is the rise of AI. What comes to mind for me are companies that are currently sounding alarms about the existential dangers of runaway, misaligned, super-intelligent AI while using these risks to justify, first, their race towards building it themselves, and secondly, towards pushing for, lobbying for, restricting open model competitors on the basis of these risks. At the same time, companies engage in ethics washing or championing their employment of philosophers and other thinkers as illustrating just how committed they are to being morally upstanding in their work. But the most important thing is that companies are well-structured and investing in and listening to privacy and security teams, as Catherine Jarmol discussed in our July episode. Otherwise, this is all a little bit like cheap talk rather than actually ensuring responsible innovation and business practices.

Finally, to get back to the topics of the episode, Tom and I also discussed the value of a great book's education. And I think that this can be applied more widely to all sorts of humanities classes that are rooted in a seminar setting. I love Tom's point about how the dangers of treating the books we read as grand authorities to which we must defer can and should be mitigated by the very nature of a well-organized discussion seminar. The books are always a part of a set of texts. And so ideally, these books are often in tension and direct contradiction with one another. The reading list then illustrates the value of disagreement and debate, the fact that history was not one uniform monoculture after another. It was defined by disagreement. And I love this turn of phrase from Tom: the inner anarchism of a genuine conversation is the necessary counterweight to the tendency to defer to the text. Students and instructors sit as equals with a goal of attaining self-knowledge, of clarifying, questioning, and refining our own commitments and ideas.

As I mentioned at the start of the episode, this is our last episode of our regular season. But next month, we'll be back with a crossover episode with my colleague Pete Becky at the Hayek Program podcast. So keep an eye out for that one. If you enjoyed this season of Virtual Sentiments, please review and subscribe so you don't miss when our next season comes out. And feel free to follow me at Substack at Theory of Virtual Sentiments.

Thank you so much for listening. It really means a lot. And I'm so grateful to be able to have these conversations with you. Till next time.

Oh —

## 一、当"美德的梦"成为自我欺骗的引擎
Merrill 对杰斐逊最锋利的诊断藏在一个看似矛盾的观察里：**让杰斐逊背叛《独立宣言》的，不是他的利益，而恰恰是他对"自己是有德之人"的信念**。传统的道德叙事总把私利视作原罪——利益扭曲原则、金钱腐蚀灵魂。但杰斐逊的悲剧走得更深：他之所以能在 1790 年后逐渐沉默、在密苏里危机中站到日后卡尔霍恩阵营的一边，不是因为他放弃了自然权利，而是因为他太确信自己"手里握着正确的观念"。**"我脑子里有对的东西"这一自信，反而成了他不必真的去做什么的许可证**。
这里有一个几乎令人不寒而栗的结构性发现：杰斐逊在《独立宣言》被删除的那段关于奴隶制的文字里，把责任全推给英王——"是他把奴隶制强加给我们"。Merrill 称之为"无辜的暴君"（the innocent tyrant）叙事。**这不是虚伪，虚伪太表层了；这是一种更精致的道德结构——把自己塑造为受制于外力的正义者，就无需真的承担改变现状的代价**。这个模式在今天几乎无处不在：AI 公司一边警告"超级智能会毁灭人类"，一边加速训练前沿模型并游说限制开源竞争者；ESG 部门的存在本身就成了

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一场加州"资源诅咒"的深层病理

Peter Thiel 那句"硅谷是加州的资源诅咒"（resource curse），在 Steve Hilton 的十分钟叙事里被反向验证了——这是全场最被低估、也最反直觉的洞察。

传统的"资源诅咒"讨论石油国家：委内瑞拉、尼日利亚、沙特。它们坐拥地下财富，反而不需要建立良治，因为税基从地下涌出而非从公民口袋。加州完成了这一诅咒模型的"知识经济版本"：硅谷替代了油井，代码替代了原油，资本利得税替代了石油特许权使用费。政府因此无需向公民负责——反正钱会来。这解释了为何"过去十年预算翻倍、人口净减 200 万"这个数学上的荒谬能长期稳定存在。加州不是一个失败的民主州，它是一个石油国家披着蓝色外衣。

"合法性"作为最深层的腐败载体

Spencer Pratt 在争辩到最激烈时说了一句极容易被忽视的话："我不是说他们作弊，问题在于——法律被设计成让他们做的事不叫作弊。"

这句话打开的问题远比选举本身要大。真正的系统性腐败从来不是违法，而是立法——把原本会被视为舞弊的行为写入法条，让批评者陷入"你连法律都不懂"的失语。街头摊贩合法化法案、非营利组织派发针管的资助结构、邮寄选票签名与信封的强制脱钩——这些都不是漏洞，是特性（feature, not bug）。

跨领域连接：这在金融领域有一个完美镜像——2008 年前的次贷证券化。没有一个环节是违法的：评级机构给 AAA 是合法的，投行打包 CDO 是合法的，贷款员发放无收入证明贷款是合法的。灾难恰恰产生于"每一步都合法"的合成物。加州的政治机制走上了同一条路：它不是被腐败入侵，它是被合法化了。

洛杉矶火灾与"倒置激励"的热力学

Spencer 讲述了整个访谈里最出人意料的因果链：加州州立公园法规保护一种叫"milk vetch"（紫云英）的植物，禁止清除枯枝——于是 6 十年枯燥可燃物在社区周围堆积，最终燃烧的不是植物而是他家、他父母家、他邻居的家。50 万美元的防火隔离带没有被划出，随后是数十亿美元的赔付黑洞。

这不是"环保过头"的老套故事。这里有个更深的系统性真相：当一个系统同时给两个不可兼容的目标写入了不可撤销的合规条款，它必然进入自燃状态。加州同时承诺（1）保护每一株濒危植物（2）在野火频发气候中维护住宅安全。这两条法规同时被立法且都不能违反——热力学上不可能，因此系统选择了让居民而非法规承受违规成本。

这与航空业有个残酷类比：波音的 MCAS 系统之所以失败，是因为它试图同时满足两个不兼容的合规要求——新发动机气动特性 + 沿用旧型号培训认证。当合规约束互相打架时，系统不会崩溃在监管上，而是崩溃在乘客身上。加州的合规约束打架时，崩溃在了 Palisades 居民身上。

一个更让人不安的观察

Steve Hilton 提到那对拉丁裔鞋店夫妇："做对的事被惩罚，做错的事被奖励。"如果你把这句话作为滤镜扫描整个转录，你会发现它不是加州的问题——它是任何一个把复杂性无限累积而不做定期垃圾回收的系统的最终状态。1,118 条年度法案的堆叠、42 万条现行法规、街头摊贩合法化叠加在鞋店 14 年的税单之上——这不是意识形态问题，这是软件工程里没有 refactor 的代码库的下场。

真正令人意外的推论是：这不能被"投票"解决。你可以换掉执行代码的 CPU（州长），但你无法通过投票让代码库重构。Steve Hilton 提出把法规从 42 万削减到 20 万——这在软件术语里就是一次 delete 50% of the codebase 的操作。历史上，任何组织自愿完成这种量级重构的案例，几乎为零。它们通常只在破产之后发生。这就是为什么 Spencer 那句半开玩笑的话可能才是真正的诊断："要等四年纯粹的毁灭后，人们才会打电话给我。"

📝 转录文本

开场：一位不寻常的加州州长候选人

A candidate for the governor of California who is extremely unique in a number of ways. First of all, he's a Republican. And second, he's a Brit. Welcome to the program, Steve Hilton.

It's a joke. I mean, what are these Democrats doing? We already have the highest taxes in the country. Your first 100 grand tax-free. Even Katie Porter agrees with that.

Prior to that, he was in Silicon Valley as a tech entrepreneur.

People are so sick of the nonsense. Is everything twice as good when they've doubled the budget? Of course not. California means to America what America means to the world.

Please welcome Steve Hilton. Wake up. Wake up, buddy. Let's go.

— Hi. — All right. Wake up, California. We have seven weeks to save our state. Are you ready? — Are we going to do it? We got seven weeks. That's all. But we can do it. — Seven weeks. Um, there's a lot of people here who aren't from California. — Well, actually, who's from California? Raise your hand. Some. Yeah.

加州为何重要

— But help explain why California is so important.

— California is not just the biggest state, the richest state and the richest most important country on earth. It's — as I said just then, and you saw — California means to America what America means to the world. I'm an immigrant, moved here in 2012, neighbors with Chamath. So how about that? I picked a good spot.

And I was inspired by this state. It represents for me and for so many people over the century-plus that this state has been growing and leading in so many ways — the absolute essence of what we love about America. Innovation and energy and ambition and hustle and that kind of rebel spirit — that's why we've created so many industries here that have completely transformed the world, starting right here in Los Angeles over a century ago: the entertainment industry, obviously tech that you're all so familiar with, but also our great agriculture — we have the leading agriculture industry in the world. In so many different fields we have led the world. That's why it's so important we don't let California go down any further.

州情诊断：全国最差的一系列指标

— What is the state of the state then?

— This state, I'm afraid, despite all our incredible advantages — and of course, we still have them: the things that the people in charge haven't managed yet to ruin, our incredible natural beauty and the weather and the energy that you see in our startup communities, the best innovation ecosystem anywhere in the world, great universities. But look at the facts. We've had 16 years of one party in control.

Today in California, we have the highest poverty rate in the country, the highest unemployment rate, the highest cost of living by far. Look at housing cost — the highest in the country. That's why people are leaving. They are leaving. Millions of people leaving California, this beautiful place.

— You got two right here.

— Exactly. Chief Executive Magazine has ranked California in its annual survey of business leaders for more than a decade 50th out of 50 for business climate. It's just incredible when you look at the range of issues where the policies that we've been subjected to have just created the worst outcomes. Not just bad in comparison to other states — the worst out of every state.

一党执政的根源分析

— So look, we know how you measure the outcome, but go back a few layers and think about the root causes. Democrats have run this state for a long time. Democrats used to be sort of peace and love and permissiveness and openness. So corral that for us — because I think this is a place that has become rules on top of rules on top of rules. How did a group of people who basically were just like peace and love and leave us alone become the rule police?

— It's exactly right. This is what happens with one-party rule, actually, and you see that in history — whether from the right or the left, it always ends up with a kind of insular, self-regarding elite that just forgets about their responsibility to everyone else and gets obsessed with their own ideology, their internal motivations, whoever their interest groups are that they represent.

And by the way, in Sacramento, we have one of the most corrupt systems anywhere in the country in terms of the power of the donors to the politicians who make the decisions — the unions, the trial lawyers. That's why we have the worst litigation risk anywhere in the country. You run a business in California, you start a business in California — 90% chance you're going to end up in litigation. So it's just a complete mess when you get one-party rule.

Now, 16 years, the Democrats have run everything. All eight statewide elected positions, the state legislature with a two-thirds majority, every big county, every big city, the state supreme court with a 6-1 Democrat-appointed majority. So this is what happens. The rules get piled up because every year they pass legislation that just adds to the burden and the bloat.

1,118 条法案的重量

Last year, the Sacramento legislature passed 1,118 bills. So we printed them out.

— Very productive.

— We'd very exact productivity going up there. We're going to be doing this year's in Sacramento on Thursday. We printed it all out. I mean, I'm not that tall, but it was twice my height. Okay. Nobody's reading this. You think Gavin Newsom is reading all this before signing it? No. It's written in the interests of the narrow groups that control that process and it benefits them but hurts everybody else.

That's why we have by far the highest regulatory blow. That's why one of the things I'm announcing today actually is that we're going to cut the number of regulations in California from where we are today — which is over 420,000 — by the end of my first term to under 200,000, which makes us competitive with the rest of the country.

打破"机器"：胜选路径

— If there's a narrow interest group that controls the legislature, is it not also the case that that narrow interest group controls the machinery that I would argue doesn't necessarily elect people, but appoints people, which makes it difficult for rational outsiders to have a shot at a true democratic campaign? That they own the ballot harvesting machines, that they own the campaigning machines, that they get everyone in the state behind them — all the unions, all the votes, everything is aligned under one controlled mechanism. And therefore, it has at this point gotten so far down the road that it is impenetrable and we cannot actually break in.

— Well, it's definitely the case that we have this very powerful and corruptly funded machine that's running everything. I agree with that. In fact, one of the ways that we're telling the story of this campaign is: the people versus the machine. That's what this is.

But there's a majority of Californians who want change. That's clear from every single poll. When we started the general election part of this campaign, if you look at the primary results on primary night in California in the governor's race — myself and the other Republican — that's 35%. I got 25%, the other Republican 10. You add up all the Democrats, 65%. That's a 30-point gap. The first poll came out, it was a 25-point gap. I know a lot of people were discouraged by that, but we were just beginning our campaign.

And look what's happened just in the last couple of months: from a 30-point gap on primary night to 25 points, 18 points, 14 points. The latest poll — an 8-point gap. We are showing that people want change in this state.

And I just don't accept that we have to put up with this — that your only choice is to put up with all this nonsense and bloat and tax and cost and all the hassles of living here, or trying to work here — your only choice is to put up with it or leave. That, if I may say so as a new American citizen, is a very un-American attitude — that it can't be done, that we can't make change happen. We've got to fight for it.

民主党选民的心理转变

— Steve, why do you think that people feel that it would be almost a betrayal, even if they want change, to not vote Democrat? There seems to be in California, at least as I've lived it, a lot of very rational people who feel sort of out of place. They're not quite sure whether they should be a Republican. They're made to feel guilty for not being completely a Democrat. So they either don't vote or they just go in and they find the D and check the box. And so all of the insanity sort of compounds. If that continues to happen, don't we need to hit rock bottom? Isn't there going to be some financial event or otherwise that needs to happen to reset?

— I got to tell you, I think it's pretty rock bottom now in terms of what it's actually like to live here. I've traveled this state. I've been to every one of our 58 counties. No candidate's done that in a very long time. We've done hundreds of events, town halls up and down the state. Every single day, I see the pain and the struggle in people's eyes to live here.

You try and own a home here. We used to have the highest rate of home ownership in the country in California and the most affordable housing. Now the median house price in California is nearly a million dollars. The median salary in California for an individual: 65,000. I mean it's just completely broken. People are broken by this and they are desperate for change.

The number one thing that people say to me when they come up to me at the airport or the street — wherever we are at my events — it's not "good luck, hope you do well." There's an intensity this year. It's almost word for word. This is what everyone says to me. I've heard it even here backstage: "You have to win." There's an intensity about it this year.

一个 911 纪念活动上的场景

I was at the 9/11 memorial event in Sacramento — not there participating, just there to show my respects. I took my seat in the back. People came up to take pictures. Just there randomly in a pretty small event. I had a number of people — must have been four or five people — just randomly all almost said the same word-for-word thing: "I'm a lifelong Democrat, but I'm voting for you this year."

I think we have reached that point. And that's why I'm saying we've got to wake up — because the other thing I hear all the time from business leaders or business owners every single day is: "If you don't make it in November, we're out." I'm serious about this. If we think it's bad now, I think the exodus of business we've seen from California in the last couple of years, if we don't show some change here and some balance in our system, it's going to turn into a stampede for the exits.
