第五贝斯蒂候选人？

— What are you doing next? Let's move on past this.

— This is it. I —

— You're joining the show? Fifth bestie.

— I have Zoom. You know, so — you have Zoom and you have time. I do love premium tequila.

— This could work. Fifth bestie.

— There's a lot of — I mean, Brad Gerstner is very popular, but I think we might need to move him to sixth bestie.

Palisades 火灾：为什么至今无法重建

— What I will continue doing because I only ever ran for mayor to increase my message of fighting these people who have destroyed my beautiful state, my beautiful city and then —

— And your home.

— My home, my parents' home, all my neighbors.

— Let me ask you a question about the incompetence of these idiots. They burn your home down because they can't keep water in the reservoir. Have you been able to rebuild? What's the state of the Palisades right now?

— Here's the best part. That empty reservoir is still empty. And the reservoir across the street from my house — that I was convinced my house was never going to burn — the one they didn't even talk about — that one's still empty. They have a hose. I just posted a video about this. They have a hose that comes all the way from Topanga through all the regrown dead brush. This is the hose now supplying the Palisades.

保险、"紫云英"与防火隔离带

But back to rebuilding. We all had Farmers and all these great insurance. But I don't blame the insurance companies, because it's our Gavin Newsom and our state parks that allowed the 60 years of dead fuels, dead brush to surround our communities knowing that there's no fire break.

All they would have had to do — I talked to the top guy that does all the cutting of this brush — I said, "How much would this have cost to cut a whole fire break, 300 yards around the Palisades?" He said under $500,000 to save billions of dollars.

Back to rebuilding: insurance dropped everybody because they were smart. They saw all this dead brush in every… It's illegal if I go cut. So if my backyard has Gavin Newsom State Park dead brush coming into it, if I cut it — those are protected milk vetch. You're going to get a fine. The LADWP got fined $1 million for cutting some dead brush around a downed pole in these state parks.

So the CARB — who's in charge of this, these people that care more about plants — they're also ruining the federal fire service right now, and they're fighting the federal government right now to protect these plants again over people.

So back to building: no, I won't be able to build until we win the lawsuit against Gavin Newsom and his state parks and the city and the LADWP, which we are.

万人集体诉讼与新年除夕的余烬

— What is the lawsuit that you filed?

— It's a mass tort. There's 10,000 victims for the negligence they let. People don't realize because they're not in the weeds — or should we say in the milk vetch — on this.

On New Year's Eve, there was a fire in the Pacific Palisades — 8 acres. They put it out. The state park did not monitor that fire, which is in their state park manual, and they let it smolder leading into a known wind event that was coming on January 6th, January 7th.

I've now had firefighter whistleblowers tell me that there was clearly smoldering coals on the side of this hill. And now in the depositions with the state park employees, we have their photos. They took photos of the hillside just smoking. And when asked, "Why didn't you do anything?" they say, "Oh, we're not firefighters."

So the state park is liable for allowing a dangerous condition to burn down the community. The LADWP is liable for leaving the reservoirs empty and having no water. And the city is liable.

参选的真正意义

— So basically you're just trying to set the record straight, hopefully get back some recompense for you and these other families — but is most of it this first part of just making the record public of all of this incompetence and the hope that people realize that it doesn't need to be this way?

— That was initially why I was out making my videos and doing the content to help my community. And then when I saw Mayor Bass was just automatically going to be the mayor again, I was like, "Oh, no way." And then I called Rick Caruso. I said, "Are you going to run or what?" He's like, "No." I was like, "Oh, it's on."

So then I ran with the intention to just try to stop her from becoming mayor. If that meant me being mayor — honestly, people are like, "Oh, you have no experience." Oh, to enforce the law. What LA needs is a mayor that enforces the law. Neither Mayor Bass nor Nithya Raman have any intention of enforcing the laws because it doesn't look good. It doesn't look good if you tell the illegal food vendors that they can't ruin a small business that's been paying taxes for 40 years. "Oh, you're messing with this community, this at-risk community." No, this is illegal — they're destroying this family's business.

So these simple things I would have been able to do as mayor. It's unfortunate that it's going to take four years of pure destruction for people to call me up in four years like, "Let's go" — and I'll be ready.

从洛杉矶到纽约：媒体、真相与愤怒

— Spencer, are you still doing content? What are you doing right now with your time?

— There's three opportunities in play. And yes — content. What I realized when I got out of this — and this sounds very pot-lies — is there's so many lies that I witnessed all day long firsthand in my city that I was like, "I need to be out here making content with the truth." It's not — it's in the center. I keep saying, people are like, "Oh, he's a Republican." No, the truth doesn't have a side. That's that simple. And these people across the country now are trying to destroy it. They truly are.

And when you start living this all day long like me, it's not for LA now. I'm like, "Damn, I got to fight for America. Like, I'm like Jason Bourne. This is crazy." So yeah, now I'm flying to New York and meeting with people in New York, trying to help them, because I don't want New York to go down even worse than —

— I have a suggestion for you. So what were the other two things? You said there was three things.

Skid Row 数据中心构想

— There there's three plays. I mean, I was going to be the big guy in AI as mayor because I was going to turn Skid Row into all just data centers.

— I mean, you're weaving. You're speaking our language.

— I actually had a call trying to get the information about data centers with a guy that knows data centers. He said — and he said — "Spencer, do you understand this is the time for a city like LA whose infrastructure is collapsing into the ground to take private business and billions of dollars, be like: 'Hey, yes, you can put this data center where we have naked drug-addict zombies and no actual human being can go for 50 blocks. We're going to put that here. But you need to redo our water pipes. You need to redo our —'"

— We can retrain the fentanyl addicts to be electricians. Meta's got a program for that.

— You know, as I drove over here, I — you know, I was going to solve a lot of problems.

为什么不做真人秀

— But Spencer, in all seriousness — you're incredibly quick-witted and entertaining on camera. You should consider doing reality TV.

— You know why I don't like reality TV? And it's the only thing worse than people in politics — is there's too much image crafting. And that's what makes bad reality shows. Now everyone is image crafting, trying to create a persona. "What's going to be in the comment section? What are people going to say on the blogs?" You cannot be… real. Like the last reality show I was on when they rebooted The Hills —

— You were on a reality show?

— A couple. A couple. You know, I am the reality candidate. That's a reality check.

But everybody was just faking their actual identity. And now what's so funny is if you watch any politician, they're just a bad TikTok influencer. You look at Abdul — say, he thinks he's Alix Earle. It's like — what are you doing?

— Honestly, I just got to tell you, I love you. And what a mistake — because not only would you have gotten some great done, this would have been the most entertaining mayorship in history.

— Well, he's got time.

— Yeah, you got to run again.

— This is — yeah, I know. What's funny is I actually am way more of a threat to these people now, because I have —

— You're dangerous.

— Two years to really get into these communities.

最后一刻：DSA 是谁？

— I suggest you torture them. Torture Karen Bass for the next two years.

— You know, Karen Bass is not our worst nightmare. And I will never say anything positive — Nithya Raman and the DSA people. People do not get — my Democrat friends do not understand what the DSA is. I keep telling them: go on their website. It's not a conspiracy. Read their website and you tell me — abolish the police. Yes.

I mean, the list goes on and on and this is what they stand by. And then I used to call them commies and everybody was like, "Oh, you can't call them commies." Now I'm like — that sounds nice.

— It's a compliment to them. They're anarchists. Like gassing them up like crazy.

— Ladies and gentlemen, Spencer Pratt. Wow. Thanks, bro. All right. Great stuff.

item.description:
## 一场加州"资源诅咒"的深层病理
Peter Thiel 那句"硅谷是加州的资源诅咒"（resource curse），在 Steve Hilton 的十分钟叙事里被反向验证了——这是全场最被低估、也最反直觉的洞察。
传统的"资源诅咒"讨论石油国家：委内瑞拉、尼日利亚、沙特。它们坐拥地下财富，反而不需要建立良治，因为税基从地下涌出而非从公民口袋。**加州完成了这一诅咒模型的"知识经济版本"**：硅谷替代了油井，代码替代了原油，资本利得税替代了石油特许权使用费。政府因此无需向公民负责——反正钱会来。这解释了为何"过去十年预算翻倍、人口净减 200 万"这个数学上的荒谬能长期稳定存在。加州不是一个失败的民主州，它是一个石油国家披着蓝色外衣。
## "合法性"作为最深层的腐败载体
Spencer Pratt 在争辩到最激烈时说了一句极容易被忽视的话："**我不是说他们作弊，问题在于——法律被设计成让他们做的事不叫作弊。**"
这句话打开的问题远比选举本身要大。真正的系统性腐败从来不是违法，而是**立法**——把原本会被视为舞弊的行为写入法条，让批评者陷入"你连法律都不懂"的失语

item.title: [Latent Space] 🔬 Google's AI Scientist Started as an Attempt to Automate Kaggle — John Platt, Google Fellow
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的核心颠覆：ERA 的真正起源，是"自动化 Kaggle"

大多数关于 AI 科学家的宣传都把它塑造成一场自上而下的"科学革命"，但 John 无意间揭示了一个更诡异的真相：Google 的 AI 科学家，起点是"打 Kaggle 比赛"。这不是浪漫的科学梦，而是一个极其功利的工程问题——如何让机器在排行榜上赢过人类。

这里有一个让人后脊发凉的观察：科学本身可能正在被"Kaggle 化"。当你能把一切科学问题映射为"可打分任务"时，你其实是在把科学的本体论从"寻找真理"悄悄替换为"最大化某个函数"。John 自己也警觉地指出——Goodhart 定律（任何指标一旦成为目标，就不再是好指标）如今应用于每一个排行榜。这意味着 AI for Science 面临的最大风险不是算法弱，而是整个科学范式正在滑向一种"高维过拟合的文明"——我们越擅长优化分数，就越可能失去对"世界真实结构"的把握。

二、跨领域连接：进化算法为何 50 年没用，却突然复活了？

这里藏着一个惊人的跨领域联系。John 提到进化式代码变异从 70 年代起就存在，但从未起飞——因为"在代码空间的随机突变几乎毫无价值，就像 DNA，大多数突变是有害的"。

真正的类比不是"AI 加速进化"，而是"AI 扮演了寒武纪大爆发中的发育调控基因（Hox genes）"。 生物学中的一个反直觉发现是：寒武纪之所以出现物种爆炸，不是因为突变率提高，而是因为发育调控网络（gene regulatory network）让突变变得"有方向"——一个 Hox 基因突变可以整体重塑一个身体分区。

Gemini 在 ERA 里扮演的正是这个角色：它不是让突变更快，而是让突变空间坍缩到"合理的梯度"上。这解释了为什么 Gemini 2.0 时代不行、2.5 时代突然可行——不是 LLM 变强了，而是它的"世界先验"密度终于足够高，能够作为一个"发育调控器"起作用。AI for Science 的关键不是计算力，而是先验知识密度的相变（phase transition）。

三、你没意识到的悖论：气候科学比生物学更"AI-抗性"

一个让人意外的洞察埋在对话深处：John 说气候比天气难做 AI，不是因为它复杂，而是因为它非平稳（non-stationary）——吸引子本身在移动。

但真正让人啊哈的是他随后的比喻："contrails（飞机凝结尾）的物理，其实和气候模型的深层不确定性直接耦合"。冰晶如何在云中沉降，取决于晶体形状；晶体形状取决于微观物理；而微观物理的近似误差，会在气候预测里放大成300 ppm 的 CO2 不确定性——几乎相当于现在整个大气浓度的 2/3。

这是一个鲜有人指出的系统性真相：气候科学的核心瓶颈，不在气候模型，而在你飞机窗外那道白线的形状。 这正是复杂系统的可怕之处——局部微观机制以非线性方式支配全局命运。

而这条线索还可以进一步跨界：这正好呼应了 John 对生物学的评价——"生物系统里全是例外和 hacks"。所以你可以推演出一个更大的假设：凡是"非平稳、多尺度耦合、数据稀疏"的系统，AI 都表现为"辅助工具"而非"颠覆者"。这解释了为什么蛋白质折叠被 AlphaFold 打穿了（数据丰富、准闭合），而气候、细胞、经济、意识这些"开放非平稳"系统，AI 至今只在边缘打转。

四、埋在角落的"啊哈"：品味 vs 严谨的隐藏对偶

John 说了一句几乎没人接住的话——"以前大家说 taste（品味）是未来的关键，但新时代的对偶是 rigor（严谨）。"

这是一个极其深刻的观察。当生成变得几乎免费时，价值不再来自创造，而来自"甄别"。 你可以让 AI 生成一千个假设，但只有极少数人能识别哪一个是真的。这某种意义上是回到了 17 世纪科学革命前夜的状态——不是缺乏观察，而是缺乏方法论。

跨界的意外映射：这与编辑（editor）在文学史上的角色惊人地相似。当印刷术让书写民主化后，真正稀缺的不再是作者，而是能筛选、结构化、批判的编辑。AI for Science 时代，最稀缺的职业可能不是"科学家"，而是"科学编辑"——那些能把 LLM 生成的假设洪流筛选成真知识的人。

而这条线最讽刺的地方在于：John 自己就是那种人。他谈自己命名小行星、拿 Oscar、听 Feynman 上课，看似炫耀，其实无意间给出了他对"未来科学家"的隐含定义——跨领域的品味 + 打不烂的严谨，二者缺一不可。

📝 转录文本

🔬 Google 的 AI 科学家源起于"自动化 Kaggle" —— John Platt, Google Fellow

引子：预测模型 vs 描述模型

问： Are you talking about introducing explicit priors that you know based upon some human intuition or maybe in this case LOM intuition?

John： When you talk about multiple hypothesis testing right there's predictive models and there's descriptive models. A predictive model is like let's say you just have a you have some inputs and you have some outputs and you just I just want to build a piece of code that tries to just have the lowest error rate on some data set — statistical model.

A descriptive model is actually what science is trying to get to, which is okay it should be able to extrapolate because it has sort of the physics or the actual some description of reality that's captured within it and then you can use it to extrapolate.

Yes, Newton thought of apples and gravity, but gravity isn't actually about apple, right? If you take the 17th century machine learning model like "oh apples will fall," but how about planets? You know, I don't know, I have no data about planets, so who knows what they do, right?

The distinction between those is a little bit blurry, right? Because when a physicist or scientist comes, they use their intuition — or maybe even more than intuition — like essentially there's maybe a solid pile of facts that they know about the world and then they make sure that whatever model they build is sort of consistent with what's known.

开场介绍

主持人： My co-host R.J. — uh, it's a pleasure to have John Platt with us today. John is a Google fellow and head of applied science at Google Research. He has really a fun background. He — I guess you described yourself when we were talking a few minutes ago as a mega nerd.

John： Oh, giga nerd.

主持人： Giga nerd. He's excited in absolutely everything, and it really shows.

You — correct me if I'm wrong about any of this stuff — but um, so you started college at 14 and started your PhD at 18 at Caltech. You were advised or co-advised by John Hopfield, right?

John： Oh, yeah. Yeah.

主持人： Who just won a Nobel Prize two or three years ago.

John： Yes.

主持人： So John created several textbook algorithms — one known as Platt scaling, another one sequential minimal optimization which is the textbook algorithm for training SVMs. Even today it's still in sklearn. John has discovered and named two asteroids, has an Oscar for technical developments from 2006 — so if you've ever watched a Pixar movie, you've seen John's algorithms and work. John has an Erdős–Bacon number of six, or three-and-three from either side.

I'm going to skip over like 20 years of your career, but then jumping to Google — working at Google Sciences, you worked on fusion, quantum computing, climate modeling and many other topics. Is that more or less right?

John： That's right, yeah.

主持人： Okay, cool. Did I miss anything important for today?

John： No, I mean I've also done lots of applied math and signal processing and all sorts of fun things.

主持人： Yeah. I think your Wikipedia has a fun story about patents and the iPhone too.

John： The iPod.

主持人： iPod, yeah.

John： Welcome. Thank you for having me.

什么是 ERA？—— AI for Science 的框架

主持人： Can you tell us about ERA — I think that's the way that the acronym is pronounced? And I know that there's a lot of different semi-related stuff out there both within and outside of Google. So what can you tell us a little bit about the details of ERA and what makes it special?

John： Well, we've been doing AI for Science in Google Research for more than 10 years now. Around 10 years ago it was very much using — I don't know what you call it now, maybe classical machine learning models — things like convolutional nets or whatever to solve specific science problems.

But about two years ago we got very excited about these more general LLMs that have popped up in the last few years, and we were wondering what can be done with them. Of course a lot of people have been playing and trying to figure out what the right thing to do is.

核心洞察：可打分任务（Scorable Tasks）

We kind of stumbled into this mapping. In other words, we found that many different scientific problems can be mapped into something we call scorable tasks. So you can often phrase a scientific problem as "gosh, I really would like to have a piece of code that maximizes some score." And it's surprising the number of different scientific problems you can make a lot of progress on by mapping into that framework.

A lot of scientists spend a lot of time building models — they might be statistical models or physically-based models. If it's a statistical model, like in machine learning, your scoring function is: "well I have some data set and I'd like to have the fit the model and the data set go up." We can talk about overfitting in a minute —

主持人： That was one of our questions.

一个非统计的例子：渐近展开

John： So machine learning is kind of a subset of this scorable task, right? But you could do other kinds of things. Especially Michael Brenner, who's the lead author on the ERA paper — he's very skilled, he likes to knock out a scientific paper in an evening now with a tool.

There's something in applied math called asymptotic expansions. You're asking: how does an ordinary or partial differential equation behave? There's some parameter — has an epsilon in it — and you're trying to say how does it behave as epsilon goes to zero. It turns out you can turn that into an empirical task by essentially asking that it proposes some solutions that are asymptotically correct, and you check to see if the asymptotic solution is correct for like epsilon equals 1e-4 or something, and then you check that fit.

But then you ask Gemini — which is the core AI underneath it — to do the mathematical reasoning, try to solve the problem while also maximizing the fit to the data. So there's a lot of tricks you can do because the underlying thing that's altering the code or making the decisions is not a random process. It's an AI itself that is smart and knows about things and knows a lot about the world.

You can solve a lot of interesting problems because that core inner loop is an AI that has huge amounts of prior knowledge. So that's the trick.

另一个例子：卫星超分辨率与 CO2 监测

主持人： So what are some of the more — the statistical one is what everyone listening will probably know about. What are some of the other interesting ones?

John： Let's see, ones that we just put a paper up on arXiv — or actually I think it might be on GitHub. You often run into this in remote sensing because there's always a trade-off. There are satellites flying above the Earth, and there's a trade-off between how frequently they can revisit a spot on Earth, what their spatial resolution is, how big the pixels are, and their spectral resolution — how many bands they have.

Ideally you'd like to have monitoring of the Earth that's constant — a frame every five minutes at hyperspectral resolution at 10 centimeters. You can't get that.

But for example, to monitor CO2 — the atmospheric concentration of CO2 — you can take data from one satellite, for example OCO-2 or OCO-3 (OCO-3 is actually attached to the International Space Station), so it gets you a little strip of CO2 measurements that are highly accurate and pretty high resolution.

You can actually try to do — because a lot of it is in the infrared — weather satellites like GOES have some infrared bands and it takes a picture every essentially 5 minutes, but the pixels are very large and it doesn't have such great spectral resolution in terms of — it wasn't designed to find CO2.

So you just ask one to estimate the other, and you shovel other data in like what's the current weather, what's sort of the long-term albedo. And so you came up with this very nice model that can do almost like super-resolution — an informed super-resolution of one satellite to another.

ERA 的工程细节：蒙特卡洛树搜索与 UCB

主持人： So any scientific problem that you can map into this framework. So the input to ERA is sort of this mapping and the output is code, is that —

John： Well, sort of. I mean the input is — the way we've got it set up in the product, you just start talking. Because a lot of times it's nonobvious how to do this mapping. Although experts like Michael Brenner know how to do it, we actually wrote an agent that helps you — it talks to you to try to help you define what your scorable task should be.

So there's already an instance of Gemini sitting there trying to help you write code. That's actually sort of almost like an intermediate result. You start talking to it about your problem and it tries to produce essentially a Python notebook underneath that has a scorable function — which essentially produces a score. And then it starts to mutate that notebook in a clever way because, again, it's Gemini, and it will try to keep proposing code that tries to maximize the score.

主持人： So what is different about this than just a generally agentic system that can optimize notebooks?

John： Right now it's — essentially it's its own — in modern 2026 parlance we actually worked on this in '24 and '25 — but in the modern parlance it's kind of a specialized harness that runs an algorithm which, for ERA, was Monte Carlo tree search.

So essentially it's keeping hundreds or thousands of possible instances of notebooks, and then it selects one — and I can explain how it selects one. It decides: well, what can I do? Gemini asks itself: what can I do to make that notebook be better? And then it will make a new one and test it and put it back into the candidate pool.

You can imagine the candidate pool is actually tree-structured because every candidate possibly has some children. What you do is you pick based on something called — it's actually a fairly standard algorithm in reinforcement learning called Upper Confidence Bound (UCB). It's an optimistic algorithm. It tries to estimate: what's the 95th percentile outcome of mutation? It tries to estimate that and picks the one with the highest optimistic bound.

So in other words, it doesn't always pick the best-performing notebook. It tries to predict "what's the current performance plus two sigma of its guess." So it always hunts around.

主持人： So high-recall basically.

John： High recall. It's trying to make its bet so that it most efficiently tries to make progress, which isn't always greedily doing the best candidate. Sometimes it's the fifth-best.

We've also played around where it recombines — it sort of takes ideas from two candidates and smashes them together and tries to make a third candidate out of that.

初始种子与并行数

主持人： How does it seed the initial candidate pool?

John： Well, that's the amazing thing — underneath, Gemini is actually good at writing code. You just ask it "write me a thing" because you have a textual description of the problem. It isn't just "oh here's your scoring function, start." You give it a textual description of the function, and you might give it — in fact we have under some things like "here are five papers that people tried to solve this problem with" — and it's kind of smart. It actually goes and reads the papers and takes a first stab at code.

It might not be great, or it might sometimes have bugs and it returns essentially minus infinity, but it will then try to mutate the code and make it better.

主持人： How many agents are you spinning up? I guess maybe not agents, or how many different tree branches at each iteration?

John： At every iteration — well, there's a trade-off. You'd like to do a lot of parallel work, but if you do too much parallel work, you can't learn from previous things. Right now the default is 10. So you try to grow 10 leaves at a time. That seems to be about the right trade-off.

主持人： When you say you can't learn from previous iterations, what does that mean?

John： Why you can't do too many things in parallel is: if you have 10 parallel searches at once, then number one can't actually see what numbers two through 10 are doing. So if you do a thousand at once, then you're using a huge amount of computation without a lot of cross-learning.

Whereas once you finish a little batch, you get the history. Obviously you have to prune it so it doesn't blow up the context, but you get the history of what it was thinking about as it was writing the code and the results of the code. So it can learn from its previous attempts.

主持人： You're really pushing Gemini's long-context abilities.

John： That's right. And you have to do the right management.

最难的部分：定义正确的评分函数

主持人： Going back to R.J.'s question — the key point being: the first key goal is to identify what specific score that you are trying to optimize, right? Sometimes that is kind of the hardest part of the problem. I find it interesting that I'm not sure I'd always trust my agent to do that part. That part seems like the more human task in the loop.

John： It is. And often you have to be careful. A lot of what you do — it's very meta. You have to make sure that — one common thing is you come up with a scoring function, or the agent does, or you do it together, and then the iteration finds a way to cheat, and you go: "oh no, I didn't mean that." So you have to go through and often have a loop around it where you iterate: "no, no, I didn't mean that," or you have to tell it in its instructions "don't do this."

So there's often iterations. Even with agent help, you don't necessarily get the right scoring function from day one.

And it's really neat because — in the old days, i.e. 2024 — a lot of grad students would spend a lot of time doing scientific software, and it's just so much effort to write code at all that you kind of try maybe a few things or a few things that are very related, and then you sort of stop because you have to write your paper, you have to do your next experiment.

This thing is kind of relentless underneath — it keeps trying and keeps trying. So the people who use it are now spending all their time almost at the right level, almost at the scientific creativity level. What does it mean to have a cost function? That's almost the essence of the scientific problem. You're not so much now in the details of "oh, I have to import this CSV file" or "I have to get this database to work." You're now thinking almost deeply philosophically about your actual scientific problem, not down in the grungy goop of worrying about databases.

One cool thing the agent can do is actually suggest data sets to you: "oh, have you thought about maybe pulling in this data set and doing a join?" So it'll make suggestions about data sets you can join with, which is kind of cool.

奖励劫持与"精灵故事"

John： Boy, I'm blanking. I know other folks have run into it. I don't know if I have enough details to sort of express the comedy of it, but you kind of get surprised. Sorry, I'm blanking.

主持人： No, it's fine. I always like to think of machine learning as sort of like the old genie stories, before Monkey's Paw — careful what you wish for, because you're going to get it.

John： That's right. And that happens very much with this. So you have to be careful.

But on the other hand, it has some knowledge. The nice thing is that Gemini knows a lot about many things — more than any one person can. It at least knows, especially if you point it at papers: "here are five papers that tried to do this in some way." So to some extent it does have that genie feel, but to some extent it also does sane things.

This is why — remember the whole idea of evolutionary coding. It's been around since the '70s. Everyone's loved to do that. "Oh, let's mutate Lisp code or whatever to do things." But the reason why it just hasn't taken off is that random mutation in code space is pretty much worthless. Just like DNA — most things are harmful.

So here it's like: "oh no, we can actually find" — it sort of knows underneath, and knows interesting gradients to try. Which is why the thing works: the underlying loop itself is an AI. So yes, it can overfit and have funny genie problems, but it also has some amount of sanity because it knows about the world.

What are your thoughts about that? Empirically, my experience — I even tried the open-source version of ERA. I kind of strapped it into Claude and it's running right now so I can't tell you how well it's working.

预测模型 vs 描述模型（再展开）

John： I guess there's two questions embedded in your question, because when you talk about multiple hypothesis testing, there's predictive models and there's descriptive models — I've been doing machine learning for a long time in statistics.

主持人： That's actually a really good point — do you mind expanding that? I'm not sure that's something everyone in the audience would be familiar with. Especially in modern days I think people are trying to obscure the two. If you started with LLMs I'm not sure that distinction would be meaningful.

John： That's right. A predictive model is: let's say you have inputs and outputs, and I just want to build a piece of code that has the lowest error rate on some data set. That's just a statistical model.

A descriptive model is actually what science is trying to get to: it should be able to extrapolate because it has the physics or some description of reality captured within it. Then you can use it to extrapolate. Because — yes, Newton thought apples and gravity, but gravity isn't actually about apples. If he had just fit the 17th-century machine learning model: "oh apples will fall," but how about planets? I don't know, I have no data about planets, so who knows what they do.

主持人： So when you say "extrapolative" — there's different ways I could think about this. One is: you said a model of physics or model of the world. Are you talking about introducing explicit priors that you know based upon some human intuition — or maybe in this case LLM intuition — or are you talking about "the physics is actually learned by the model"?

John： The distinction between those is a little bit blurry, right? Because when a physicist or scientist comes, they use their intuition — or maybe even more than intuition. Essentially there's a solid pile of facts they know about the world, and they make sure whatever model they build is consistent with what's known.

Currently in ERA it is sort of LLM intuition — that's what I was trying to say about having a good gradient underneath. Especially if you point it at existing papers, it will try to build models that are kind of sane underneath. Especially if you give it guidance like "oh be sure to incorporate this" or "look at these papers," you get these things. So you can introduce a bias towards certain model choices, and it will have a bias because its own little world knowledge is accumulated inside itself in pre-training.

具体例子：物理先验

主持人： Can you give us examples of what that might look like? For example if you're doing something with partial differential equations, there's these formalisms people have — neural operators for example, or physics-informed neural networks — for fluid and PDE-type modeling systems. Or for molecular systems there's often this idea about equivariance. Is the model picking up on these tricks which have been developed in the literature, or are they adding some weights for some physical prior?

John： I don't know if I have enough data to say "oh, 73% of the time it does this." But especially when you point it at existing papers, it will do very well at adapting the methods described in the papers for the problem. In fact, we'll do an amazing job. You can actually often just recreate or reverse-engineer a paper — that's what Michael Brenner actually likes to do. He'll say "oh that sounds like an interesting paper."

Oh — we did this for the — we had this thing, it was actually kind of a hack, I suggested this to Michael. There's this one MIT professor who came up with some code: if you have a rooftop with fixed area and you want to maximize the amount of solar power you capture over a day, you can build up — which of course captures more sunlight — and you can have it design a widget involving mirrors or struts or solar panels to stack at whatever angles or sizes you like, usually with a maximum height, and then let it explore that design space.

I believe Michael — we can ask him — I believe it actually just — I don't think he actually installed the simulator, I think the code just reproduced the code, because it has a coding agent inside of it. So it just reproduced the code from the paper and figured it all out.

So yes, it's very good, especially if given a pointer to what other people have done. It's good at — I haven't seen it try equivariant modeling. That can get very hairy if you know about Clebsch-Gordan coefficients, it's pretty fun. So I don't know if it'll do the true equivariant stuff, but it actually knows a lot.

I remember when Gemini 2.5 came out — I know this is not exactly about ERA — but I remember thinking "oh, this is a new world." The day 2.5 came out, I said "hey Gemini 2.5, can you write me some boosted decision tree code?" And it did. And it worked. It just did. I said, "yeah, this is a new world."

So yes, to loop back to your question: if you give it guidance about "oh, it's important to put this kind of thing in," it will. At least not that we've seen — it won't necessarily discover completely new physical models from scratch, but it will certainly, if you tell it about interesting constraints about the world that are known, evolve.

主持人： So there's still room for humans for the next year or two?

John： Oh, in fact — going back — I think there's totally room for humans. I don't know, we have co-scientist that tries to help you come up with hypothesis generation, but really I still haven't seen the creativity and the philosophy and the careful rigor. You totally need the humans. I don't see humans going away. They can make strange suggestions — I've used co-scientist for an interesting problem in geochemistry and I learned about a new kind of ion I didn't realize happened in magma. It'll tell you interesting things and you'll learn stuff, but I don't think it substitutes for human creativity.

参差不齐的边界（Jagged Frontier）

主持人： Going back — we were just talking about two years, 2.0 to 2.5, you already saw a leap, and now it's been another year or two and now we're at 3.5. Whenever you look at a graph, if something looks like an exponential, it can either be in a sigmoid or you can be at the beginning of a takeoff. Every exponential turns into a sigmoid eventually. But the question is: where are we on that?

John： I'm a big believer in the whole jagged frontier. So certainly there's some big spikes out in jaggedness in terms of coding ability and just gathering knowledge and finding related things — and that's huge and wonderful, which is great for scientists.

So far, it's less in terms of rigor. We can talk about things like the International Math Olympiad and math in general, but in terms of philosophy and creativity, it's still kind of not there. Maybe everything will inflate and pass — some people are saying that — but I'm still seeing a lot of very strong jaggedness. Maybe it'll get to be extra good at coding, extra good at fitting models, extra good at making suggestions — but I don't know. So far, you need the humans.

回到过拟合：Power Tool 的双刃剑

主持人： I want to get back to the question about the multiple hypothesis testing. Sorry, totally love the tangent.

John： Multiple hypothesis testing is when you have a descriptive model and you're saying "this is the way the world works," and you have a bunch of data and you take a billion darts and throw. So you have to be careful — there's something called false discovery rate.

The question is: is this finding descriptive models, or is this finding predictive models? Fundamentally the scientist is there to make sure that whatever it's saying is descriptive. We haven't been able to make a system so far, out of these pieces, that can really discover completely new physics or completely new science — but this is a power tool to help you discover completely new science.

主持人： But then — what about just pure over — okay, let's set aside. It's not trying to figure out a descriptive model of the world, that's still up to the scientist. But what about just plain old overfitting?

John： Yes. You have to be very careful because it's a power tool. It can — I shouldn't probably say — it can slice your fingers off. You have to be very careful and very rigorous.

In fact, now you have to be more careful, more rigorous to not fool yourself. You really need to be just excruciatingly careful about having very hidden hold-out sets you don't look at. You have to be super rigorous to make sure you don't completely — because it is a total power tool.

主持人： So the answer to "how do I not slice my fingers off" is: you need to use the same techniques but be very careful with them.

John： Yes.

主持人： That's a very clear answer. Yeah — okay, I actually don't think I've heard any guests say that. It's a very important skill. People talk a lot about taste.

John： Yeah.

主持人： Maybe this is a variation of taste — but the taste is the other side. It's like rigor.

John： Yes. In fact, if anything —

主持人： Taste or rigor, which is more important?

John： Well, I don't know. The aspect that researchers are software developers — there's a lot of overlap. I'm seeing that software engineers — obviously there's a lot of concern like "oh no, what am I going to do, coding seems to be getting automatic." I think there are both. There's a lot of people getting pulled into "well I'll be the creative source, I'll try to figure out new science, I'll try to figure out new products, I'll be very very creative." I'm a strong believer that's not going to go away.

There's also people pulled toward rigor: "oh, I want to make sure this doesn't crash, I want to make sure this scales, I want to make sure this isn't wrong." I think you need both. You need people who are really good at both — but they don't necessarily have to be the same people.

I think this is even broader than science. As software engineering evolves, it'll be the people who bring the creativity and the people who bring the rigor. Those will be sort of anchors.

ERA 的起源：Auto-Kaggle

主持人： There's a really cool leaderboard for scientific problems from Stanford. It seems like a really interesting idea to me — different agents kind of competing on the leaderboard. It seems like if you squint a little bit, what ERA is doing is kind of a leaderboard, but it's internal and it's recombining ideas. What are your thoughts about this?

John： Ironically — people may not realize — Kaggle is actually part of Google. And so it was called the Auto-Kaggle problem. That's what it was: let's have a system that can win at Kaggle competitions. That's why it has the shape. That's how the project started.

And it goes back to overfitting, right? If you've ever competed in a Kaggle competition —

主持人： I have done Kaggle competitions — I've done one. It is a really interesting phenomenon because overfitting is rampant. It's really impressive how people can overfit to certain data sets.

一个 Contrails Kaggle 事故

John： We have a fun project I can talk about more — that tries to mitigate contrails, gen contrails. We had a contrail Kaggle competition, and people actually beat us. But they found that we had a half-pixel error in our labels — it had to do with the center versus the lower-left, like where is (0,0)? Is it in the lower-left of the pixel or in the center?

They found that and exploited it and squeezed a little bit extra out. It turns out when you make artificial data and you rotate it, you have to make sure you take into account that half-pixel offset.

So people themselves will act like these LLMs and try to reward-hack. It goes back to Goodhart's law: any metric that becomes a target is no longer good as a metric.

You have to be very careful. You have to have layers of rigor — "okay, we'll do this and optimize for this, but you have to realize Goodhart's law applies, and be careful." That's why the whole AI field has been constantly exhausting these things — Goodhart's law applies individually to every leaderboard you make. You just have to step back and be very careful.

Auto-Kaggle 的成绩

主持人： Given Auto-Kaggle, how often was it successful?

John： Well, we tried it on various "playground competitions" and it did very very well in the playground competitions. We've entered into different competitions — some of them, in the last few years, the number of leaderboards and competitions have just exploded far beyond Kaggle.

One thing we're super proud of: the CDC set up this competition where you try to predict next week's number of COVID and flu cases that will happen in every state and territory in the US. You try to predict a week in advance, and ERA did super well on that.

主持人： It's funny because Google invented the concept of using data to track disease progression with Google Flu Trends. So it's funny that you're going full circle 20 years later.

John： Other ones where we entered, we weren't quite as good, often because — sometimes how well you do in these competitions is a measure of how much TLC you put into it and how much you're willing to squeeze the last 0.001. ERA did well, got pretty close, but didn't close the jump in the last 30 places or whatever because no one was there to shave the last 0.01 off.

人在回路

主持人： Is it very iterative? You get to it, you sort of get these step changes as it discovers something, then flat. Is it very human-in-the-loop like "okay, you've stalled on the problem, try this kind of thing"?

John： Yes, at the outer loop — which is I think the almost more fun creative part. "Oh, here, have a look at this paper" or "oh you're doing something bad." It's almost like having a hyper-eager grad student who doesn't sleep. You tell it things and you guide it around.

主持人： So it's very much designed to be human-in-the-loop then. Interesting — a lot of the other tools I've tried tend to be very one-shot.

Obviously you talk to it and start it and it'll go for some number of hours and then come back — but then that's where the human creativity kicks in, and you're doing the outer loop. Depending if you want to sleep, every few hours you go and give it another try.

Contrails：飞机凝结尾与气候干预

主持人： One of the things you optimized was contrails. Can you talk a little bit about that?

John： Let me maybe spend a minute or two talking about the contrails problem.

主持人： Yes, please.

John： For context: contrails, not chemtrails, which is a conspiracy theory. Yes, you should also dislike contrails, but maybe not for the same reason.

Contrails — if you've ever seen those white clouds formed behind jets, those are condensation trails, or contrails. It turns out they add — at least according to estimates — about 1% of all anthropogenic global warming.

为什么 Contrails 会变暖？

There are two counter-vailing effects. Sometimes if you've seen them, they streak and then go away — those don't really do anything. But sometimes they last for a long time. You'll see in the sky an almost waffle-like pattern of persistent contrails.

Two effects: 1. They're thin white clouds — they reflect sunlight. But that only happens during the day. 2. All objects emit black-body radiation. The Earth does, at about 300 Kelvin — it's in the far infrared around 10 microns. At those wavelengths, contrails have very low albedo. They're almost black. So they absorb some of the outgoing infrared radiation and re-emit it in both directions. So they trap heat like a blanket.

Because that happens 24 hours a day, they tend to be warming.

It's surprising — there's some uncertainty — but contrail cirrus that comes from contrails might cover, especially in places like Europe which has a lot of airline traffic, a few percent of the actual sky. In places like Europe it adds about one watt per square meter of forcing locally.

Just to give you a sense: all anthropogenic warming, averaged across the whole globe, is about three watts per square meter. So in places of high airplane traffic, it can be a lot of warming locally.

如何干预：绕开冰过饱和区

What can you do? Contrails are caused by areas in the atmosphere that are ice-supersaturated. They're a little bit like rock candy — when you have rock candy, you get a water solution with too much sugar in it, and any little bit of sugar will just crystallize all the sugar out.

Just like that: in these contrail regions, they tend to be kind of pancake-shaped, only a few hundred meters tall. If you fly through it, the jet exhaust has a little bit of moisture which turns into droplets and then freezes. And then, for every gram of water, ice, or soot you put out, it's about 10 kg of water gets sucked out — so there's this enormous 10,000-to-1 ratio.

So it's a big problem. What you can do: figure out where these regions are (they're invisible), and tell the plane to go underneath. You only have to drop essentially two flight levels. It costs a little bit of fuel, but not very much, to avoid these bad regions.

We built a system that looks at satellite images and tries to detect where contrails are. We have essentially a continuous monitoring system, and then try to build a model — because it turns out weather models are not quite accurate enough to find these places of ice supersaturation. So we build a custom model — a convolutional net or a UNet — to predict where they're going to happen. Then we give maps to flight planning software so they can dodge it and inexpensively reduce the climate impact of aviation by a lot.

主持人： What's the physics behind why you can predict that?

John： Because you're trying to detect these regions of ice supersaturation — they're very persistent.

主持人： Oh, they're persistent.

John： Yeah, no one knows exactly, but they could last for days. They're caused by, they think, warm moist air being injected just at the boundary of the tropopause, at the bottom of the stratosphere. When humidity gets up there, it sticks for a long time and gradually dissipates. So they're like bad spots in the atmosphere you don't want to fly through.

反事实模型

主持人： And the models you're using are CNNs?

John： That's right. We haven't replaced those with ERA-level models yet.

But there was a very interesting problem: you want to know how much warming did this contrail make and how much did it add to global warming? Because you might want to find the biggest ones — there's some fuel cost and it might cost a bit of money for airplanes to avoid them.

But that's actually what they call a counterfactual problem. Okay, you made a contrail, and a certain amount of infrared radiation happened. We can measure that if we're careful — but what would have happened if there hadn't been a contrail there? That's very difficult because you can't access the universe where the contrail didn't happen.

So you have to make these things called counterfactual models. Those are pretty tricky to fit and make.

Remember there were two effects — reflecting sunlight and the infrared. It turns out measuring the effect of reflecting sunlight is more difficult, and we were stuck on it for two years. We had a model that worked okay for outgoing longwave radiation, but not for reflected sunlight.

ERA actually helped us find a model that searched all the confounders and figured out how to estimate it. We even had test code on artificial data sets where we injected contrails — because we knew how much it was because we injected it. Our own attempts didn't even pass our own tests, but ERA did, and unstuck this problem.

We have a paper about the outgoing longwave radiation, and we have another paper — not submitted yet but talked about at EGU — where we actually solved this problem.

主持人： The models that ERA comes up with — are they a big monstrosity of code, or pretty basic?

John： In this particular case, more the latter. It essentially helped identify — it was a very simple model with some number of confounders that we just hadn't tried that combination before, and it worked very well. So yeah, it came up with the answer, and it was clear in retrospect. That was a big win.

气候建模的深层困境

主持人： I know you've done a lot of work in climate. What other stuff have you done?

John： I talked about the CO2 thing. That was pretty fun because the reason estimating CO2 in the atmosphere is interesting: we actually don't know what the carbon flux is into the biosphere.

We know the biosphere captures — we emit a bunch of CO2, some gets absorbed into the ocean mostly through inorganic chemistry (some phytoplankton), and a lot gets absorbed on land. But the error bars are moderately large. The error bars about what will happen 50 years from now are very large. Models in 2100 — we don't know how the biosphere will react to ever-increasing temperatures and CO2.

We don't actually know how much CO2 will be absorbed, and the error bars are 300 ppm of CO2 just from the uncertainty of what gets absorbed. Right now there's about 440-450 ppm. So 300 ppm is enormous uncertainty. It would be really nice to reduce that.

天气 vs 气候

主持人： I know that Google has made some really big improvements in climate modeling and weather prediction. I was at NeurIPS this year and stopped by the climate track — it really blew my mind the step change that's happened in the past 10 years or so in climate modeling.

John： People often collapse climate and weather together. They're fundamentally the same physics — although obviously when you start having ice and land, climate is long-term weather. The complexity of a full Earth system model, which is a climate model, is much bigger than an atmospheric model. You have to measure water flux, CO2 flux in and out of the land, what happens with ice.

Weather is up to 15 days — approximately, because the atmosphere appears to be chaotic. Essentially the butterfly effect: small perturbations, like a butterfly flaps its wings, and the weather will be completely different in 2 or 3 weeks. Weather is trying to predict the actual trajectory of the atmosphere over 2 weeks.

That has been a huge step change — a lot of not even the new LLM stuff, that was based on 2018-era machine learning and a large amount of data and compute. There's been a lot of very clever work, a lot from Google, making new weather models. It's been great.

We had a neat breakthrough — we can predict tracks of cyclones much more accurately many days in advance. Places like Jamaica got hammered by a terrible hurricane, and a lot of the classic models didn't predict it, partially because the intensification is driven by surface temperature. Hurricanes are heat engines, essentially — they convert heat in the ocean to big atmospheric motions.

为什么气候比天气更难

Climate is much more difficult because you don't actually care about whether it's going to rain in Seattle in 2070. You're trying to get averages. What makes it difficult is that it's non-stationary. The underlying physics is behaving differently — plants behave differently, ice behaves differently. It's very difficult to use classical ML on true climate models.

That's why the whole discussion — descriptive models and multiple hypothesis testing — is incredibly severe in climate, because we have no data from 30 years out, and we don't want to wait 30 or 50 years to find out whether we were right or that we overfit.

So whatever we do, you have to be careful and try to peel off sub-problems. The problem of exactly how do you build a big model that can predict into the future but is still constrained by what we know — it's a fascinating problem. I think it's still unsolved. It's a great problem to have because of these uncertainties. We really would like to know what will happen in 60 years to the climate. So far AI has not revolutionized it because it's very resistant, because of this data problem — it's a low-data problem.

混沌和吸引子

主持人： Does the butterfly effect impact climate too, or is the time scale so large that you have a closed system?

John： It's unfortunately non-stationary in a different way. The original chaos stuff — in meteorology it was Lorenz who had this very simple ODE.

The difference between climate and weather is: weather is where you are on the attractor, and climate is about the statistics of the attractor itself.

The trouble with climate is that we're altering it. So the attractor itself is moving, and there could be — everyone talks about tipping points — that means the attractor suddenly changes, and that's very difficult to predict. Even the attractor's shape changes quickly, or could.

The trouble is: when you run a simulator, you don't know — did it go unstable because my model's not great, or is it an actual physical instability? That's extremely difficult to tell.

数据的稀缺

主持人： What do you do, when you don't have future data, and you really don't have much past data? Maybe you have if you're lucky 50 data points in any one location.

John： So whatever we do has to be very constrained by what we know. People — in applied science in general, but climate is the most extreme — make these things called process models. What you do is: "well, I'm going to be reductionist and take the horrible complicated climate thing and boil it down to a thousand pieces, and then find the expert who wrote a paper about piece number 763 and fit a cubic to some data."

One mysterious thing related to contrails: how does ice behave in clouds? Everything is complicated once you dig into it. When you make a contrail, how long does it last? It depends on — because the way contrails evaporate: ice starts to accumulate, ice crystals get big and then fall. But how quickly they fall depends on their shape, which is not known. How much does the contrail mix from the moist inside to outside? People have approximations, but they don't know.

The uncertainty is very confounded. It's not just "oh, John cares about contrails" — the microphysics of ice has strong implications for what climate models do. And we just don't know. So it's very gnarly.

My hope is that with tools — maybe not today's ERA but tomorrow's ERA — because it not only can fit data, it can read papers. And it can read a lot more papers than we can. Maybe we can integrate all the knowledge people have carefully evaluated, much more than any one person writing a piece of code and fitting data. That would be utterly glorious. We don't have that today, but that's one of the hopes I have for a more amazing tool in the future — something that can write code in a sane way, constrained by all the scientific knowledge we've accumulated.

类比：生物学

主持人： That strikes me as being very similar to biology.

John： Oh, yes. If you've ever played with biology, there are so many exceptions and so many hacks in biological systems. It would be amazing if we could have a thing that could integrate all known scientific knowledge with data and synthesize new models.

主持人： So AI can be an unlock here because the models are so piecemeal, necessarily piecemeal. Being able to assemble the jigsaw puzzle — having just scale and capacity actually helps a lot.

John： That's right. Somehow humans — even I'm pretty well-read — it's difficult to integrate across the N-squared of different papers I've read. Somehow there's so much data in those billions of parameters, and you can give it access to read PDFs, that it can start to pull things together that people wouldn't. John： It boils down to almost the difference between weather and climate. If you're in a data-rich regime — like weather, or even proteins because of PDB — you can feel "yes, I've got enough data to cover it." A statistical model like AlphaFold does. In fact, a lot of people happily use AlphaFold — I'm not a biochemist, but people seem to love it. One amazing thing they did: they exhaustively ran it on all of PDB and published it — six billion protein predictions. The vast majority are quite accurate. So that's amazing. But it feels closed.

When it's like climate — open and non-stationary — or you have to make big extrapolations, you have to be much more cautious. Maybe biology, too. There was this Virtual Cell Challenge from the Arc Institute — I know that people were — there may have been some overfitting, at least so I'm told. Or the simple baselines worked very well.

主持人： One of the classic things in biology: always start with a simple baseline. Understand your simplest case. In biology there are many problems extremely resistant to anything beyond the simple baseline, even with a lot of data.

John： That's right. I tell people: just fit linear regression. Just do it. Or SVMs — SVMs are just a different form of linear regression, yes.

When do you need the more process-modely thing? It's when — climate is on one end, weather maybe on the other. It's about where you are on the data-richness thing. When can you feel "oh, I really have a closed problem, I can cover it"?

主持人： I guess if you're in a cold climate and you want to warm it up, this is now your own —

So it's rare — there are contrails where uncertainty bounds are in terms of warming. Many contrails, mostly at night of course, where it's largely warming, and we're very sure. 关于核聚变

主持人： Fusion is one of those things where the joke was always "fusion is 30 years away," but I think it's actually now less than 30 years away, maybe.

John： Yeah, there's a definite probability that someone will make commercially relevant fusion even by the end of this decade. So it's like three years away, not 30.

John： Sure, sure. Well, we could talk about fusion —

主持人： There were two things. One is fusion, the other is better control systems.

John： Yes — Google DeepMind has been working on control systems for tokamaks to make sure they don't go unstable and disrupt.

主持人： Disruptions are quite interesting themselves.

John： Basically the entire energy in the tokamak collimates into one little beam —

主持人： And it hits your vacuum chamber and you're very sad.

John： Very sad. I think people believe ITER could be turned on after $30 billion, disrupt, and then basically have a $30 billion brick.

Before LLMs, we worked with a fusion company called TAE. I was in their control room. Yes, it was kind of sad — you have to be very careful. We were making systems to recommend new experiments, and they were very skeptical and jaundiced, which they should be, because even under human control it was like — they were doing some experiment and then you hear this big bang and it was like "oh no," and then the apparatus is down for two weeks as they patch it.

主持人： You were there during a disruption?

John： Oh no, this is — they have Field-Reversed Configuration, which has arcs. So what is that?

主持人： Sorry, I'm not familiar.

John： Field-Reversed Configuration — tokamaks are perhaps the most studied form of plasma, but there are many different architectures, ways to stabilize and compress plasmas. There's a shape — essentially a self-contained football plasma — called a Field-Reversed Configuration where the magnetic field inside and outside are opposite, separated by something called a separatrix.

That is in theory unstable, but in practice stable. When you run magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) code, it's unstable under that assumption — but that's an assumption that's not the way the real world works. So it was disfavored for many years, but TAE and Helion have FRCs because they're relatively robust. You can actually knock them against walls and they'll stay stable. But you can still get discharges that punch holes in your vacuum chamber, which is kind of unfortunate.

主持人： For clarification: you have these fusion reactors — you create a plasma, the plasma is magnetically confined. So you have some sort of magnetic system that's tunable by a computer.

John： FRCs — once you make them, they're sort of sustained. There are different ways.

Okay, so all of fusion boils down to something called the Lawson criterion. It explains why fusion is hard. On the back of an envelope you can just show that the density, the temperature, and the confinement time (one over the amount of time it takes for the energy to decay by 1/e in a plasma) — the product of those three numbers has to be bigger than some constant, and then you can get fusion. If not, you don't.

That's a product of three numbers, and that explains why fusion is so hard — because every approach has an Achilles heel where one of those numbers is not very big, and they try to desperately make it higher. Every approach to fusion is different.

You have to be a bit skeptical when there are all these breathless news things about fusion, because it'll say "now confinement time is X for X minutes" — talking about only one of the three numbers. You have to have all three before you can get fusion. The whole field is making a lot of progress and it's very exciting, but you have to be cautious about breathless news articles.

主持人： So what is the computational part of that?

John： For tokamaks, it's — there's this instability that takes all the energy and smacks it into one place, so you have to keep everything under control. It's a control system.

FRCs have very simple instabilities — a Z-instability. It's stable, it'll just wobble back and forth, but you just make what they call a PID controller that keeps the football in the center of the reactor, and things are fine. It adjusts, I think, the electric field. It knocks it back and forth. The issue people have depends on which plasma architecture they're using.

气候韧性

主持人： Instead of interventions, one thing I'm curious about is: how does this affect decisions — what do we build, how do we build? You're from LA, right?

John： Well, I spent 11 years —

主持人： So you spent a lot of your life in LA. LA basically — large parts of it just burned down. This is something a lot of people saw coming, maybe due to regulatory issues, but also other issues. We were completely unprepared. Have you worked on predicting risk assessments or suggestions of what we actually change to harden society?

John： That's right. There's a big effort at Google into climate crisis resilience. We had a very fun project called FireSat.

For wildfires: if you could catch them early enough, it's very easy to put out a wildfire the size of this room. But even if it's an acre, it gets much harder. Under certain circumstances they can grow exponentially. They often start small and spend a while.

We figured out: if you had a global constellation of low-Earth-orbit satellites that could detect in the midwave IR — which goes back to the black body, that's the temperature of fire — fires stand out in the midwave IR.

We designed a sensor — depending on their orbits, roughly 50 to 80 of them — you could find fires about 5 meters on a side anywhere on the planet, within 15 to 20 minutes. You'd have to put up 80 to get within 15 minutes. Then you could intervene — or decide not to, if you thought it was safe to let the fire burn fuel.

We worked with a nonprofit called Earth Fire Alliance. They're starting to — we've launched one satellite, which is a prototype. We worked with a company named Muon Space to make the satellite.

We have wildfire boundary detection and propagate that through Google — figuring out from existing satellites where the boundaries of fires are, then telling people through Android phones or Search about fires. We've worked with the US Forest Service on new models for how fires propagate — that goes back to process-based models from the '70s by Rothermel. We made a little neural network proxy model to run it very quickly.

The World Health Organization estimates there are 300,000 excess deaths a year across the world from wildfire smoke.

主持人： I remember a few years ago there was this cloud of smoke that crossed all of northern US and Canada and caused a lot of respiratory issues.

John： It's very hard to track — you have to estimate these excess deaths from statistical means. But it's a very serious public health problem, and just very scary and burns people's houses down.

AI for Science 的演进：给年轻人的建议

主持人： You've been at the intersection of AI and science for quite some time. How do you see the field has evolved? What lessons have you learned, and how should this change how a young scientist or practitioner should approach the future?

John： There has been a phase change in the last 12 to 18 months. A lot of what we used to do was build specialized models to solve individual problems. If you think that's your job, it's kind of fun — you find a problem, you solve it. But now we have these much more general AI things, and the whole AI for Science community is still feeling around. The fact that they're working is so new that collectively we're not sure what's the best thing to do — maybe there's no one best, maybe there's a tool chain.

What should young scientists do? I have a son who's 21 who's really into AI and coding and chemistry. I look at him and think he's doing the right thing — he's both learning a lot and trying to be a domain expert about RNA, but he's also using vibe coding and all the tools. That's the right answer. Because everyone's figuring it out.

Be a deep domain expert — I don't think domain expertise is going away. It goes back to taste, and figuring out how people get taste without doing all the grunt work. That's an interesting open question. Develop domain expertise, but also play with all the different tools that are available.

There's still the huge open issue of what do you do about physical lab work. That's not going away because experiments are the ground truth — and a bottleneck. People are talking about a "lab in the loop" but that's very open. No one has a general lab that does everything.

Advise people to play with whatever tools are available, develop deep domain expertise and taste. And don't be scared — try stuff. I'm always happy — we have student researchers at Google, and they come and do wild and crazy things, and that's just delightful. People should be trying wild and crazy things and seeing what happens.

主持人： When I think about how I developed expertise, it was by starting with a simple defined problem and hammering it. In that process, you learn more, you go broader, you go deeper. John： You know, I don't know. Maybe it's a bit like hiking. You obviously can't drive everywhere. Or you could drive up the mountain. But maybe it's okay, even fun, to hike up the mountain occasionally even if you can drive.

In the old days — I'm going to sound like an old man. In the old days of six months ago —

主持人： In the old days of six months ago —

John： Well, I was thinking of the '80s and '90s. A lot of people take it: "oh, there are open source packages, there's all sorts of things." We didn't have that. I had to write my own numerical library, my own machine learning. I've rewritten boosting probably four times in four different languages. Now I know boosting.

So maybe not taking the totally easy route — obviously there's a trade-off, you want to be as productive as possible, but you also have to develop the muscles. It's like being an athlete. 主持人： Even if locally that one moment you are not being maximally productive by not exploiting an LLM, that feeds into something.

John： I hope so. The thing I don't know is — I hope people in their careers, it's hard, because the whole world seems to want to optimize everything.

At Google, especially in my group, we have this concept of 20% time, which I very strongly in my own group try to protect. I know 20% time is unusual. There seems to be this strong impetus to just optimize and squeeze everything out. But you lose something when you hyper-optimize — you sort of overfit.

主持人： You overfit to productivity.

John： So my advice might be swimming upstream against cultural norms.

哪些技能持久？

主持人： The problem is not stationary. There's a new skill set that will be the right skill set for the future. Is this a skill that's enduring? John： No. I mean, I don't know. I have a little management work, but you can't be an empty suit — because things might get it wrong, especially LLMs that are really weird. They don't make the same kind of mistakes humans make. So you can't fully trust them. You have to be rigorous and poke at it.

Although you should be poking at software that you write yourself too. That's one thing I've learned. What did Feynman say? "You absolutely can't fool yourself, and you're the easiest person to fool."

I don't know if I can quantify what's enduring. Fundamentalness — really learning a domain that is about the world, like biology or physical sciences. Those are enduring. Math is very enduring.
