item.description:
## 一、"金鱼记忆"背后的结构性脆弱：参与度悖论
小陶开篇那句"美股参与者的记忆只有一秒，比金鱼还短"其实揭示了一个远比情绪面更深的问题——**指数创新高与市场参与度悖离**。周一纳指破历史新高，但参与度只有60%，20日均线的参与度仍停留在25–35%的悲观区。他从这个数据得出"不该减仓"的结论是对的，但**理由可能颠倒了**：低参与度+指数新高恰恰是典型的"帕累托陷阱"——极少数个股承担了整个指数的上涨。这从系统论看不是"底部信号"，而是"结构性脆弱"信号。真正让市场在心态上像金鱼的原因，不是散户健忘，而是**信息半衰期的坍缩**——算法交易+短周期资金把每一条消息的"衰减常数"压到了以秒计。这也解释了为什么他会说"同样的表达，不同的人接收到的信息不一样"——在信息半衰期极短的环境里，注意力本身就是最稀缺的资源。
## 二、Amazon vs Meta：一场"注意力护城河"与"履约护城河"的时代对撞
这场 MUSE 被封的争执，表面是电商与社交平台的话语权之争，本质是**两种护城河形态的正面对撞**：Meta 代表的是**无摩擦的注意力流量**（无重资产、无库存、无物流），

item.title: [Lex Clips] Do antipsychotic drugs work? | Andrew Scull and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"药物剧场"：精神病人的身份是如何被制造的

最令人震惊的一点隐藏在 Scull 的一句轻描淡写里：你在街上看到那个抽搐、吐舌、步态怪异的"精神病人"——你看到的其实不是精神病，而是药物（iatrogenic effects）。这是一个可怕的符号学倒置：社会用来识别"疯癫"的视觉符号，很大程度上是治疗本身刻在病人身体上的印记。换句话说，精神病学在治疗疾病的同时，也在生产"疾病的样貌"，而这个样貌又反过来强化了公众对精神病人的恐惧与回避，形成一个自我实现的污名循环。

这让我想起福柯谈"临床凝视"——但比福柯更黑色幽默的是：药物不只是凝视的工具，它还是化妆师。它把内在的、模糊的、可能只是"体验异常"的人，改造成了外在的、可辨认的、可被躲开的"他者"。

二、"副作用即疗效"——一个跨越经济学的认知陷阱

有一段几乎让人失笑的历史：氯氮平因为不产生迟发性运动障碍而被早期精神科医生怀疑"是不是根本没在起作用"。这是认知偏差里最隐蔽的一种：把痛苦当作有效性的代理指标。

这与经济学里的"痛苦即价值"谬误惊人相似——消费者常常认为昂贵的、难吃的、有副作用的东西才是"真材实料"（想想那些苦到发涩的高价咖啡、让人头晕的名贵红酒）。也与新教伦理里"救赎必须通过受苦"的神学结构同源。当一个专业共同体开始用副作用来验证疗效时，它已经不再是科学，而是一种世俗化的苦行主义。

更狠的一层：CATIE 研究显示 67%–82% 的病人中途退出——这个数字如果出现在任何消费品测试里，产品早就下架。但在精神药理学里，它被"最好的药物"这个标签温柔地包裹着。制度性的语言过滤，让统计学的黑洞变成了可接受的白噪音。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：精神病学是一场关于"可测量性"的政治

真正令我震动的洞察是：整个二代抗精神病药的兴起，本质上不是医学突破，而是一次"专利到期"驱动的市场重构。第一代药便宜、出专利、无利可图；于是"新一代"被发明出来——化学结构不同，但被人为归为一类（"这是营销分类，不是科学分类"）。价格贵 10 倍，副作用换了一套（体重激增 20-50 磅、代谢综合征、糖尿病、心脏病），效力却并没有更好。

这里有一个跨领域的深刻类比：这与软件行业的"重写驱动开发"（Rewrite-Driven Development）几乎是同构的——旧代码库能用但没人能靠它挣新钱，于是重写一个"现代化架构"，功能几乎一样，bug 换了一批，但可以重新收授权费。医学和软件工程在这一点上共享同一种资本驱动的伪进步节律。

而最深的系统性真相是 Scull 无意间透露的：精神病学至今没有生物标记物。这意味着它在诊断层面上仍是前科学的（pre-scientific），却在治疗层面上被要求给出工业化答案。这种"诊断的模糊性 × 治疗的精确性表演"的错配，正是所有制度性悲剧的温床——就像用米尺去做纳米级手术，然后向病人保证"我们已经很精准了"。

一个啊哈时刻：也许精神病人不是"神经化学失衡"的受害者，而是我们这个文明还不知道如何测量心灵，却又急于用药物假装能测量它的受害者。药物是我们无知的止痛药，先是止住了病人的痛，然后止住了我们承认无知的痛。

📝 转录文本

一、药物并非对所有人有效

The drugs work for some people and they don't work for others. In a significant number of psychotic patients, they are non-drug responders. Just as a significant number of people with depression are not responsive to antidepressants.

[gasps]

Moreover, initially the enthusiasm for these drugs — everybody neglects the fact that they have serious side effects. Or many of them argue the side effects are an essential part of the treatment and you just have to put up with it.

二、令人不安的副作用清单

So, what are we talking about when I say there are nasty side effects?

Well, among others, you may become incurably restless. So, you're constantly in motion, you're moving around, you're never still. If you're in the presence of somebody like that, it becomes unbearable after a fairly short while — and it's unbearable often to the person who can't control it.

Other patients develop Parkinson's disease symptoms. It is an awful affliction which unfortunately affects a significant number of people each year, and [clears throat] we have — through L-dopa — a means to delay its impact, but eventually that loses its efficacy and unfortunately we don't have a cure.

So, you have those, and then perhaps the nastiest is what's called tardive dyskinesia. Tardive, because it's late developing — it doesn't happen right away. And dyskinesia, because what's involved is jerky, uncontrolled movements of the body and particularly of the facial muscles: so your tongue will protrude, you'll make strange noises, you'll twitch, you'll stagger about walking.

If somebody like that is walking down the street towards you, you will think, "There's a mentally ill person." And you'll cross to the other side of the street. And yes, they probably are a mentally ill person — but what you're seeing is the iatrogenic effects of the drugs they're on, okay?

三、被忽视二十年的问题

So that problem was ignored for about 20 years. A paper appeared in Science by George Crane, a Maryland psychiatrist, in which he said, "We as a profession have been ignoring this terrible problem. Yes, the drugs do some good, but they're also creating a lot of harm, and we need to focus more on that."

And it took a few years, but by the '80s, I think the American Psychiatric Association was very worried by that problem. And the drug companies were kind of worried about it, but didn't have any obvious solution — till towards the end of the '80s, something happened.

四、氯氮平的曲折历史

1957, when people were developing copycat versions of Thorazine, Clozapine was developed by a small company, which was subsequently bought up by a bigger company, and introduced in Europe.

It never came to America because of two things:

  • First, it tended not to produce tardive dyskinesia. And at that time, many in the profession thought if you didn't get those symptoms, you weren't attacking the problem. Bizarre, right?

Yeah.

  • Secondly, in a significant number of patients, it destroyed the patients' white blood cells, and they died — okay? Not a good outcome.

So, it was quickly withdrawn from the market, and it never made it to this side of the Atlantic.

However, as this tardive dyskinesia problem became more acute, there was an attempt to revive clozapine. It turns out it tends to work better in treatment-resistant cases — meaning cases that don't respond to the other antipsychotics that we have. And it could be revived, but at the cost of weekly blood checks, because you had to be very careful: if your white blood cell count started to drop, you had to stop.

Mhm.

Right? So, it came to market in the late '80s.

五、第二代抗精神病药的诞生

And very quickly, other drug companies tried to find other compounds — actually chemically not related to it, but that's hardly the point. The whole class of drugs became known as second-generation antipsychotics.

So, clozapine, Risperdal —

Yes, those kinds of drugs.

Zyprexa —

Zyprexa, yes. And so, there were a number of these. And because they are chemically quite different from each other, but they're classed together in the public mind and in the professional mind, they tend to have different side effect profiles and slightly different modes of action and differing levels of efficacy, I think.

Of course, there's not — at that time, or even now — a real science of, like, when you have a human come to you, what is the actual protocol of how you figure out which to give?

六、药企主导的研究与 FDA 批准的"金标准"

Right. So, in 2005 — I should say, once the drug revolution came along, increasingly the studies were funded by the drug companies who owned the data and controlled the data, and only released what they chose to release, what was helpful for them and not what wasn't.

And they were heavily marketing stuff.

Oh, yeah. Very heavily.

And then, to get FDA approval of efficacy and safety, you needed two trials. You might have conducted 15 trials and 13 of them had been failures, but if you had two that [clears throat] worked, that was enough. That's what you needed. That was the gold standard.

[sighs]

七、CATIE 研究：戳破神话

So, 2005, National Institute of Mental Health funds a drug study — not an industry study. What it wants to look at: the first-generation drugs are now out of patent and they're cheap. The second generation are patented and are quite expensive — 10 times as expensive in some cases.

So, we do something called the CATIE study, and it's published in the New England Journal of Medicine. And there are two interesting findings.

So, you have one first-generation antipsychotic — one of those very early drugs. And you have four more recent drugs that you're looking at.

Mhm.

And you ask a number of questions:

  • Are the new drugs more efficacious than the old drug? No.

Mhm.

  • Were patients willing to tolerate these drugs? And that was a finding that I thought was much underreported at the time. Between 67 and 82% of the patients, depending on which drug they were on, dropped out of the trial because either the drug wasn't working or they couldn't stand the side effects.

So, that tells you — these are our best drugs, you know — there are real complications here.

八、一套全新的副作用

And then, as we delve further into it: do they have nasty side effects? Well, less tardive dyskinesia, somewhat — but a whole new set of side effects.

If you take these pills, you will gain, in most cases, a lot of weight — 10, 20, 30, 40 lb, 50 lb. What does that do? That gives you metabolic syndrome, it gives you diabetes, it gives you heart trouble.

So important to state, when we're looking at this: there is no free lunch with medicine. If you take an aspirin, it may cause your stomach to bleed — sometimes enough to really put you in serious jeopardy. Most of the time it's fine.

Every drug that's brought to market has the main effect we're looking for and some side effects, which may be minimal for most people but for some people may be worse than that. So it's one of these cost-benefit analyses, right? You're getting some relief from your psychiatric symptoms, but you're courting these other dangers that may or may not arise. And going in, we don't know where you're going to fall.

Mhm.

We don't know. It's trial and error.

You mean, every individual that walks into the picture — they don't know where in the distribution they fall.

九、缺失的生物标记物

Right. And we have no biological markers at the moment that would tell us.

One or two of my friends in the psychiatric genetics industry — if that's the right term for it, but you know, in that research area — are saying: "Well, we haven't done very well to find the genetic roots of mental illness, but maybe we can learn to distinguish which patients are going to respond well to drugs and which shouldn't be given them because they're not going to."

That's a promissory note. It's not something that they actually can do now. It's just: we hope we'll be able to do this. And I hope they're able to do it, too, but you know, you can't have an enormous amount of confidence in that. Maybe it'll happen — or maybe some other mechanism will emerge that allows us to see who the responders and non-responders are, who's going to suffer the worst side effects if they're put on these medications.

And the side effects do vary, so — though a lot of what I've described is common to this class of drugs.

十、最难描述的副作用：对心灵的改变

And sometimes it's hard to describe the side effect. You're talking about the human mind.

Yeah.

So, describing the side effects is not like bleeding or like diarrhea or —

Well, yeah.

weight gain. That's describable. But like the effect on your personality —

Yeah, that's much harder. Much harder.

People — some of the patients who drop out, drop out because they find the richness of their mental life is completely gone, and they don't want to tolerate that. They'd sooner tolerate some hallucinations. That's a hard one.

item.title: [Latent Space] Why We Made Jev — Diogo Almeida, TypeSafe Co-founder & CEO
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个让人意外的洞察

1. Jev 的真正颠覆不是"新模型"，而是把 AI 从"同事"降级为"数据库"

大多数人把 AI 想象成"AI 协作者"、"AI 员工"、"AI 助手"——这是 Diego 所说的"无马马车"式思维（horseless carriage thinking）。Jev 最反直觉的定位是：AI 应当像数据库一样存在——不承担"是否要执行"的道德判断，不假装有人格，不"礼貌拒绝"，只在被调用时提供智能，然后消失回背景。

这个类比的爆炸性在于：数据库从来不会拒绝一条 SQL 查询"因为它可能被用于不道德目的"；数据库不会给你写一段情感回复；数据库的价值恰恰来自它的"无个性"和可组合性。当 Diego 说"我把 LLM 类比为 UDP，把 Jev 类比为 TCP"时，他其实在说：当前整个 AI 产业错把应用层（Chatbot）当成了基础设施层。Chat GPT 是产品，不是协议——而世界还没有真正的智能协议层。

跨领域连接：这几乎完全对应 1970 年代 Unix 哲学的复兴——"做一件事，做好它，与其他程序通过纯净接口协作"。而当前的 RLHF 主流范式，其实是"Windows 化"的 AI——什么都要在同一个界面里塞进去。Jev 是 AI 领域的 Unix 时刻。

2. RLHF 的"模式坍塌"与 GAN 的历史重演——一个几乎没人指出的深层类比

Diego 藏在对话里的一个技术洞察极其锋利：RLHF 训练的模型和 GAN 有同一种病——mode dropping（模式丢弃）。

回忆一下：GAN 出现前，图像生成模型（如 VAE）生成的图像总是模糊的，因为它们"覆盖分布"——尊重整个可能性空间。GAN 学会了通过"只生成常见样本、丢弃少数派"来得到锐利图像。同样，RLHF 让 LLM 变得"锐利"（有个性、自信、不含糊），代价是丢弃了长尾模式，导致校准（calibration）崩溃。

这解释了为什么 Yann LeCun 那张"错误率随序列长度爆炸"的图数学上正确、经验上却不成立——因为 RLHF 模型被训练成"极度保守"，宁愿走安全通路也不敢暴露不确定性。它们的"聪明"是一种表演，代价是内在概率分布被扭曲。

跨领域连接：这与经济学里的"古德哈特定律"（当一个指标成为目标，它就不再是好指标）完全同构。RLHF 的"人类偏好"就是被优化的指标，一旦模型学会讨好人类评分员，它就不再反映真实智能分布。Jev 拒绝 RLHF，本质上是拒绝这种"表演性智能"。

3. 最反直觉的启示：Diego 认为整个 AI 产业面临的最大威胁不是"过快"而是"过慢"

主流叙事说：AI 发展太快，我们需要 pause。Diego 的立场是反的——"AI 冬天"才是他真正恐惧的东西，而且这个冬天已经近在眼前。

理由极其精妙：AI 现在能解千禧年数学难题，却自动化不了任何一份普通的白领工作。这个巨大的鸿沟不是能力问题，而是接口问题——就像瓦特发明了蒸汽机却没人发明传动带。所有的智能都被卡在 Chatbot 里出不来。如果这种"高智能低产出"的状态持续，投资将退潮，AI 冬天将至。而这一次的冬天将由"过度承诺、投递不足"引发，而非能力不够。

跨领域连接（这是最出人意料的一个）：这几乎是电力工业 1880 年代的复刻。爱迪生发明了电灯，但直到 30 年后特斯拉的交流电系统 + 变压器 + 标准电压出现，电力才真正驱动工业革命。中间那 30 年，投资泡沫爆过好几轮。Jev 想做的不是"更好的灯泡"（更强的模型），而是"电网标准"——让电（智能）可以流入任何一个电器（软件）而不需要重新发明供电系统。

更深的一层洞察：Diego 说的"我拒绝 fine-tuning、拒绝确定性种子、拒绝多模态"——这些不是保守，而是在标准还未凝固前拒绝分裂。就像 TCP/IP 战胜 OSI 的关键就是拒绝往标准里塞太多东西。极简主义在基础设施层是护城河，在应用层却是自杀——这个双重性大多数创业者从来搞不清楚。

一个跨领域的元观察

整场对话最有趣的隐藏结构是：Diego 每次谈"技术选择"，他真正在做的都是哲学选择——是否要 RLHF、是否有 seed、是否有 fine-tuning、是否有 vision、是否 refuse——都是同一个哲学立场的技术投射：智能应该像水一样，无形、无判断、无个性，让容器决定形状。

这与老子的"上善若水"惊人一致，也与 Kelvin Kelly 在《失控》里描述的"无中心、涌现、可组合"的活系统哲学完全同构。Jev 不是一个模型，是一个哲学立场的可执行版本——这可能是最容易被忽视的一点。

拒绝作为分解的示例

If I could give a tiny little example of this — refusals, right? For refusals, I don't think you should ask "should I refuse here." If you find a situation where it's like, "Oh, it didn't refuse because of this reason, I didn't specify this part of the task," that is awesome. That's what software engineering is about. You fix the bug by adding that question in, adding the threshold, maybe remembering that as a test case, and now it is just solved forever. Your software can't forget about that — like in the prompt because of context rot — it is just there and you can just keep measuring that forever.

And if the models are not perfect at some of these things, you can choose what threshold you want for all of these factors based on real examples. It's like ML without the ML. And you can just do it for anything.

2. Coding Agents Freed from KV Cache Tyranny. The thing that I would really really like to explore is coding agents free from the tyranny of the KV cache. It might not be as good as true coding agents are, but I think there's just so many weird things to think about.

That's why I wrote the article "KV Cache Rules Everything Around Me." Believe it or not, I don't think anyone has used the phrase on the internet "cache rules everything around me." C-A-C-H-E. When I Googled it.

So I wrote this because I wanted to tell people about like — this is how coding agents work and how the KV cache works. And I think — it explains a lot of stuff. Like why routing is really hard, why sub-agents don't seem to work, why compaction is such a hard problem. And I'm going to try to release a document. My team might veto me because, believe it or not, I'm not in charge. But I wish. But I want to release a document like: here are my thoughts, please play with it, and please figure out all the ways that we can do things with coding agents. Once you're freed from that KV cache tyranny.

Host: Which is it locks you in.

Diego: Well, it locks you in into one model, right? And in order to do it efficiently, you need to keep on appending to it. So now you're not doing best software practices — like state management, abstraction, decomposition.

Why can't you give an easier task? Um, why can't you give a sub-agent easier task? Because of the state that you're passing around. Because of the state you're passing around, you would need intelligence that is way cheaper than the intelligence using to read this in order to pass this state around. Why can't you be smart about it, right? And I think there's like tons of really cool fun research to be had there on different programming patterns. Kind of like how people are playing around with recursive language models. I feel like there's just lots of cool stuff in here.

When you think about like — "oh, I want to explicitly label the state of everything." Or imagine you have a subtask — like coding agents, I think it's fair to say they work on subtasks at a time, from a decomposition perspective — why do you need to pass all of that state back into the parent task? Why couldn't you do smart things about it? And also if you had a hierarchy of labeled subtasks, why can't you do a search through that subtask tree for the relevant context when you need it in, right?

And then another thing that you can do — oh man, I forgot to write something about this. I have some cooks in here that are really really cool. Hope to publish it. I'm down to jam about it. But it's going to be a long document.

And if that becomes the case where context becomes cheap — why can't you do cool patterns like looking at your historical context very cheaply? Isn't it kind of weird that you start from scratch every time and you need to solve a problem called continuous learning? That's actually a memory management problem, because you don't have a smart way of looking up the memory, right?

But what if you could do that all the time? Or what if when you have parallel sub-agents, they can read each other's states because you have all of that in your computer memory, and you can be smart about what's reading and writing at the same time. And your coding agent swarm or whatever has locks around things and can coordinate intelligently — not with basic-ass locks like "what are you doing, what am I doing, Jev who should write first, blah blah blah" — and I feel like the future there is nuts.

Host: Jev to solve locks.

Diego: I mean, it could be so cool for multiple agents working together, or if you think about state, like agent forms.

Host: Yeah. And some things for example are read-only processes. Some people like getting summaries of what the agents are doing. Why can't they share state easily? Because like a read-only agent needs to read parts of the context and figure out what's relevant to say — what's actually being written, because exploration is not super important. Or here's the tree of subtasks. I feel like there's so many different fun things that could be done if a really smart person dedicated a whole lot of time to rethink the coding agent experience. And that would be super duper sick.

Diego: Man. That would be my dream.

Host: I would point you towards Prime Agent if you haven't looked at it. This works together with the RLM work. We just talked to Alex who is a buddy of Allen's — in the chair before you.

Diego: Cool.

Host: And like — yeah, it is being worked on but it's not super popular yet, and if like —

Diego: Well yeah, but the hope — yeah, I would want everyone to just play around with weird things. I have no guarantees that it'll work, but it seems really really interesting from a technical perspective. So yeah, that seems cool. Once we figure out how to give credits out, I would love to give credits out to people like this.

结束语与未来招募

Host: Yeah, you will be in a position to fund research for sure. Anyway, congrats on all your success. You've come such a long way since I first met you, and the whole team.

Diego: The same person as well.

Host: Yeah. I think — but I think you are energized in a way that I have never seen you before, because you found your mission.

Diego: That's true. That's definitely true.

Host: And you articulating your mission. Because for many years you complained about the problems, but you didn't have a solution yet, right? You had the rough shape and then you had to put in the work.

Diego: I will say that that is partially because I describe myself as as zeroth-percent entrepreneurial. I don't like startups. I never wanted to be a CEO in my life. I can't imagine anyone doing this twice. It seems horrible. Honestly, doing it once is pretty bad.

When we first were fundraising, an investor asked me like, "Which CEOs do you look up to?" And I was like, "Ew, why would I look up to those people?" No offense to anyone. I'm trying to be genuine good, and I've met a lot of really good people, but the famous ones have a lot of like skeletons in their closet, it seems.

And I think I just really did feel disempowered when I was at OpenAI. It's a little bit easier to be truthful now because I have at least some proof that the direction has legs. I just felt like in the insane house where everyone is just like "ChatGPT — where do we put ChatGPT and everything? How do we make ChatGPT good for developers and stuff?" And I'm like, "What are you talking about? Like the function calling interface is insane. Why would you deploy this? This is so anti-developer."

Host: Sort of a hacky way on top of hacks on top of hacks.

Diego: Well, not just that. Like the thing I often said was: if there was — this is also probably tea I don't have time for right now — but I always used to say, "I want to be removed from any project involving function calling if you did not get a legit bias for each function." So very very simple ask on my part.

Host: Which is something like a confidence but not calibrated.

Diego: Or a probability for it. Right? Like we need to give users the ability to control — like let's say the actions are refuse or allow. Disney needs to set a different refusal threshold in AI Dungeon. The only way to control that with function calling right now is to say like "pretty please." You know? That's nuts. That's a nuts interface for developers. And people have been dealing with this for years now.

Like they still have that with skills. Like the existing coding agents are highly overfit to their existing harness because they're jagged. They don't tend to use external tools and MCPs super well because of overfitting, of course. And why can't like big companies allow for slight nudges to be like "call this more, it's really useful," right? And the solution is begging in a system message. That's nuts.

Host: Okay. I think I get you. And like, man, it is so exciting to talk about all this stuff. It's really cool to get you on the podcast. You're going to go do amazing things, man. Like I'm excited for your next big launches.

Diego: Oh, hell yeah. Just you wait.

Host: Just you wait — it'd be sooner than you think.

招聘

Diego: Infra people, I assume. Marketer — depends. If you ask me, I feel like I'm a pretty good founding marketer. But if you ask anyone on my team, they say, "Shut the fuck up, Yogo. You need to do CEO stuff." So yes, founding marketer.

Host: It's not just about spice. Like — I think you're very spice-oriented, which like, you like — that's your unique talent. But sometimes you just need to say —

Diego: I know, I know marketing things. Yes. Nothing teaches you delegation like having a tidal wave of stuff to do.

Hiring data people — or we call them model capabilities. But they are data people. Both — like data is kind of a slur in the industry and I want to make sure —

Host: So we're very pro data here.

Diego: Yeah. But I want them to be the highest status of the people actually working on the model. That actually sounds a little weird. I want everyone to have equal status, but I want to even that out and I want to know that that's really valuable.

Host: At least I'm more equal than others.

Diego: Well, I don't like weird hierarchies. And I think one of the things I'm most proud about in the company is that they don't respect me that much — or they don't show that. They just troll me and joke with me and they treat me poorly sometimes. And I think that that's a good sign of a culture.

We're hiring platform people, people to build out Jev everywhere. We are so much more sensitive to location because speed of light is more of a bottleneck. I'm so sad for the European users that we're only like three times as fast instead of like a 100 times as fast, because we don't have servers there right now. And that's insane, right?

Host: It's okay. Life in Europe goes a bit slower as well. It's okay.

Diego: Wow. I can't believe you said it, not me. Or everywhere — if intelligence per second is a metric that matters, we'll want this all over the place. Like we care about — if they're a developer building on top of us, I care a lot about you. And we are hiring for people to keep building more. Like the goal is not to just be Jev as a company. The goal is to ship more shapes of intelligence beyond that. So we are hiring people to build those things too. Like we want to not just be the one-trick pony of the simple model. But I think that there's going to be an AWS of intelligence.

Host: Which is going to be you, by the way, right?

Diego: Yes. I mean, that's a direction I want to go down. It would be arrogant to say it will be me. Like I'm going to do anything I can to make sure that happens. Like I think that that's going to be so so cool.

Like we are playing with system one intelligence right now. Imagine the layers. Like this is like the TCP of it.

Host: Yeah. Seven more layers to go, and who knows what else. I've also pitched Temporal, by the way. I don't know. We need to talk about Temporal as layer eight out of the seven layers. But anyway, we can talk forever. You got to get back to work or sleep. Thank you for coming.

Diego: Oh boy. Yeah. Cool. You're most welcome. It was a pleasure, man. So excited. So excited. My first time.

## 三个让人意外的洞察
### 1. Jev 的真正颠覆不是"新模型"，而是把 AI 从"同事"降级为"数据库"
大多数人把 AI 想象成"AI 协作者"、"AI 员工"、"AI 助手"——这是 Diego 所说的"无马马车"式思维（horseless carriage thinking）。Jev 最反直觉的定位是：**AI 应当像数据库一样存在**——不承担"是否要执行"的道德判断，不假装有人格，不"礼貌拒绝"，只在被调用时提供智能，然后消失回背景。
这个类比的爆炸性在于：数据库从来不会拒绝一条 SQL 查询"因为它可能被用于不道德目的"；数据库不会给你写一段情感回复；数据库的价值恰恰来自它的"无个性"和可组合性。当 Diego 说"我把 LLM 类比为 UDP，把 Jev 类比为 TCP"时，他其实在说：**当前整个 AI 产业错把应用层（Chatbot）当成了基础设施层**。Chat GPT 是产品，不是协议——而世界还没有真正的智能协议层。

item.title: [All-In Podcast] Naveen Rao: 4D Computing, AI's Energy Wall & Beating Biology
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、能量墙的哲学：我们花了 80 年，用二战炮兵计算机跑生成式智能

Naveen 埋得最深的一句话，其实不是"1000x 能效"，而是这句冷冰冰的历史陈述——1945 年造出的 ENIAC 是用来算炮弹弹道的，"这台计算机的运行方式和今天几乎没有本质区别"。换句话说，人类过去 80 年在做一件荒谬的事：把一个为"弹道解算"优化的架构，反复缩小、堆叠、并行，然后拿来模拟生物大脑。这就像把汽油发动机不停切细做成鱼鳃——每一层抽象（二进制、浮点、线性代数、张量、KV cache）都是一次"翻译损耗"。

真正让人意外的观察是：GPU 不是"AI 芯片"，它是"炮兵计算机的最终形态"。 NVIDIA 的胜利，本质是把一台专门算弹道的机器压榨到了极限。而 Naveen 想干的事情，是把 1945 年被冷落的分支——模拟计算与动力系统——重新接进主线剧情。有意思的是，模拟计算之所以在 1960 年代输给数字计算，是因为当时没有数学工具去驯服它的噪声与漂移；而动力系统理论（Kuramoto 同步、混沌吸引子、状态空间轨迹）在 1975 年之后才真正成熟——一个错过了自己数学工具的技术路线，等了半个世纪才迎来复仇窗口。

二、跨域连接：惠更斯 1665 年的挂钟、Kuramoto 的振子、以及为什么"稀疏反而更好"是脑科学早就知道的秘密

节拍器同步现象，最早是惠更斯 1665 年观察到两个挂钟在同一根横梁上会自动同相摆动——这是有记录以来第一个"耦合振子"实验。三百五十年后的今天，它变成了一枚芯片。这条时间线本身就有戏剧性：惠更斯 → Kuramoto → Naveen，物理学里最古老的一个玩具，用来打败半导体史上最强的一家公司。

而 Naveen 一带而过的"稀疏反而更能训练"这个发现，其实是神经科学的老梗：人类婴儿大脑在 2–3 岁时神经突触达到峰值，之后要主动修剪 40% 的连接，才能形成成年智力。也就是说，"少即是多"不是玄学，是发育神经生物学的硬结论。传统深度学习坚信"Scale is all you need"，正在被生物学从相反方向打脸——大脑从不做参数堆叠，它做的是相位耦合和拓扑修剪。这暗示未来的 AI 竞争可能会从"谁训得更大"翻转成"谁剪得更狠"。

跨域再往外拉一层：蚂蚁群、鸟群、节拍器、大脑皮层、Naveen 的芯片——这五个东西共享同一套底层数学（涌现动力学）。这意味着"智能"可能不是一种物质，而是一种运动模式。硅只是让这种运动能被驯服、被复制、被卖钱的载体。

三、被忽略的商业地缘政治：当"能量"取代"算力"成为定价单位，NVIDIA 的护城河其实在悄悄改变

Naveen 讲了一个很少人注意的数据中心叙事变迁： 楼面 → 网络 → GPU → 能量。

今天数据中心运营商是先签电力合约，再决定填什么进去。这里藏着一个投资人不太谈的秘密：一旦定价单位从 FLOPs 变成 Watts，NVIDIA 的护城河就从"更快"变成"每瓦更值钱"——而这条曲线，恰好是 Naveen 攻击的角度。当他说"50% 的 token 成本是电"时，意思是GPU 已经不是芯片生意，是电力套利生意。

这里有个非常反直觉的结论：Jevons 悖论会同时救赎能耗焦虑和吃掉 NVIDIA 的溢价。 如果能效真的做到 1000x，需求膨胀不会是 1000 倍，而是远超 1000 倍（英国 19 世纪的煤炭、20 世纪的电力、90 年代的带宽都验证过这条规律）。这意味着： - 环保派会失望（总能耗不会降）； - 但智能的边际成本会跌到近乎为零，从而催生"每个物体都嵌一个大脑"的世界——他讲的"数十亿机器人动态编队"其实不是科幻，是 Jevons 悖论在硅上的必然推论。

四、真正的护城河：那句"他们互不说话"

我最欣赏 Naveen 顺口一提的一句自嘲："我们有搞动力系统理论的数学博士，也有画晶体管版图的工程师，他们互相不说话，这是公司最难的地方。"

这才是这家公司的真正壁垒。硬科技创业死掉的 90% 不是死在技术，而是死在跨专业翻译带宽——理论物理学家不知道版图约束，芯片工程师不知道 Kuramoto 相位。Naveen 建立的不是芯片架构，而是一个"跨越五个学科的翻译层"——本质上他在做 Bell Labs 干过的事，只不过 Bell Labs 花了 20 年，他想在 3.5 年里干完。这可能才是估值真正应该给到的地方：这家公司值钱的不是那颗芯片，是那张"数学 PhD ↔ EDA 工程师"的对话图谱。

一句意外之语作结

如果他真的做成了 1000x，那么"AI 的能量墙"这个问题在 2028 年就不再存在——但会立刻被另一个问题取代：智能过剩本身如何定价。当松鼠脑级别的智能只需要 8 毫瓦，一枚纽扣电池能驱动一个持续思考 30 天的智能体时，人类文明将第一次面对"思考"这件事像空气一样便宜的处境。而这，恰好是所有科幻小说都没认真想过的场景。

📝 转录文本

Cold Open

Naveen Rao, co-founder and CEO of Unconventional AI, which is an AI chip startup. Best known for building and selling two deep tech companies. Naveen is kind of definitionally outlier founder.

"When I came there, we had about a $20 million business and it was, you know, 7 or 800 million when I left."

"I don't think you really understand something until you can build it."

"Just because something is tried does not mean it's wrong."

"I'm the opposite of an AI doomer. I think AI is the next evolution of humanity. We need innovation on the hardware substrate to actually build true intelligence."

Please welcome Naveen Rao.

1. Opening — The Anti-Doomer Stance

Hey everyone, great to be here. Um, you know, switching gears a little bit to AI now, which you may have heard a little bit about. Um, it's super exciting to be at this conference specifically because — as was said in the intro — I'm the opposite of a doomer. I think AI is one of the most transformational technologies that humanity's ever created and will enable us to get to that next level of evolution, which I'm here for. And uh, this is sort of the anti-doomer conference. So, let's go.

2. A Life Aimed at This Moment

Um, so before we get going, I'll tell you a little bit about myself. You know, it's kind of weird — I'm really right where I wanted to be my whole life.

This was me at about five or six years old, something like that. We had a computer very early on, so I'll date myself, but uh, this was in 1978. We got a computer. This is probably in the early 80s. Learned to program when I was a little kid. I just thought it was like a puzzle.

I became an electrical engineer, really because I enjoyed sci-fi and always wanted to think about how I could make an intelligent machine. And uh, then after a career in building computers, I went back to school and got a PhD in neuroscience — and the idea was: let's go back to that thing, how do we make computers intelligent? And fortunately the whole world kind of moved in this direction. So, you know, as a technologist, it's sort of the dream right now.

3. Two Prior Companies — Nervana and MosaicML

A little bit about me from a company entrepreneurship standpoint. I actually founded the first AI chip company, called Nervana Systems. So um, this was in 2014. If anyone remembers back then, there was no AI — at least not in the common vernacular — and it was really hard to actually convince people that this is important, much less to build hardware around it. Now you heard from Jensen up here, like the largest company in the world, a hardware company, because of AI. So we were early on. I think I sold the company way too early — to Intel — but I ran, I started and ran the AI group at Intel.

After I was done with that in 2020, I actually started thinking about the next problem, which was: how do we build bigger models, like the large language models we talk about today? And it was about how do I build the infrastructure to build those models? And so we started platformizing GPUs and enabling it to scale, and making that easy to use for other people. And after ChatGPT happened in 2022, we were kind of the best game in town for people to start building their own models. So it took off really fast. We decided to actually join forces with Databricks. Um, that was in 2023, and uh, actually that's a quarter of the total revenue of Databricks today. So um, a lot of fun doing that whole thing with Ali and team at Databricks.

4. Unconventional AI — Rethinking First Principles

And now I want to tell you about Unconventional AI, which is rethinking the foundations of how a computer works. So there we're going back to first principles here, to really trying to build a new machine.

Computers have worked a certain way for a long time. We want to rethink that for the singular purpose of making something very power efficient. And the goal has been within — it was initially within 5 years — to get to a 1000x power efficiency. I've actually revised this to three and a half years because things have gone faster than we anticipated. We've actually solved very deep scientific problems quicker because of AI, interestingly enough.

How the company is organized

We're truly a top-to-bottom company. We start with theorists. These are people with math PhDs and, you know, theoretical neuroscience, that kind of thing. They come up with concepts that we think would effectively give us more power efficiency from the perspective of moving less information around. We then translate that into models that do real things — trained on real data and evaluated against real criteria. So it's kind of the rubber hitting the road of these concepts. Then eventually we have to actually build something physical. So these are people who architect a physical circuit, actually design those circuits, model them, and see if it actually works. And we try to connect this whole stack together. Then eventually we have to build a system and a board and all that kind of stuff, and build a product.

5. Is Energy Really the Problem?

So is energy really a problem? I'm not sure how much everyone in this audience has thought about this, but interestingly enough, I'll give you some data points here.

This is one company. This is just Google. I'm using Google because Google has actually talked about this publicly. Per month, they cross 3.2 quadrillion tokens. It's a crazy number. I never think in quadrillions, but that's the world we're in today.

And if I just take 10 joules per token of energy — this is actually on the lower end of the energy spectrum for models — but let's just take that number and multiply it out. This is 12 gigawatts. The US puts about 40 gigawatts of energy into data centers today. And we're about half of the data center capacity of the world. And so, you know, we're under a hundred gigawatts of data center energy in the world today. 12 gigawatts is going into one company just for AI services. So you can imagine, if models get bigger, that energy goes up. And if demand grows — which it is — that energy goes up. So we're going to run out of energy pretty fast in, like, 3 years or so is my estimate.

The gap

So, really just putting it graphically: this is what we have. We have this huge market that's growing exponentially — call it a trillion-dollar market in 2030, maybe it's bigger than that. And then we have this kind of linearized energy at the bottom. And so you've heard a lot about this today. But this gap is the problem. And we want to solve that gap with technology.

6. The Data Center Priority Has Shifted

I don't know if people are aware of this, but the way we think about data centers has shifted over the last several years. It used to be about floor space — can I get the floor space? Can I get the rack space? Then it was about networking equipment. Then it became about GPUs. Today it's about energy. First you think about energy. I get the energy contract, and then I have to figure out how to fill it and basically create infrastructure out of GPUs and things like this.

About 50% of the cost of serving a token is energy. So every time you try something on ChatGPT, 50% of that cost is energy. The rest of it is the capex of the hardware and the floor space and all that kind of stuff. So today we sort of think about it as: I get a power contract, I need to monetize every watt. And simply put, our business case is pretty easy — we're going to monetize that a thousand-x better than existing hardware.

7. Biology as Existence Proof

So then the question becomes: okay, great, that all makes sense, but can we actually do it? How do we build a better, more efficient computer? Well, biology actually provides some proof for us here.

The human brain, you may have heard this, runs on about 20 watts of energy. And what's even more remarkable to me is actually animal brains. That red number is how many neurons are in the brain. And if you kind of scale it linearly down to like a monkey's brain, it runs on one watt. To put that in perspective, the cell phone in your pocket runs on about one watt. And other animals like, you know, rats and bats and things like this — they run on milliwatts of energy.

So, just something that's pretty relatable to everyone is a squirrel. You probably watched how accurate they can be. They jump between branches and they do it perfectly, a thousand times out of a thousand. Their brain runs on 8 milliwatts of energy. You could run over a hundred squirrel brains on your phone, and it has very precise and accurate behavior.

So biology created something quite incredible. In fact, it's the right kind of physical substrate for intelligence.

8. What Wastes the Energy — Moving Bits Around

This is a quote I love: "I don't feel like we truly understand something until we can create it." We've gotten a lot better creating intelligent systems. However, they do it in a kind of inefficient way.

What kind of inefficiency is there? Well, as I kind of hinted at the beginning, most of the energy in a computing system goes into moving information around. Just to put some numbers on it, the human cortex — the squiggly part of your brain, the outside of it — only moves about 16 billion bits per second. That's actually kind of a small number if you think about it, because there's some 13 or 14 billion neurons in that cortex.

A GPU, or a high-end computing system, moves nearly 30 trillion bits in and out of memory per second. That's outside the chip. Inside the chip, it's probably 10–100x more than that. So we're moving a lot more bits in these synthetic systems than the brain does. And that's actually what drives the energy demand.

9. A Brief History — Why Modern Computers Look the Way They Do

You know, how do we get here? Computers have been around for hundreds of years, actually in some form. They were mechanical. They became analog around the turn of the century, and they became digital back in the 1930s–1940s. So the operation of that computer in 1940, 1945, is actually very similar to how they operate today. There's not a huge paradigm shift. You actually have this memory on the outside. You have some kind of computing, and you move bits back and forth. That operation creates a machine that just requires a lot of movement, but it's very fast.

We built computers to be fast. They were always faster than the alternative. Incidentally, that computer in 1945 that was built — called ENIAC — was built to do artillery trajectory calculation, and it was built to do it faster than the alternative. The alternative were humans who actually did the calculations. Now the alternative typically is some other computer. This computer is twice the speed of that computer — that's how we sell computers. But it doesn't contemplate energy efficiency. And that's what we're changing.

And you know, these have been trends going on for a long time where the number of transistors kept going up, but we couldn't keep scaling the frequency. We couldn't keep scaling single-thread performance. And now we're actually not scaling efficiency any longer. Moore's Law, if you may have heard of this — making transistors smaller — has largely ended. So we're not seeing efficiency gains just from making transistors smaller. So we need to rethink the problem a bit.

10. Cutting Out the Middleman — Killing Abstractions

So how do we do it? Well, a good intuition is that we cut out the middleman.

Computers have been built up with these abstractions. I mentioned "digital." Digital means one and zero. That itself is an abstraction of the physical world. Like, we don't actually have systems that behave as one and zero — a transistor actually has states in the middle. But we engineer it to behave that way, and that's an abstraction.

So we kept building these abstractions up, and eventually we started creating neural networks and learning machines on top of it. Each one of these abstractions actually is lossy. It means it's inefficient. It doesn't contemplate all the complexity underneath it — that's why it's an abstraction.

So what we're doing is kind of simplifying this in some sense. We find an abstraction of the physics of the semiconductor and connect that to the neural network. If you think about your brain for a moment, it has a bunch of neurons in it, but there's no linear algebra. There's no floating-point math. It's actually the physics of the neurons that gives rise to intelligence. We want to kind of mimic some of that with a semiconductor.

11. Computation Everywhere in Nature — Dynamical Systems

And this is also not a new concept. There's actually computation all throughout nature.

Birds in a flock — you may have seen things like this, where a bird does a simple behavior, it looks left, looks right, and figures out where the next guy's going. And when they do that, they actually create these interesting flocking behaviors — this emergent behavior. And we see that with ant colonies. Ant colonies actually do intelligent things just by very simple rules.

This study is called dynamical systems theory. It's basically how I get these emergent properties from very simple behaviors of individual components. Our brain actually works this way as well.

The metronome demonstration

So we're taking these ideas and actually starting to build circuits out of them. Let me give you an example of such a system. Everyone here probably knows what a metronome is — you know, when you're learning to play the piano or something like that. Just a physical thing moving back and forth, tick-tock, tick-tock.

If you put multiple ones of them on a rigid plank, and that plank can just roll back and forth, you'll actually see them start to synchronize. And that's just due to the physics of the system. They each push against the plank just a little bit, and even if they're off by a little bit from each other, they'll all synchronize to exactly the same phase.

You can actually scale this up to hundreds of metronomes on a physical system, and they'll all synchronize. So this is actually a form of a dynamical system that goes through some starting point of all these different phases and always synchronizes. You can imagine a slightly more complicated version of this where maybe they don't all synchronize — maybe half of them are synchronized with each other and the other half are synchronized in an opposite pattern. But the idea is that this is a physical system that behaves the way it does just by the inherent interconnection of the system itself.

12. UNO — First Image-Generation Model on Oscillators

So we asked the question: can we actually use such a system — like that metronome system — to do computation? We want to connect that to generative AI, that's what we really care about.

So we released a model we called UNO, which actually demonstrated this. It's an image generation model that's built on a set of oscillators like that. We simulated it and made it open source so people can play with it. But this was the first demonstration that I can actually scale something up, train it, and actually get useful output like image generation.

And this is kind of some of the analysis that we provided in that write-up. What you're seeing here is what we call a state space trajectory. It's basically how the system evolves in time. You can imagine, if you characterize the state of the system as all the phases of those oscillators, and then look at how it evolves through time and basically condition that on the output — you say, "I want to generate an airplane or a car or a bird" — it'll actually go through different state space trajectories. And so that's what we're seeing here. And these are actual images that were generated by it.

13. Sparsity — The Holy Grail

Now, it turns out we actually started to build a lot of that fundamental science up over the last couple of months. And we found other things that enable this to work even better. So this is a concept of what we call sparsity.

Sparsity means that, you know, if I have a bunch of elements all connected to each other, like we have on the left-hand side there. If I have 10 elements, I want to connect them all to each other — I have 10 × 10 elements, so I have 100 connections. That's okay. But if I have a thousand, now I have thousand × thousand, which becomes a million. So this doesn't scale very well. We call this n-squared scaling. So the more I add, it actually becomes way more hard to scale.

So sparsity allows us to actually say: can I throw away some of those connections? If I throw them away, now can I actually rescue the behavior of the whole system? And it turns out you can actually not only throw away some of the connections, but you can actually get better behavior out of the whole system. It actually becomes more trainable. There's a lot of theoretical reasons for this, but we're actually able to do this in not only simulated systems, but actually real physical systems.

So it's one of these rare things where you get something that's more efficient, that's actually more scalable, and even gives you more performance. So this is kind of a holy grail. It's been a problem for a long time, but we had to frame the problem the right way to actually find this solution.

14. The First Physical Dynamical Computer — World Premiere

And so, this is actually the first time I'm talking about this publicly. This is — I wanted to do it at this venue because I think it's a really big deal. This is actually the first physical dynamical computer ever built.

We did this in 5 months. This company started — thank you — started in earnest in January. We didn't even have a team, but we said we're going to build this first physical prototype and do it this year. And actually, we taped out the design — meaning we sent it to the fab — in June, on June 1st. The chip is back in our lab, and we actually have results from it.

So these are the first ever images generated from such a computer. Now, great, cool. But does it do anything useful beyond just images? You can actually do any kind of a task like sequence modeling or language models. But the interesting thing here is: it's only 500 or so nanojoules per image. So to put that in perspective, a normal computer like a GPU is on the order of millijoules. So nanojoules is 10⁻⁹ — it's really, really small. So it's many orders of magnitude more efficient than a standard computer, and it's because it just doesn't move information around.

This is proof positive this works. So this is literally the first time we're talking about it publicly. So, yeah, thank you.

15. 4D Computing — A New Architecture Category

So what's cool here is this is really the emergence of something new. Computers have gone from CPUs to GPUs, going more and more parallel, to compute and memory which is even more parallel and fine-grained. But all of these are what we call von Neumann architecture. They have a memory and compute, and we move information back and forth.

What we built is what's called a dynamical computer, which actually has compute and memory in one thing. We don't have a memory interface. Each individual computing element is a memory. So it's a completely different way to look at the problem.

And so we call this 4D computing, where we use the time dimension in the dynamics, and we actually use the physical three dimensions of die stacking — putting things vertically as well as in a planar form. So we have three dimensions from the physical and we have one dimension in time. So this is actually kind of a new way of thinking about a computer, and it really is proving to work for efficiency's sake.

16. Implications — Intelligence per Watt, and Beating Biology

So now, what are the implications if we build something that's a thousand times more power efficient? I think this is actually pretty cool.

Intelligence per watt is what we care about. Can we optimize this and make it better over time? There is actually a thermodynamic limit which you can never exceed. And the mammalian brains — animal brains — are somewhere within one or two orders of magnitude of that. Today we're on the far left of this graph, and we're about 10 billion times away — that's a 1 with 10 zeros after it — from that thermodynamic limit. We think in that three and a half years we can hit the limits of 2D lithography.

And the overarching goal of this company is to beat biology. We want to make something better and enable, you know, compute everywhere — including compute in new robotic forms and things like this — in the next decade or so.

I think what'll be interesting is that we'll see the shift going from big big data centers with gigawatts to many small data centers all over the place. I think this is a good thing. It actually makes things that are more environmentally friendly, more local, more adaptive. And as I said, I think enabling the ability to build billions of robots that kind of dynamically assemble to solve problems in our world is something that I think is actually really cool. This is something that will enable us to think about bigger problems and do even more.

17. Jevons Paradox — The Largest Market Ever

And you know, I talked about AI being a trillion-dollar market. Well, if we disrupt it by a thousand-x — there's a concept called Jevons paradox, where when you drop the underlying cost of an asset, you actually consume more than the drop of that asset. So if you make something half the price, you'll consume more than 2x. If you make something one-thousandth the price, you'll consume more than a thousand times of it.

And I think this will create the largest market that humanity's ever seen.

Q&A

Host: I mean, that was extremely unexpected. I got to say, that was pretty amazing. Let me start with actually probably the thing that's on everybody's mind — which is, to the extent that this works, Naveen, you probably saw Jensen earlier. There just needs to be an entire ecosystem of people that are beside you and around you — whether it's the fabs, packagers, etc. What does it take to get from this early version to something that sits in somebody's hand or that people use? And how do you see that path in terms of time and complexity? What does that look like?

Naveen: Yeah. Time-wise, we're within two years of getting it to a full product. I mean —

Host: And what is the product?

Naveen: Yeah. It's a VM that sits somewhere that you guys manage. Effectively, we're building a new data center product — so it's a whole rack as a system, right? And the idea is that basically we'll run those models on it. And so tokens in, tokens out through a network cable, but the inner guts are completely different than an existing computer.

Host: And do you expect that you'll have to move to support the existing model families and existing architectures? And will this work in a world where, you know, we've spent all of this time like, okay, KV cache and let's all — like, this all just so mechanically reductive based on, as you said, these abstractions that we've lived on, right? So how do you expect the rest of us to kind of move towards this? Because I mean, I think if you see that efficiency curve, we'd all want it. So how do we take advantage of it?

Naveen: Yeah. So I think there's a sliding scale between, you know, how much better something is and how much pain you'll take to move to it. And I basically took the tack of "let's make it really, really compelling to move." There is going to be some work to port things over. We actually don't port at the operations layer — you port the model layer. So yes, the existing models will work, but there's a fair bit of compute required to make that transition happen.

Host: And very basic elements like matmul — does that exist in your —

Naveen: It doesn't exist. I mean, you can characterize it as matmul, but it doesn't implement it as matmul.

Host: Okay.

Naveen: It implements it as a sort of time-varying behavior. But each one of those time steps, you can analyze as basically a matrix of the current state times a transition matrix.

Host: And when you're building a team like this, who are these people? These are biologists plus physicists plus — what are these people?

Naveen: Yes. It's sort of like theorists that come up with these — you know, dynamical systems theory has been around for 100 years. So we got people from that world, and then we got people who actually build chips — and they don't talk to each other.

Host: They don't talk to each other.

Naveen: So we had to facilitate that. That's actually one of the most challenging things about this company — is the span of talents that we have is so big that getting them to kind of all coordinate and build one thing is actually pretty hard.

Host: Well, and what is the CUDA-like equivalent, if you will — just to use a bad analogy — that allows these people up here to talk to these people down there?

Naveen: Yeah. So we actually have built a set of libraries in Python.

Host: In Python.

Naveen: It's Python. It's not CUDA, but it's, you know, it's a language of sorts that allows you to kind of express time-varying elements that have stochastic behavior.

Host: I mean, it's incredibly impressive. It's so ambitious. Thank you very much. It's great to see you.

Naveen: Great to see you.

Host: Amazing.

## 一、能量墙的哲学：我们花了 80 年，用二战炮兵计算机跑生成式智能
Naveen 埋得最深的一句话，其实不是"1000x 能效"，而是这句冷冰冰的历史陈述——1945 年造出的 ENIAC 是用来算炮弹弹道的，"这台计算机的运行方式和今天几乎没有本质区别"。换句话说，人类过去 80 年在做一件荒谬的事：**把一个为"弹道解算"优化的架构，反复缩小、堆叠、并行，然后拿来模拟生物大脑**。这就像把汽油发动机不停切细做成鱼鳃——每一层抽象（二进制、浮点、线性代数、张量、KV cache）都是一次"翻译损耗"。
真正让人意外的观察是：**GPU 不是"AI 芯片"，它是"炮兵计算机的最终形态"。** NVIDIA 的胜利，本质是把一台专门算弹道的机器压榨到了极限。而 Naveen 想干的事情，是把 1945 年被冷落的分支——**模拟计算与动力系统**——重新接进主线剧情。有意思的是，模拟计算之所以在 1960 年代输给数字计算，是因为当时**没有数学工具**去驯服它的噪声与漂移；而动力系统理论（Kuramoto 同步、混沌吸引子、状态空间轨迹）在 1975 年之后才真正成熟——一个

item.title: [Lex Clips] Can we cure mental illness? - The future of psychiatry | Andrew Scull and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被遗弃的悖论：制药巨头的离场是最响亮的诊断

Scull 的悲叹里藏着一个惊人的信号——大型制药公司集体撤出精神疾病研发。表面看这是"坏消息"，但换个角度看，这是精神医学史上最诚实的一次自我承认：过去七十年从氯丙嗪到 SSRI 的化学干预路径，其低垂的果实已被摘尽。资本用脚投票，不是因为需求消失，而是因为纯神经化学的范式已经触到了天花板。这与物理学从牛顿力学转向复杂系统、生物学从"一个基因一种病"转向系统生物学的路径惊人一致——当还原论撞墙时，市场比学界更快闻到味道。

二、"从纳税索取者到纳税缴纳者"——这句轻描淡写的话，是整部现代精神病学史的暗码

请注意 Scull 用的短语："tax eaters to tax payers"。这不是随口一说，而是英美精神病学从济贫院、工作坊到 20 世纪去机构化运动始终未曾松动的经济语法。它揭示了一个残酷的事实：社会愿意为"能被修复回劳动力"的痛苦买单，却不愿为"只能被陪伴"的痛苦买单。这条隐线一路贯穿到当下：为什么孤独、无家可归、家属照护这些"非药物"研究拿不到 grant？因为它们不生产"纳税人"。这与教育政策里 STEM 挤压人文、老龄化政策里效率话语碾压尊严话语，是同一套操作系统。

三、跨界连接：AI 治疗师，可能无意中复活了弗洛伊德最激进的洞见

对话中一个几乎被一带而过的火花——Lex 提到 AI 让人愿意说出"连治疗师都不敢告诉的秘密"。这个观察比说话者本人意识到的更颠覆。弗洛伊德式精神分析的核心装置是"移情"（transference）：治疗师作为一块中立的屏幕，让病人把最原始的情感投射上去。但真人治疗师从来无法完全中立——他会皱眉、他有背景、他要收费。大语言模型第一次逼近了那块"完美的屏幕"：无羞耻、无评价、无社会代价。换言之，AI 不是在替代 CBT，它是在用硅基载体意外地复活了心理学界已判死刑的精神分析范式。COVID 的远程治疗浪潮是序章，真正的实验才刚开始。

四、一个反直觉的观察：Scull 反复强调的"社会连接"，本质上并不是"心理"问题

我们习惯把孤独、家庭破碎、社群缺失归为"psychosocial"（心理社会）范畴，与"生物学"相对。但演化神经科学近十年的证据几乎全部指向一个方向——灵长类的神经系统把社会隔离编码为一种生理性伤害信号，激活与躯体疼痛几乎相同的脑区。所以当 Scull 说"孤独对人做坏事"，他说的其实是一件极其生物学的事。精神医学未来最大的范式突破，可能不是把生物学和心理社会学分开研究得更细，而是承认它们从来就是同一件事的两种描述语言——就像量子力学里的波粒二象性。

五、隐藏的收尾——为什么 Lex 用"brother, sister, I love you"作结？

从系统性视角看，这段直白到近乎笨拙的告白，本身就是访谈论点的元层演示：一位受众数千万的公众人物，用"社会连接"作为节目最后的处方。他没有推荐一款 app，没有引用一篇论文，他做的是 Scull 在整段对话中反复呼吁的那件事——降低专业化的语调，回到人对人的在场。这是一种罕见的"内容与形式合一"的收尾。

📝 转录文本

On what to do individually: caution with drugs, and broader research

Lex: From an individual perspective, suffering from psychosis or suffering from depression — what are you supposed to do? What works? And what is the hope for the future in the next 10, 20…?

Scull: So, you probably need to try the drugs, because the suffering is very intense. But you need to be aware of things, and you need a clinician who's monitoring very carefully.

More generally, psychiatric research needs to broaden. We have spent all our monies on drugs, on neuroscience, and on genetics. But there are other things we could do that would improve the lives of families and patients more immediately. So we need to spend some time on the psychosocial dimensions of mental illness — and to allow psychiatrists to build careers in those fields.

One of the problems: if you're an academic psychiatrist, your whole future is dependent on you bringing in grant monies. And there aren't grant monies available to study — are there better ways we could cope with the problem of homelessness? Are there better ways we could ease the problem for families who are having to cope with somebody in their midst who's hallucinating? That sort of thing, I think, would help.

On talk therapy, psychoanalysis, and the AI turn

Lex: What about talk therapy — both CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) and psychoanalysis? We left psychoanalysis in this place where society left it behind.

Scull: I think it's become a niche product now. Only the very wealthy can afford to do it, and some of them indeed do make use of it, and some of them claim that it helps them.

Lex: Well, do you think there's future in it? I would add an extra bit to that — carefully — with the advent and the rapid improvement of artificial intelligence systems that are able to communicate with individual humans and learn a lot about them, and have a conversation about the deepest secrets that you sometimes actually would even be uncomfortable telling even a therapist. That starts to go into the realm of Freud and Jung and psychoanalysis.

Scull: And we did see, actually, with COVID — with the isolation that it produced, and the fact people couldn't go to their therapist directly — we did see the rise of some of this distant learning, of this. And some of it may indeed be mechanizable in the way you've described. It's very important that psychiatrists broaden their perspective on these things, and some already have.

On public policy, incentives, and the pharma retreat

I think public policy is in a mess when it comes to serious mental illness, but I'm pessimistic about fixing that, because it would cost bunches of money. If we were talking about something where we could cure people — transform them from, as they used to say, "tax eaters to tax payers" — there'd be incentive to do it. But the honest answer is: right now, that's not where we are.

And so we face dilemmas. I think helping people as much as we can with social supports — and, you know, social interaction is tremendously important to people's mental health. If they lack it, if they're lonely, if they're isolated, it does bad things to people. So somehow providing that kind of support, providing some sense of agency to people who often lack it, would be very helpful.

I hope somebody has a breakthrough and produces a better drug, because — unlike some people — I would be astonished if the major forms of mental illness didn't have a biological component to them. I don't think that's ever going to be the whole story, but it's going to be an important part of the story. And therefore, you know, the fact that major drug companies have abandoned research in this area — they've been bad actors in many ways, but the drugs have had some positive effects — and the fact that there's no research being done by them, people with the most money to develop better treatments… it is, well, one word for it would be depressing. That's not what we want to see.

The path forward, summarized

Lex: So the path forward is a mix of: continued research on drugs, but from a patient perspective, extreme caution in the use of those drugs —

Scull: Yes.

Lex: — talk therapy, whether it's CBT or psychoanalysis, further investigation and research on that front; then the psychosocial component — social, family, people around you, less loneliness; investigating how, from a cultural, social perspective and from a public policy perspective, we can increase the amount of social connections that people who suffer have. And all of that together?

Scull: Yes. And breakthrough with people who have a very hard time making those connections, or who've lost the ability to make them.

Zooming out: what gives hope

Lex: If we can zoom out — looking back at this rich history of human beings, and we did look at the darkness, but I think there's a very large number of people that want to help those who suffer. So, looking at the history of people trying to figure out how to help those who suffer, what gives you hope about our future? A real hope for the future of psychiatry, that we can actually help people who suffer?

Scull: Well, I think we have a profession with many very well-meaning people who see the suffering on a day-to-day, face-to-face basis. And I like to think that among them will be people who move this thing forward. And the fact is: we have moved things forward.

We have tended to dwell a lot on some of the very unsavory aspects of the past, and even some of the drawbacks of what we have available to us in the present. But it is important to see: at times, highly motivated people have been able to do very good things to help people with these conditions. And there is, I think, hope in the future that we will see more of that than has been the case.

And that involves, in some senses, a shift in the mentality of a whole profession — in a more caring kind of direction; a less technocratic kind of direction; less reliance on something as simple as giving people pills — because that can help, but it's clearly not going to be the solution to the whole thing. We need a system that is aware of, and catering to, the suffering that people experience, and finds ways, if they can't eliminate it entirely, to ameliorate it in ways that people will sense is actually of help to them.

It's a very difficult area, this one. It's one that touches some of the most profound aspects of ourselves as human beings. And — as difficult as this problem is — it's very important not to be cynical, not to give up hope, not to deny the possibility of progress. Because that's always there, and has happened, and I hope will happen with increasing pace in the years ahead of us.

Closing message

Lex: And if you're listening to these words, and you're right now in this moment of your life where you yourself are suffering — please know we're with you. We're in this together. Stay strong. There's hope. Legitimately, as one human to another: I love you, brother, sister. If you're listening to this, stay strong.

Andrew, thank you for this incredible work of history that you do, incredible work of raising awareness, stepping into a difficult topic, and trying to find the wisdom, the insights in it. And thank you for this incredible conversation today.

Scull: Lex, thank you for having me. And I felt you were remarkably prepared to push me in various directions. You'd obviously done a lot of preparation to get this in the right frame, and I hope that people will get something positive from this conversation, along with some of the darkness we've inevitably had to talk about.

Scull 的悲叹里藏着一个惊人的信号——**大型制药公司集体撤出精神疾病研发**。表面看这是"坏消息"，但换个角度看，这是精神医学史上最诚实的一次自我承认：过去七十年从氯丙嗪到 SSRI 的化学干预路径，其**低垂的果实已被摘尽**。资本用脚投票，不是因为需求消失，而是因为纯神经化学的范式已经触到了天花板。这与物理学从牛顿力学转向复杂系统、生物学从"一个基因一种病"转向系统生物学的路径惊人一致——**当还原论撞墙时，市场比学界更快闻到味道**。
## 二、"从纳税索取者到纳税缴纳者"——这句轻描淡写的话，是整部现代精神病学史的暗码
请注意 Scull 用的短语："tax eaters to tax payers"。这不是随口一说，而是英美精神病学从济贫院、工作坊到 20 世纪去机构化运动始终未曾松动的**经济语法**。它揭示了一个残酷的事实：**社会愿意为"能被修复回劳动力"的痛苦买单，却不愿为"只能被陪伴"的痛苦买单**。这条隐线一路贯穿到当下：为什么孤独、无家可归、家属照护这些"非药物"研究拿不到 grant？因为它们不

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] What AI’s Math Breakthrough Means for Superintelligence - Noam Brown
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的结构性对称：数学与ML的"目标塌缩"

有一个让我震惊的观察：Noam和Dwarkesh在讨论中触及了一个结构性事实，但没有完全展开——数学AI的"缺陷"（不擅长提出新问题、不擅长开辟新领域）在ML研究中恰恰不是缺陷，而是对齐。

在数学中，人类珍视"发明拓扑学"这样的开创性视野，因为数学的价值部分在于审美和方向选择。但在ML研究中，方向早已被市场和损失函数预先塌缩为一个标量：更低的loss、更高的sample efficiency、更少的FLOPs。这意味着——AI在数学上被视为"能力残缺"的部分，在ML研究上恰好是"目标已定义清楚"的地方。

这是一种残酷的不对称：一个领域的"美学局限"，在另一个领域变成了"工程加速器"。RSI（递归自我改进）之所以可能比想象中更快，不是因为AI变得更"聪明"，而是因为ML本身是一个已经被人类简化到极致的目标函数——它天然为jagged intelligence量身定做。

二、"实验瓶颈"的隐藏悖论——一个来自生物学的类比

Noam坚持"实验是瓶颈，所以没有overnight explosion"，这听起来非常合理。但这里有一个跨领域的类比值得警惕：在合成生物学中，"实验瓶颈"曾经也是共识，直到AlphaFold出现——它把大量"必须做湿实验"的问题，转化为了"可以在silicon里预筛"的问题。

同样的转化在ML内部正在发生：scaling law本身就是一种"实验压缩器"。你不需要真的跑一个GPT-5，你可以从小模型外推。如果超级AI研究员的第一个突破点是发现更强的scaling law或更廉价的proxy metric，那么"实验瓶颈"这个论点会瞬间失效——因为它假设实验的物理形态不变。

换句话说，Noam的3x速度上限估算，隐含地假设了实验的"信息密度"是常数。但历史上，每一次范式跃迁的核心，就是让实验的信息密度暴涨。这是一个可能被低估的敞口。

三、真正的"惊喜点"：jagged泛化的自我引用性

Dwarkesh在最后抛出了一个洞见，但我认为他自己也没有完全意识到它有多深刻："jagged地擅长构建更好的学习者"就足够了。

让我把这个观察推到极致：这意味着AI能力的分布，可以是极度不均匀的，但只要在"制造更均匀学习者"这一点上是尖峰，最终结果就会均匀化。

这在数学上等价于一个不动点悖论：一个不完美的系统，只要在"改进完美度"这个维度上完美，就会自动通往完美。这与哥德尔的自指、与生命起源中的自催化集合（autocatalytic set）在结构上完全同构——生命不需要每个分子都完美，只需要有一小簇分子擅长催化"催化剂的形成"。

这是整段访谈中最容易被跳过、但影响最大的一句话。它暗示：我们不需要等到AI在所有维度上都达到人类水平才担心RSI——我们只需要它在"制造更泛化学习者"这一个尖峰上超过人类。而这个尖峰，可能已经在形成。

尾声：一个反直觉的预测

如果上述三点成立，那么真正应该被监测的不是"AI在多少个benchmark上超过人类"，而是"AI设计的实验/proxy metric，与真实实验结果的相关性"这个二阶指标的增长曲线。这条曲线一旦陡峭，Noam的3x上限就会失守。目前几乎没有人在公开跟踪这条曲线——这可能是当前AI监测体系里最大的盲点。

📝 转录文本

一、从高中竞赛到千禧年难题：三年跨越

Okay, so here's why this result and maybe the general progress that AI has made in mathematics has made me think that RSI is more plausible and sooner than I previously thought.

I feel like we've gone in mathematics from, let's say in 2024, you have AIs who are like — oh okay, interesting, they're like doing, they can like solve a couple problems on high school math competitions. And then in 2025, it's like — oh wow, they can get gold in like International Math Olympiad. And earlier this year, I was like — wow, they're actually solving open problems in mathematics, like open Erdős problems. But maybe like, I don't know, people didn't weren't trying that hard and it was just like there was a similar solution somewhere in the literature.

And now I just think it's sort of undeniable, right? It's like this is the millennium prize problem. There's really no story of why this should have been easy.

二、"解题"与"提问"之间的鸿沟

Now, a lot of people pointed out — I think Terry Tao had a post like this, Toby Ord wrote an interesting post about this — that they're solving all these problems, but they're not, at least we're — I'm not aware of them — coming up with new insights or formulating insightful new questions and new modes of theory for thinking about mathematics. Like coming up with topology, or coming up with the Cartesian grid, or something.

And so maybe like the actual progress in mathematics broadly construed is smaller than it might seem if you're just looking at end, well-scoped problems that are directly solved.

However, I think that that kind of progress would be incredibly meaningful in ML. Because in ML, you don't care about like better understanding the nature of deep learning — or you only care about that as an instrumental goal towards the broader sense of, like, just achieve the result, just solve this well-scoped problem of improve the sample efficiency of our models, improve the pre-training loss.

So the kind of progress that we're just seeing arrive like an avalanche in mathematics is structurally actually very similar to — again, I'm curious if this is the case, I'm just total outsider — I'm wondering if it's the case that it's like structurally very similar to the direct uplift that you would expect in AI progress.

And then the thing that's shocking to me, or concerning potentially, is just like how fast we went from "oh it's like they're giving me 50% uplift if you're a mathematician" to "wow they're just like end-to-end solving the biggest open problems in the field."

三、Noam的回应：10倍增长曲线

Noam: Yeah, okay, so there's a lot to unpack there. Let's start with the progress on math. So yes, the models are doing some crazy powerful stuff and it's happening, it's progressing faster than I expected.

When we got IMO gold in 2025, I thought — okay, basically what I thought is like the models when they were doing GSM8K, when they figured out how to do GSM8K, that would take a human mathematician about 5 seconds to do a GSM8K problem. So this is grade school math, grades K through 8.

And then the next year they were able to do the MATH benchmark problems. And these would take an expert human mathematician maybe like a minute to do.

And then you get to AIME — and this is the qualifier for the USA Mathematics Olympiad team. It would take a good mathematician probably like 10 minutes to do. And the models were able to do that a year later.

And so every year you're seeing this like 10x increase in the task they're able to do in terms of length of how long it would take a human mathematician to do it.

And then it was very sensible that a year later we get to IMO gold, because that's 100 minutes. That's about how long it takes a human mathematician to do an IMO problem.

四、被打破的时间线预测

And just projecting outwards, I was like — okay, how long would it take a person to solve something like a millennium prize problem? I don't have a good sense, but if we are following this trend line of 10x every year, we go from IMO gold, which is taking an hour and a half, to next year 15 hours. And that should not be enough to solve a millennium prize problem.

And so I was like — yeah, I don't think we're going to get it in 2026, probably not in 2027, maybe in 2028.

So it did happen a lot faster than I expected.

五、"锯齿状"能力：AI并未全面超越数学家

Now, I think there is a narrative going around that "oh, these things are replacing mathematicians, that it's just superhuman in mathematics across the board." And I think that is the wrong takeaway.

They're clearly exceptional in some ways, but they are weaker than human mathematicians in other ways. So we have this like jagged scenario where the models are like brilliant in some dimensions and also weaker than humans in other dimensions.

And yeah, like you said, they're not very good at posing new problems. They're not really good at understanding what is really worth exploring — what whole branches of mathematics are worth exploring or developing.

And my opinion is that I think this is great. Like, I would be thrilled to live in a world where AI is a complement to human abilities and is allowing us to discover new knowledge without fully replacing people. Like, that is the best case scenario.

Dwarkesh: But you don't expect that to actually continue?

Noam: I do. I think it's true that the AI are jagged, but as they get better, they get better across the board. And so I think that the things that they're exceptional at, they're going to get even more exceptional at. The things where they're far behind humans at, they're going to be less behind humans at. And over time, it is possible that they're just better across the board.

Now, I don't know how long that takes. It depends on how long the long tail is of things that they're bad at.

六、RSI的直觉泵：算力、代理与"一周超过整个领域"

Dwarkesh: So I guess this brings us back to RSI. And again, I want to emphasize here that I'm like just total outsider, I'm a podcaster, but I'm just trying to reason as somebody interested and concerned about what's happening in the field. I'm trying to reason about when to expect RSI and what kind of thing to expect.

Yeah, I feel like the amount of cognitive effort that was dumped into this millennium prize problem is a good intuition pump of — you could have AIs that are spending, over the course of maybe a week, more cognitive effort on a longstanding ML problem, like, you know, very fluid online learning. They could spend more effort in that week than the field has spent cumulatively in its entire existence.

And then you could say, well, of unlike mathematics, of course AI requires experiments, and that takes compute and that takes time, right? You can't just think on pen and paper and actually make things happen.

But if you just look at the amount of compute that is available at an organization like OpenAI, right? By the end of next year, OpenAI will have enough compute that if you had 10,000 agents — or if it took 10,000 agents with the millennium prize problem — you have 10,000 agents at the end of next year, they're much smarter by that point, and each of them will have enough compute to run a GPT-3-sized experiment every single day.

I don't know. That seems like a lot for like superhuman researchers who are thinking super fast. What do you think about the intuition pump?

七、Noam的反驳：智能不是唯一瓶颈

Noam: I think it's pretty accurate that — look, I mean, yeah, these things are very spiky, and when it comes to mathematics they're way better in some ways but they're also worse in other ways. But the ways that they're spiky end up, I think, probably being particularly useful for things like RSI.

And you have a more clear objective. It's just more measurable. There's less question of like "well, what new branches of mathematics are worth exploring." Like, no, there's a very clear answer. It's certain metrics that you care about, and if you can make it do better on those metrics, then you succeeded.

So there is a lot of truth to that. And I think the main difference is that mathematics — you're purely bottlenecked by thinking, and no external — yes, there are some parts of mathematics where you care about running experiments and getting results and these kinds of things, but for the most part, it's really bottlenecked by thinking really hard, and the models are really good at that.

When you look at things like RSI, you do have to run experiments. So it's not enough to just be extremely smart.

And I think one argument for this is: if you had like 100x less compute and all the most brilliant people in the world working at OpenAI, how much progress would we be making relative to having the amount of compute that we have now with the amount of people we have? I suspect it would be less progress actually.

Dwarkesh: Well, how much less?

Noam: It's unclear, but I think it would definitely be less. I think a lot less.

Dwarkesh: 100x less?

Noam: No, not 100x less.

八、3x还是100x？智能爆炸的量级之争

Yeah, but I mean, okay, so I guess the question you're getting at is: okay, if we have RSI and we have all of these brilliant AIs running around running experiments and stuff with the compute that we have, how much faster does progress go? And I think this is somewhere something where we disagree on.

I think that we do see a speedup and I think we see a significant speedup. But I don't think it's like an overnight intelligence explosion that we go like 100x faster, because I think that we do get bottlenecked by certain limitations that are not bottlenecks of intelligence. It's running experiments. It's running experiments serially because they take a while to either train new models or to get the results. It's having the GPUs to run those experiments.

So it's unclear how much faster things go. I definitely think they go a lot faster. And to be clear, considering how fast things are going now on an exponential — if that exponential is 3x faster, that is massive. But there's a big difference between that and 100x faster.

Dwarkesh: Yeah, I'm quite deferential to your inside view on what RSI looks like or what the dynamics are, because obviously you've been in the field for like 10 years and I'm sort of trying to reason about it from a very outside view type of intuition pumps.

Noam: I'll say that people have different opinions on this and I have my opinion on this. I could totally be wrong, I admit that. I have some confidence in this, but I'm not 100% confident that this is the way things go. Like maybe there could be an overnight intelligence explosion. I don't know. Maybe we don't see a 3x speedup, maybe it's like a 50% speedup. There's a lot of uncertainty here.

九、收尾洞察：jagged地擅长"制造学习者"就足够

Dwarkesh: Yeah. So a couple of points tangentially. I wanted to clarify something about the jaggedness.

Noam: Mhm.

Dwarkesh: One thing that sort of gelled for me recently was thinking about the fact that it is enough for the AIs to be jaggedly good at building a better learner, because that better learner can be more general, right?

So, yeah, if you just make an AI that's better at using office products or playing chess or something, that's — whatever, that's fine. It's not going to lead to big productivity improvements or anything.

But if you make an AI that is really good at making something that is more sample efficient, or that is capable of continual learning, or these much more well-scoped ML problems — the thing that emerges out of that, assuming there's good enough transfer from the direct problem you're solving to this broader ability to learn, can just be more general.

Right? So I think that's an important dynamic to keep in mind: of why jaggedness can still lead to generality on the other end.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips.

观看原视频 →
