item.description:
## 一位无神论者的护身符：Constâncio 悖论
这段访谈最耐人寻味的时刻，不在他反复宣称的"黄金是神话"，而是他不经意的一句自白——**葡萄牙央行的黄金储备排名全球第十二**。一位刚刚论证黄金"非理性、迷信、无收益"的前央行行长，坐镇于一个人均持金量惊人的国家。这就像一位无神论哲学家，抽屉里始终放着一枚圣物。他把这称为"集体非理性向个体理性的转化"，但这个用词本身就是一次无意识的降维——他用"非理性"命名了一种他所在体制无法建模的**价值维度**。
## 他的论证里藏着黄金最好的辩护词
Constâncio 定义资产价值为"未来现金流的贴现"，因此黄金"没有收益流 = 投机品"。**但他随后自己拆解了这个定义**：谈到"安全资产"时，他承认——没有任何资产是绝对安全的，安全性来自"低通胀""法治""对财产权的保护""对机构可信度的信任"。也就是说，他推崇的"安全"完全**寄生于制度信任**。而黄金的全部特征恰恰是：它是唯一一种"制度信任崩塌时依然工作"的资产。当他说新兴市场买金是因为"美元资产会被冻结制裁"时，他等于承认了：黄金正在履行的，正是他框架里根本无法定价的功能—

item.title: [a16z] Why the People Who Built Hip-Hop Ended Up With Nothing
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：这不是慈善，是"债务的迟到清算"

大多数人会把 Paid in Full 基金会读成"富人回馈给穷艺术家"的温情叙事。但看完整段，你会发现一个更冷峻的真相——Ben Horowitz 反复强调的关键词不是"给予"，而是"credit where credit is due"（该归谁的功劳就归谁）。他花 10 美元买的一张专辑，让他在硅谷创业地狱里挺过来，最终转化成 500 万美元的商业价值——这是一笔从未被记账的知识产权授权费。

真正让我意外的是 Nas 那句"在 hip-hop 里你不能直接给钱"。这句话表面是文化敏感性，深层其实是产权哲学：当你直接给钱，等于承认对方是"受救济者"；当你以"荣誉"的形式支付，等于承认这笔钱本来就该是他的版税。基金会的整个仪式设计，是一次对未签署合同的追溯性履约——他们不是在扶贫，是在补交欠了 40 年的许可费。

二、跨领域连接：Tommy Hilfiger、Adidas 与"未被资本化的文化 alpha"

访谈中最惊人的一段是 Steve Stoute 讲 Tommy Hilfiger 开车穿越 Harlem，看到年轻人露出 Calvin Klein 内裤边——于是他把自己的 logo 放大放在腰带上，救活了整个品牌。这个细节看似八卦，其实揭示了一个至今仍未被主流经济学建模的现象：

文化生产者（hip-hop 艺术家）持续为消费品牌生成"隐性 beta 因子"，但资本市场把这笔 alpha 全部算在了品牌方的市值里。

Adidas 在美国的市场份额从 2% 起飞、Hilfiger 从卖领带到街头之王、Louis Vuitton 请 Virgil Abloh——这些商业史转折点的因果贡献者从未被列入损益表。这和什么现象结构相同？开源软件维护者与万亿美元云计算产业的关系。Linux 内核维护者的处境和 Grandmaster Caz 的处境是同一个数学问题：基础设施提供者被系统性地从价值分配链中除名。

Ben Horowitz 作为顶级 VC 干这件事的深层动机，很可能不只是"报恩"——他见过太多技术领域的"Grandmaster Caz"，他知道一个不奖励基础层的生态系统最终会枯萎。Paid in Full 本质上是一次针对文化产业的"OSS Sustainability Fund"实验。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：为什么"骄傲"比"贫穷"更难解决

访谈里最容易被略过、但最有分析价值的一个细节是：有些老艺术家收到电话时不相信是真的，甚至有人拒绝领奖——"我不需要施舍"。Ben 说他们"很难帮助人"。

这是一个经典的博弈论悲剧：当一个群体被系统性伤害了 40 年，接受帮助的心理成本会高于继续贫穷的物质成本。这个现象在心理学叫"defensive pessimism"，在博弈论叫"信任崩溃后的次优均衡"。基金会真正的天才设计不是筹钱，而是用"荣誉"这个语义包装解构了防御性骄傲——你不是在收钱，你是在被加冕。

更深一层的观察：Nas 在场是关键的"信号发射器"。Ben 一个白人科技富豪打电话，会被当骗子；但 Nas 出现在董事会名单上，等于给整个项目盖上了文化 KYC 的印章。这是一个用"社会资本"启动"金融资本"流动的完美案例——放在 crypto/DeFi 领域，几乎就是一次"文化 DAO"的原型。

四、彩蛋洞察：Ben 那句"从'正确'开始，而不是从'可能'开始"

这句话在访谈末尾轻轻一带，但它其实是 Ben Horowitz 整个投资哲学的暗号——a16z 押注加密货币、AI Agent、生物科技这些"看起来不可能但正确"的赛道，用的是同一个决策框架。Paid in Full 不是他的副业，是他的世界观在低风险场景下的一次公开演示。你可以把这个基金会看作 Ben Horowitz 的一份"人格白皮书"。

📝 转录文本

开场：为什么要做这件事

Ben Horowitz: I think in life it's impossible to do anything great if you start with what's possible. You have to start with what's right. Hip-hop's not that big. Like the guys who made the art form are not that many. And so why can't we honor them?

Steve Stoute: Acknowledging and celebrating and then bringing this group of people together is something that the industry should have done a long time ago.

Grandmaster Caz: When people see me and they see my passion, this [ __ ] still got it. He's still doing it because I have to. Hip-hop don't have social security. You have to work.

Nas: The whole thing about hip-hop is about to grow to be better. And I think we are living our lyrics — paid in full.

Steve Stoute: I want everybody to know around the world what Grandmaster Caz looks like and to celebrate him and applaud this man for what he's done and celebrate Roxanne and celebrate Melly and the DOC and everybody else who's had these achievements. The thing is the honor. The thing is putting you in the light that you deserve to be in. If you're watching this and love hip hop.

一、基金会的缘起：一张 10 美元的专辑，与一笔无法偿还的债

主持人: So, this is the first time this group has gotten together to publicly talk about the Paid in Full Foundation. Guys, welcome to the podcast.

All: Thank you. Yeah.

主持人: So, Ben, why don't you introduce the foundation and maybe let's get into the origin story as far back as you want to go as to how this came to be.

Ben Horowitz: Yeah. So, Paid in Full is an organization meant to honor the legacy of the people who created one of the most important musical art forms of all time, hip-hop, and make sure that they're paid in full — financially, spiritually, and culturally.

The idea kind of started with me, Steve and Nas. It always bothered me that, you know, I bought Paid in Full — the album — for $10, and in my career (those of you in tech know this) I probably got at least $5 million worth of value out of that record. But there was no way to pay it back. And it needed to be paid back.

So I had the idea originally, and I called Steve. Steve and I have been friends for many, many years, and I said, "Steve, I have this idea, what do you think?" And he said, "Well, it's not only a good idea, but it's a very timely idea because people are talking about this right now — but they're not doing anything." So, like if you listen to the podcasts, people are saying, "Oh, these rappers, these old guys, they don't have any money. They're dusty, they're this, they're that." And these are very, very important guys. But nobody's doing anything. And so, I thought, well, let's do something.

And then the next call I made was to Nas. And Nas had a great insight — a lot of the concept was inspired by our dear friend Quincy Jones, who had a thing called the Jazz Foundation where he would get money to the old jazz guys. And I told it to Nas, and Nas said, "You know, that's not going to work that way in hip-hop, because in hip-hop you can't just give somebody money. It has to be more than that. It has to be a recognition of what they did and who they are."

And so that's when we got the idea of, well, let's have a big award show — have this idea of the Grandmaster Award for the true greats of hip-hop — and invite everybody to honor these guys. And we started it off with two all-time greats: Scarface and Rakim.

二、Scarface 的电话：当"荣誉"遇上"救命"

Steve Stoute: Before we even got to the first show, it was also timely because Scarface was going through a medical condition.

Ben Horowitz: Yes.

Steve Stoute: And I remember I was in the south of France, and I called him — he needed to get his kidney, to get his kidney from his son, a kidney transplant, and it wasn't the right doctors. There was a lot of care and concern on that anyway, but more specific was the money and the doctor who was performing the surgery. And I called him — I've known Scarface for years — but when I called him literally from the south of France in June, and he got that phone call from me about what we were going to do, he was in shock.

I mean, just imagine — a phone call coming randomly from a guy you hadn't spoken to in two years, and I'm calling you about your medical condition and I'm telling you that we got you financially, we're going to help you. And I remember calling Ben after that and saying, "Look, I spoke to Scarface, man, and he was in disbelief."

In fact, early on, people were in such disbelief they didn't believe that it was real.

Ben Horowitz: Yeah. We had a hard time actually helping people because they didn't believe it. I have some stories on that — I don't even know if I can mention the names, but we had people who literally didn't get the award because they thought it was a scam. They just didn't want to mess with it.

And that's actually what reinforced the belief that if you celebrated the artist — and it didn't feel like you were giving them reparations, but you were actually celebrating them and giving them the honor and dignity they deserve that they had not received properly — then that would be the way it would be accepted and celebrated.

It wasn't until we did the first one — and, you know, like any other startup, duct tape and whatever we got to do to get this thing going — but we had Scarface and Rakim, and obviously the support of the board, having Nas on the board, that all helped. Then it started to go through the community: "There is something that's happening." And that's when it worked. But literally, it was disbelief from the initial phone calls.

三、Nas 的诊断：Hip-hop 为什么"不爱自己人"

Nas: Why would anybody do this? That's how [ __ ] they've been for so long. Like why would anybody come look and try to help us now? And how [ __ ] the rap community has been — like, to not show love, to be so divided, to act like it's every man for himself. Rap is competitive, but at some point we got to bring it around to what it's supposed to be.

It was funny, like nothing like this ever existed. When you were talking to me, I was like, why hasn't this happened? I'm in the right circle of people to be talking about the right thing. And it was almost daring for us to even do something like this.

Ben Horowitz: Yeah. Well, it's one of those things where somebody's got to step up at some point. And that's the thing about history in general — people act like things are inevitable, but they're not. Somebody's got to do something. Once it's done, it's very obvious, but until somebody steps up it doesn't happen.

四、Grandmaster Caz：被偷走的第一首 Hip-hop 金曲

Ben Horowitz: Actually, I met Caz in New York kind of right around the first year. And I remember, we had a great conversation, but then going back and rereading how important Caz was — like, Steve, let me ask you this. In a different circumstance, in a different kind of timing, how big would Caz have been?

Steve Stoute: You know, Caz — I talked about you after I met you, I speak about you. The fact that you are so charismatic still, right now, that you hold no bitterness in your heart and you present yourself as a star — I mean, it's clear. If you would have been — I mean, 12 years later, just forget it — by the way, if you would have actually just got the credit you deserved from the beginning, we wouldn't even have to fast-forward it 12 years. But I'm just saying: when you walk into a room, it shifts. You have that level of presence and talent and star power. So I think it's definitely ageless — the time period. But it was shocking to me that, again, everybody had known what had happened to Caz. Everybody.

Nas: It's the original.

Ben Horowitz: Not enough people knew, though.

Steve Stoute: At the same time — not enough people knew, but the right people knew. The industry knew.

Nas: Yes.

Steve Stoute: The music industry knew.

Nas: Yeah. I mean, Caz wrote the rhyme that became Rapper's Delight. Those were his rhymes.

Ben Horowitz: With his name in the rhymes. The first hit.

Nas: And it was stolen. The first hip-hop hit was stolen from him — and he didn't get what he deserved. And everybody knew it, but no one ever did anything about it. Never said anything about it. Didn't give a [ __ ] about it.

Steve Stoute: When we were having our board calls and thinking about who we were going to honor — one of the privileges of having this group of people looking at the cases and deciding who we're going to give the award to — you say certain people's names and it's unanimous.

Nas: It's like everyone's arguing why their "yes" is more "yes." It's like, "Yo, Caz — but you don't understand why I said yes." Because everybody's so delighted that we nailed the person. And then you meet the person and it is so beautiful when they walk in the room.

Steve Stoute: We've been blessed to have honored people who not only deserve it, but when they got the phone call, they didn't come in with "about time" energy. They came in with smile, bright, glowing.

五、Roxanne Shanté：她要的是"对的奖"

Steve Stoute: I think about Caz and Shanté when I just think about, like, just glowing. When Roxanne got the award, her child had said, "Mom, you see all these female rappers getting all these awards. Don't you ever feel bitter about that?" She's like, "No, I didn't want that award. I wanted the right award."

Nas: Paid in Full.

Steve Stoute: And I was like, "Yeah, that's awesome. That's awesome that we were able to do that."

And to be able to give these artists that recognition right now — and then having the artists be a part of voting for the future recipients. So Caz is now a recipient and he's part of the committee who's voting for future recipients. And that's the gift that keeps giving about this foundation.

Nas: And Shanté is one of the reasons I'm here. She's from my neighborhood, same neighborhood. And when she released Roxanne's Revenge back in 1984, 1985, she was a kid — older than me, but a kid. And when I saw that she could be on the radio rapping and going after men, it was like she was an activist and beating them — she was a woman's activist. Because that was unheard of in hip-hop. And when I saw her be that bold and to challenge a whole established rap group and change the course of this whole thing for me, that was incredibly inspiring. So to have her be a part of this — to me is still crazy. I love it.

六、Grandmaster Caz 亲述：被"审核"的过程

Grandmaster Caz: For me, when I was kind of brought in — I had no idea what was going on. I just know somebody that I knew from a while back reached out to me — I hadn't heard from in years — and that was Quincy Q3. And I'm like, "Q, what's up?" He's like, "This and that." He was pretty vague, but he was like, "I want you to come downtown." And that's when I met Ben and everybody. And I really wasn't fully — you know — but I was being vetted to some degree. "We want this guy. Let's see what his — you know — let's see where his head is at, where his attitude is." Because I've seen or heard about other people who deserve but don't, you know what I mean?

I just came with my spirit. And the fact that so many people — these guys had alluded to earlier — had brought up the subject, "Yo, we should give the old-school dudes a million dollars." I think Swizz Beatz made it public — shout out to Swizz.

Nas: Not to interrupt you, but I just did. Sorry, but I had to say it. When you were saying that, you reminded me of something. I spoke about this in a magazine, I think in the 90s — or maybe the year 2000. They asked what would I do — or maybe they asked a bunch of hip-hop artists — and I described this to a tee. Somebody pointed that out to me like last month, that I forgot I even said that. So we all been wanting this type of thing. Sorry to cut you off again because I just got excited at that memory.

七、这是"班级聚会"：Dr. Dre 也想被介绍给 Kool Moe Dee

Nas: I would debate hip-hop with Ben. I would debate hip-hop with Steve forever. Me and Steve will stop speaking about disagreeing. Me and Ben will analyze the album to death. Ben got with you and sent me a video of your conversation about Sugar Hill Gang and everything. I couldn't believe that you cared so much — being from the Bay — about the origin story of some of the greatest hip-hop history ever. But I shouldn't have been surprised. The care that we have for the culture is the same.

Like, Caz — every time I approach you, I'm stalking you about what happened this year and that year. So it's not just Paid in Full — it's a way that we convinced ourselves that we can be together, and we can get together and not just talk about it from afar. We can actually talk to Caz. We could actually be in a room with Rakim. It's not just this thing that's so spread out — it's bringing us together.

Steve Stoute: It feels like a class reunion.

Nas: Yes. And last year when Dr. Dre heard about Paid in Full and decided to come, I was in shock that he asked me could I introduce him to Kool Moe Dee. He never met him before. And I was like — this is — first of all, I would never even think of that. Not that Dr. Dre never met Kool Moe Dee before.

Steve Stoute: Dre did this to me too in Vegas. He said, "Could I introduce him to Slick Rick?" He never met him before.

Nas: Oh my god.

Grandmaster Caz: It's wild that it took this foundation to bring these type of people together.

Steve Stoute: And the bond is that strong. The bond is so strong that 25, 30 years removed, Dr. Dre with all of his glory and success is like, "Man, could you please introduce me to Slick Rick and Kool Moe Dee?" But at the same time — that it took this celebration in order to bring these legends together in the same room, to create that moment.

八、行业为什么割裂了艺术家

Grandmaster Caz: I think the industry itself separates us — by success, status. Who's hot, who's signed, who this and that. If I see Nas, it's like by happenstance or something all these years. Mutual respect. But I don't see him all the time. If he reaches out — as he's done in the past and done a project — "Yo, Caz, I want you to be a part," I'm on it automatically. I ain't got to see him or none of that. Just say it and I'm there. Now I see him every year. I can call him on the phone. Steve Stoute — you hear about Steve Stoute, big business, man. He done made this person rich. It's a special moment that is growing every year.

Steve Stoute: And to Caz's point, this idea of separating artists — I'm not sure why that happened. I'm not sure if it was the industry doing the industry's doings on purpose, or was it just the fact that rap was broken into old school, new school, this that and the third. So there was no connection. But the truth of the matter is that the real artists have respect for the person that they had their poster on their wall, the first CD they bought, the first tape that they bought. And that respect that inspired either me as a businessman, or Nas as an artist, or Ben as a businessman — that'll never ever go away. Like sports heroes — it never goes away.

And so the foundation acknowledging and celebrating, and then bringing this group of people together, is something that the industry should have done a long time ago. And there's been attempts — like the VH1 thing.

Nas: Yeah, the VH1 Hip-Hop Honors.

Steve Stoute: It's putting a light on these artists. But it's not putting anything in their pockets. It's not investing in the artist. It's not making them feel like they've been acknowledged for everything that they contributed. That was the point.

It was two things: starting Paid in Full, but also Ben investing in United Masters. The idea was — how do you contribute so much culturally, but yet the financial take is so meaningless? How do you pour so much in and get so little out?

Grandmaster Caz: No respect, I'll tell you.

Steve Stoute: And everybody became comfortable with that idea. They just accepted it as, "Oh, that's just the way it is." Meanwhile, you're changing the way people are dressing. You're changing dialect. You're changing so much in the world. And yet your bank account or acknowledgement for what you've contributed is not even partner. It doesn't add up. That's not inspiring. It doesn't incentivize creativity. It incentivizes people to feel like they've been robbed and stolen from.

九、Nas：Hip-hop 的歌词早就在说这件事

Nas: And, not to cut you off — in the lyrics of hip-hop, we speak about the total opposite. We speak about breaking down barriers. We speak about changing the system. We speak about love. We speak about being entrepreneurs and taking this thing into our hands and keeping it real. But then the action of keeping it real wasn't happening outside the studio.

You play a record — this dude sounds like he's the realest ever. Then you see him, he won't speak to you. He's posted up and he's not talking to you. You could be like, "Yo, I need some help." He's looking at you, he's laughing at you. It's a competitiveness to the max. And it doesn't wind up being like what the lyrics said.

You hear the lyrics of rap — since the beginning, since Caz was talking and inspiring and putting his DNA into this thing, and bigger groups will come from Caz, and bigger soloists, and the rap game will be shifted with what Caz put down — and the lyrics represent one thing. But how we going to be real and we say we're hip-hop, we're real, and then the actions are not happening? It's just going to be on record. It can't just be on record.

The whole thing about hip-hop is about to grow, to be better. And I think we are living our lyrics. We're paid in full.

十、Ben 和 Felicia：把钱押在正确的事上

Steve Stoute: And it takes the courage of Ben and his wife Felicia and that foundation to put the money up, to match the contribution, to be able to fund something like this. You would think — or you would hope — that it would come from an organization that benefited financially from —

Nas: One would guess. If you just say who do you think will help these guys, you'd be like, "Oh, definitely the record company."

Steve Stoute: So-and-so, this person. No. It takes somebody — it is hard for me to sell him a ticket. It takes a crazy rap fan. And Felicia — an entrepreneur who has deep soul and belief in and respect for creativity — that made this one of his missions to help solve this and make sure the right guys get properly awarded and the respect they deserve.

十一、第四年，找到节奏

Ben Horowitz: I think this year is going to be a pivotal year for the organization. This is our fourth year, and we have a great, great, great lineup. It's very well produced. Like, you don't walk in — first year, lucky you wasn't there.

Nas: We were feeling our way through. It was a little long, it was a little this that and the third — where we learned like anything else. We refined, got tighter, got smarter. And I think we got it now.

In year four where it's going to be our biggest year — and hopefully, as well as produced as this show will be, that it's something that we could take wider. At the same time, I feel like I want everybody to know around the world what Grandmaster Caz looks like, and to celebrate him and applaud this man for what he's done, and celebrate Roxanne and Melly and the DOC and everybody else who's had these achievements — that they get a chance to see their heroes on the platform that they respect.

I think when you do something big and important — not only in hip-hop, but in anything — people are going to emulate it. People are going to want to follow. If they see a formula that works, Ben, you're a testament to this. You see a formula that works, you want in. And a lot of people lost face because nobody did it yet.

Ben Horowitz: Steve and I have conversations about this kind of thing all the time. But I think in life it's impossible to do anything great if you start with what's possible. You have to start with what's right. And if you start with what's right, then — it may not be possible, but at least you have a chance to do something great.

That's always how I came at it. I was like, "Look, we ought to be able to figure this out. Hip-hop's not that big. The guys who made the art form are not that many. So why can't we honor them?" It just didn't make any sense to me.

And by the way — you guys were very kind saying, "You know, I wasn't a beneficiary." I'm a big beneficiary of Caz and Nas and Rakim, in that you all were the inspiration to my career — and got me through very, very difficult times in business. So hard that I wrote a best-selling book about how hard it was. And in the book, I had the rap lyrics. But in Silicon Valley, I actually got a lot of criticism for it — like, "What are you doing with hip-hop? Is that some kind of gimmick?" And I was like, no, this is credit where credit is due. The ideas that I had in business came from those lyrics. And that's why the chapters — that's why the idea started with the lyric — because that's where the idea started. And it was just credit where credit was due. And so it was my chance to, in my mind, just do what was right and pay it back.

And, you know, look — I'm an entrepreneur. I know how to build things. So building a foundation didn't seem that hard.

十二、把"没兴趣的人"变成信徒

Nas: If I got pushback or people talked about it bad, I don't listen. I can't even hear it.

Steve Stoute: No, he doesn't hear it. But you — you bring people. You invite people who would probably have no interest in this topic. And you bring them there — and you know what they do? I've seen it convert. They go there and they're like, "I'll go for Ben. Whatever. I'll go for Ben. It's Ben." Then they go there and they're like, "Oh [ __ ], I didn't even know this, I didn't know that."

And it connects a lot of dots. And there's obviously a lot of empathy. How do you not feel empathy for somebody who's invented something and didn't get what they deserved? But the theme of the night isn't that. The theme of the night isn't "get what you deserve" — that's the underlying foundational truth. On top of that, we celebrate the fact that you are getting now what you deserve. You are getting the acknowledgement, the light put on you, in the right way, by a bunch of people who respect you.

I mean — come on, man. Last year — I've known my man Grand Puba for so long. To see Puba out there — that made me feel so proud.

Nas: Why would you skip that? It's easy to skip it. "Oh no, not that." And you got Grand Puba, at one point the greatest rapper.

Steve Stoute: By the way, did it over three different — it's funny about rap. Eras — it's not like decades, but eras could be four years. And if you're not part of it, you don't even realize how fast it changes. Masters of Ceremony, Brand Nubian, Puba, solo career.

Nas: Three eras.

Steve Stoute: He went through three eras. Crazy. And got through that and got to the other side. Very few artists have done that. Those changes during that period of time were drastic. It was like you were out — a lot of our favorite artists couldn't jump that fence, and they got stuck on the other side. Then all of a sudden you're considered old school, or washed, or not dope anymore, whatever the thing was. And Grand Puba did that. No one else is going to sit and turn around and watch this man go on stage and get his props. No one else is going to put the time in to have the people that understand that nuance.

It's easy to write a check. People write checks to things and check that box. There's so much time going into making sure we get it right.

Nas: Yeah. Because of the love. And in the room, there's love. Even if you didn't think you'd be walking in a room like that — you think it's going to be like some typical award show — it's genuine love. It's no egos. Nobody's putting their chest out in front of nobody. Doesn't matter if a billionaire's over there and over here at that table. Everybody's here on a real thing of learning what's happening on the stage. You're being educated.

And then we're talking about our man Quincy Jones, who I spent a lot of time with — with Ben — before he passed. And then QD3 being there, and we getting to see a Quincy Jones award happen through this — because Quincy, had he been here, he would have been a part of this. And last year George Clinton went — he brought the mothership. He did a mothership thing for us. And it was just mind-blowing to see him reciting Rakim's lyrics to Follow the Leader. This is George Clinton. He is the outer space guy. He is the guy who shifted music. And then him reciting at 83 years old Rakim's lyrics on stage. This is a room of love on another level.

十三、Quincy Jones 奖：因为格莱美搞砸了

Steve Stoute: To the Quincy Jones Award. Quincy Jones — obvious legend. The legend of legends. The triple OG. The foundation of it all. No disrespect, but the Grammys botched his celebration.

The idea for the Quincy Jones Award was literally because of how bad the Grammys did it. It wasn't like we thought we had to check that box. We couldn't believe they got that wrong. They didn't pay tribute to this man properly — to the point that his son, QD3, was like, "Let's do this." And now it's part of what we do in the foundation on an annual basis.

Nas: That's love. Can we say who the new recipient of the Quincy Jones Award is?

Ben Horowitz: Yeah, we got to let Steve say it because he works so hard on it.

Steve Stoute: Nile Rodgers, man.

Nas: Yes. How do you not — Nile Rodgers?

Steve Stoute: Nile Rodgers, who came up with a guitar lick that's been used — Good Times. By the way, that's just hip-hop connection. That's Hip-Hop Chic. Look at Sister Sledge. Go down the myriad songs he's produced — all the way up to Get Lucky. For Daft Punk. He's that guy.

So boom — we got Nile Rodgers this year getting the Quincy Jones Award. What we're doing is, obviously, making sure that — within our purview, whether it's old-school hip-hop or Quincy Jones, who should have gotten celebrated a little bit more properly with his Grammys — we're making a contribution to make sure we get it right. We're holding ourselves accountable to get it right.

This is obviously a big thing to do because you got families, estates, other artists looking at this. "Are these real? Is this going away anytime soon? Is this another facade? What are they selling on the back of this? They must be selling t-shirts out the trunk."

十四、Kool G Rap、Kurtis Blow：都以为是假的

Nas: I called Kurtis Blow, and Kool Rock-Ski from the Fat Boys, like, "Yo, man, we want you in this." And I think for a second he didn't think it was real.

Grandmaster Caz: Yeah, I heard.

Nas: I ain't going to lie to you. He was there last year — an award — and didn't think it was real.

Grandmaster Caz: He walked off the stage not thinking it was real.

Ben Horowitz: What did Kool G Rap say?

Nas: G Rap I called him. He was very appreciative. One of the greatest MCs of all time, man. One of my biggest inspirations. When people come — again, it's love, man. It's real love. It's your time. It's your show. We're here for you.

And I think it's surprising for them to feel like it's nothing like — like you said, we're not selling shirts out in the back. This is not for us. It gives us joy that we're doing this. But it's beautiful to see these people show up and be appreciated.

十五、真正的巅峰时刻：Scarface 和 Rakim 谈"写作"

Nas: You just talked about the ego thing. Of course it is. First of all, at the end, you start going crazy on the mic. You and Mod last year — y'all go crazy on the mic. So that's still there. Let's be clear. It's a celebration, but the park-jam part is not going anywhere.

But because there's so much ego in rap, at least in this moment, in this room, it comes down to the point where Ice Cube came two years ago. And he says, "I wouldn't even put out an album until I listened to what Scarface had to say."

Ben Horowitz: You remember when he said this?

Nas: Hell yeah. "I knew before I dropped anything, I'd had to make sure what this guy was saying — you would know." And Scarface came after Cube. But when Scarface came — woo. And to watch Scarface and Rakim acknowledge each other's writing skills —

Ben Horowitz: Oh, dude. If you love hip-hop — if you're watching this and love hip-hop — you got to know: to have Rakim and Scarface have a conversation about writing and respect that they have for each other in a real, pure way — you're talking about two of the greatest writers in anything. I don't give a [ __ ] what it is. Anything. Having a real discussion about —

Nas: And every hip-hop guy in the world before, since, would acknowledge what you said. Nobody would even — some of the greatest writers of all time, in hip-hop, Scarface and Rakim. Not even a question. Nothing to discuss.

Steve Stoute: Nothing to discuss.

Nas: And they're discussing it for the first time at Paid in Full. That's how special this room is.

十六、Ben 的呼吁

Ben Horowitz: Okay, let me give the plug. paidinfullfoundation.org. You can come and be a part of it. Felicia and I match every donation two-and-a-half to one, which means that all your money goes to the artist. There are no paid employees at the foundation. Everything is volunteer. If you want to be part of it, if you want to contribute, paidinfull.org. That's my plug.

And I want to ask Caz —

Nas: That was pretty good. That's like a radio.

Ben Horowitz: Thank you. Caz, we've been talking about it — but as a recipient, what has it meant to you from an honor standpoint, from a financial standpoint? How did it affect you?

十七、Grandmaster Caz 亲述：它买了我一间房，也买了我的尊严

Grandmaster Caz: I definitely was gonna address that at some point, because it's not specifics — like, yo, this and that, this one gets that. It's like you get a grant, so to speak, and it's over a five-year period. And it's helped change my life.

I was on a path to self-improvement, trying to get things. LL Cool J called me a few years back and was like, "Yo, it's time. I want you on the radio." But when Paid in Full called me, it was like, "Yo, now this is going to change your life."

I bought a house.

Ben Horowitz: Wow.

Grandmaster Caz: I moved out the projects. And I've lived in the Bronx all my life. I only did a three-year stint in Cali for a while, but I lived in the Bronx all my life. And I thought I would always end up here. And my last thoughts in my head for the last like 10, 15 years — I don't want to die in the projects. I don't want to end here. I don't want it to end here.

And it didn't. You know what I mean? I got a nice house in Pennsylvania. Me and my wife. And my life has improved drastically. I got a comfort, I got a cushion that I never had. Everything was day-to-day. Everything was run out, grind, hustle.

And when people see me and they see my passion — this [ __ ] still got it. He's still doing it because I have to. I didn't have no — hip-hop don't have social security. Hip-hop don't have no health benefits or none of that. You have to work. You got to stay out there. For me anyway, I got to keep working. So when you see me on radio, you see me doing park jams, you see me doing hip-hop sightseeing tours — all that was to maintain, to keep me up and at it.

And I think my attitude that went along with it, and the way that I deal with people, kept me in people's consciousness — which I'm so [ __ ] grateful for. Like I said, I can't speak for everybody, but I'm sure what it's done for me, it's done for everybody.

One thing I want to say — I don't want to say what person — but when you was talking about some people didn't know if it was a scam or whatever, a couple people thought was like, "Yo, I don't need this. Like, I'm good." Like a handout — "I don't need nobody to give me." Nah, it's not about that. It's not all about that. That's a part of it. The thing is the honor. The thing is putting you in the light that you deserve to be in.

And I got to salute LL Cool J for that, too. He put us — he put Shai Rock on the radio — when he didn't have to. He created a whole lane. He's like, "Now that's y'all, go. Monday through Friday, y'all on the air." So that kind of recognition, it resonates. And when people see important people giving you your props, they feel obligated — like, "Yo, I got to say that."

What this does — how you just ended it — is it brings recognition. And that's the gift that keeps giving, because it's done out of love. And it inspires more people to think that we can do things like this, too. We got to remember: let's take care of each other.

I'll say this. I was getting reached out to by a few hip-hop artists for a while, probably the later end of the 90s on. And I would do things for different artists — won't say it, won't mention the names. Even up to someone who passed away recently, a musical hip-hop producer. I was there. And I wonder how many more of us were doing that — but it's on the low. This is on the high. This is on an even bigger level. And you can show the world: we're taking care of our own. We're taking care of the thing that took care of us.

十八、隐藏的商业史：Adidas、Tommy Hilfiger 与 Hip-hop 的未支付版税

Grandmaster Caz: In Ben's book, he has pieces of lyrics that inspired him. These things are important, because if we forget, if we sweep it all under the rug — if you don't know that Puba took Hilfiger to another level, if you don't know —

Nas: Sprite.

Grandmaster Caz: Sprite — the fashion industry, period.

Steve Stoute: By the way, that's exactly why I wrote The Tanning of America. It was specifically so that all of the things that hip-hop created —

Ben Horowitz: In your book, when you talk about the Run-DMC concert — I go from — everybody holds up their Adidas. What that did for Adidas.

Steve Stoute: Adidas was kind of dead at the time.

Nas: Hold on. Dead.

Steve Stoute: Oh yeah. 2% market share in America.

Ben Horowitz: 2% market share in America. And three-quarters of that 2% was coming from the Northeast region. And all they knew is that — why is everybody up there buying this one specific SKU, and why are they throwing away the shoelaces?

Nas: Hip-hop, baby.

Steve Stoute: But — Puba: "Obey your thirst" is his line.

Nas: "First things first, obey your thirst." That's his line. That's their tagline.

Steve Stoute: No one would ever pay attention to these things. These guys are pioneers above and beyond hip-hop. They created the culture around the music that lives on to this day. The fashion, the language, the brands that only exist as a result of their contribution.

I love Tommy Hilfiger. Tommy Hilfiger is a great guy. He's done a lot with artists. He should be part of contributing to Paid in Full. If it wasn't for hip-hop, he was dead in the water. They were selling ties. He says that he was selling ties. He was trying to be Ralph Lauren. And they were like, "You're not Ralph Lauren, dog."

And on his way home — because he lived in Greenwich — when you leave the city you can obviously get to Greenwich by the traditional way taking the highway, or you can cut through Harlem and get up to Westchester. So he's cutting through Harlem, and he sees everybody wearing their pants low and their Calvin Klein — the top of the Calvin Klein brief showing. And literally that's where he got the idea to make underwear and use that where Calvin the — the top —

Ben Horowitz: Yeah, and put Tommy there. Whatever this [ __ ] is called — the elastic band. And he put Tommy Hilfiger there and made the waistband bigger, thicker, so that you could really see it.

Steve Stoute: And that's how the whole thing got going. Seriously — literally — and he talks about it. He'd seen it driving through Harlem.

Nas: That's crazy.

Steve Stoute: And that's when the brand took off — and went from selling ties that wasn't working to now selling streetwear. The hottest fashion trend in the world. Streetwear. That Louis Vuitton sells, designed by skateboard P. You know what I'm saying?

Ben Horowitz: God bless. And Virgil.

Steve Stoute: These are the things that these guys have been a part of contributing that they never got their fair share of.

And by the way — what we're doing is, we're just trying to get momentum. We're not trying to solve the world's problem here. We need others to either come and donate to the organization, or start other organizations that also have the same motive: to help celebrate, give back to the guys who have helped contribute to your business, to inspire you — on some real, with love and respect.

Nas: With love and respect.

十九、Felicia 与 Scarface 的开胸手术

Ben Horowitz: And actually, on that, I want to tell a story. Because the love and respect part goes beyond even the award.

So Scarface had a heart condition. And, you know — look, he comes from a place where people don't even really go to the doctor, let alone go in for open-heart surgery, which is what he needed. And he was on the phone with my wife Felicia, and she knew he was scared. And she flew out to Houston to see him before he went to the doctor. And he didn't want to go in. He's like, "No, I don't want to go to the doctor. I'm not going to the doctor."

And she said, "No." And he calls her "the bully." She's about 5 feet tall, weighs maybe a buck 05. And she says, "No, I'm taking you to the doctor right now."

And right as they got into the doctor, his aorta burst — and they got him in just in time and saved his life. And that doesn't happen without her caring so much about him.

And a lot of what the foundation is about — because she runs it, he's the president — is how much she cares about these artists and how much she's committed to taking care of them regardless. Forget the award, forget what the actual contract is and all that kind of thing. She's going to do that work. And that creates the whole culture of the thing — which is why that feeling at the award is so different.

Grandmaster Caz: Agreed. Definitely kudos to Felicia. None more serious than that. She makes it — like it's love involved here. Beyond the award, beyond the check. It's not over. You'll get a call — "How are you doing? How's your wife?" "Oh, she's sick." "Give me your address." She sends — the next day flowers come. The next day like some Dior glasses come. That's how Felicia is. And it's not about what's going on. She'll randomly call you just to check on you, to see if everything's good. And that's the difference between this and anything I've ever experienced in an award, grant, foundation. The love. The genuine love.

I just can't speak enough about the event that's coming up — the next Hip-Hop Grandmaster Awards. It's going to be monumental. And if you haven't been abreast of what's going on with Paid in Full, definitely check in this year, and then look back at what we've done in the past four years. And then get on board. Don't play with it. Stay with it.

Nas: Yes, sir.

二十、结尾：Nas 的父亲、Quincy Jones、以及被隐藏的谱系

主持人: Now Steve, I'm curious — if you could talk about when was the moment you knew that you and Ben were going to be friends for life?

Nas: Steve invited me to a dinner years ago. That's the craziest — way up.

Steve Stoute: Oh yeah, it was an interesting room of people, right? He put together a great room, great restaurant.

Nas: It was Mr. Chow's downtown. Mr. Freddy. Yeah. So this room was dope, right? And he put this together. And I heard about Ben through him, and I met Ben right there. And our love for music and love for food was a thing that connected me and Ben at that point. And we just been cool since then.

Ben Horowitz: Yeah. Some of my best times listening to Rakim with Nas. By the way, Nas hears things in Rakim songs that nobody else hears. It's unbelievable. And then listening to Prince. We listen to Prince together — and then break it down. Going and visit triple OG Quincy Jones together. Music fans who just — Nas is like, as great an artist as he is, he's that great a music fan.

Nas: By the way — I was at Quincy's house when he had just moved into the house. Or redecorated the house, rather. And it was me and Chris Tucker. And he goes and shows — he was showing us the casting tapes for The Color Purple.

Ben Horowitz: The Color Purple.

Nas: Right. He's showing us — and there was Whoopi Goldberg. And she's talking. She's just talking to the camera like this or whatever. And then she starts reading the script — and then within a second starts crying. I was like, "Oh." It was the first time I seen acting and I was like, "Oh, I mean — I knew for a fact this is a skill that is beyond." She was like, regular normal talking — and they said, "All right." And Steven Spielberg's holding the camera. And boom, she just starts crying.

Ben Horowitz: Yeah, she was great in that role, by the way.

Nas: So anyhow — Chris Tucker, we all were blown away by the fact that she did that. And we just started talking about a bunch of different [ __ ], and I bring up Nas — I bring up my dad, Olu Dara. Yo, this guy — Quincy Jones at that age was still moving very quickly, like a quick guy — quickly went and grabbed a bunch of vinyls and came back with pictures. And he showed me a picture of him with Nas's dad in Saint-Tropez in the 60s.

Ben Horowitz: That's amazing.

Nas: I was like, "Holy shit." Like, I knew Nas's dad was obviously a jazz legend, but I didn't know at what level it was that these guys were running around.

Grandmaster Caz: He would tell me stories of people he'd been around, but I didn't listen. I'm like, "Oh, yeah. Okay, pop." Yo, my pop told me — about Mtume. The song Juicy came out. He's like, "Yo, that's my man." I'm like, "Come on. You probably met him in passing." I ain't thinking nothing about it. What year was that? 83, 84 or something. I got into the rap game and I met Mtume — and he's like, "Yo, your dad is my man." And I said — I didn't believe him when he told me that. Not that he's a liar or anything, but I didn't know it was like y'all were like that. He was like, "That's my guy, man." I was like, yo, you understand? Juicy Fruit was the biggest song in the world. So how could I believe that at the time? I'm a kid. I don't know. I think he's just trying to make me feel good or something. But he knew a lot of people when he was younger, man. Quincy knew everybody.

Ben Horowitz: Everybody. Everybody knows your kids.

Nas: Yeah, we know. But the fact that Olu — now you got to understand, like in anything else, the DNA thing, right? Your dad's a famous football player, right? The son. This I didn't know. I mean, obviously I know Nas is a brilliant artist. I had no idea the connection was that his dad was that level of brilliant. I thought his dad — I didn't know it was that level of brilliant, that Quincy Jones within a second go find a picture of them together. And I'm like — these guys were in Saint-Tropez in the 60s doing their thing.

The whole thing was profound to me — that whole evening of going from The Color Purple to Olu Dara, and then reflecting on the fact that Nas comes from this great lineage of talent.

Nas: Yeah. They come from Mississippi. My pops. He comes from Natchez, Mississippi, and his dad was in a band. And it just — music in the family.

Ben Horowitz: Yeah. It's crazy.

尾声

主持人: So, one more time. Paid in Full.

Ben Horowitz: paidinfullfoundation.org. All your money goes directly to the artists. And it is — everybody who's ever been to it will tell you it's the greatest charitable event in the world. Like, there's nothing like it. I guarantee nobody's ever gone and not had a great time. And a time that will be a memory for the rest of your life.

主持人: Oof. All right. Thank you guys. That was great.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：这不是慈善，是"债务的迟到清算"
大多数人会把 Paid in Full 基金会读成"富人回馈给穷艺术家"的温情叙事。但看完整段，你会发现一个更冷峻的真相——**Ben Horowitz 反复强调的关键词不是"给予"，而是"credit where credit is due"（该归谁的功劳就归谁）**。他花 10 美元买的一张专辑，让他在硅谷创业地狱里挺过来，最终转化成 500 万美元的商业价值——**这是一笔从未被记账的知识产权授权费**。
真正让我意外的是 Nas 那句"在 hip-hop 里你不能直接给钱"。这句话表面是文化敏感性，深层其实是**产权哲学**：当你直接给钱，等于承认对方是"受救济者"；当你以"荣誉"的形式支付，等于承认这笔钱本来就该是他的版税。**基金会的整个仪式设计，是一次对未签署合同的追溯性履约**——他们不是在扶贫，是在补交欠了 40 年的许可费。
## 二、跨领域连接：Tommy Hilfiger、Adidas 与"未被资本化的文化 alpha"
访谈中最惊人的一段是 Steve Stoute 讲 Tommy Hilfi

item.title: [Lex Clips] Hitler's role in development of psychoanalysis and psychology | Andrew Scull and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个未被言说的悖论：希特勒是美国临床心理学的"意外奠基人"

这段访谈表面在讲精神分析的兴衰，但隐藏着一个几乎没人明说的因果链条——纳粹的种族灭绝，实际上是二十世纪心理治疗产业化的第一推手。犹太分析师被驱逐 → 精神分析在美国翻倍 → 二战爆发，美国军队照搬"心理学思维"应对 shell shock → 战后 VA 和 NIMH 巨额拨款催生临床心理学 → CBT 帝国崛起。也就是说：如果没有 1933 年那次驱逐，Menninger 不会成为陆军精神病主管，Beck 也不会先做精神分析师再叛离，而美国今天可能仍然是一个"生物精神病学 + 州立疯人院"的国家。大屠杀是现代心理健康基础设施的隐性催化剂——这是一个我们在心理学教科书里从不写下的句子。

结构性弱点：为什么"完全自控"反而成了死亡陷阱

Scull 提到一个精妙的观察——精神分析的悲剧在于它"完全控制了自己的培训"。这听起来像优势，实则是一种生态位错配。战后知识的重心迁移到大学，谁能写联邦拨款申请、谁能做 RCT、谁能被 NICE 和 Cochrane 收录，谁就活下来。精神分析拒绝进入大学，或大学拒绝接纳它，结果它在评审体系里成了"不可测量的对象"。这里有一个跨领域的隐喻让我震撼：精神分析对于二十世纪医学官僚体系，就像 Smalltalk 对于九十年代软件工业——纯粹、自洽、封闭，因此在开放的 API 生态里被绞杀。同样的故事在 Betamax 对 VHS、传统中医对循证医学、甚至今天的独立作家对算法平台之间不断重演。能测量的东西吃掉不能测量的东西——这不是关于精神分析的教训，而是关于所有"深度手艺"在标准化时代的宿命。

症状论 vs 结构论：一场被误解为"哲学之争"的政治经济学冲突

访谈把 CBT 和精神分析的分歧描述为"打地鼠还是重构人格"的方法论争论。但真正的驱动力其实是美国医疗支付模式。Scull 隐晦地点破：美国没有社会化医疗，所以人们习惯付钱看私人心理医生。而保险公司只报销"可打包、可复现、可短期结束"的疗程。CBT 之所以赢，不是因为它更"科学"，而是因为它契合了保险精算表的时间颗粒度。想想看：如果美国 1946 年通过了全民医保，CBT 可能只是无数疗法中一支；正因为治疗要按疗程标价，Beck 的六周方案才成为标配。这就带出一个更让人不安的观察——你以为你选择的治疗方法反映了心灵的真相，其实它反映的是账单周期。这和城市规划里的一个古老命题异曲同工：巴黎的林荫大道不是审美的产物，而是拿破仑三世为了让骑兵能镇压街垒起义。技术形态是政治经济的化石。

一个尚未有人问的问题

那 175 万被"筛掉"的美国人是谁？他们被判定为"心理脆弱者"从而不能入伍，却仍在战后的经济中生活、结婚、育儿。这可能是二十世纪最大规模的、几乎从未被追踪的心理学自然实验——被国家标签为"不稳定"的百万级人群，他们的一生轨迹去了哪里？没有人做过这个纵向研究。这个盲点本身，就是关于精神病学"预测能力"的最诚实评估。

📝 转录文本

The Freud Diaspora: How Persecution Redistributed Psychoanalysis

Hitler starts killing off Jews and killing off psychoanalysts. The ones who can escape, some of them go to England and some come to America. The most famous escapee is Freud himself and his daughter Anna — Princess Bonaparte, who's one of Freud's great supporters, bribes the Nazis to get him out. And he travels by train to London, very sick with cancer of the jaw as he has been since the mid-20s. So he sets up shop in London, and Anna succeeds him really as one of the central figures in British psychoanalysis.

But other analysts come here to America. So the numbers of analysts probably by 1940 — America's not yet in the war — have a bit more than doubled. And more importantly, psychoanalytic training has become much more organized here. The institutes outside the universities control psycho— And the universities are not yet the knowledge factories they become after the war.

Mhm.

The Structural Weakness: Purity Outside the University

That's a crucial mistake that psychoanalysis makes. It's great because it controls its training completely. The bad thing is: when the center of gravity moves to the university, it's not there. And it either resists being incorporated, or the university resists incorporating it. So I think that's a structural weakness for them. But what really transforms things is World War II.

To backtrack, what's officially the process for psychoanalysis as Freud and Carl Jung saw it? He said 5 hours a week. So this is long, deep dive.

Five 50-minute hours, famously. They lost 50 minutes cuz then there's 10 minutes for the analysts to recover before the next patient arrives.

And literally, I mean — you think it's not important, but I guess they were pretty strict about this — you're lying on the couch.

Yes, you are free associating on the couch. And gradually being coaxed to see, as the material emerges, what you're hiding from yourself.

From Hypnosis to Free Association

I mean, initially they tried — this is in the early early days — they tried hypnosis.

Yes.

But this is where Freud took the big leap and expanded to free association.

Right. So I mentioned Freud training under Charcot. Charcot hypnotized his hysterical patients.

Mhm.

We now know a lot of that was fakery. Not — I don't think he was conscious of the fakery, but the patients were on display over and over again, and they worked their routines up very well, and they deceived him, and they deceived the audience.

But Freud came back from Paris bringing with him the idea that hypnosis was the way forward. But after the break with Breuer — and Breuer had a general medical practice and lost interest in hysteria and didn't want anything to do with the revisions of Freud's work on hysteria — after that happened, Freud, who was a very clumsy hypnotist by his own account, began to develop this alternative of free association, and getting people to speak whatever came into their head without a censor. That was the important thing: that the half-buried memories were being hidden from you, and the constellation of psychological forces in your unconscious was squashing them down, but they were re-emerging as other kinds of symptom.

The Unmeasurable Cure

So how would the psychoanalysis work? How much do we understand? We've talked about all these approaches that didn't work.

Mhm.

How well did it work at that time?

You know, one of the things after World War [II] — when psychoanalysis was making great strides in America and the Rockefeller Foundation was still heavily involved in promoting psychiatry and developing what they hoped would be new tools in it — the then heads of the Institute of the funding program, Alan Gregg and Robert Morrison, especially Morrison, kept pressing the analyst: provide us proof that what you do works.

Mhm.

And the analyst kept resisting and resisting and resisting, saying: "It's much more complicated than that, and there's no easy measure, because what we're doing is reconstructing entire personalities, entire ways of being, and people's sense of themselves, their ways of being in the world — and we don't have easy ways to measure that."

So, contrast that with the 80% promises.

Yes.

Over and over and over and over.

And it's a long and complicated process. That was very important, because another kind of psychotherapeutics is emerging in the aftermath — during and then the aftermath of the war — as a rival for both psychiatry and for psychoanalysis. Initially not terribly successful, but as time goes on, a more and more important part of the story.

World War II: The Great Amplifier

So to focus on the war for a minute — America's psychiatrists went to the military brass and to the politicians before America entered the war, and they had some advance warning because America didn't enter till Pearl Harbor, but the European war being going on. And they said:

"Look, if we have to fight, we're going to have the same problem we had in the First World War. We're going to train these soldiers, going to equip them, we're going to put them in the battlefield, and the psychologically vulnerable among them are going to break down."

Mhm.

"They'll be shell-shocked all over again. So we should screen all recruits to make sure they're not psychologically weak and susceptible."

And they screen out 1 and 3/4 million people and say: "These men are not fit. So now we won't have the problems we had in World War I."

Except it quickly turns out that those problems reemerge. Industrial warfare exposes people to seeing things and doing things that all of us in normal life would recoil from. And when we're forced to do them as soldiers — many of us... I can't speak from experience, but from talking to people who have gone through all this — many of them find the experiences and the memories they create intolerable, and they emerge in symptoms, and they break down.

So it became a huge problem for the American army, as it did for all the armies, actually. The Nazis just shot people. Break down, you're banned, you're dead. We're not dealing with you. But obviously, the allies — that was not the response. And they quickly had to try to treat these troops: maybe get them back into the fighting lines, maybe get them into support positions, something to cope with the problem. Which was both — it created extraordinary morale problems among the troops, and it invited malingering, claiming you had these conditions when you didn't. It obviously cost a lot of the fighting force. In combat conditions, as much as 25% of the soldiers broke down. So it was a big, big problem.

The Menninger Moment: A Freudian in Uniform

Before the war, there were about 2,000 psychiatrists in North America. In the US.

[gasps]

At the end of the war, there were more than 2,000 psychiatrists in the US military. Okay. So you had to train people in a hurry. And even still, it was hard to get enough people trained.

And it turned out that the head of the US military [psychiatry] — not the first, but the first one died — the second one was a man named William Menninger, from the Menninger Clinic in Kansas, where he and his brother ran a psychoanalytic treatment facility. So Bill Menninger became the head of the army psychiatry. He concluded that the best treatment for these soldiers breaking down was psychotherapeutic in nature. The origin of their condition was trauma. And so, in a watered-down way, Freud's ideas were the ones that the people recruited quickly and retrained as psychiatrists absorbed. So they formed after the war a fairly coherent group of people, separate from the psychiatrists in the state hospitals, who were still very biologically oriented.

The Psychologists Enter Stage Left

Another group emerged during the war, precisely because you couldn't produce enough psychotherapists who were MDs quickly enough — psychologists were drafted in and asked to treat.

So what the psychologists discovered was: "Hey, we could do this stuff, too, and we really like it. It's interesting. It's challenging. We should do that." So after the war, similar kind of problem — mental illness is a massive problem. The returning soldiers, it's a big problem, but it's also a problem in the community.

[gasps]

These guys — the psychiatrists — don't go and work in the mental hospital. They start outpatient treatment. And by 1958, about 80% of psychiatrists are working in outpatient rather than in the hospitals.

So the psychologists organize themselves, and federal money — again, "we need you, we need you, we need more of you." So the VA, the Veterans Administration, and then, once the National Institute of Mental Health is established, they start providing a lot of money for training. And they train not just psychiatrists, they train psychologists.

So the question is: how are the psychologists going to set up clinical training? What the psychologists come up with — the clinically oriented ones — is a training program where would-be clinical psychologists spend 2 years learning basic scientific psychology and research methods. And then they have 2 or 3 years of clinical work and experience. And that's very clever, because it means when they start looking for grants, they know how to do that. And the psychoanalysts don't have a clue how to apply for federal grant money, and they don't get any, almost.

Symptoms vs. Structure: The Great Schism

Beyond that, these people begin to work on treating symptoms. The psychoanalysts think to treat a symptom is to play whack-a-mole. If you don't deal with the underlying problems of the personality — the interaction between your id, ego, and superego — you suppress that symptom, and another one will pop up over here.

The clinical psychologists go: "We're going to treat the symptoms of what are troubling people. We're going to treat the symptoms, and we're going to develop techniques that allow people to cope with those symptoms and eliminate them." And how are we going to do that? We're going to do it primarily through what initially is cognitive behavioral therapy, and later interpersonal therapy, and some other variants emerge.

But basically what they try to do with those techniques is develop things that work relatively quickly, work specifically on one set of problems or a small subset of problems, and try to get those under control. And how does it work? "You've developed really bad habits — the way you react to being socially snubbed or being ignored, or the way you deal with your coworkers and the trouble you're having with your disruptive child. [We'll] help you see the patterns that you've fallen into, and will give you exercises that will work to give you a better way of coping with those things that don't produce these symptoms." I'm oversimplifying, obviously, but basically, that's the fundamental thrust of this.

The CBT Advantage: Packageable, Reproducible, Fundable

And one of the other contrasting things about CBT, cognitive behavioral therapy, is that it doesn't have necessarily that heavy requirement of 5 hours a week.

Exactly. So these therapies could be packaged. They could be reproduced. They could be tested to see whether they worked. So they had an evidentiary foundation. The psychoanalysts would say: "It's going to take us years, and it's hard to measure." These guys were: "Well, we'll measure what happens when we treat people this way."

Psychologists.

Yeah. The symptoms are what matter, not the underlying, you know, the underlying more complex thing that psychoanalysts claim to be treating. And so, it's shorter. It's reproducible. Whereas psychoanalytic, you know, every patient is a new patient, with a new set of complicated things going on. Here we are — we're going to do this.

Bandura, Ellis, Beck — And a Defector from Freud

And the key figures here is Albert Bandura, Albert Ellis, Aaron Beck.

Yes, Bandura and some other psychologists launching this movement. And then later on, Aaron Beck, who went by Tim Beck, who just recently died at — I think he was 99. It's extraordinary.

He crossed 100.

Maybe 100.

Yeah.

Yeah, maybe 100.

There's videos of him talking at that age, and he's still killing it. So wise.

Aaron Beck is a remarkable figure because he was also one of the first in the 1960s to look at psychiatric diagnosis and show how unreliable it was — how difficult it was to get psychiatrists to agree on what was wrong.

So, he was a psychoanalyst, right?

He had been trained as a psychoanalyst. Became disillusioned with it. And so there were two strands, two important strands that stemmed from his work. First: he was one of the ones within the community itself who said to his fellow psychiatrists, "You know, we're not very good at this diagnosis business, and maybe we need to work on that."

Yeah.

Okay? And that was very important for the movement towards DSM-3. The other side of the coin was: he broke with the idea that treating symptoms was a waste of time. And joined with the psychologists who already embarked on that journey, to say: "How can we develop techniques to overcome these self-destructive ways in which people are responding? How can we help with their ability to interact?" So interpersonal therapy is much more with the way in which — if your relations with other people break down, that damages your emotional stability. If you repair those relationships, that helps your emotional stability come back.

Payment, Politics, and the American Exception

So all of this develops, and Americans are unusual. Most of the rest of the world has what we call socialized medicine. America doesn't have that, so we're used to paying for medical care. And so, Americans were more willing, I think, to pay for clinical psychologists. And they attacked some of the problems of everyday living — the more... I was going to say minor, but these are often quite distressing things — but those were the things they were most successful at doing.

Evidence, Honestly Read

If I look at the literature on CBT, for example, and its uses in cases of schizophrenia, the evidence is pretty poor that it works. And even the evidence for the milder conditions is a bit more ambiguous than they like to pretend. The Cochrane reviews, which are a systematic attempt to assess how strong the evidence for particular approaches to disease of all sorts are, say that at best the evidence for CBT is of low and medium confidence, you know?

But I think, again, there are patients for whom this helps. And indeed, for the milder forms of depression, I think CBT works better than the drugs, without some of the side effects that the drugs have. And indeed, NICE, which is the British organization that passes on what treatments the National Health Service will support and which ones are sufficiently evidence-based, has come to that same conclusion.

So I think one thing to say about cognitive behavioral therapy — I mean, it has some elements of kind of surface-level intuitive kind of things, like

Mhm.

being aware of and adjusting your thought patterns, being aware of triggers that get you down a negative spiral, and then basic behavior changes, habit changes that lead to a healthier life. So I think this kind of "getting your life together" kind of process

Right.

is intuitive that that would have a positive effect on some percent of the population. But as you get more serious and serious into the land of mental disorders, it starts to be a little bit less conclusive.

Yes, I think that's an accurate statement of the way I read the literature. And it's not a cure-all, but for some patients, this really does seem to improve things quite a lot. And it does make sense that you have developed poor ways of responding to signals from the outside world. And they've become habitual — and habits, as we know, are very hard to break. You know, there's a lot of homework, there's a lot of exercises you have to do to try to reconfigure the ways you deal with the world. And it's not for everybody, and it doesn't work for everybody. But there's some subset of people for whom this seems to have positive effects.

item.title: [Business of Sport] Have UEFA Missed Their Opportunity To Get Rid of Infantino?
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被揭示的权力，是一种正在贬值的资产

节目里 UEFA 的"核选项"——威胁抵制世界杯——被反复描述为一次权力的"显影"：一旦亮出，皇帝没穿衣服的事实就再也藏不住。但这里藏着一个被主持人们几乎忽略的悖论：权力一旦被揭示，就开始折旧。这非常像冷战核威慑逻辑——威胁的价值在于"从未使用"。UEFA 现在处于一个尴尬的窗口期：它证明了自己能掀桌子，但也同时暴露了它对这张桌子的依赖（欧洲球员、欧洲转播、欧洲赞助商同样需要世界杯这个舞台）。所以 Charlie 说"必须在最强的时候动手"——这不只是政治策略，这是期权定价：UEFA 手里的是一个正在向到期日靠拢的看跌期权，时间价值每天都在流失。

二、Infantino 真正精妙的一招：把"反 Infantino"重写为"反小国"

大多数人以为 Infantino 的护城河是加勒比小国的"贿赂式忠诚"，但这只是表层。他做的事其实是议题重构（reframing）——把"要不要留下 Gianni"偷换成"要不要让 UEFA 直接统治 FIFA"。这一招在政治学上有个名字叫 issue ownership，特朗普、勒庞、贝卢斯科尼都玩过：我不是主角，我只是恰好挡在你和你的敌人之间的那个人。牙买加足总 Ricketts 那句"Montigani 想说什么随便他说，只要 Infantino 给我 4000 万美元"看似赤裸，其实已经进入了 Infantino 的叙事框架——他不再讨论 Infantino 的对错，只讨论"要钱还是要 UEFA 的人"。UEFA 如果没有意识到自己在打的是一场"叙事战"而不是"制度战"，那它 6 个月后大概率会输。

三、一个跨领域的意外连接：这是一场"愤怒的半衰期" vs "利益的复利"之战

Charlie 无意间说出了一个非常深刻的行为经济学观察：愤怒是新鲜时最强。这其实就是心理学里的 hyperbolic discounting（双曲折现）——情绪回报快速衰减，而现金流回报持续累积。7、8 个月后，加勒比小国代表脑子里的画面不再是那个"可耻的商业化方案"，而是"下个月发不出的工资单"。

这套动力学在完全不同的领域里反复上演： - 气候政治：一次山火之后大家愤怒，两年后集体投票给了石油补贴。 - 企业并购中的股东反抗：怒气驱动的委托书争夺战几乎从未战胜稳定分红承诺。 - 国际制裁：制裁初期道义高点最高，随后每一天都在耗损联盟凝聚力。

真正让人意外的洞见是：UEFA 面对的其实不是 FIFA，而是"时间"这个对手。它的敌人不是 Infantino 的狡猾，而是人类神经系统对痛苦记忆的自然稀释速率。Sepharin 说"必要时不惜以丑陋方式解决"——翻译成系统语言就是：他隐约意识到，走"合法路径"会被时间腐蚀掉；而"非常规路径"（让欧洲 U20 女足球员成为附带损害）本质上是一次强行冻结时间的操作——用不可逆的伤害来防止情绪衰变。

四、被节目忽略的一个结构性真相

Infantino 治下的 FIFA，已经在悄悄地从"体育治理机构"演化为"跨境财政再分配机器"。加勒比、非洲、亚洲小国得到的每一笔 200 万、4000 万，本质上是一种足球版的"发展援助"，只是没人这么叫它。这就是为什么 UEFA 的攻击很难落地——它在攻击一个已经被小国重新定义为"福利体系"的组织，而 UEFA 恰好长得像那个"想要削减福利的富国北方"。这场斗争因此不是治理之争，是分配正义之争。而分配正义之争，历史上几乎从没有靠"规则内的程序"解决过——它只被两种东西终结：革命，或者钱变多到不用打这场架。UEFA 目前两样都没有。

📝 转录文本

引言：一个月的沉默之后，重新回到 Infantino 问题

We should just quickly touch on Infantino himself. Um, because we've left that topic alone for the last month um or so since in the aftermath of the World Cup.

Obviously what happened was UEFA stamped their foot and said this isn't good enough. Um, right. So, we are now going to press for not just the rejection of the plan to create a separate investable um commercial rights vehicle which is ultimately probably going to be run by Gianni Infantino — but we're also now going to push for, first of all, Infantino not to carry on being president at the end of his term in March next year.

Um, but also on top of that, there was you know quite heavy messaging around: we also need to see fundamental change within FIFA itself. And that's something which we on this show have been pushing for, right? Saying that UEFA have a moment in time where they could use their authority — which has been revealed to be that if UEFA threatened to boycott the World Cup, then the World Cup has no value. And not just the World Cup, but the women's World Cup and other FIFA tournaments — effectively all FIFA tournaments are fundamentally the [property] of UEFA. Because once UEFA boycott them, there ain't [anything]… the emperor's got no clothes.

Sepharin 的野心：不是阻止某件事，而是根本性改变

And um, we referenced the interview that um uh The Rest is Politics did with Aleksander Čeferin, the head of UEFA, about 3 weeks ago — in which Čeferin was making it pretty clear: we're not in this just to stop that one thing happening; we are in this now to make fundamental change. Um, and he made very clear in that, that part of that fundamental change was that Gianni Infantino would have no future in global football politics whatsoever.

Right? UEFA was being backed in that — is being backed in that — by um a couple of other federations, right? The Asian Federation on the one hand and CONCACAF on the other hand. And CONCACAF was particularly notable in their support. Why? Because CONCACAF includes all the um smaller Caribbean nations — well, in fact, all the Caribbean nations and Central American nations who had been a bit of a cornerstone of Infantino's power base, and indeed prior to him, [Sepp Blatter's] power base.

If you remember the old Jack Warner days, when Jack Warner would deliver the Caribbean bloc vote in return for, as we now know, um various um rewards.

Montagliani 的签名，与加勒比的真实立场

So it looked like — and we sort of questioned it at the time — that Victor Montagliani, the Canadian boss of CONCACAF, who would put his name to Čeferin's letter… I effectively sort of speculated at the time: I wonder if he's got all the Caribbean nations on side with this? Because it's those small federations — and I've seen it firsthand through my work in the Caribbean — for whom every extra 2 million bucks counts, right? Counts partially for the stuff that they might want to do with football, but also counts for them and their federations and them personally, right? How much they're able to pay themselves, whether they're able to travel around the world in first class — all these types of things.

So —

Which was referenced in the head of Jamaica Football, Michael Ricketts' statement.

I was going to go on to Ricketts.

No, no, but please, if you have it in front of you, please.

I I don't have it in front of me, but I can paraphrase it as such, which is: Montagliani can say whatever he wants, but if Infantino is going to promise to put an extra 40 million bucks into Jamaican football, then I'm all for it.

Yeah.

Right. Followed by: we will not follow UEFA because they will always have a problem with something — insinuating that the power should and will, in UEFA's eyes, always lie with them, not the small countries that Gianni has been trying to cajole together. He's consolidated —

Infantino 的反击叙事："我只是那个恰好在这里的人"

Well, what Infantino is doing — Infantino is going around behind the… this is going to end up being a big fight, right? Infantino is going around behind the scenes, and his various um henchmen are going around behind the scenes, speaking to the small federations and saying:

Do you understand what's fundamentally um you know at the heart of this? Right? Do you want a FIFA going forward that is run in your interests, or do you want a FIFA that is effectively just run on behalf of UEFA? Right? 'Cause that's what Čeferin wants. So you might think that Montagliani supporting Čeferin and getting rid of Infantino is just about Gianni. It's not just about Gianni. I'm just — I'm just the guy who happens to be here right now. If you let them get rid of me, you will end up with a UEFA placeman in that position who will make damn sure that you don't get your extra 30, 40 million bucks. So whatever you think about what went on a month or two ago, put it to the back of your mind. I'm your man.

距离选举还有六个月：战术图谱开始成形

Right. So here we are. We're six months out from the election for the FIFA president, and the battle lines are starting to be drawn, right?

And I think it's going to become really, really interesting to see the tactics that are employed by UEFA. The tactics employed by Infantino are clear. The tactics employed by UEFA to ensure that it gets its way — because I don't know if you remember, Charlie, in that interview with Alastair Campbell on The Rest is Politics, what Čeferin made quite clear is: he is going to get his way, and he doesn't really care how he does it. If I have to do it the formal way, I'll do it that way. If that doesn't work, we'll do it some other way.

一个不得不接受的丑陋结论

So, I agree. The challenge I have is — we've spoken previously about the different ways you could remove him. You can beat him in an election. You can call special meetings. There is most likely one way — only one way — that you are going to have to do this, and it's going to have to be the ugly way.

They may not want to do that, but if you're really going to get this change through, because of the reasons you've just described — and now the time he has running up to the next election — let's not forget the furore that existed, right? But as we know with everything, anger is at its most strong when it's fresh.

Yeah. And in seven, eight months' time — I may remember all the reasons that really pissed me off. But as you've said, I am continually reminded of all the financial pressures that my federation is under. And that's really shown in the last seven, eight months. So I'm pissed. But am I pissed enough to shoot 40 million away? [snorts] That's a big ask. That's a big ask.

Infantino 的最后一层防御："我已经道歉了"

And don't forget — and also don't forget — that what Infantino is going to do is he's going to say:

Look, I've already said that I'm not going to come back with that particular scheme, right? So you made your point, right? Hands up. I should have dealt with it better.

Yeah.

Does that mean that you want UEFA running FIFA?

You can see how that sort of, you know… in other words, it enables — it gives permission to — the federation bosses of the smaller countries in world football to say: look, you know, he's made it very clear he got it wrong, but overall he's been great for world football, so therefore we are going to vote for him. As you say — and at a moment in time when that sort of furore around it has died down, counting on the fact that he can get up to 120, 130 such countries. You know, it's going to be really interesting.

结论：现在不动手，就永远动不了手

But you have to act when you're strongest. And UEFA was strongest — and still are probably strongest — just about now, and in the last few weeks.

Yeah. If they want the change, they are going to have to break with the rule book as to how you would remove [him], and they will have to rebel. And they will have to accept — if they really want to do it — that the players will be collateral. That European players who are going to compete in the women's under-20 tournament going on… will not be able to compete.

That is the cost of the change that they want to make. Yeah. Because we know the power structures — that this has been designed, set up and formalized to protect someone like an Infantino.

item.description:
## 一、被揭示的权力，是一种正在贬值的资产
节目里 UEFA 的"核选项"——威胁抵制世界杯——被反复描述为一次权力的"显影"：一旦亮出，皇帝没穿衣服的事实就再也藏不住。但这里藏着一个被主持人们几乎忽略的悖论：**权力一旦被揭示，就开始折旧**。这非常像冷战核威慑逻辑——威胁的价值在于"从未使用"。UEFA 现在处于一个尴尬的窗口期：它证明了自己能掀桌子，但也同时暴露了它对这张桌子的依赖（欧洲球员、欧洲转播、欧洲赞助商同样需要世界杯这个舞台）。所以 Charlie 说"必须在最强的时候动手"——这不只是政治策略，这是**期权定价**：UEFA 手里的是一个正在向到期日靠拢的看跌期权，时间价值每天都在流失。
## 二、Infantino 真正精妙的一招：把"反 Infantino"重写为"反小国"
大多数人以为 Infantino 的护城河是加勒比小国的"贿赂式忠诚"，但这只是表层。他做的事其实是**议题重构**（reframing）——把"要不要留下 Gianni"偷换成"要不要让 UEFA 直接统治 FIFA"。这一招在政治学上有个名字叫 **issue ownership*

item.title: [Lex Clips] Prison system is an insane asylum | Andrew Scull and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：监狱是「疯人院」的赛博朋克回归

美国最大的三家精神病"住院机构"——洛杉矶县监狱、库克郡监狱、雷克岛监狱——不是医院，是监狱。这里藏着一个令人毛骨悚然的历史闭环：我们花了两百年时间把疯人从监狱里"解放"出来，建造了充满乐观主义的精神病院；又花了半个世纪把这些病人"解放"出精神病院，结果他们又回到了监狱。

这不是简单的倒退，而是一种更糟糕的"精神病收容制度2.0"——因为原始的疯人院至少是带着治疗意图的建筑，而现代监狱则是带着惩罚意图的建筑在偶然扮演治疗角色。这就像用榔头做外科手术。

跨领域连接：这是一种"公共政策的庞氏骗局"

Scull 说 community care 是 "a shell game without a pea"（没有豆子的三杯赌骗局）——这个比喻精准得可怕。让我把它拉到一个你可能没想过的领域：这和 2008 年金融危机的"资产证券化"是同构的。

两者都遵循同一个逻辑套路： - 打包：把复杂、烫手、需要长期承担的责任（次贷/精神病人） - 重命名：换一个听起来进步的名字（金融创新/社区照护） - 分散：让责任落到无法追责的分布式节点上（下游投资者/根本不存在的社区设施） - 崩盘：当账单到期，最脆弱的人承担全部代价

去机构化（deinstitutionalization）本质上是一场"精神病照护的次贷危机"——只不过它的"雷曼时刻"没有一次爆发，而是分散成了每天在旧金山街头、纽约地铁里、洛杉矶帐篷城里的一万次微型崩溃。

最让人意外的洞见：寿命差距在"扩大"，而不是缩小

15到25年的预期寿命差距——这个数字本身惊人，但真正让我脊背发凉的是 Scull 那句轻描淡写的话："that gap has been growing rather than diminishing"。

在一个抗精神病药物、脑成像、循证治疗、心理健康去污名化运动都在飞速进步的时代，重症精神病患者的寿命差距反而在扩大。这意味着什么？

这意味着 医学进步和公共政策正在朝相反方向奔跑。我们制造出了越来越精密的治疗工具，同时系统性地拆除了让这些工具能够抵达病人的社会基础设施。这就像不停研发更好的心脏支架，却同时关闭所有心脏专科医院。

更深一层的系统性真相是：精神疾病是唯一一种"技术进步反而恶化患者处境"的重大疾病领域。这暴露了一个被忽视的模式——当一种疾病的核心症状是"让患者无法为自己的治疗发声"时，医疗技术的进步无法自动转化为社会照护的进步。声音，才是治疗真正被兑现的货币。

附加视角：19世纪的乐观主义是一种失落的智慧

那些早期的"alienists"（精神病学先驱）相信 60-80% 的治愈率——今天我们会嘲笑这种天真。但请注意他们的哲学起点："治疗环境本身就是治疗"——不是驱除恶魔，而是"把它们控制住"（keep them under some sort of wraps）。

这几乎预言了今天的神经可塑性研究和创伤知情照护（trauma-informed care）：环境塑造大脑，虐待会激活并强化病理，尊严与结构性生活能够重塑神经通路。

具有讽刺意味的是——我们抛弃了asylum的建筑物，也抛弃了它最有价值的洞见：人是被环境治愈的，不只是被药物治愈的。而监狱，正是那种系统性地摧毁一个人自我调节能力的环境。

📝 转录文本

一、被公共政策辜负的重症精神病患者

For people with serious mental illness, public policy has screwed things up badly. So, if if you are a person with serious mental illness, you will die on average 15 to 25 years before the rest of us. And that gap has been growing rather than diminishing, so that's not a good thing.

It it's not something I want to lay in entirely at the door of psychiatry, so don't get me wrong. I think a lot of this is public policy that has really abandoned treatment for the seriously mentally ill, and you see it on the streets of our cities. You see the sidewalk psychotics. You see people who are cycling between brief periods of inpatient care, uh the gutter or the flop house, and the jail, you know?

二、监狱成为美国最大的"精神病院"

So, the three largest centers of inpatient psychiatric care, if you can call it that, in the United States today, are the Los Angeles County Jail, Cook County Jail in Chicago, and Rikers Island in New York.

That's shocking, because by their very nature, of course, prisons aren't equipped to deal with serious mental illness.

So, some dark way to return to the asylum era.

Yeah, well, you know, the asylums had acquired a very bad reputation, and I've written of some about some of the reasons why that happened.

三、疯人院最初的乐观主义起源

But when asylums were founded, it was a period of enormous optimism that we were going to be able to cure these people, that we would rescue them from addicts and from jail cells, and through providing a therapeutic environment, coaxing them to work, creating a system where they learn to control themselves — not necessarily to drive their demons out, but to keep them under some sort of wraps.

The expectation was when the asylums came along that they'd not only rescue people from horrendous conditions in the prisons and the jails, but they'd actively cure them. And the earliest alienists, as they called themselves then, uh thought that they could cure a 60, 70, 80 percent, maybe even more, of patients as long as they came in early.

And really asylums were built out of that sense of optimism, that sense that we, you know, that so much was environmental and so much was not exacerbating the condition by treating people like animals or treating them, you know, beating them and in other ways uh horrifically maltreating them, that that would create um a sense of cure. And really that that underlay the construction of the asylums.

四、"社区照护"：一场没有豆子的赌局

And now, having abandoned the asylums — which we did starting a little bit in the 1950s, but really the late 1960s onwards — uh that was because there was going to be something miraculous called community care.

But community care is a shell game without a P. It's like one of those confidence tricks. There were no substitute community facilities for dealing with the really serious mentally ill.

观看原视频 →
